Opening with a lengthy prologue on the duties and dangers of the historian, the work surveys the condition of Christians under Muslim rule, the rise of the Turks, Peter the Hermit and the preaching of Urban II at Clermont, and the deeds of the crusading princes through the capture of Jerusalem and its aftermath, drawing on Greek and Arabic sources as well as oral testimony. The opening books circulated widely, and the chronicle's mixture of royal biography, character sketches, and episodic narrative made it a staple source for later retellings of crusading history; its rare vocabulary and idiosyncratic diction have also furnished frequent parallels for readers tracing the Latinity of medieval historiography.
la.ambrose.apologia_altera_prophetae_david: A late antique Latin prose treatise of theology, the Apologia Altera Prophetae David is a second apologetic work by Ambrose in defense of King David, composed to defuse the scandal of David's adultery with Bathsheba and his contrivance of Uriah's death. Taking its cue from the superscription of the penitential psalm and from the Gospel reading in which Christ dismisses the woman taken in adultery without condemnation, it arranges its defense in three parts, answering the objections of pagans, Jews, and Christians in turn. Ambrose argues that David's fall illustrates the common frailty of human nature, exalts his humility and penitence, and reflects on how royal power must remain subject to justice and how rash judgment of another's sin can outweigh the sin judged. Readers tracing patristic exegesis of the David narrative or the afterlife of the adulteress pericope will find here a compact instance of Ambrosian moral and homiletic argument.
la.ambrose.apologia_prophetae_david_ad_theo: A brief Latin treatise of some 85 lines, addressed to the emperor Theodosius Augustus and transmitted among the works of Ambrose, defending the biblical king David against readers scandalised by his adultery with Bathsheba and his contrivance of Uriah's death. Drawing on the narrative of 2 Kingdoms (2 Samuel) and on Pauline sayings against judging others, it argues that David's fall was permitted by divine providence so that penitent sinners might find a model of confession and restoration, and that the lapses of the saints instruct later believers in both innocence and repentance. For readers of intertexts, the work offers dense quotation and paraphrase of the David narrative and the apostolic letters, together with an influential patristic pattern for moralising the sins of exemplary figures.
la.ambrose.de_benedictionibus_patriarcharum: A Latin exegetical treatise in a single short book, attributed to Ambrose and of uncertain date, expounding the final blessings pronounced by Jacob over his sons in Genesis, prefaced by an account of Jacob's cross-handed blessing of Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh. Ambrose treats the patriarchal sayings as prophecy rather than mere benediction, finding in them figures of Christ, the apostles, and the Christian people, and argues against Jewish interpretations at length, notably on Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, whom he links with the passion of the Lord and the obduracy of the Jewish people. For readers hunting parallels, the work repays attention for its dense scriptural quotation, its explicit vocabulary of type and mystery, and its recurring comparisons between Jacob and Isaac in the conferral of blessing.
la.ambrose.de_cain_et_abel: A late-antique Latin prose treatise on theology and biblical exegesis by Ambrose, De Cain et Abel presents itself as a sequel to the author's De paradiso, turning from the fall of Adam and Eve to the story of their sons. Across its 85 lines it reads Cain and Abel allegorically as two opposed 'sects' of the soul, Cain as acquisitive self-assertion and Abel as the devout mind that refers everything to God, and then extends the typology to Rebecca's twins, to Isaac and Moses, and finally to synagogue and church. For readers of intertexts the work is valuable as a dense specimen of Ambrosian allegory, combining etymological wordplay on the brothers' names, arithmetical and philosophical digression, and continuous scriptural citation and paraphrase in the Schenkl edition of 1897.
la.ambrose.de_fuga_saeculi: De Fuga Saeculi, a brief work of Late Antique theology in Latin prose, presents flight from the world as the central task of the Christian soul. Opening with a meditation on how readily the mind is drawn back by the allurements of the senses, it warns against the vanities of circus, theater, and pleasure, and allegorizes the Old Testament cities of refuge as figures of the sinner's flight to God, with the Levites as a type of those who renounce family and possessions for the divine service. Its dense fabric of scriptural quotation and allusion, from the Psalms and Ecclesiastes to Lot's wife, Paul's race toward the prize, and Elijah's solitude, makes it a rich hunting ground for readers tracking biblical phrasing and ascetic motifs across Latin literature.
la.ambrose.de_helia_et_ieiunio: De Helia et Ieiunio is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on fasting by Ambrose, printed in Karl Schenkl's 1897 Vienna edition of his collected works. Taking the prophet Elijah as its central exemplar, the work unfolds in a sermonic mode through Christ's temptation in the desert, John the Baptist's ascetic life, the primeval fast of the six days of creation, and the breach of abstinence in Eden, presenting fasting as the food of the mind and the life of the angels. Its dense accumulation of scriptural quotation and typological parallel, from Elijah's drought and miraculous journey to the tempter's snare for Adam and Christ, offers rich material for readers tracing ascetic motifs and biblical commonplaces across patristic and later Christian writing.
la.ambrose.de_iacob: A late-antique work of theology in Latin prose, De Iacob is attributed to Ambrose and takes the patriarch Jacob, together with Joseph, as an exemplar of temperance and the rule of reason over the passions. Its opening chapters argue that good speech alone is insufficient for moral correction unless reinforced by right reasoning, survey a catalogue of the passions arising from pleasure and pain, and illustrate the curbing of concupiscence through David's renunciation of the water of Bethlehem, the parable of the barren fig tree, and Joseph's resistance of temptation. Intertextual readers will find it densely threaded with scriptural quotation and allusion, from the Decalogue and the Psalms to the Genesis narrative, and it offers a rich point of contact between philosophical moral psychology and biblical exegesis in late-antique Latin.
la.ambrose.de_joseph: De Joseph is a Latin prose treatise in a homiletic vein of Late Antique theology by Ambrose, expounding the biblical patriarch Joseph as a moral and spiritual exemplar. The work presents Joseph above all as a mirror of chastity and patience, exhorting readers to forgive their enemies and to govern familial love without partiality, while reading the Genesis narrative typologically: the boy's dreams prefigure the resurrection and adoration of Christ, the father's sending of his son to his brothers anticipates the Father's mission of the Son, and the variously colored tunic signifies the manifold virtues. Drawing continually on direct scriptural quotation and allegorical interpretation of Genesis, De Joseph offers rich material for readers tracing patristic typology, biblical allusion, and the afterlife of the Joseph story in Latin Christian exegesis.
la.ambrose.de_mysteriis: A Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date on the sacraments of initiation, De Mysteriis is attributed to Ambrose. It presents itself as the sequel to a preceding course on morals and now expounds the rites conferred at baptism: the renunciation of the devil, the turn toward the east, the opening of the ears with the word Epheta, and the washing in water, while explaining why such mysteries were withheld from the as-yet unbaptized. Its argument proceeds chiefly by typology, tracing baptismal prefigurations from the Spirit moving over the waters at creation through Noah's flood, the dove, the cloud, and the crossing of the Red Sea, and it cites scripture continuously. For readers of intertexts, the work offers dense biblical allusion, early liturgical formulae, and a Late Antique example of Old Testament types reinterpreted as Christian sacrament.
la.ambrose.de_nabuthae: De Nabuthae is a Late Antique Latin prose work of theology by Ambrose. It takes the biblical story of Ahab's seizure of Naboth's vineyard as the starting point for a sustained moral assault on avarice, arguing that Ahab is reborn wherever the rich covet the inheritance of the poor, and it interleaves close paraphrase of the scriptural narrative with rhetorical meditations on wealth, naked birth, the common endowment of the earth, and the equality of the grave. Its dense weaving of scriptural diction with moralising commonplaces on poverty and riches makes it a valuable witness to the Late Antique reception of the Naboth episode and a productive source of parallels for later Christian writing on wealth and dispossession.
la.ambrose.de_noe: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise on the patriarch Noah, attributed to Ambrose and of uncertain date, preserved in the Vienna edition of 1897 prepared by Karl Schenkl. In a compact span of 128 lines it expounds Noah's life, character and deeds, allegorising the flood, the renewal of mankind, and the sons Sem, Cham and Iapheth as an ordered array of good, evil and indifferent elements within the soul. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense quotation of Genesis and the Psalms, an appeal to an unnamed Greek poet on placing evil in the midst of battle, and a characteristic Late Antique fusion of biblical exegesis with moralised philosophy.
la.ambrose.de_paradiso: De Paradiso is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on the Garden of Eden by Ambrose, printed here in Karl Schenkl's 1897 Viennese edition of his works. Taking its cue from Genesis 2:8, the work asks what paradise is and where it lies, weighs Paul's rapture to the third heaven as a limit case, and then reads the trees of Eden, the tree of life as wisdom, the tree of knowledge of good and evil as the discernment of good and evil, and the serpent as figures within the soul's moral economy. Its dense weave of scriptural citation and allegorical exegesis makes it a rewarding source of parallels for readers tracing paradise imagery, the allegorization of Genesis 2–3, and patristic interpretive diction.
la.ambrose.epistula_ad_sororem: A short Latin prose letter attributed to Ambrose and addressed to his sister, of uncertain date, giving a first-person account of a confrontation over the basilicas of a city in Late Antique Italy. The author recounts his refusal to surrender the churches to the emperor's officers, 'the temple of God cannot be handed over by a priest', the occupation of the principal basilica before daybreak, and the sermon on Job that he preached to a congregation in which even soldiers came to join, the crowd's cry 'rogamus, Auguste, non pugnamus' encapsulating the stance of prayerful resistance to Arian pressure. Its compact narrative of episcopal defiance of imperial power offers rich material for parallels within the Ambrosian corpus and for later literary traditions of church-state conflict.
la.ambrose.epistulae_variae: A collection of miscellaneous Latin prose letters of Late Antique date, attributed to Ambrose, who signs the opening epistle as a bishop addressing the emperor Gratian. The opening letter excuses the writer's absence from court, praises the emperor's confession of faith in the full divinity of Christ, and passes to a defence of the Spirit's godhead, closing with an extended allegory of Scripture as a sea fed by many rivers and the Church as a ship upon the waters. Across its 278 lines the corpus blends courtly panegyric, pastoral counsel, and exegesis. Readers tracing intertexts will find dense scriptural quotation and allusion, from Abraham's hospitality and Pauline paradox to psalmic imagery of floods and harbours, in a formative example of the bishop-emperor correspondence.
la.ambrose.expositio_evangelii_secundum_luc: A late-antique Latin prose exposition of Luke's Gospel, attributed to Ambrose and edited by Henricus Schenkl in 1902 (Vienna). The work moves through Luke more or less verse by verse, opening with a meditation on the 'many' would-be narrators of Luke 1:1 that catalogues apocryphal gospels ascribed to Basilides, Thomas, and Matthias and defends the fourfold canonical gospel. Its argument advances by sustained typological comparison between the two Testaments, true and false prophets, the seeing of God by Abraham and Isaiah versus the blindness of contemporary Jews, and the prose is saturated with quoted and reworked biblical phrasing. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it a dense repository of scriptural allusion, allegorical reading, and the Latin exegetical vocabulary of the late empire.
la.ambrose.expositio_psalmi_cxviii: A Late Antique Latin prose commentary on Psalm 118 (the Beati immaculati), attributed to Ambrose and printed from Michael Petschenig's 1913 Vienna edition. The exposition follows the psalm's acrostic arrangement, treating each Hebrew letter and its eight versicles in turn, and reads the text chiefly through a moral and allegorical lens, weaving a dense web of scriptural citation that ranges from Genesis and the Wisdom books to the Song of Songs and Pauline teaching on baptism and resurrection. Readers hunting textual parallels will find it a rich witness to patristic intertextual practice, since nearly every phrase of the psalm is glossed against other biblical passages and against the moral and mystical senses of scripture more broadly.
la.anonymous.laudes_domini: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, preserved in 152 lines and printed in Pieter Van Der Weijden's 1967 edition with Dutch translation and commentary. The poem opens by questioning the slow pace of divine rewards, then recounts an exemplum of conjugal piety from the Saône valley among the Aedui, where a husband and wife vow a shared tomb, before unfolding a hymnic catalogue of Christ's works as Creator: the ordered sea and shores, the seasons, vines, honey, the service of animals to humankind, navigation, and the starred heavens. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a medieval instance of the hymnic creation topos and of the devoted-couple exemplum, both with rich antecedents in late antique Christian and classical verse.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_agobardum: A medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, transmitted anonymously under the title Carmen ad Agobardum and running to sixty lines arranged in fifteen quatrains. It takes the form of a penitential prayer to God as immense creator and universal judge, voiced by a speaker who presents himself as a condemned man thrust into prison and dreading death, pleading for pardon, the aid of kinsmen, and Christ's strengthening grace. The stanza initials spell out the name Agobard, a device the poem itself flags when it invites the addressee to read his name in the first letters of the verses. For readers of intertexts it offers penitential and judgment imagery, an explicit acrostic dedication, and a closing doxology that invites comparison with other medieval prayer verse.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_exordio_francorum: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de Exordio Francorum sets out in 146 lines the origins of the Frankish people, addressed to a Charles praised as the heir of his forebears' titles, arms, and piety. Opening amid Rome's thunderous dominion and Gaul's subjection, it passes through the marriage of Ansbertus to Blithild, daughter of Hlotharius, to the birth and sanctity of Arnold, Feriolus, Modericus, and Tharsicia, and onward along the episcopal line of Arnulf toward the ancestry of its royal addressee. The poem announces itself as verse rendering what prose had already celebrated of the Frankish gens, and its epic diction, morning-star simile, and hagiographic episodes make it useful for readers comparing Frankish foundation narratives and their classical echoes.
la.anonymus.carmina_augiensia: The Carmina Augiensia is a brief collection of anonymous medieval Latin devotional verse, 97 lines in all and in places fragmentary; its title points to the monastery of Reichenau (Augia), though the date of composition and the poet's identity remain unknown. Its poems celebrate an altar dedicated in honour of Saint Mary by a priest-monk and his fellow devotees, invoke Peter, Paul, John the Baptist, Sebastian and Valentine, record a cross-trophy dedicated by one Egino, and close with verses on the four evangelists and the raising of Lazarus. Readers hunting textual parallels will find here the stock formulas of monastic dedication and cross poetry, altar, trophy, evangelist praise, Lazarus summoned from the tomb, motifs that circulate widely in medieval Latin verse.
la.anonymus.carmina_bibliothecarum_et_psalt: Carmina Bibliothecarum et Psalteriorum is an anonymous medieval Latin collection of verse, of uncertain date, devoted to libraries and psalters. Its opening section addresses Charlemagne, invoking the psalmists David, Asaph, Eman, Ethan, and Idithun, praising Jerome's translation of the Psalter, and noting the scribe Liuthard at whose completion the pen came to rest, while offering the king a bibliotheca of the two Testaments and cataloguing the many offices of Scripture, from correction, exhortation, and consolation to fasting, almsgiving, and the ordering of daily life. The verse then proceeds to a versified survey of the biblical books, beginning with the five volumes of Moses and with Joshua. For readers hunting intertexts, its 835 lines offer a compact example of how psalmic diction, biblical epitome, and royal dedication rhetoric could be recombined in medieval Latin poetry.
la.anonymus.carmina_de_ludovico_ii: An anonymous medieval Latin piece of uncertain date, transmitted as Carmina de Ludovico II, preserves two short poems in 51 lines on the emperor Louis II. The first, in narrative verse of a popular cast, recounts the treachery of the Beneventans under Adelferio, who seize the pious emperor, remove him from his palace like a martyr ('Tamquam ad latronem venistis cum gladiis et fustibus'), and are answered by a demon-tormented schemer's fall and a Saracen advance on Calabria and Salerno; the second, a set of elegiac couplets, laments his death and the mourning of Rome, Latium, and Gaul. Readers of intertexts will find the transfer of Gospel passion diction to an imperial biography alongside classicising epitaph topoi, a compact instance of biblical and antique modes interwoven in verse on a ruler's fall and death.
la.anonymus.carmina_libris_saec_viii_adiect: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of 309 lines, of uncertain date, whose title points to verses added to books of the eighth century. It opens with a plea that Christ preserve a certain Ragnardus and records that a boy of noble stock, Hieronymus, of the line of Charles and Pippin through Ragnard son of Ragnerus, wrote the verses at nine years of age. The poem then praises King Charles as defender of the church who subdued the Lombards and their king Desiderius and entered Pavia in triumph, and frames the presentation of a gift-book to Pope Hadrian through imagery of Davidic music and mystic songs sealed with a sevenfold seal. Readers of intertexts may note its fusion of biblical motifs, Judas's betrayal, the patient lamb, Christ's enthronement, with Carolingian dynastic panegyric and the conventions of book dedication.
la.anonymus.translatio_sancti_mercurii: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Translatio Sancti Mercurii recounts in 122 lines the translation of the relics of Saint Mercurius and directs its readers to a Passio of the saint in the verses that precede it. The narrative follows the emperor Constans as he campaigns to subdue Apulia, destroys the wealthy city Quintodecimum near Benevento, and dies in Sicily, where his companions bury the martyr's body beneath a marker stone; it then turns to the devout prince Arechis, who entombs twelve brother martyrs, born of one womb, in his new basilica of Saint Sophia at Benevento and, spurred by a vision and the martyr's appearance to the bishop, has Mercurius's long-hidden grave opened and the relics borne in procession. Readers hunting parallels will find the standard machinery of the translatio genre, concealment of the tomb, dream revelation, communal excavation under episcopal supervision, solemn reburial, together with the learned diction and Phoebus-rising dawn scene typical of medieval Latin versified hagiography.
la.anonymus.translatio_xii_martyrum: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, running to about a hundred lines, the Translatio XII Martyrum commemorates the transfer of the relics of twelve martyrs from Apulia to Benevento under Prince Arechis, who dedicated a marble shrine to them and enriched the new foundation with lands, gold, gems, and textiles. The verse recounts the prince's demand for the relics, the triumphant procession of clergy and populace, and the civic gifts and privileges that followed, closing with internal dating by regnal year, indiction, and the month of May. Readers of intertexts may note its fusion of hagiographic translation narrative with classical and epic diction, including an explicit comparison of Arechis's temple with the buildings of Justinian, and its affinities with panegyrical descriptions of princes and civic ritual.
la.apuleius.apologia: Apuleius' Apologia, also transmitted under the title Pro se de magia, is a Latin prose speech in which the Platonist of Madaura defends himself before the proconsul Claudius Maximus against an accusation of magic, composed in the Later Imperial period. The opening section rebuts the slanders of the accuser Aemilianus, vindicates philosophy against popular prejudice, and begins dismantling an indictment that turns on the speaker's marriage to Pudentilla and on alleged maleficium. Readers hunting parallels will find the speech dense with quotation and exemplum, Homer is cited in Greek, while Pythagoras, Zeno and Plato are invoked as precedents, and its epigrammatic, highly ornamented Latin makes it a productive source of verbal echoes.
la.apuleius.florida: The Florida is a compilation of short prose extracts from the public speeches of Apuleius of Madaura, the Platonist philosopher and orator of the later Roman imperial period, transmitted under the title Apulei Platonici Madaurensis Florida. The selections showcase an orator's repertoire: a reverent prologue likening entry into a city to a traveller's devotional pause at a sacred grove, reflections on Socrates's way of judging men, an elaborate retelling of Hyagnis and Marsyas's musical contest with Apollo, an anecdote about the piper Antigenidas, and remarks on theatrical genres and their effects on an audience. Its dense quotation and allusion, to Plautine verse, Homeric and Virgilian imagery, and Greek musical lore, makes it fruitful ground for readers hunting literary parallels, and it preserves in excerpt form much of Apuleius's otherwise lost oratorical output.
la.arnobius.adversus_nationes: A seven-book Latin prose apology written in the Late Antique period, Arnobius's Adversus Nationes defends Christianity against the pagan charge that the world has decayed since the rise of the Christian religion. The opening book confronts the accusation that pestilence, famine, earthquake, and other calamities beset humankind because the gods have been provoked or have withdrawn, answering it by appeal to the chronic misfortunes of earlier ages. Across the seven books the treatise rehearses pagan myth, cult practice, and philosophical teaching in order to refute them, and its dense allusive engagement with classical religious and literary traditions makes it a fruitful source of parallels for readers of intertexts.
la.augustine.adnotationes_in_iob: A set of terse Latin prose annotations on the Book of Job, transmitted among the works of Augustine and dating from Late Antiquity, the Adnotationes in Iob moves through the biblical narrative in sequence, appending a brief gloss to each phrase. The notes read Job's history morally and allegorically: his daily feasts and victims signify charity and confession, Satan's appearance before God figures the soul's temptation, and details such as the myrmicoleon and Babylon receive figurative senses tied to the devil, the church, and the earthly city. The annotations are densely interwoven with scriptural cross-references, quoting or echoing Paul, the prophets, and the speeches of Eliphaz, so that Job becomes a lens for the whole Christian interpretive apparatus. For readers hunting intertexts, the work offers a compact witness to Late Antique Latin exegesis of Job and to the stock of allegorical equivalences on which later commentators drew.
la.augustine.breviculus_collationis_cum_don: A short late-antique Latin prose work by Augustine, the Breviculus Collationis cum Donatistis is an epitome designed to condense the protracted official record of the colloquy held at Carthage, by imperial command, between catholic and Donatist bishops before the tribune and notary Marcellinus. It proceeds through numbered sign-posts, recapitulating in order the imperial rescript, the commissioner's edicts, the notoriae and letters of both sides, and the early procedural maneuvers in which the Donatists sought to prevent or delay debate on the merits of the case. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a compact rendering of the arguments, formulae, and scriptural appeals of the conference transcripts, valuable for tracing Augustine's anti-Donatist polemic and the legal and ecclesiological language it disseminated.
la.augustine.contra_academicos: A Latin prose dialogue of Late Antique date by Augustine, the Contra Academicos opposes the sceptical teaching of the Academy, according to which truth cannot be grasped and the wise man can follow only what is probable. Set as a debate on a country estate and framed by a consoling dedication to Romanianus, it stages the question whether happiness is possible without possession of the truth, discussed among Trygetius, Licentius, Alypius and Navigius with Alypius as judge, and argues that living according to reason in the search for truth is itself blessed, dismantling the Academic case in the course of the discussion. Its declared debt to Cicero's Hortensius, its Ciceronian dialogue form, and its philosophical vocabulary make it a key witness for the reception of Cicero and of Academic scepticism in Latin Christian writing.
la.augustine.contra_cresconium_grammaticum_: Augustine's Contra Cresconium Grammaticum et Donatistam is a late antique Latin prose treatise of theological polemic, written in response to Cresconius, a Donatist grammarian who had attacked Augustine's reply to Petilian, bishop of Cirta. The work defends the catholic church's case against Donatist rebaptism, answers Cresconius' accusations of over-reliance on eloquence, and argues that rhetorical skill serves Christian truth when directed by right belief. Readers hunting intertexts will find sustained biblical citation, engagement with earlier Donatist writings, and discussion of classical authorities such as Plato on rhetoric and civic order.
la.augustine.contra_faustum: Augustine's Contra Faustum is a late-antique polemical treatise in Latin prose directed against the Manichaean Faustus of Milevis, an African whose eloquence Augustine had already recalled in the Confessiones. In keeping with the plan announced in its preface, the work sets Faustus's words under his own name and appends Augustine's reply under his, defending Catholic faith and the authority of Scripture against Manichaean objections, such as the denial that Christ's genealogy and birth belong to the gospel. For readers hunting intertexts, it offers a dense weave of biblical citation and verbatim quotation of the Manichaean adversary, making it a principal witness both to Augustine's scriptural argumentation and to the language of the anti-Manichaean controversy.
la.augustine.contra_gaudentium_donatistarum: A short Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date by Augustine, directed against Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Tamugada, who had threatened to burn himself and his followers in his church rather than submit to the imperial laws enforcing Catholic unity. Written in the form of a reply to the tribune and notary Dulcitius, it quotes Gaudentius's two letters verbatim and refutes them point by point, defending the coercion of schismatics and rebutting Donatist claims to innocence and persecution; the preface also explains Augustine's method of quotation in contrast with his earlier answer to Petilian. Readers of intertexts will find Gaudentius's epistolary wording cited directly, scriptural allusions applied to the controversy, and references to the conference held at Carthage, making the work a useful witness to the exchanged language of the Catholic-Donatist dispute.
la.augustine.contra_mendacium: Contra Mendacium ('Against Lying') is a late-antique Latin theological treatise by Augustine, cast as a long-delayed reply to his correspondent Consentius, whose materials on the Priscillianist heresy reached him through the messenger Leonas. Augustine argues that no lie is ever permissible, even for pious ends such as unmasking heretics: he sorts lies into kinds, weighs the claim that falsehood harms only the liar, and rebuts the Priscillianist appeal to patriarchs, prophets, apostles, angels, and Christ himself as exemplars of holy deception, pointing instead to Jehu's condemned deceit and to the martyrs, who confessed rather than lied under persecution. The argument proceeds through dense quotation and allusion to scripture, the Psalm on God's destruction of liars, Paul on doing evil that good may come and on confessing with the mouth, so readers hunting intertexts will find both a rich vein of biblical commonplaces on truth and mendacity and a record of how rival readings of those same passages were contested in patristic polemic.
la.augustine.contra_secundinum: The Contra Secundinum is a brief Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date, written by Augustine in reply to a Manichaean correspondent named Secundinus who had suggested that fear of hardship and desire for ecclesiastical honour, not conviction, drove Augustine out of the Manichaean sect. Across twenty-nine lines the author defends his conversion by citing Pauline passages on seducing spirits and forbidden foods, then turns Secundinus's own words against him, arguing that Christ can be called king of the lights only if he made rather than begat them, and so exposing the incoherence of the Manichaean division between the kingdom of light and the kingdom of darkness. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense quotation of Paul, direct engagement with Manichaean writings on the two natures, and a compact specimen of Augustine's polemical method against his former coreligionists.
la.augustine.de_agone_christiano: De Agone Christiano is a Latin prose theological treatise by Augustine, composed in the late-antique period, on the Christian life as a contest in which the crown of victory is promised to those who overcome the devil. Augustine argues that the unseen adversary is defeated within the soul itself, through victory over cupidity and love of the passing world, and expounds the Pauline passage on the struggle against principalities and powers by interpreting the heavens in which such powers dwell as the air rather than the highest heaven. A substantial section refutes the Manichaean myth of a primordial race of darkness and the divine substance supposedly mixed with and degraded by it. For readers of intertexts the work matters for its dense quotation and reworking of Pauline verses and for the witness it bears to how contested scriptural loci were read in late-antique polemic against Manichaean exegesis.
la.augustine.de_baptismo: De Baptismo is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, directed against the Donatists and printed in Michael Petschenig's 1908 Vienna edition of the Scripta contra Donatistas. Fulfilling a promise made in the books written against Parmenian's letter to Tychonius, Augustine argues that baptism conferred outside the catholic communion, though given illicitly, remains a valid sacrament, that it is not lost by schism and therefore need not be repeated, and that rebaptism rather than the practice of the universal church wrongs the sacrament. He also confronts the Donatist reliance on the authority of Cyprian, contending that the martyr's writings refute rather than support their position. The sustained engagement with Cyprianic tradition, with Parmenian, and with the Tychonius correspondence makes the work a productive locus for tracing the reworking of earlier patristic authority in Latin anti-Donatist polemic.
la.augustine.de_bono_viduitatis: The De Bono Viduitatis, a brief Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date by Augustine, is framed as a letter from the bishop to the widow Juliana, urging her to persevere in her profession of holy widowhood. Arguing from the Pauline epistles, above all 1 Corinthians, it ranks the continence of widows above the good of faithful Christian marriage while insisting that second marriages, though inferior, remain licit, a point sharpened by criticism of the Cataphrygians, the Novatians, and Tertullian's harsher verdict on remarriage. Readers hunting textual parallels will find a dense lattice of scriptural quotation and allusion, exempla drawn from Ruth and Anna, and an explicit Augustinian rebuttal of Tertullian on second unions. The work is printed in Joseph Zycha's 1900 Viennese edition of Augustine's Opera.
la.augustine.de_conjugiis_adulterinis: De coniugiis adulterinis is a short Latin prose treatise by Augustine, addressed to a correspondent named Pollentius, in which the author defends the indissolubility of marriage against Pollentius's argument that an abandoned spouse may remain unmarried rather than return. Working through the Pauline teaching of 1 Corinthians 7 and the Matthean exception clause concerning fornication, Augustine argues that separation without cause is itself forbidden and that continence within marriage requires the mutual consent of both partners. Readers tracing intertexts will find dense, verse-by-verse engagement with scriptural passages on divorce, remarriage, and conjugal debt, as well as implicit appeal to Augustine's earlier De sermone Domini in monte, making the work a useful node for parallels among Late Antique exegetical treatments of these themes.
la.augustine.de_consensu_evangelistarum: De Consensu Evangelistarum, Augustine's Latin prose treatise On the Agreement of the Evangelists, opens by ranking the gospel above all other divine scriptures as the fulfillment of law and prophets and by arguing that only the four evangelists, Matthew and John from among the apostles, Mark and Luke from their faithful followers, bear canonical authority, while other would-be gospel writers introduced fabrications that the church rejects. Augustine then treats the order in which the four wrote (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), the symbolic aptness of their number to the four parts of the world, and each evangelist's distinctive emphases, above all the royal and priestly figures he finds reflected in the differing genealogies of Christ. A late-antique landmark of gospel harmonization and of the defense of scriptural consistency, it weaves a dense web of biblical quotation and exegetical patterning of value to readers hunting textual parallels; the Latin follows Franz Weihrich's 1904 Vienna edition.
la.augustine.de_cura_pro_mortuis_gerenda: De cura pro mortuis gerenda is a short Latin treatise of Late Antique date in which Augustine, replying to a letter from the bishop Paulinus, examines whether burial near the memorials of saints brings any benefit to the departed. Taking its cue from a widow's request that her son be laid to rest in the basilica of the confessor Felix, the work argues that funerary care profits the dead only where merits acquired during life make such aid effective, and that the lack of burial does no harm to the soul. Scriptural authorities, including the sacrifice for the dead in Maccabees and the apostle's words on the tribunal of Christ, are set against the Virgilian fiction of unburied souls barred from crossing the infernal river, and funeral rites are judged to be comforts of the living rather than aids to the dead, as in the Gospel contrast between the rich man and Lazarus. Readers hunting parallels will find explicit quotation of the Aeneid, a cross-reference to the first book of De ciuitate dei, and dense allusion to psalm and Gospel material within a compact epistolary frame.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_operibus: A prose theological treatise by Augustine written in Late Antiquity, De Fide et Operibus takes up the question whether catechumens living in open and notorious sin, such as adulterers and those in illicit second unions, should be admitted to baptism before amending their lives. Augustine opposes those who would baptise first and instruct afterwards, citing scriptural passages on the mixture of good and evil in the church, and argues instead for prior correction, penitence, and ecclesiastical discipline. The argument weaves together Pauline texts on excommunication and deliverance to Satan with dominical sayings on fraternal correction, binding and loosing, and the tares among the wheat, making the work a valuable witness to late antique baptismal practice and to Augustine's handling of scriptural authorities.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram_imperfec: An unfinished Latin prose treatise by Augustine on the opening of Genesis, a work of Late Antique theology edited by Joseph Zycha in the 1894 Vienna edition of the author's opera. It opens with a summary of the Catholic faith, the consubstantial Trinity as maker of all creation out of nothing, evil as sin or its punishment rather than a natural substance, and the renewal of humanity through Christ, and then sets out four traditional modes of scriptural exposition, historia, allegoria, analogia, and aetiologia. From there it probes the meaning of 'in principio fecit deus caelum et terram,' asking whether the beginning is temporal or the divine Wisdom itself, whether angels were made before or with time, and whether time can exist apart from the motion of bodies, concluding that time itself is a created thing with a beginning. For readers of intertexts the work supplies compact parallels for creation exegesis, patristic classifications of interpretive method, and the doctrine that time is a creature, themes that recur throughout Augustine's Genesis commentaries and later medieval writing on Genesis.
la.augustine.de_mendacio: De Mendacio is a brief Late Antique theological treatise in Latin prose by Augustine, of uncertain date, presented in Joseph Zycha's 1900 Vienna edition. Opening with the observation that the question of lying disturbs everyday actions and must be pursued cautiously alongside the reader, it excludes jokes from the outset, distinguishes speaking what is false from lying proper, and defines the liar as the one whose words carry a doubled heart, saying otherwise than the mind holds with a desire to deceive. Its casuistic core weighs paired examples, the man who tells a falsehood about robbers on a road in order to save a traveller, and the man who tells the truth in order to deceive, to test whether lying resides in the falsity of the utterance or in the will to deceive. Readers tracing intertexts will find a fountainhead of definitions and exempla on truth-telling that later moral theology repeatedly quotes and reworks, delivered in a deliberately plain style whose hasty composition the author himself thematises in the opening lines.
la.augustine.de_natura_boni: De Natura Boni is a short Latin prose treatise on theology by Augustine, a Late Antique work printed in Joseph Zycha's Vienna edition of 1892 and running to only forty-eight lines. Arguing from the premise that God, the supreme and immutable good, transcends all measure, species, and order, the treatise holds that everything made from nothing is good insofar as it is a nature, and that evil is nothing other than the corruption of a nature's measure, species, or order. Against those who would posit an evil nature of wicked spirit and mortal body that God did not make, it ranks created goods from the unchangeable God through rational spirits down to bodies, allowing corruption to diminish but never annihilate natural goodness. Its terse, axiom-like formulations, omnis natura bona, evil as corruptio modi, speciei ac ordinis, the comparison of the changing universe to a well-composed speech, recur throughout Augustine and later writers, making the work a dense source of verbal and doctrinal parallels.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_gratia: A late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine on nature and grace, written in reply to the book that Timasius and Jacobus had sent him. The argument defends the necessity of unmerited grace for the salvation of both infants and adults, the inheritance of sin from Adam, and the insufficiency of unaided human nature to fulfill the law, against writers who excuse human wrongdoing by accusing nature rather than the will. Dense with Pauline material on law, justification, and the free gift of Christ's blood, and citing the verdict of secular literary authors, 'falso queritur de natura sua genus humanum', the compact work (84 lines) offers readers of intertexts a clear specimen of Augustine's scriptural argumentation and of the late-antique debate over grace and free choice. The text follows Zycha's 1913 Vienna edition.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_origine_animae: A Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology by Augustine, cast as a letter to his brother Renatus and written in answer to Vincentius Victor's recent books on the nature and origin of the soul. It quotes Victor's positions directly, that the soul was made from God's own substance rather than out of nothing, and that soul is body rather than spirit, and refutes each in turn, defending the soul's creation ex nihilo and its mutable but spiritual nature. The work combines epistolary courtesy with doctrinal polemic, touching also on Victor's recent conversion from Donatist and Rogatist circles. Because Victor's own words are embedded in Augustine's argument, the treatise offers fertile ground for tracing verbal parallels and shared formulations between the two writers.
la.augustine.de_opere_monachorum: De Opere Monachorum is a short Latin theological treatise in prose of Late Antique date, written by Augustine at the prompting of Bishop Aurelius of Carthage, as the opening address 'sancte frater Aureli' records; the corpus text derives from Joseph Zycha's Vienna edition of 1900. It rebuts monks who interpret Paul's injunction 'qui non uult operari, non manducet' as referring to spiritual labour alone, defending manual work by setting Paul's own example among the Thessalonians against the Gospel's counsels against anxiety over food and clothing. In the course of the argument it quotes and paraphrases scripture densely, 2 Thessalonians 3, Matthew 6, 1 Corinthians 3 and 9, the parable of the talents, making it a rich source of biblical commonplaces and a well-marked instance of patristic argument built on the juxtaposition of passages.
la.augustine.de_ordine: De Ordine, a Late Antique prose dialogue by Augustine addressed to Zenobius, takes as its theme the order of things, both particular and universal, by which the world coheres and is governed, a reality so hard for human beings to see or expound that few attain it. The opening argument weighs how divine providence can care for human affairs amid such perversion that evil seems everywhere diffused, rejecting the impious alternatives that providence does not extend to the last things or that God wills all evils, and locates the remedy in self-knowledge, recovered by receding from the senses and by the liberal disciplines that purge and cultivate the soul. A framing passage recalls conversations, taken down with a stylus, at the villa of Verecundus with Alypius, Navigius, Licentius, and Trygetius, after a stomach ailment had compelled Augustine's departure from the school. For readers of intertexts, the dialogue supplies dense loci on providence, cosmic order, and the soul's dispersal in multiplicity, including the mosaic-pavement analogy for perceiving artistry in the whole and the geometric figure of the circle's center, imagery much reworked in later treatments of order and unity.
la.augustine.de_patientia: De Patientia (On Patience) is a short Latin prose treatise on the virtue of patientia by Augustine, a theologian of Late Antiquity, printed in Joseph Zycha's 1900 Vienna edition of Augustine's works. Opening from the paradox that Scripture calls a God who cannot suffer 'patient', the work defines human patience as the even temper with which temporal evils are borne so that eternal goods are not lost, and contrasts such endurance with the tolerated 'madness' of those who suffer long and hard for wealth, honour, lust, and even crime. It cites the apostle on the lightness of present tribulation weighed against future glory, quotes the Lord's saying that in patience souls are possessed, and argues that true patience is the companion of wisdom and good conscience rather than the servant of desire. For readers hunting intertexts, the treatise offers a compact Late Antique instance of biblical quotation woven into a Christian reworking of classical virtue vocabulary, with exempla drawn from secular letters, and serves as a useful comparand for moral prose on endurance.
la.augustine.de_sancta_virginitate: De Sancta Virginitate is a short Late Antique Latin theological treatise in prose by Augustine, printed in Joseph Zycha's 1900 Vienna edition of his works. Composed as a sequel to the De Bono Coniugali, to which its opening lines refer, it urges virgins dedicated to Christ to hold their gift in humility without despising the married faithful, arguing from Mary that virginity is a vow freely chosen before God, and that Mary's blessedness rests on hearing and keeping the divine word rather than on bodily kinship with her son. Its dense scriptural texture, the wild olive grafted into the olive, the Gospel sayings on Christ's true mother and brethren, the counsel 'qui potest capere capiat', and its account of the church as at once virgin and mother make it a natural hunting ground for parallels in later writing on marriage, celibacy, and Mariology.
la.augustine.de_spiritu_et_littera: De Spiritu et Littera is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, printed here from Joseph Zycha's 1913 Vienna edition, its title drawn from the Pauline antithesis between the killing letter and the vivifying spirit. Framed as a reply to Marcellinus on whether anyone in this life can be wholly without sin, it argues that the human will cannot attain justice by its own force, since the law's prohibitions only inflame concupiscence until the Spirit pours charity into the heart. Its sustained exegesis of the apostolic dictum 'littera occidit, spiritus autem uiuificat', woven together with allusions to the Gospels and the Song of Songs, makes the work a central witness for readers tracing the vocabulary of grace, free will, and the letter-and-spirit topos in Latin Christian writing.
la.augustine.de_utilitate_credendi: A short Late Antique prose treatise by Augustine, cast as a letter to Honoratus, directed against the Manichaeans and their demand that reason precede belief. It defends the priority of faith, arguing that those who follow the authority of the Catholic faith before they can behold truth with a pure mind are prepared and illumined by God rather than deceived, and it answers the Manichaean onslaught on the Old Testament with an account of how its mysteries are to be received. The argument draws on autobiographical recollection, since Augustine recalls spending nearly nine years among the Manichaeans as an Auditor before returning to the Catholic faith. Readers hunting textual parallels will find a dense weave of scriptural allusion and recurring Augustinian formulae concerning faith, purification, and the reading of the Old Testament.
la.augustine.epistulae: The Epistulae of Augustine, transmitted in Alois Goldbacher's 1895 Vienna edition of the Operа Sancti Aurelii Augustini, collect the letters of the late-antique Latin author in continuous prose, some 2,231 lines with no division into books. The opening correspondence, addressed to friends such as Nebridius and Alypius, debates Academic scepticism, the Platonic inheritance, and the pursuit of the happy life, while looking back on Augustine's own early philosophical writings, including the Soliloquia. For readers of intertexts the collection offers dense engagement with Plato, Carneades, and Epicurus, together with Augustine's habitual self-reference to his earlier dialogues, making it a productive ground for verbal and philosophical parallels.
la.augustine.gesta_cum_emerito_donatistarum: A brief Latin acta preserving a verbatim disputation between Augustine of Hippo and Emeritus, a Donatist bishop, held at Caesarea in the greater church before bishops including Deuterius, Alypius, and Possidius, with the consuls Honorius and Theodosius named in its heading. Late Antique theological prose, the record belongs to the aftermath of the celebrated conference at Carthage: Augustine presses Emeritus, who has come of his own accord, to state what he would still argue in defense of the party of Donatus, while Emeritus refuses to speak except through the official proceedings, which will show whether he was defeated by truth or overborne by power. Though very short, the exchange cites Pauline verses on again travailing in birth until Christ be formed in converts and on the troubler who shall bear his own judgment, and its phrasing echoes the formulae of Augustine's wider anti-Donatist polemic, making it a compact witness to that controversy's argumentative repertoire.
la.augustine.liber_de_divinis_scripturis_si: A short Late Antique Latin prose work transmitted among the writings of Augustine in the CSEL edition of Weihrich (1887), the Liber de divinis scripturis, sive Speculum arranges scriptural doctrine and moral instruction under a long sequence of numbered chapter headings, moving from the unity of God and the distinction of the divine persons through penitence, almsgiving, and prayer to precepts on oaths, false witness, idolatry, fornication, usury, tithes, and the duties of priests, parents, and judges. Many of the headings are phrased as biblical commands and echo Old Testament legal and sapiential material, in keeping with the title's promise of a mirror of the divine scriptures. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in the work a dense repertory of late antique scriptural diction and ethical commonplaces, useful for tracing Latin biblical phrasing and the topical organization shared by catechetical, penitential, and mirror literature.
la.augustine.liber_de_unico_baptismo: A brief late-antique Latin treatise of Augustine on baptism, addressed to a brother named Constantine and preserved among the anti-Donatist writings in Petchenig's 1910 Vienna edition. Written in prose, it answers a Donatist composition which argued that the baptism once bestowed should never be repeated by the 'sacrilegious', countering that the sacrament belongs to Christ and not to the minister, so that baptism validly received from schismatics or heretics need not be iterated; an extended analogy likens such recipients to the Jews, who held God's good law while erring. Heavily laced with quotation from Paul, especially Romans, and compact enough to be read at a sitting, it offers hunters of parallels a dense witness to the vocabulary and scriptural argumentation of the rebaptism controversy.
la.augustine.sermo_ad_caesariensis_ecclesia: A brief Latin prose sermon addressed to the people of the church of Caesarea, attributed to Augustine and printed among his writings against the Donatists in Petschenig's 1910 Vienna edition of the Scripta contra Donatistas. The preacher welcomes the congregation's desire for unity and reports the pledge of Emeritus, hitherto in the communion of the Donatist party, to accept reconciliation with the Catholic Church. In answer to those who object to treating schismatics as brothers, he distinguishes their heresy from the divine goods they carry, above all baptism, which belongs to Christ and bears the character of the emperor rather than of the deserter. Dense with scriptural quotation and allusion, from Paul on the Church's peace to the soldier's seal as an image of the baptismal character, the work offers a compact witness to late-antique anti-Donatist argument on schism, heresy, and the validity of baptism conferred outside communion.
la.aurelius_victor.de_caesaribus: The De Caesaribus attributed to Aurelius Victor is a Late Antique Latin prose history of the Roman emperors, opening with Augustus and proceeding reign by reign in terse biographical notices. Each ruler receives a compressed character sketch of virtues, vices, and scandal, interspersed with brief notices of wars, provinces, and dynastic upheaval, as in the extended treatments of Tiberius, Caligula, and Claudius at the work's opening. Its epigrammatic moralising and stock formulas for tyranny, luxury, and civic decline make it fertile ground for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels across Latin imperial historiography and biography.
la.aurelius_victor.epitome_de_caesaribus: The Epitome de Caesaribus, a Latin prose work of imperial historiography attributed to Aurelius Victor and of uncertain date within the Late Antique period, offers compressed biographies of the Roman emperors from Augustus onward. Each notice assembles anecdotes on an emperor's lineage, character, virtues, vices, wit, and death, as in its opening account of Octavian's rise to sole power, his rebuilding of Rome 'latericiam... marmoream', and the rumours that Livia poisoned him at Nola. The terse, often sententious prose condenses earlier historiographical tradition into a sequence of moralised imperial portraits, moving on from Augustus to a pointedly dark sketch of Tiberius. For readers of intertexts the work serves as a compact reservoir of imperial anecdote, aphorism, and phrasing that circulated widely in later Latin writing.
la.ausonius.de_xii_caesaribus: De XII Caesaribus is a Late Antique Latin sequence by Ausonius comprising epigrammatic characterisations of the Roman emperors, opening with a monostich for each of the twelve Caesars and explicitly modelled on Suetonius, whom the preface credits with a full account of their names, deeds, lives and deaths. The series then continues with longer poems extending the imperial gallery through the Flavians, the adoptive Antonines and the Severan age, each ruler dismissed with a pointed moral verdict. Compressing Suetonian biography into memorable verse, the work is useful to readers of intertexts as a late witness to the reception of Suetonius and to the moral typology and phraseology of imperial biography in later Latin poetry.
la.ausonius.gratiarum_actio: The Gratiarum Actio is a Late Antique Latin prose oration by Ausonius, a formal speech of thanks addressed to the emperor Gratian for the consulship conferred on the speaker. The orator insists that gratitude must be paid everywhere, in every place and mood, and adduces proofs of the emperor's virtues, including peace restored in a single year to both the Danubian and Rhine frontiers, a richly endowed army, and a father consecrated with divine honors. The latter part celebrates a consulship attained without canvassing, bribery, or expense, for whom the Roman people, the Campus Martius, the senate, and the curia were all one Gratianus, and closes by setting the emperor's golden saying beside the eloquence of Homer's Menelaus, Ulysses, and Nestor. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact specimen of late antique panegyric densely engaged with classical and epic models of oratory.
la.ausonius.libri_de_fastis_conclusio: The Conclusio to the Libri de Fastis of Ausonius, a Late Antique poet writing in Latin lyric metre, rounds off his verse consular calendar in twenty-four lines. It recalls the fasti assembled from the age of the kings down to Ausonius's own consulship, sets out a numerical scheme for reckoning the years of aeternal Rome from its foundation, and addresses a certain Proculus, who is invited to carry the annalistic series forward into future Olympiads. Playfully self-referential throughout, the poet offers the fruit of his vigilae under the studious lamp and directs the reader to a title elsewhere in the collection, the piece also invites whoever comes after to add to the list if fate permits. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact late example of Roman calendar poetry and an authorial epilogue that comments on chronology, consular lists, and the mechanics of verse commemoration.
la.ausonius.precationes: The Precationes, a brief work of sixty-nine lines in lyric metres, is a collection of prayers by the late antique poet Ausonius. Its principal piece is a new-year prayer addressed to Janus and to the sun, invoking seasonable weather, favourable planets, victory over Frankish, Sarmatian, and other enemies, and the consulship of a Caesar who is to succeed the speaker, who styles himself consul Ausonius. The refrain 'Iane, veni' and the catalogues of winds, zodiacal signs, and the courses of sun and moon recast Roman hymnic and calendrical conventions in the idiom of consular panegyric. For readers hunting parallels, the poem offers late antique reworkings of the new-year invocation, seasonal catalogue, and prayer formulae familiar from Horace and the Latin lyric tradition.
la.ausonius.versus_paschales_pro_augusto_di: A short Latin poem of thirty-one lyric lines in which the late antique poet Ausonius marks the Easter festival on behalf of an emperor, as the phrase pro Augusto dicti in the title records. The opening celebrates the returning solemnities of Christ the giver of salvation and the fasts of his devout devotees, and the central section addresses God the Father as ruler of earth, sea, air, Tartara and the milky belt of the painted heavens, rehearsing the deception of Adam through Eve's blandishments, the gift of law and prophets, and the sending of the son, true from the true and living from the living source, whose baptismal precept quickens mortal limbs and grounds a threefold faith in a single author. The close draws a pointed analogy between that indivisible divine order and an earthly Augustus, begetter of twin Augusti, who embraces brother and son alike and shares his rule without dividing it, before a final prayer commends the placid rulers of earth and ministers of heaven to Christ. Readers tracing intertexts will find a compact fusion of Trinitarian doctrine, the Adam and Eve narrative and baptismal imagery with classical lyric metre and the conventions of imperial panegyric.
la.bede_the_venerable.de_locis_santis: A short early medieval Latin prose treatise by Bede the Venerable describing the holy places of Jerusalem, opening with the city's near-circular plan, its walls, towers and gates, and then surveying the Constantinian complex of the Martyrium, Golgotha and the rotunda of the Anastasis with the Lord's tomb, its altars, lamps and measurements carefully recorded. Further sections treat Mount Sion with its monastic cells, the church housing the site of the Last Supper, the pool of Bethsaida, the spring of Siloe, the rock of Saint Stephen's martyrdom, and the rectangular house of prayer that the Saracens maintain on the temple platform. A closing citation of Victorinus of Pettau on Golgotha as the center of the earth underscores the work's value for readers tracing how the scriptural geography of Jerusalem was transmitted and elaborated in the medieval West.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: A Latin poem of 173 lines on the life and miracles of Saint Benedict, attributed to Bertharius of Monte Cassino and preserved in a version whose title marks it as interpolated. Its couplets run through the familiar Benedictine miracle cycle: the sieve and poisoned loaf made whole, the rescue of the drowning Placidus by Maurus, poison taken back by the priest who brewed it, visionary combats with the devil, and the prophecy granted to Totila concerning the span of his reign. The poem closes with an address to Rome foretelling the city's endurance and warning a cleric against profiting from holy orders. Readers of intertexts will find it useful for measuring how Carolingian verse reshapes episodes known from earlier prose hagiography and for tracing formulaic language shared across the Benedictine legend.
la.boethius.consolatio_philosophiae: The Consolatio Philosophiae of Boethius, a Late Antique Latin work in five books alternating prose and lyric verse, opens with the author-figure lamenting the sudden reversal of fortune that has left him, condemned on false charges, in exile and near despair. Personified Philosophy appears at his bedside, banishes the theatrical Muses who have been dictating his complaints, and undertakes his cure through a therapy of recollection, argument, and song. The dialogue moves from meditation on the mutability of luck toward larger questions of providence, free will, and true happiness, with the lady's ascent toward the heavens figured throughout. Steeped in Platonic and Stoic allusion, Socrates, Seneca, Canius, and Soranus are named among philosophy's martyrs, it serves as a dense hub of classical echoes and a touchstone for readers tracing intertexts between antique philosophy and later literature.
la.boethius.de_fide_catholica: A brief Latin prose treatise ascribed to Boethius and of Late Antique date, De Fide Catholica sets out the foundations of Christian doctrine: the coeternal Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the creation of the world from nothing by the divine Word, the fall of Adam with the transmission of sin and death to his posterity, and the refutation of heresiarchs such as Arius, the Sabellians, the Manichaeans, and Pelagius. It grounds the faith in the joint authority of the Old and New Testaments and distinguishes historical, allegorical, and composite modes of scriptural meaning. The work is printed in H. F. Stewart's 1918 edition of the Theological Tractates and the Consolation of Philosophy. For readers hunting textual parallels, its compact dogmatic formulae and heresiological catalogue offer a rich touchstone for the vocabulary of Latin patristic theology.
la.boethius.quomodo_substantiae_in_eo_quod_: A short Late Antique philosophical treatise in prose by Boethius, framed as a reply to a correspondent who asks for a plainer exposition of the problem raised in the author's Hebdomads: how substances can be good in so far as they exist without being substantial goods. It begins from a series of axioms on common conceptions, distinguishing esse from id quod est and simple from composite being, and then resolves the paradox by arguing that created things are good because their being flows from the first good, in which alone being and goodness are identical. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a compact source of the vocabulary of participation and of the esse/essentia distinction on which later scholastic discussion of being and goodness repeatedly drew.
la.boethius.quomodo_trinitas: Quomodo Trinitas is a short Latin prose treatise on philosophical theology by Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, composed in late antiquity and addressed to his father-in-law Q. Aurelius Memmius Symmachus. It argues that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and not three gods, contending against the Arian ranking of persons that numerical difference arises only from accidents, whereas the divine substance, being pure form without matter, admits no plurality. In the course of the argument Boethius recalls the seeds of reasoning drawn from Augustine's writings and sets out the division of the speculative sciences into natural, mathematical, and theological, reserving intellectual rather than rational understanding for divine things. Readers hunting parallels will find a dense web of Augustinian phraseology and Aristotelian ontology, matter, form, accident, genus, species, number, that later medieval discussions of the Trinity and of divine simplicity repeatedly echo.
la.caesar.de_bello_civili: Caesar's De Bello Civili is a work of Republican historiography in Latin prose, preserved here in three books, giving an account of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey told from the Caesarian side. It opens with the senate's final deliberations over Caesar's command, the hostile senatus consultum, and the flight of the tribunes to Caesar at Ravenna, before tracing the collapse of negotiation into open hostilities. Its spare, rapid style and openly partisan viewpoint made it the baseline prose narrative of the Republic's fall, and later historians and epic poets treating the civil war write continually with and against it.
la.caesar_augustus.res_gestae_divi_augusti: The Res Gestae Divi Augusti is a Latin prose account, presented as a copy of an inscription once set up on two bronze pillars at Rome, in which Augustus enumerates the deeds by which he brought the world under the power of the Roman people and the sums he spent on the state. Writing near the end of his reign in the first person, he records his youthful private levy against the dominating faction, his civil and foreign wars, the offices and priesthoods he held or declined, his censuses, his settlements of veterans, and the honors voted him, from the title of Augustus to the consecration of the Ara Pacis and the closing of the gates of Janus. Its terse, formulaic inventory of achievements became the archetype of imperial self-presentation, and readers hunting parallels will find its phrasing, themes, and catalogues echoed throughout later historiography, panegyric, and inscriptional literature.
la.cicero.brutus: Cicero's Brutus is a rhetorical dialogue in Latin prose of the late Republican era, framed as a conversation between Cicero, Atticus, and the younger Brutus in the aftermath of Quintus Hortensius' death, which Cicero mourns at length in the opening. From that lament the discussion broadens into a history of eloquence, tracing its Greek origins and surveying the great Roman orators down to Cicero's own contemporaries, with a celebrated eulogy of Hortensius at its centre. For readers hunting intertexts it offers a dense web of allusion: Hesiod on repayment of gifts, Marcellus and the recovery after Cannae, and a running catalogue of orators whose reputations and phrases recur throughout Ciceronian rhetorical works and later accounts of Roman literary history.
la.cicero.cum_populo_gratias_egit: A short Latin oration by Cicero, belonging to the oratory of the Roman Republic, spoken to the Roman people upon his recall from exile, in which the speaker gives thanks to the gods, the senate, Italy, and above all the citizen body for his restoration and that of his brother. The speech dwells on the sweetness of recovered blessings, children, brother, property, friendships, honours, and the fatherland itself, likening the joy of return to health regained after grave illness, and contrasts Cicero's recall through popular supplication with Marius's armed return. Its dense rhetoric of gratitude, its catalogue of intercessors (Popilius, the Metelli, the Luculli, the Servilii and Scipiones), and its self-fashioning after political ruin make it a rich hunting ground for parallels on exile, restoration, and public thanksgiving.
la.cicero.de_fato: Cicero's De Fato is a brief Latin prose dialogue of the late Republic, set at Puteoli after Caesar's assassination, in which Cicero converses with the consul-designate Hirtius on whether all events happen by the necessity of fate. The discussion treats the problem of future contingents and the Stoic theory of causes, weighing the positions of Chrysippus, Posidonius, and Antipater on antecedent causes, celestial influence, and the freedom of the will. The preface connects the work to the De Natura Deorum and De Divinatione, where arguments were set out on both sides, and renders Greek technical vocabulary such as axiomata and peri dynaton into Latin philosophical prose. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable for tracing Cicero's handling of Hellenistic philosophical sources and for the formulas of causation and determinism that recur throughout Latin literature.
la.cicero.de_finibus_bonorum_et_malorum: A prose philosophical dialogue in five books by Cicero of the late Republic, on the ends of good and evil, treating the highest good and greatest evil through successive Greek ethical doctrines. The opening prologue, addressed to Brutus, defends composing philosophy in Latin and reflects on translation, imitation, and Roman literary taste, while the work as a whole brings Epicurean, Stoic, and Academic teaching into Latin philosophical vocabulary. Its dense texture of quotation and allusion, to Plato, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Chrysippus, and Posidonius, and directly to Ennius, Pacuvius, Caecilius, Terence, and Lucilius, makes it a central witness to the transmission of Greek thought and poetry into Roman letters and a rich source for readers hunting intertexts.
la.cicero.de_inventione: De inventione, a Latin prose treatise on rhetoric attributed to Cicero and belonging to the Republican era, is transmitted in two books here edited by Stroebel. It opens with a celebrated prologue debating whether eloquence has brought human societies more good or harm, tracing speech's power to found cities and its capacity for corruption, before turning to technical instruction. The work sets out the definition, office, parts, and material of the art, then expounds the divisions of a judicial speech, the theory of status or issues, and the topics from which arguments are drawn. Its doctrines run closely parallel to the anonymous Rhetorica ad Herennium, and its vocabulary of exordium, narratio, status, and argumentative topoi became common coin in Latin rhetorical education, making the treatise a central point of reference for readers tracing rhetorical formulas and shared diction across later prose.
la.cicero.de_officiis: A Latin philosophical treatise in three books from the Republican era, De Officiis was composed by Cicero as an essay of moral instruction addressed to his son Marcus, then studying philosophy under Cratippus at Athens. Drawing avowedly on Panaetius and the Stoics while insisting on independent judgment, it treats the definition of duty (officium, rendering the Greek kathēkon), the distinction between ordinary and perfect duty, the conflict between the honorable and the useful, and precepts for conduct in public, private, forensic, and domestic life. For readers hunting intertexts, the work is a principal conduit by which Greek ethical vocabulary and doctrine entered Latin prose, and its dense allusions to Plato, Aristotle, Demosthenes, Isocrates, and the Hellenistic philosophers make it a rich source of parallels.
la.cicero.de_optimo_genere_oratorum: The De Optimo Genere Oratorum is a short Latin rhetorical treatise by Cicero, written in prose during the Republican era and printed in Wilkins's Oxford edition of the Rhetorica. Against those who would confine 'Attic' speaking to a thin and plain manner, it argues that oratory has a single perfect genus, embodied in the orator who teaches, delights, and moves his hearers, and it holds up Demosthenes as the model a Roman should imitate. Framed as a preface, it announces Cicero's Latin renderings of the opposed speeches of Aeschines and Demosthenes, translated 'not as an interpreter but as an orator.' Readers of intertexts will find it densely stocked with named Greek and Latin exempla, from Ennius, Pacuvius, and Terence to Lysias, Thucydides, and Plato, and with formulations on decorum, copia, and the three offices of the orator that reverberate in later stylistic debate.
la.cicero.de_provinciis_consularibus: A deliberative oration of the Roman Republic, Cicero's De Provinciis Consularibus addresses the Senate on the assignment of the consular provinces, urging that Syria and Macedonia be taken from the commanders Gabinius and Piso while the two Gallic provinces are decreed under the lex Sempronia. The speech catalogues their misgovernment, extortion and violence in Macedonia, the plundering of Byzantium and Achaea, and frames the question of provincial command as a matter of public welfare rather than personal grievance. Readers of intertexts will find dense Ciceronian invective, recurring administrative and legal vocabulary (provincia, imperium, senatus consulta), and allusions to Hannibal and the Mithridatic wars that echo across Republican oratory and historiography.
la.cicero.epistulae_ad_familiares: The Epistulae ad Familiares gathers the prose correspondence of Cicero with friends, family, and political allies, preserved in sixteen books of Republican Latin. Its letters move between private courtesies, commendations, consolations, domestic news, and detailed dispatches on senatorial maneuvering around figures such as Pompey and Cato in the crisis of the late Republic. The collection offers readers of intertexts a dense storehouse of Ciceronian idiom and contemporary allusion, much of its phrasing echoed in Cicero's own speeches and in later Latin prose.
la.cicero.letters_to_brutus: A brief Latin prose collection of correspondence, the Letters to Brutus belong to Cicero's epistolary output of the late Republic and are addressed to Marcus Brutus during the civil war waged against Marcus Antonius. The letters survey the military and political scene in close detail: Dolabella's operations in the East, Antony's flight, the eruption of Brutus's forces in Macedonia, the deaths of the consuls Hirtius and Pansa, and the emergence of the young Caesar, together with a pointed disagreement over whether clemency or severity should govern the treatment of defeated citizens. Readers hunting parallels will find an explicit quotation of Plautus's Trinummus, an allusion to the oracular response of Apollo Pythius, and a dense register of late-Republican political and rhetorical diction.
la.cicero.letters_to_quintus: The Letters to Quintus is a Latin prose epistolary work of the Republican era, attributed to Cicero from the source record, comprising correspondence addressed to his brother Quintus during the latter's three-year governorship of the province of Asia. The letters blend fraternal encouragement with practical and moral counsel on provincial administration: restraint toward allies and citizens, management of publicani and negotiatores, oversight of legates and quaestors, and the integrity expected of a Roman magistrate abroad. Readers hunting parallels will find Cicero's periodic syntax, ethical exempla, and recurring themes of virtus, moderation, and reputation, phrasing that resonates with his speeches, treatises, and other correspondence and repays intertextual comparison across Ciceronian and Republican Latin.
la.cicero.lucullus: Lucullus, a Latin philosophical dialogue in prose by Cicero of the Republican era, is transmitted as the second book of the Academica. Taking its name from the consul L. Licinius Lucullus, whose career, memory, and devotion to letters the opening encomium celebrates, it stages a debate on the criterion of truth and the possibility of knowledge, with Lucullus defending the epistemology of Antiochus of Ascalon and Cicero replying for the sceptical Academy. Readers of intertexts will find dense engagement with the Greek philosophical tradition alongside allusions to figures such as Hortensius, Themistocles, Cato, Panaetius, and Scipio Africanus, connecting the dialogue to the wider literary culture of the Roman elite.
la.cicero.orator: A Latin prose treatise on rhetoric by Cicero, composed during the Republic and addressed to Brutus, edited by A. S. Wilkins in the Oxford Clarendon edition of 1911. In answer to Brutus's repeated questioning, Cicero defines the perfect orator and the highest kind of eloquence, treating the dependence of eloquence on philosophy, the character of the supreme style, and the Platonic doctrine of ideas as a pattern for ideal form. Named exempla range from Demosthenes and Plato's Phaedrus to Phidias and the sculptors of the Coan Venus and Olympian Zeus, making the work a dense locus of allusion. It is a standard point of comparison for readers tracing Cicero's rhetorical vocabulary and his engagement with Greek thought alongside De Oratore and Brutus.
la.cicero.paradoxa_stoicorum_ad_m_brutum: The Paradoxa Stoicorum, a brief Latin prose treatise by Cicero addressed to Marcus Brutus in the late Republican period, sets out six notorious Stoic doctrines, that only the morally honourable is good, that the good man lacks nothing for a happy life, that all offences are equal, that all fools are mad, that only the wise are free, and that only the wise are rich, and argues them in an ornate oratorical style to show that even the harshest Greek school positions can be made persuasive in the forum. The fourth locus, on the madness of the foolish, survives only in fragmentary form, with the opening of a further paradox on the wise man as the sole citizen now lost. The preface frames the work as a small literary gift to Brutus and an exercise in transferring scholastic philosophy into forensic eloquence, a programme articulated with pointed reference to Cato's Stoicism and to Socratic precedent. Readers of intertexts will find dense allusive material in its digs at Cicero's contemporaries, including Clodius, Lucullus, Hortensius, and Crassus, alongside echoes of famous exempla such as Bias carrying his goods with him.
la.cicero.post_reditum_in_senatu: A brief prose oration of the Roman Republic, delivered by Cicero before the senate upon his return from exile and preserved in Albert Clark's Oxford edition of 1918. In thirty-nine lines the speaker heaps gratitude on the senators whose decrees secured his recall, praises the consul P. Lentulus, Q. Metellus, Cn. Pompeius and Q. Catulus as agents of his restoration, and rounds on the unnamed adversaries whose legislation had driven him out. For readers of intertexts the speech offers a concentrated specimen of Ciceronian gratiarum actio, with its rhetoric of beneficium and immortal memory, its veiled invective, and its self-portrait of the returning exile as a man raised from the dead by the senate's care.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_postumo: A defense speech by Cicero, composed during the Roman Republic, in which he pleads the case of Gaius Rabirius Postumus, a wealthy Roman financier charged under the Julian law over money alleged to have reached Aulus Gabinius after Gabinius's conviction for extortion. Cicero argues that his client lent money in good faith to the exiled Ptolemy of Alexandria, whose restoration the Senate had commended, and that Postumus's liability must be severed from the causes of Gabinius and of the Senate itself.
