The speech draws on legal procedure surrounding the assessment of damages, exempla of familial virtue such as the Decii and the Scipios, and an allusion to the Sibyl, making it fertile ground for parallels with Cicero's other forensic oratory and with the political and financial vocabulary of the Republican era.
la.cicero.pro_m_caelio: Cicero's Pro M. Caelio is a forensic defence speech in Latin prose from the Roman Republic, preserved in Albert Clark's Oxford edition of 1908. Speaking for the young Marcus Caelius against charges brought by Atratinus, the orator opens by professing astonishment that a private case should occupy the courts on public holidays, and then sets out to dismantle the prosecution's portrait of a dissolute youth: the accusations touching his conduct, his standing with his father and municipality, and above all his alleged familiarity with Catiline are met point by point with irony and rejoinder. The speech is a showpiece of Ciceronian wit, invective, and characterisation, drawing on the diction and situations of Roman comedy, and its exploitation of the commonplaces of accusation makes it fertile ground for readers tracing intertexts in Latin oratory and literature.
la.cicero.pro_marcello: Pro Marcello is a brief senatorial oration in Latin prose by Cicero, belonging to the late Republican era, in which the speaker publicly thanks Julius Caesar for pardoning Marcus Marcellus after the civil war. Over some thirty-five lines it unfolds as a sustained encomium, contrasting Caesar's conquests with his greater triumph of clemency, moderation, and mercy toward the defeated, culminating in the celebrated claim that Caesar has conquered victory itself. Students of intertexts will find it a dense repository of panegyric topoi, the merciful victor, self-mastery in power, praise of character over deeds, that echo through later Latin oratory and praise poetry, and its terse formulation of clementia offered a touchstone for imperial and medieval writers alike.
la.cicero.pro_murena: Pro Murena is a forensic oration in Latin prose by Cicero of the late Republican period, delivered during his consulship in defence of Lucius Murena, the consul elect standing trial for electoral bribery (ambitus) under the very law Cicero himself had carried. The surviving opening answers the objections of the accusers, above all Marcus Cato and Servius Sulpicius Rufus, before an appeal grounded in the authority of the consulship, an old friendship, and the lingering threat of Catiline's conspiracy. Edited in Albert Clark's Oxford text of 1908, the speech repays readers hunting intertexts with its celebrated humour and mockery of Stoic austerity, its formulaic legal and political diction, and its dense verbal echoes of Cicero's other consular orations.
la.cicero.pro_rege_deiotaro: A short Latin forensic oration of the Roman Republic, spoken by Cicero before Caesar in defence of King Deiotarus, who stood accused of plotting against Caesar's life. The opening argument dwells on the indignity of a king tried for his life, the impiety of the accusers, notably a grandson, Castor, prosecuting his own grandfather, and the delicate task of appealing to a judge presumed to bear the defendant lingering anger. Delivered outside the normal public venues of advocacy, the speech turns the constraints of its private setting into an exordial appeal for Caesar's clemency and fairness, while recalling Deiotarus's loyalty to the Republic and his former alliance with Pompey. Its compact exordium offers dense material for intertextual comparison with other Ciceronian speeches and with Republican oratorical topoi of judicial bias, friendship, and clemency.
la.cicero.pro_s_roscio: A Latin forensic oration of the Republican era, in which Cicero defends Sextus Roscius of Ameria against a charge of parricide; the opening itself signals that the advocate had not yet entered public office. The speech argues that the prosecution was contrived so that the powerful freedman L. Cornelius Chrysogonus, who had bought the murdered man's estate in connection with Sulla, might rid himself of the heir, and it dwells on the climate of fear and servility that the Sullan settlement had bred in the courts. Short by the standards of Cicero's corpus at 154 lines in Clark's 1908 Oxford edition, it is nonetheless among his most celebrated speeches, above all for its exordium on the dangers of speaking freely under a compromised regime. Readers tracing intertexts will find a wellspring of phrasing on patronage, proscription-era greed, and the corruption of justice that later rhetoric and literature draw on repeatedly.
la.cicero.pro_sestio: Cicero's Pro Sestio is a political prose oration of the Roman Republic, delivered in defence of Publius Sestius, the tribune whose efforts had helped secure Cicero's recall from exile. The speech sets out Sestius' lineage, quaestorship under C. Antonius, and conduct during the Catilinarian conspiracy, while framing the trial as a contest between loyal citizens and those who had overturned the state, and it contains Cicero's celebrated treatment of the optimates and their opponents. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense quarry of Republican political vocabulary and of recurring references to Cicero's consulship, exile, and restoration, phrasing that echoes across his other orations and letters. The text follows Albert Clark's Oxford edition of 1909.
la.cicero.pro_sulla: The Pro Sulla is Cicero's forensic oration in defence of Publius Sulla, a prose speech of the Roman Republic transmitted in Albert Clark's 1909 Oxford edition. Speaking after the conspiracy he had exposed as consul had been crushed, Cicero answers the objection that having testified against Autronius he now defends a man implicated in the same affair, and turns the plea into a sustained meditation on clemency, constancy, and his own public record. At ninety-three lines the oration offers a compact specimen of Ciceronian judicial argument, rich in reflexive self-defence, antithetical balancing of severitas and misericordia, and sententiae that echo throughout the Ciceronian corpus, making it a rewarding quarry for verbal and thematic parallels.
la.cicero.pro_tullio: Pro Tullio is a Republican-era forensic oration by Cicero, preserved in part, defending Marcus Tullius before a panel of recuperatores in a claim for quadruple damages against Publius Fabius, whose armed household was alleged to have inflicted loss by violence on Tullius' farm in the territory of Thurii. The speech recounts the institution of the judicium de damno dato under M. Lucullus, sets the case against the lex Aquilia, and dwells on boundary disputes, the purchase of neighboring estates, and the character of the opposing advocate Fabius. Gaps in the transmitted lines indicate that only a fraction of the original oration survives. Readers of intertexts may find its legal vocabulary, familia, damnum datum, recuperatores, the quadruple assessment, and its portrait of violence by armed rural households useful points of comparison in later juridical and literary passages.
la.cicero.timaeus: Cicero's Timaeus, a short prose philosophical work of the Roman Republic, preserves a Latin version of the opening cosmological sections of Plato's Timaeus, prefaced by a brief conversational frame involving P. Nigidius Figulus and the Peripatetic Cratippus. The surviving passage treats the distinction between what is eternal and what is generated, the benevolent maker who fashions the visible world as a single, intelligent living being after an everlasting exemplar, and the rational limits of such inquiry. As Cicero's rendering of Plato's account of the world's origin, it supplies an influential body of Latin cosmological vocabulary and phrasing, and readers hunting intertexts will find it a principal vehicle through which Platonic doctrine and diction entered Roman philosophical prose.
la.cicero.tusculanae_disputationes: Cicero's Tusculanae Disputationes, a Latin philosophical prose work of the Roman Republic, presents five disputations held at the author's Tusculan villa and framed by an address to Brutus, conducted in the old Socratic manner of question and answer. The opening question whether death is an evil sets the pattern, and the five books proceed through the endurance of pain and grief, the control of the passions, and the sufficiency of virtue for the happy life. Its preface surveys Greek learning and Roman achievement from Homer and Hesiod to Ennius and Cato, presenting the work as a deliberate transfer of Greek philosophy into Latin literary form. Readers tracing intertexts will find in it a reservoir of philosophical Latin repeatedly reused by later writers, together with a dense weave of allusion to Greek and Roman poets, exempla, and antiquarian detail.
la.cicero_pseudo.in_sallustium: A short Latin prose invective in twenty-three lines, transmitted under a pseudonymous attribution to Cicero and of uncertain date, with a dramatic setting in the oratorical politics of the Republican period. Speaking as Cicero before the patres conscripti, the author answers an attack by the historian Sallust, defending his own career, his consulship, his exile and recall, and his famous verses 'cedant arma togae' and 'fortunatam me consule Romam', while heaping abuse on Sallust's life, eloquence, and household. Though brief, the speech offers readers of intertexts a dense tissue of Ciceronian self-quotation and pointedly reversed Sallustian themes, illustrating how each writer's diction and famous phrases could be turned against him in forensic vituperation.
la.cicero_pseudo.pridie_quam_in_exilium_ire: A Latin oration of uncertain date and authorship, transmitted under Cicero's name and presented as a speech delivered before the Roman people on the day before his departure into exile. The speaker, who identifies himself as M. Tullius, pleads with the citizens to defend the man whose consulship, as he portrays it, rescued them from a conspiracy against the state and from servitude, arguing that gratitude to a public benefactor is owed as a debt and that his own destruction would endanger all who live by virtue. Rhetorically it gathers the recognizable furniture of Ciceronian self-justification: the father-of-his-country motif, the catalogue of services rendered, the contrast between merit and the envy of enemies. Readers tracing parallels will find a compressed quarry of Ciceronian phrases and topoi reworked in a declamatory register, valuable for mapping the afterlife of Ciceronian oratory and the exile theme.
la.claudian.de_bello_gildonico: Claudian's De Bello Gildonico is a late antique Latin panegyric in 526 hexameter lines on the defeat of the African rebel Gildo and the restoration of unity between the twin halves of the Roman world under a single ruler. The opening celebrates a victory so swift that the laurel outruns the news of battle, then turns to an extended supplication in which personified Rome begs Jupiter to end the famine caused by Gildo's seizure of the African grain supply, rehearsing Punic War exempla such as Regulus and Cannae and lamenting the city's reliance on Libyan harvests since the empire's division. The poem repays readers of intertexts through its dense panegyric rhetoric and its allusive recasting of earlier Latin epic diction, offering a compact specimen of late antique praise poetry in the classical hexameter tradition.
la.claudian.panegyricus_dictus_manlio_theod: A late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, celebrating the consulship of Manlius Theodorus. The poem of 360 lines opens with a programmatic address to the poet's Thalia and the allegory of Jupiter's twin eagles sent from east and west to survey the world, before charting Theodorus's judicial and administrative career across Spain, Germany, Britain, Gaul, the Danube lands, and the eastern empire. Its dense mythological exempla, personifications such as Virtus, and classicising diction make it a rewarding point of comparison for readers tracing allusion to earlier Latin verse and the conventions of imperial panegyric.
la.claudianus_mamertus.de_statu_animae: De Statu Animae by Claudianus Mamertus is a late antique Latin prose treatise on the nature and condition of the soul, edited by August Engelbrecht for the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum latinorum (Vienna, 1885). Cast as a reply to a revered priest, the opening portion confronts Arian claims that the begotten Son must be junior to the unbegotten Father, arguing that terms such as 'begotten' and 'unbegotten' signify rather than constitute the divine nature and that what proceeds from another need not be later in time. The discussion then takes up scriptural sayings that attribute anger, hunger, or sorrow to God, reading them as accommodations of divine power and language to human understanding. Readers of intertexts will find in it a compact witness to late antique anti-Arian argument and to the accommodationist interpretation of biblical anthropomorphism current among Latin Christian writers.
la.claudianus_mamertus.epistolae: The Epistolae of Claudianus Mamertus, a Late Antique author writing in prose, survive as a small group of letters edited by August Engelbrecht in the 1885 Vienna volume of the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum latinorum. The correspondence comprises a mock-indignant protest at a correspondent's long silence, with a comic threat of literary revenge, and a florid encomium praising the addressee's treatise on the state of the soul and his hymns, likening him in sweeping catalogues to classical orators and philosophers from Demosthenes and Cicero to Cato and to church fathers from Jerome and Lactantius to Augustine and Ambrose. Readers of intertexts will find in these letters a highly wrought, allusive Latinity, enumerative lists of auctores, and a self-conscious play on the obligations of friendship and literary patronage characteristic of late antique epistolary style.
la.commodianus.instructiones: The Instructiones of Commodianus, a Christian author of the later imperial period writing in Latin, consist of a long series of short theological chapters, preceded in the file by sigla for the manuscripts and early editions and by a list of contents. The chapters attack the classical gods one by one, Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Apollo, Bacchus, Hercules and the rest, then address pagans, judges, the wealthy and Jews, before turning to instruction for catechumens, the faithful, penitents, apostates, infants and soldiers, and closing with chapters on the Antichrist, the day of judgement and the resurrection. The work offers readers of intertexts a compact repertory of classical myth handled polemically and of biblical phrasing in later imperial Christian idiom.
la.couplet_et_alii.confucius_sinarum_philos: A Latin prose work of uncertain date attributed to Couplet and associates, opening with a florid dedicatory epistle to Louis XIV that presents Confucius as the supreme master of moral philosophy and politics among the Chinese and flatters the French king as the ideal ruler whom the sage's doctrine had foretold. The dedicatory speaker, a traveller newly returned from the far shores of China, extols both Confucian teaching and the king's suppression of heresy as kindred triumphs of piety over false doctrine, promising that Confucius himself here stands before the reader in Latin dress. The work is transmitted in three book files totalling some 350 lines. For readers of intertexts it is significant as a channel through which Confucian names, maxims, and the image of Chinese moral and political wisdom entered Latin and, by translation, European vernacular writing.
la.cyprian.ad_quirinum_aut_testimoniorum_li: The Ad Quirinum, also known as the Testimonia, is a late antique Latin theological work in three books attributed to Cyprian, assembled as a manual of scriptural proof-texts drawn from the Old Testament. Its prose preface, addressed to a beloved son and composed at his request, explains that the excerpts were gathered under short headings so that readers might be instructed and strengthened in faith from the divine scriptures. The numbered chapters argue that the Jews fell into idolatry, slew the prophets, and forfeited the law, circumcision, sacrifice, priesthood, and Jerusalem, while a new people drawn from the nations received the new law, baptism, and the promises fulfilled in Christ. Because each claim is supported by runs of biblical quotation attributed to named books, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Judges, Jeremiah, Malachi, Kings, and Esdras, the collection offers a dense witness to how early Latin Christian writers excerpted, attributed, and repurposed scriptural material, making it fruitful ground for tracing biblical lines and their patristic afterlives.
la.cyprian.de_bono_patientiae: De Bono Patientiae is a short late antique Latin prose treatise on patience by Cyprian, presenting the virtue as the foremost of the heavenly disciplines and the mark of those who are philosophers in deed rather than in word. Setting the genuine patience of believers against the false patience professed by pagan philosophers, the work holds up God's own forbearance, which lets the sun rise and the rain fall upon the just and the unjust alike, as the supreme pattern for Christian imitation. Its argument is woven from close quotation and allusion to the gospels and the Pauline epistles, from the Sermon on the Mount to the warnings against worldly wisdom, so the treatise repays attention from readers tracing patristic scriptural reception and the Christian transformation of classical moral vocabulary.
la.cyprian.de_dominica_oratione: Cyprian's De Dominica Oratione is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology expounding the prayer that Christ himself taught, which the author presents as surpassing all other forms of petition because it comes from the mouth of the Son. The work prescribes the inward and modest disposition proper to prayer, citing biblical exempla such as Hannah, the three children in the fiery furnace, and the Pharisee and the publican, before turning to a running commentary on the petitions of the Lord's Prayer, beginning with its communal rather than private character. Dense with direct quotation and allusion to scripture, it offers a rich witness for readers tracing biblical intertexts and early Christian interpretive traditions.
la.cyprian.de_habitu_virginum: Attributed to Cyprian and of uncertain date, the Latin treatise De Habitu Virginum exhorts consecrated virgins to preserve continence in body and appearance alike, warning against adornment, cosmetics, and any desire to please others than Christ. Its argument opens with a meditation on disciplina buttressed by scriptural proofs from the Psalms, the Pauline epistles, and the prophets, before addressing virgins directly as the flower of the ecclesiastical flock and citing the dominical saying on those who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven and the vision of those undefiled who follow the Lamb. For readers hunting textual parallels, the work is valuable for its dense verbatim quotation and reworked biblical formulae, its imagery of the body as temple of God and of the Church as fertile mother, and its place in the lineage of Latin Christian writing on virginity that later ascetic authors echo.
la.cyprian.de_opere_et_eleemosynis: A brief late-antique Latin prose treatise on almsgiving, De Opere et Eleemosynis is ascribed to Cyprian and survives here in Hartel's 1868 Vienna edition. The work argues that works of mercy and almsgiving purge sins committed after baptism, portraying them as a divinely given remedy that complements the single forgiveness granted in baptism, and it supports the claim with a dense chain of scriptural authorities drawn from Isaiah, Daniel, Tobit, the Psalms, Solomon and the Gospel. For readers tracing intertexts, its compact twenty-six lines offer a concentrated example of how an early Christian Latin author stitches together Old and New Testament citations, paraphrases and allusions to build a doctrinal argument.
la.cyprian.de_unitate_ecclesiae_catholicae: De Unitate Ecclesiae Catholicae is a Latin prose treatise on church unity attributed to Cyprian, opening with an exhortation to vigilance against the devil's hidden assaults, which work through heresy and schism rather than open persecution. The argument centres on Christ's commission to Peter ('tu es Petrus') as the origin of the one church and of the single, undivided episcopate, and closes with the figures of the sun's rays, the branches of a tree and streams from one fountain to show unity preserved in its source. Woven throughout with direct and allusive quotation from the Gospels, the Pauline letters and the Song of Songs, the work became a locus classicus for later Latin writing on ecclesiology and offers rich material for tracing patristic biblical idiom.
la.cyprian.de_zelo_et_livore: A brief Latin treatise on zeal and envy (De zelo et livore) by Cyprian, preserved in Hartel's 1868 Vienna edition of his works. Addressed to the 'fratres dilectissimi' in the episcopal style customary of Late Antique Latin theology, it opens by arguing that envy seems a slight and tolerable fault yet works as a hidden perdition, and traces the vice to its origin in the devil, who fell through envy of the first man and thereafter inspired Cain's murder of Abel, Esau's hatred of Jacob, the sale of Joseph, Saul's pursuit of David, and the Jews' blindness before Christ. The closing pages make envy the root of all evils and the fount of hatred, avarice, ambition, pride, and discord, culminating in heresies and schisms born of resentment against bishops and priests. For readers of intertexts the treatise offers dense scriptural tissue, quoting 1 Peter 5:8 and Wisdom 2:24 ('inuidia autem diaboli mors introiuit in orbem terrarum') and retelling the Genesis narratives, and stands as a compact witness to the topos of envy as the first sin and mother of schism.
la.cyprian.quod_idola_dii_non_sint: A short Latin apologetic treatise of Late Antique date, attributed to Cyprian and printed in Hartel's 1868 Vienna edition of his works, arguing that the gods of the pagans were merely deified mortals rather than deities. It assembles a rapid catalogue of classical exempla, Melicertes and Leucothea, the Dioscuri, Aesculapius, Hercules, Apollo, Jupiter's Cretan tomb, Saturn at Latium, and a series of Roman cult figures from Romulus to Febris, to show that temples, sacrifices, and festivals arose from the memory of dead kings, and that Roman dominion rested on fortune rather than religion. The closing section recasts pagan worship as the work of lurking demons who inspire poets, govern oracles, and possess bodies, yet yield to Christian adjuration. Readers tracing intertexts will find it a dense repository of mythological, antiquarian, and philosophical references, Homer, Plato, Socrates' daimonion, Hermes Trismegistus, redeployed in Christian polemic.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_iona: De Iona is a short Latin poem of later Roman imperial date, transmitted under the name of Cyprian (hence pseudo-Cyprian), which versifies the biblical book of Jonah. Its hundred and five lines open with a meditation on the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah and the Dead Sea, then follow the prophet from God's warning to Nineveh through his flight by ship from Joppa toward Tarsos, the storm raised against him, the sailors' prayers and casting of lots, and his confession and surrender to the waves. In retelling scripture in classicizing diction, the poem offers readers of intertexts parallels for late-antique biblical epic conventions, storm-narrative topoi, and the interplay of divine wrath and deferred mercy.
la.cyprian_pseudo.orationes: A short Latin prose collection of prayers transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage as the work of Pseudo-Cyprian, of uncertain date within the later imperial period. The prayers invoke God through an accumulating series of titles and biblical precedents, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the deliverer of Tobias and Sara, of the three youths in the furnace, of Daniel, Susanna and Hezekiah, and of Thecla, asking for purity of heart, forgiveness of sin, and protection from the devil. Their interest for readers of intertexts lies in the dense weave of scriptural allusion, from Tobit, Daniel and Jonah to the penitential idiom of the Psalms, together with liturgical formulas such as the trisagion-like 'hagios, hagios, hagios', which document the circulation of prayer language and exempla of deliverance in early Latin Christianity.
la.cyprian_saint.de_exhortatione_martyrii: De Exhortatione Martyrii is a short Latin prose treatise of theology by Cyprian, written in the Later Imperial period and addressed, as its opening shows, to a brother named Fortunatus. Composed amid the weight of persecutions and the approaching 'time of antichrist', it gathers scriptural precepts under numbered headings as arms and fortifications for the soldiers of Christ, urging steadfastness in confession and framing martyrdom as a second, greater baptism in blood that crowns the virtues where the baptism of water remits sins. Its dense weaving of biblical testimonia, its miles Christi and agonistic imagery of contest, palm, and crown, and its program of arming readers with divine lection make it a rich source of phrases and motifs echoed in later martyrological and ascetic writing.
la.dracontius.orestes: The Orestes of Dracontius is a Late Antique Latin dramatic poem of 973 lines that reworks the tragic cycle of the house of Atreus: the rescue of Iphigenia among the Taurians, the murder of Agamemnon, and the vengeance of Orestes upon his mother and Aegisthus. The prologue summons Melpomene and her tragic buskin while announcing dactylic verse, a deliberate hybrid of tragedy and epic in the manner of late Roman mythological poetry. Readers of intertexts will find dense engagement with the Orestes legend as transmitted through Greek tragedy and through Virgil, Ovid, and Seneca, so the poem serves as a valuable witness to the continuing recasting of classical myth in the Christian era.
la.ennodius.epigrammata: A Latin collection of short poems attributed to Ennodius, a Late Antique author, preserved in roughly 930 lines of uncertain date. The epigrams open in a funerary register with laments for the untimely dead and meditations on mortality, then move through dedicatory and panegyrical pieces, including an address to a Faustus that catalogues moral, natural-historical, and comic material, and poems concerned with church figures and foundations such as Lawrence and Xystus. Readers hunting intertexts will find a dense mingling of classical epigram diction and topoi with Christian themes, in phrasing that later medieval verse repeatedly absorbed.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.de_laude_heremi: De laude heremi is a brief Latin prose treatise by the late-antique author Eucherius of Lyon, preserved among his works in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum edition of 1894. Framed as a letter to a correspondent who had embraced the desert life and later attained episcopal rank, it praises the heremus as God's chosen dwelling and assembles scriptural exempla, Moses at the burning bush, Elijah veiling his face, the Israelites led by the pillar of fire and through the Red Sea, to show that solitude brings the soul closest to God. In only some forty-five lines it models how biblical motifs of the wilderness could be woven into a rhetorical defense of withdrawal, making it a compact witness for readers tracing the literary afterlife of desert imagery and scriptural allusion in later praise of the eremitical life.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.unknown: The opening lines correspond to the Passio Agaunensium martyrum of Eucherius of Lyon, a Late Antique prose martyr narrative, printed here with Eucherius' other treatises in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum edition of 1894. The work recounts how the Theban Legion, six thousand six hundred soldiers summoned from the East, refused Maximian's order to persecute Christians, endured decimation rather than obey, and, encouraged by their leaders Maurice, Exuperius, and Candidus, went to execution at Agaunum in the Alpine valley of the Rhone, whose sacred site Eucherius describes some sixty miles from Geneva. The soldiers' formal address to the emperor, declaring that they owe him military service but God their obedience, and the citation of the gospel precept to render to God what is God's and to Caesar what is Caesar's, give the narrative its doctrinal spine. Readers of intertexts will find here the classic formulation of the Theban Legion legend, with its themes of conscientious refusal, martyrdom freely accepted, and loyalty divided between emperor and God, which circulated widely in later hagiography.
la.eugippius.epistula_ad_probam_virginem: Eugippius's Epistula ad Probam Virginem is the prefatory letter to his late antique florilegium of excerpts from Augustine, compiled at the urging of Abbot Marinus and offered to the virgin Proba. The writer excuses the modest scale of his collection, explains that each chapter carries an indication of the book from which it was taken, and urges readers either to seek out more of Augustine or to refine the excerpts into a better-ordered corpus. He arranges the anthology so that it begins and ends with material on charity, recalling Augustine's subsequent letter to Jerome on the question of the soul and the four virtues hanging from the twofold command of love of God and neighbor. For readers tracing parallels, the letter offers a witness to how Augustinian doctrine circulated through excerpting and a compact web of scriptural quotation, from Solomon's honeyed words to the imagery of feeding the Lord's flock.
la.eugippius.exerpta_ex_operibus_augustini: A Late Antique Latin theological compilation in which Eugippius gathers excerpta from the works of Augustine. The opening item reproduces Augustine's letter to Jerome on the origin of the soul, weighing whether each soul is newly created, rejecting the Stoic claim that all sins are equal, and treating the unity and unequal degrees of the virtues under caritas as the fullness of the law, with James 2:10 as the governing crux. For readers hunting parallels, the anthology presents Augustinian prose in excerpted form, offering a compact locus where discussions of sin, virtue, and charity recur in phrasing readily matched against patristic and later Latin writing.
la.eugippius.vita_sancti_severini: Eugippius' Vita Sancti Severini is a Late Antique Latin prose hagiography recounting the deeds of the holy man Severinus among the Christian communities of the Danube frontier in the troubled aftermath of Attila's death. The narrative moves from Pannonia into Noricum Ripense as Severinus predicts barbarian assaults, relieves famine, secures the release of captives, and urges fasting, almsgiving, and prayer upon towns whose Roman defences are failing, presenting divine protection as the province's last effective guard. Written in unadorned but scripturally saturated prose, the work weaves biblical allusion and established hagiographic topoi, the man of God who foresees disaster, nourishes the hungry, and defeats raiders without arms, into a connected series of miracle episodes and moral exhortations. For readers hunting parallels, it offers a dense field of scriptural diction together with a vivid literary portrayal of a disintegrating Late Antique frontier society.
la.evagrius_monachus.altercatio_legis_inter: A short Latin dialogue in prose, of Late Antique date but transmitted under the name of Evagrius Monachus, framed as a letter to a brother named Valerius reporting a recent dispute. It stages an altercatio legis between Simon, a Jew, and Theophilus, a Christian, in which Simon's objections to Christ's divinity are answered with a chain of proof-texts from Genesis, Deuteronomy, the Psalms and the Prophets, treating the unity of God, Christ's two advents, the Mambre theophany and Christ as the true 'prince of the host'. Its dense and sometimes distinctive scriptural citations reward readers tracing biblical testimonia and the stock arguments of the adversus Iudaeos tradition in late antique Latin apologetic.
la.evodius.de_fide_contra_manicheos: A brief Latin anti-Manichaean treatise of Late Antique date, transmitted under the name of Evodius and printed among Augustine's works in Zycha's 1892 Vienna edition. After a credal opening affirming the one invisible and incomprehensible God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it attacks the Manichaean claim that an unbegotten prince of darkness stands opposed to God, and argues instead that evil is neither nature nor substance but sin freely committed by the rational soul and punished by God's justice. To make the case it cites the apostle Paul on God's unique immortality and on cupidity as the root of all evils, and turns Manichaean authorities against themselves, quoting the acta compiled by Lencius, Mani's Thesaurus, and the Epistula Fundamenti to show that Mani himself conceded that souls sin by their own will. Readers tracing intertexts will find a compact witness to Latin anti-Manichaean polemic and to verbatim Latin excerpts of Manichaean scripture embedded in orthodox argument.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_ratione_fidei: A short Late Antique Latin treatise attributed to Faustus of Riez and cast in question-and-response form, which defends the full divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit against readers who take the Gospel saying 'the Father is greater than I' as implying subordination. Its answers reconcile apparently unequal sayings about Christ by appealing to his two nativities and his twofold divine and human substance, and they uphold Mary's inviolate virginity and the Spirit's godhead almost entirely through strings of biblical testimonia drawn from the Gospels, the Pauline epistles, Isaiah, Job, and the Psalms. For readers hunting intertexts, the work offers a compact witness to the scriptural proof-text method in the defence of the Son's equality with the Father, and to the catechetical responsa genre in Late Antique prose theology.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_spiritu_sancto_libri_: A Late Antique treatise in Latin prose, the De Spiritu Sancto Libri Duo of Faustus of Riez defends the full divinity of the Holy Spirit against the errors of Arius and Macedonius. It opens with a sequence of chapter headings outlining its case, on the creed's confession of the Spirit, on why belief is directed 'in' the Spirit but only with the preposition removed in the catholic church, and on the Spirit's operation in Christ's conception, before proceeding through sustained exegesis of the creed interwoven with scriptural testimony, including a symbolic reading of the 318 priests who condemned Arius and Macedonius. Faustus grounds his argument in the distinction between believing God and believing 'in' God, and in witnesses from Isaiah to Acts to the apostolic preaching of the Trinity. Readers of intertexts will find a dense lattice of biblical citation, creedal formulae, and anti-heretical polemic characteristic of Late Antique trinitarian debate.
la.faustus_of_riez.epistulae: Epistulae of Faustus of Riez, a late antique Latin epistolary work in prose, edited by August Engelbrecht in volume 21 of the Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (1891). The opening item is a letter of fraternal correction in which the author urges an erring brother to hold together the operation of divine grace and the obedience of the baptised, arrays a series of anathemas against Pelagian tenets, such as salvation by human labour alone and the denial that Christ died for all, and closes with a roster of episcopal subscriptions. An appended recantation condemns in turn a catalogue of predestinarian claims, among them that free will perished wholly in Adam, that some are appointed to death, and that the fires of hell do not exist. Its scriptural quotation, anathema formulae, and carefully balanced theology of grace and human effort offer rich material for readers hunting verbal and doctrinal parallels in late antique Latin.
la.favonius.disputatio_de_somnio_scipionis: Disputatio de somnio Scipionis is a short Latin prose treatise on philosophy by Favonius Eulogius, a writer of the Later Imperial period. Addressed to a dedicatee named Superius, it defends Cicero's Somnium Scipionis as sober philosophy rather than fable, replying to Epicurean mockery by showing that the dream teaches the soul's immortality and that Scipio's allotted span of fifty-six years and his dwelling in the Milky Way rest on arithmetic necessity. The work then expounds Pythagorean number symbolism, explaining the monad, dyad, and triad and their operations in god, the world, justice, and the structure of nature. Readers tracing the reception of Cicero's dream in Latin literature will find here a compact witness to its numerological and Neopythagorean interpretation.
la.flavius_josephus.de_iudaeorum_vetustate_: An Early Imperial prose treatise in Latin, transmitted under the title De Iudaeorum Vetustate sive Contra Apionem, in which Flavius Josephus defends the extreme antiquity of the Jewish people against Greek detractors, Apion chief among them. Addressed to Epaphroditus as a companion to the author's books of Antiquities, it contrasts Egyptian, Chaldean, and Phoenician record-keeping with the late origins and mutual contradictions of Greek historiography, and marshals non-Jewish witnesses to the early history of the nation. Readers hunting intertexts will find it useful for its dense catalogue of Greek historians, Hellanicus, Acusilaus, Ephorus, Timaeus, Herodotus, Thucydides, and for its influential ethnographic argument about the reliability of ancient memory.
la.fulcher_of_chartres.historia_hierosolymi: A medieval Latin prose chronicle of the First Crusade and the early Frankish East, the Historia Hierosolymitana covers the years 1095–1127 and is the work of Fulcher of Chartres, a cleric of the expedition who presents himself as an eyewitness of the events he records. Opening with the Council of Clermont, it preserves a full rhetorical version of Pope Urban II's call to crusade and then follows the Franks from their departure through the conquest of Jerusalem to the consolidation of Latin rule in the East. Fulcher writes in a classically colored historiographical manner saturated with biblical language, explicitly comparing the crusaders to the Israelites and the Maccabees and quoting Scripture directly, as in the 'salt of the earth' passage woven into Urban's sermon. Readers tracing intertexts will find the chronicle a rich vein of scriptural echo and typological analogy, presented here in Heinrich Hagenmeyer's 1913 Heidelberg edition.
la.gellius.attic_nights: The Attic Nights (Noctes Atticae) is a Latin prose miscellany by Gellius, a writer of the Later Imperial era, whose preface explains that its materials were collected in whatever order they came, from Greek and Latin books and from anything worth hearing or noting. The title derives from winter nights spent in the land of Attica, and the collection ranges from grammar, dialectic, and geometry to augural, pontifical, and civil law, offering selected 'first fruits' of learning for the civilly educated reader rather than an indiscriminate heap of excerpts. The work is distributed across twenty-one book files in the corpus. For readers hunting intertexts it is a rich storehouse of quotations, anecdotes, and verbal borrowings from authors both Greek and Latin, and its deliberately promiscuous ordering rewards searching book by book for parallels of word and matter.
la.giraldus_floriacensis.carmina: Carmina is a medieval Latin verse work of 754 lines attributed to Giraldus Floriacensis, whose byname points to the monastery of Fleury (Floriacum) on the Loire. The opening section recounts in verse the Lombard devastation of Italy and of Benedict's monastery at Monte Cassino, expressly referring readers to Gregory the Great's Dialogues for fuller details, before turning to the Frankish king Clovis son of Dagobert and Abbot Leodebodus, whose exchange of the royal estate of Floriacus enabled the founding of the abbey there. Blending hagiographic episode drawn from Gregory with an institutional foundation narrative centered on Fleury, the poem offers useful material for readers tracing the reception of the Dialogues and the motifs of monastic foundation poetry in medieval Latin verse.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carmina: The Carmina of Godescalcus Saxus constitute a modest corpus of medieval Latin verse, some 1,068 lines transmitted in two books, by a poet of the Carolingian period. The collection opens with an extended prayer to Christ for pardon, cleansing, and firmness of purpose, composed in rhymed, rhythmical lines whose diction is steeped in biblical and liturgical language. Readers of intertexts will find the poems useful as a witness to the shared vocabulary of Carolingian devotional poetry and hymnody, where scriptural phrasing and rhymed rhythms converge.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_minora: A small gathering of Latin prose fragments attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, the late-antique Gallic bishop and theologian, transmitted through quotation in later sources and printed by Alfred Leonhard Feder in his 1916 Vienna edition of Hilary's works. The excerpts concern the incarnation, including a writing addressed to the emperor Constantius with the paradox that God the Son, made man, remained God, together with comments on the book of Job and the devil's warfare as an occasion of purgation, the petition for daily bread, and passages from the prologue of the commentary on Matthew and from an exposition on the epistle to Timothy. For readers hunting intertexts, the collection preserves Hilary's Christological phrasing in the excerpted form in which later authors encountered it, making it a convenient source for tracing verbal echoes and doctrinal parallels in patristic and medieval citation.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.hymni: A compact Latin collection of hymnic verse transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, the late-antique bishop whose Opera Feder printed at Vienna in 1916; it runs to only 141 lines. The hymns speak in the voice of a congregation at prayer, rehearsing Christ's eternal generation from the Father before the ages, his birth from the Virgin, his agency in creation, and his triumph on the cross. Their blend of Trinitarian doctrine, scriptural allusion (David as the first to proclaim Christ in song), and formulas such as light from light makes them a natural point of comparison for readers tracing Christological hymnody and credal phrasing in late-antique Latin.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.oratio_synodi_sardice: A brief Latin prose address of Late Antique date, attributed to Hilary of Poitiers and printed with his works in Feder's Vienna edition of 1916, though its title presents it as the petition of the council of Sardica to the emperor Constantius. The bishops implore the ruler's clemency on behalf of a church suffering Arian persecution, ask that secular judges desist from trying clerics, and request the recall of exiled bishops, while defending the absolution of Athanasius and naming Ursacius, Valens, and their associates as corrupters of the apostolic rule. Its plea that God accepts no coerced confession and that faith must remain free gives the piece a set-piece on religious liberty characteristic of anti-Arian polemic, and readers of intertexts will find here the recurring vocabulary of episcopal exile, heretical blasphemy, and appeals to imperial clemency.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_super_psalm: A Latin prose work of Late Antique theology, the Tractatus super Psalmos presents Hilary of Poitiers' exegesis of the Psalter, in 1323 lines edited by Anton Zingerle (Vindobonae, 1891). The prologue debates the division of the Psalter into five books, the attribution of individual psalms to David, Solomon, Asaph, Idithun and other named authors, and the claim that the whole book stands as prophecy sealed until Christ, who holds the key of David, opens it through his advent, body, passion, resurrection, kingdom and judgment. Expositions of individual psalms then unfold their allegorical and typological sense for the faithful. For readers of intertexts the work offers a dense lattice of scriptural citation, Acts, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Kings and the Apocalypse are all marshalled in the opening pages alone, and a major witness to how Psalm language and Christological reading circulate in Latin Christian prose.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.libri_tr: A three-book Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology directed against the bishops Valens and Ursacius, written by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, amid the fourth-century Nicene controversy. The surviving material, much of it lacunose and arranged under editorial section dates ranging from 356 to 367, assembles a documentary dossier, synodal acts and letters, imperial correspondence from Constantius, creedal texts including the Nicene symbol, the records of Sardica, Ariminum, and Seleucia, and letters of Bishop Liberius of Rome, joined by narrative passages. For readers tracing intertexts, the work preserves a dense collection of fourth-century creedal and epistolary formulae, some otherwise lost, against which phrasing in contemporary and later authors can be measured.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.spuria: Preserved among the spuria of Hilary of Poitiers and hence of uncertain authorship, the work is a short Late Antique Latin prose piece cast as a letter from an absent father to his daughter. He recounts a journey along long and difficult roads to a surpassingly beautiful youth who possesses a garment and a pearl of inestimable worth, gifts to be granted only to one who renounces silken, gilded, and dyed clothing along with every other pearl. The allegory opposes a heavenly reward, immune to moth, wear, age, and death, to the luxury and adornment of worldly dress, in the idiom of ascetic exhortation. Readers hunting intertexts will find in the peerless pearl and the unwearing robe evident points of contact with gospel parable and with Late Antique ascetic symbolism.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.vita_mariae_aegypt: Vita Mariae Aegyptiacae is a medieval Latin verse life of Mary of Egypt by Hildebert of Lavardin, recounting the penitent harlot's withdrawal to the desert beyond the Jordan. Its opening sections centre on the monk Zosimas, whose ascetic renown is checked by a warning vision and a journey to the monasteries of the Jordan, where he is destined to meet the hidden saint; the narrative then moves on towards their encounter and her confession. Running to some 910 lines, the poem weaves biblical quotation, monastic exhortation and the stock imagery of desert asceticism into hagiographic narrative, offering abundant points of contact for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels across medieval Latin verse.
la.italicus.ilias_latina: The Ilias Latina is an Early Imperial epic in 1,075 hexameters attributed to an author known as Italicus, presenting a compressed Latin version of Homer's Iliad. Its opening ('Iram pande mihi Pelidae, Diua, superbi') recasts the invocation of Achilles' wrath, and the poem proceeds through Apollo's plague, the quarrel of Agamemnon and Achilles, and the subsequent course of the Trojan War in condensed narrative form. Because Homeric matter is rendered in the diction of Roman epic, the poem offers intertextual readers a dense field of Virgilian and post-Virgilian phrasing attached to Iliadic scenes, and a key witness to the reception of Homer in Latin.
la.john_cassian.conlationes: John Cassian's Conlationes, a Late Antique work of Latin prose theology, reports a series of ten conferences held with the foremost fathers of the desert of Scetis, framed as dialogues in which Cassian and his companion Germanus question figures such as Abba Moses on the goal of the monastic life. Presented as the sequel to his Institutio coenobiorum and dedicated here to Pope Leontius and the brother Helladius, the work moves from the external discipline of cenobitic observance toward the interior perfection of unceasing prayer and contemplation. Its dense weave of scriptural allusion, ascetic doctrine, and Egyptian monastic teaching rendered into Latin makes it a rich source for readers tracing verbal echoes and thematic parallels in patristic and later Christian literature.
la.john_cassian.de_incarnatione_domini_cont: John Cassian's De Incarnatione Domini contra Nestorum is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise of theology in 461 lines. Written at the urging of Leo, an ornament of the Roman church, it presents itself as a labour of obedience undertaken after the Collationes, turning from the spiritual instruction of that earlier work to the defence of the incarnation and majesty of the Lord against the newly arisen heresy that the title identifies with the Nestorians. An opening rehearsal of earlier errors from the Ebionites to the Apollinarians frames the refutation, and the fable of the many-headed hydra that regrows with every wound supplies the governing image for the perpetual rebirth of heresy in the churches. Readers of intertexts will find dense scriptural allusion, deliberate classical borrowing from the fables of the poets, and a studied rhetoric of unworthy authorship that shapes the whole argument.
la.john_cassian.institutiones: John Cassian's Institutiones is a Late Antique prose treatise of monastic theology, written at the request of Castor, whom the author addresses as 'beatissime papa', for the guidance of a newly founded monastery in Gaul. It sets out the institutions and rules of the coenobia that Cassian reports having observed in Egypt and Palestine, and announces an account of the eight principal vices together with their origins, causes, and cures, as handed down by the elders. The preface frames the enterprise through the allegory of Solomon's temple built with the help of Hiram of Tyre, and positions the work against earlier treatments by Basil and Jerome, claiming the authority of direct experience over merely heard report. As a Latin witness to Eastern monastic practice and its scriptural typology, the work supplies abundant parallels for readers tracing the transmission of ascetic tradition into the West.
la.lactantius.de_ira_dei: De Ira Dei is a short Latin prose treatise of theology by Lactantius, a Christian apologist of the late antique period, arguing against the philosophical position that God neither benefits nor punishes, and defending divine anger as an aspect of providence alongside divine favor. Addressed to Donatus, it presents itself as a continuation of the author's Divinae Institutiones, recapping that work's treatment of false religions, the one supreme God, and God's legate before refuting those who would strip deity of both anger and grace. The opening opposes revealed doctrine to philosophical conjecture, invoking Socrates' profession of ignorance as Plato reports it, and the argument then proceeds through a systematic partition of the possible views on whether anger, favor, or both may be attributed to God. Its close engagement with classical philosophical commonplaces about divine impassibility, together with its dense allusive style, makes it a productive hunting ground for parallels between late antique apologetic and earlier Greco-Roman literature.
la.lactantius.de_mortibus_persecutorum: De Mortibus Persecutorum is a late-antique Latin prose treatise attributed to Lactantius, addressed to a correspondent named Donatus, and edited by Samuel Brandt in the Vienna corpus of 1897. Its governing argument is that God repays the persecutors of the church with fitting vengeance: beginning with the restoration of peace after a recent persecution, it surveys Christian history from the crucifixion under Tiberius onward and recounts the careers and violent ends of emperors such as Nero, Domitian, Decius, and Valerian. Alongside its moralizing historiography the work offers dense scriptural paraphrase, apocalyptic motifs, and Sibylline allusions, including the legend that Nero will return as forerunner of the Antichrist, making it fertile ground for readers tracing parallels among apologetic, historical, and prophetic traditions.
la.lactantius.de_opificio_dei: De Opificio Dei is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on theology by Lactantius, addressed to a certain Demetrianus whom the author undertakes to instruct in truer and better doctrine. Its 276 lines argue from the functions and uses of the human body, and from the rational soul contained within it, to the providence of the creator God, while warning the addressee against the deceptive sweetness of worldly prosperity and censuring the conduct of the philosophers. The work explicitly takes up a task that Cicero attempted but, by the author's account, left incomplete in De re publica, De legibus, and De natura deorum, quoting the De legibus directly and aspiring to a fuller treatment, with a passing rejection of the Prometheus myth along the way. Readers of intertexts will find it a principal witness to the Christian recasting of Ciceronian physico-theology and to the polemical engagement between Christian and philosophical traditions.
la.lactantius.divinarum_institutionum: The Divinae Institutiones is a seven-book apologetic treatise in Latin prose by the Late Antique Christian author Lactantius, edited here from Samuel Brandt's 1890 Vienna edition of his Opera omnia. Its prologue announces the work's design: to correct the errors of pagan philosophy and supersede the manuals of civil law with 'divine institutions,' directing the learned to true wisdom and the unlearned to true religion, a project the author explicitly grounds in his earlier career teaching oratory. Written in deliberately Ciceronian Latin, the work reworks and answers the classical rhetorical and philosophical tradition it inherited, making it a rich hunting ground for readers of intertexts tracing how Late Antique Christian prose absorbs and repurposes Greco-Roman literary material.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_conven: De Non Conveniendo cum Haereticis is a very short Latin theological polemic of Late Antique date, attributed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, preserved in Wilhelm von Hartel's edition in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (volume 14, 1886). Written in prose, it replies to an adversary who has branded the author and his associates enemies of peace, unity, and fraternal charity, insisting that Christians must refuse communion with heretics. Its argument rests almost entirely on Old Testament exempla: Moses pitching the tabernacle outside the camp, the destruction of Dathan, Abiron, and Core, Mosaic prohibitions of intermarriage and peaceful greeting with idolaters, and the fall of Jericho with the sparing of Rahab. Readers of intertexts may find it valuable as an instance of scriptural typology deployed to justify separation from the Arians, whom it styles pseudo-bishops and spiritual adulterers.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_parcen: De Non Parcendo in Deum Delinquentibus is a brief late antique Latin treatise of polemical theology transmitted under the name of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, edited by Wilhelm von Hartel in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (vol. 14, 1886). Addressed directly to the emperor Constantius, whom it charges with introducing Arian idolatry into the church, the work argues from scriptural exempla, Moses' slaughter of the golden-calf idolaters, Phinehas' zeal, and the Deuteronomic commands against false prophets and kin who entice to other gods, that no mercy is owed to apostates, and it appeals to the continuous faith of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs in the one God and his Son. Dense with quotation from Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and the Gospel of John, and running to only 35 lines, the treatise rewards readers tracing biblical citation practice and the rhetoric of anti-Arian invective in late antique prose.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.epistulae: The Epistulae of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, is a brief Latin collection of letters transmitted under his name and edited by Wilhelm von Hartel in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (1886). The correspondence runs in both directions: Lucifer writes to the bishop Eusebius and to the magister officiorum Florentius, while Liberius, Florentius, and Athanasius address letters to him concerned with the Arian controversy, the exile of confessing bishops under Constantius, and consolation among persecuted clergy. At only nineteen lines, the collection affords a compact Late Antique witness to the epistolary networks of anti-Arian bishops and to the rhetoric of confessorship and ecclesiastical perseverance echoed across patristic prose.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.moriendum_ess: A brief Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology, addressed as a fierce invective to the emperor Constantius, whom it brands an Arian apostate for persecuting those who confess the Son of God. Written by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, and printed in Hartel's edition in the Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (1886), it argues that Christians must be ready to die for their faith, presenting the martyrs slain by the emperor's cruelty as victors who win eternal life in heaven. Constant scriptural quotation and allusion, the Beatitudes, the indwelling of God in his temples, the trial of the just as gold in the furnace, are marshalled around its central theme, that one must die for the Son of God. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a compact treasury of martyrdom commonplaces, biblical tags, and the language of anti-imperial polemic in late fourth-century Latin Christianity.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.ennodius_ambrosio_: A late-antique Latin paraenesis by Magnus Felix Ennodius, addressed to a correspondent named Ambrosius, urging that moral virtue and liberal learning be pursued together. Combining prose exhortation with inset versified speeches, the work stages personified guides, Verecundia, Pudicitia, Fides, Grammatica, and the lordly power of eloquence, who successively commend their gifts, with Grammar and Rhetoric delivering the most substantial declarations. Its diction weaves biblical precept, such as the summons to correct the wise man, into classical topoi of education and oratory, from the 'Tullian' ideal of eloquence to martial figures like Mavors. Readers of intertexts will find it a compact witness to late-antique allegory of the liberal arts and a quarry of formulae circulating between patristic exhortation and secular literary culture.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.libellus_adversus_: A brief Latin prose polemic of thirty-three lines by Magnus Felix Ennodius, a Late Antique author, written against those who had opposed a synod and attacked the Roman pontiff. The libellus opens with an elaborate preface on the duty of speech (tempus tacendi, tempus loquendi) before answering the schismatics' objections in turn: that not all priests were summoned to the council, that accusers of the pope should not be called adversaries, and that the pope ought not to have convoked a synod at all. Its sustained invective is densely laced with scriptural citation and forensic rhetoric, making the work a useful quarry for readers tracing biblical commonplaces and the diction of Late Antique ecclesiastical controversy.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.panegyricus_theodo: A Latin prose panegyric addressed to King Theodoric, composed by Magnus Felix Ennodius in the Late Antique period. After a prologue on the duty of subjects to repay a ruler's benefits with praise, the speech celebrates Theodoric's victories across peoples from Scythia to the tropics, his upbringing in Greece, and his defeat of a usurper and restoration of the sceptre to an exiled prince. As a fully worked example of late antique ruler-praise, it offers abundant material for readers tracing the topoi, diction, and rhythmic prose of the panegyric tradition and its afterlife in medieval encomium.
la.maximianus.elegiae: The Elegiae of Maximianus is a Late Antique Latin composition in elegiac couplets, 686 lines long and of uncertain date, edited by Richard Webster (Princeton, 1900). The poem opens with an aged speaker who begs senectus to hasten his end and release him from the prison of his failing body, cataloguing the gifts of his prime, eloquence, poetic fame, athletic prowess, beauty, endurance and capacity for wine, before the later elegies turn to reminiscence of his amatory career. Old age serves as the lens through which the conventions of Roman love elegy are reworked, with explicit appeal to exemplars such as Socrates and Cato and self-conscious reflection on poetic fiction ('poetarum mendacia dulcia'). Readers hunting parallels will find a dense late-antique summation of elegiac motifs, from the glorification of the lover's body to the lament of the man excluded from desire.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.carminum_appendix: A Carolingian Latin collection of 221 lines attributed to Milo of Saint-Amand, the 'Carminum Appendix' gathers dedicatory and colophon verses, an account of the shrine of Saint Amandus, epitaphs for the abbey's sacristan Lotharius, its abbots, and an epitaph of the poet Milo himself, closing with a rhythmic hymn to the saint. The opening lines record that Lotharius had the book written for the honour and praise of the Lord, and the poems commemorate those who enriched the church's structures, relics, and library. The verses combine inscriptional and funerary forms with scriptural and hagiographic diction in varied patterns of verse. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the conventional formulas of the Carolingian scribe's colophon and tomb poetry, echoes of the Psalms and classical idiom, and hagiographic praise diction characteristic of the Saint-Amand milieu.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.appendix_: A collection of ten documents (decem monumenta veterum) transmitted as an appendix to the seven books of Optatus, bishop of Mileve, against the Donatists, gathering judicial proceedings and official correspondence from the Constantinian era. Its contents include the Gesta apud Zenophilum, the proceedings on the purgation of Bishop Felix (Acta purgationis Felicis), a letter of the Council of Arles to Sylvester, and several letters of Constantine to African officials and to bishops of both the Catholic and Donatist parties. Together these records bear on the origins of the Donatist schism, above all the accusation of traditio, the surrender of the scriptures during the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, with the cases of Silvanus and Felix at their centre. Readers tracing intertexts will find here the documentary matrix behind Optatus's own polemic and the standard points of reference for later African writers on the schism.
la.ovid.amores: Ovid's Amores is a three-book collection of Latin love elegies in elegiac couplets, an Augustan work transmitted here in 2,515 lines. Its opening poems announce that five books have been reduced to three, then stage a comic recusatio in which Cupid steals a foot from the epic couplet the poet was attempting, followed by the lover's capitulation and the triumphal procession of Love. Across the collection the stock materials of Roman elegy, the locked-out lover, the vigilant door, the procuress, the deceitful puella, receive an ironic treatment that at once continues and parodies the conventions of the elegiac tradition. Readers tracing intertexts will find in the Amores a deliberately bookish digest of those conventions and, in turn, a rich quarry of motifs and phrasing for later poetry.
la.paulus_orosius.historiae_adversum_pagano: The Historiae adversum paganos, written in Latin by Paulus Orosius, is a universal history in seven books of prose composed at the request of Augustine, to whom the opening letter is addressed, and it is printed here in Karl Friedrich Wilhelm's Vienna edition of 1882. Arguing against pagans who blamed contemporary calamities on the abandonment of the old gods, it surveys wars, plagues, famines, earthquakes, floods, and other disasters from the creation and the reign of Ninus down to the author's own day, maintaining that suffering under Christ is no greater than before his birth. Its assembly of material from Greek and Roman historians, framed within a providential Christian chronology from Adam to the present, makes it a dense locus of borrowed and reworked material, and it circulated widely as a storehouse of exempla for later writers, so that readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels will find it both a source and a transmission point for classical historiography.
la.petronius.fragmenta: A collection of 374 lines of Latin verse attributed to Petronius, a satirist of the Early Imperial period, composed in a mixture of meters and transmitted as fragments. The pieces include a poem on the vulture gnawing the false poet's breast, an aetiology of the gods born of fear, reflections on the impossibility of keeping court secrets, on the deceptions of sight and taste, and on dreams as self-made visions, together with an elegiac lament for an Indian bird that has exchanged barbarian sounds for Latin speech. Their epigrammatic polish and dense verbal texture make them a recurring point of comparison for readers tracing allusive patterns and verbal parallels across Latin poetry.
la.plautus.aulularia: A Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Titus Maccius Plautus, transmitted in the text of F. Leo's 1895 Berlin edition of the Plautine plays and running to about 847 lines of dramatic verse. The Aulularia opens with a prologue spoken by the Lar familiaris, the household god of Euclio's family, who recounts how a treasure of gold buried in the hearth by an earlier generation has made the miserly Euclio guard it obsessively, even as his daughter, seduced by a young man during the festival of Ceres, is sought in marriage by the wealthy old neighbor Megadorus. Readers hunting parallels will find here the classic plot of hidden treasure and the paranoid old man who hoards it, together with stock comic scenes of abuse, eavesdropping, and household deception that later European drama repeatedly reworked.
la.plautus.captivi: Captivi is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Plautus (T. Maccius Plautus), transmitted in F. Leo's edition of Plauti Comoediae (Berlin, 1895) and running to 1037 lines of dramatic verse. Its prologue outlines the plot: Hegio of Aetolia, with one son stolen in childhood and sold into slavery in Elis and the other captured in the war between the Aetolians and the Eleans, acquires two prisoners whose secret exchange of names and status drives a story of loyalty, deception, and recognition. The speaker pointedly announces that the play contains none of the stock figures of the genre, the perjured pimp, the wicked meretrix, the braggart soldier, and that the battles will be fought off stage. Readers of intertexts will find here a canonical Roman treatment of captivity, mistaken identity, and master-slave exchange, whose relatively serious tone has repeatedly invited echo and adaptation in later drama.
la.plautus.casina: Casina is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Plautus, transmitted in 961 dramatic lines from F. Leo's edition of the Plautine plays (Berlin, Weidmann, 1895). Its prologue, one of the wittiest in Plautine comedy, names the Greek original, Diphilus's Kleroumenoi, known in Latin as Sortientes, and sketches the plot in which a father and son contend for Casina, a foundling exposed sixteen years earlier and raised in their household, while the wife sides with her son against the husband's designs. Metatheatrical banter about old comedies, old wine, and the departed poets, the discussion of servile marriages in Greece, Carthage, and Apulia, and the stock situations of New Comedy refashioned as Plautine farce make the play a natural point of comparison for readers tracing the transmission of Greek drama into Latin and the echoes of Plautus in later comedy.
la.plautus.mercator: The Mercator ('The Merchant') is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republican period, composed in the varied metres of Roman comic drama and preserved in the Leo edition of 1895. Its prologue, spoken in the person of a young lover whose father sent him to trade at Rhodes, catalogues the miseries that attend love and wryly comments on the conventions of comedy itself, while announcing that the play adapts the Greek Emporos of Philemon. The plot turns on the entanglements that arise when both the merchant's son and his father become infatuated with the same purchased slave girl, generating the deceptions and reversals typical of Plautine comedy. Readers tracing intertexts will find the prologue's self-conscious mediation between Greek New Comedy and Roman palliata a particularly rich locus for parallels.
la.plautus.persa: Persa is a Latin comedy attributed to Plautus and belonging to the Roman Republican stage, preserved in an 863-line text printed in F. Leo's edition (Berlin, Weidmann, 1895). The play follows the enslaved Toxilus, who with the parasite Sagaristio's help devises a fraud to raise the money needed to free his courtesan beloved, tricking a wealthy pimp into buying a girl passed off as a Persian captive from whom the title is drawn. Its opening, which ranks the torments of Love above the labours of Hercules before passing into banter between lover, slave, and parasite, displays the stock figures and scheming of Roman comedy at full stretch. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the cunning-servant plot, the satirised parasite, and the commerce in bodies that the Plautine stage transmitted to later European drama.
la.plautus.poenulus: Poenulus ('The Little Carthaginian') is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a dramatist of the Roman Republic, printed in F. Leo's edition (Berlin, 1895) and running to some 1,441 lines of dramatic verse. Its prologue, delivered by the 'imperator histricus', burlesques tragic prologue style and issues mock-edicts regulating lictors, ushers, slaves, nurses and matrons before turning to the plot. Two cousins of Carthage drive the action: one dies, and his only son, stolen at the age of seven and sold at Calydon to a rich old man who wants children but hates women, is adopted and made heir. The sustained parody of tragic and official language, the metatheatrical address to the audience, and the Carthaginian setting give readers tracing dramatic intertexts abundant ground for comparison.
la.plautus.pseudolus: A comedy in dramatic meter from the Roman Republic, the Pseudolus runs to 1355 lines in F. Leo's 1895 edition and announces itself in its opening verse as a 'long Plautine comedy' stepping onto the stage. The plot turns on the crafty slave Pseudolus, who comes to the aid of his lovesick young master Calidorus, found weeping over a letter from the courtesan Phoenicium: the leno has sold her to a Macedonian soldier, whose signet-ring seal must be matched before the deadline of the Dionysia, and the slave schemes to outwit both seller and buyer. Intertext readers will find here a rich vein of New Comedy material, including the servus callidus, the intercepted love letter, and a celebrated scene in which the written characters themselves are made the object of jest ('these letters are looking for children'), motifs that echo throughout Roman comedy and its later imitators.
la.plautus.rudens: The Rudens ('The Rope') is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a dramatist of the Roman Republic, surviving in some 1,428 lines of dramatic verse and printed here from F. Leo's 1895 edition. Its prologue, spoken by the star Arcturus, opens a tale set on the coast of Cyrene: a pimp carries off a kidnapped Athenian girl by sea, but a storm wrecks the ship and washes her and her companion ashore near the villa of the exile Daemones, leading to rescue and recognition. The prologue names the Greek poet Diphilus as the source of the plot. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact assembly of comic stock types, a shipwreck-and-recognition sequence of lasting influence, and meditations on perjury and divine justice that later comedy repeatedly echoes.
la.plautus.trinummus: The Trinummus is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Plautus, printed here from F. Leo's 1895 edition and running to some 1200 lines of dramatic verse. Its prologue, spoken by the personified Luxuria, announces that the play translates the Greek Thensauro of Philemon and takes its title from the three nummi at the center of an intrigue involving a prodigal son, a father's concealed treasure, a staged transfer of the family house, and a friend hired both to chide and to assist him. Reflections on friendship, avarice, and the decay of old-fashioned mores supply some of Plautus's most moralizing passages, and the play's stock characters and devices reward comparison with Greek New Comedy and its Roman and later imitators.
la.pliny_the_elder.naturalis_historia: The Naturalis Historia of Pliny the Elder, an Early Imperial Latin prose encyclopedia, opens with a dedicatory preface addressed to the emperor, in which the author justifies a work on the natural world, rerum natura, 'which is life itself', as worthy of serious letters despite its technical and even barbarous vocabulary. As the preface advertises, the work compiles material drawn from hundreds of earlier volumes and exquisitis auctoribus, deliberately avoiding the digressions, speeches, and marvels that ornament other genres. Its preface alone quotes and discusses Catullus, Cicero, Livy, Varro, Lucilius, and Persius, and the encyclopedia as a whole transmits a vast web of earlier Greek and Roman learning, making it an exceptionally rewarding source for readers tracing intertexts and the reuse of prior authorities.
la.pontius_diaconus.vita_caecilii_cypriani: A Latin prose life of Caecilius Cyprian, the bishop and martyr, attributed to a deacon named Pontius and assigned to the Later Imperial period. The surviving opening preface justifies the undertaking by invoking earlier accounts of the martyrs, then praises Cyprian's rapid progress from conversion to the priesthood, his almsgiving and continence, and the constancy with which he withstood temptation and worldly loss, presenting his passio as an enduring document for posterity. The corpus preserves only a brief opening portion of nineteen lines. Readers hunting parallels may care because the preface dwells on Cyprian's eloquence and prolific writing, and the narrative models his virtues on scriptural exempla such as Job and the Ethiopian eunuch of Acts, inviting comparison with both biblical and Cyprianic diction.
la.priscian.carmen_in_laudem_Anastasii_impe: A Latin panegyric in praise of the emperor Anastasius, attributed to Priscian and of uncertain date within the Late Antique period. In 334 lines across two books the speaker renounces the customary habit of poets who raise emperors to the stars with false claims, promising to speak nothing but the truth, and then celebrates Anastasius's justice, clemency, and victory over the Isaurian tyrants. The poem frames its praise through a catalogue of earlier exempla, from Pompey to Antoninus, Marcus, Nerva, Titus, and Trajan, against whose virtues the reigning emperor is measured. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense allusion to classical panegyric and epic diction, together with the era's characteristic fusion of imperial praise and providential theology.
la.priscillian.tractatus_undecim: The Tractatus Undecim ('Eleven Tractates') is a Latin prose work of late antique theology attributed to Priscillian, edited by Georg Schepps in 1889 together with Orosius's Commonitorium de errore Priscillianistarum et Origenistarum. Cast as a confession of faith addressed to the bishops ('beatissimi sacerdotes'), it responds to slander and accusations of heresy by setting out the author's credal position, cataloguing and anathematizing a long series of heresies (Patripassian, Novatian, Nicolaitan, Manichaean, Ophite, Arian, and others), and defending the allegorical and spiritual interpretation of scriptural animal imagery drawn from Daniel, Job, and the Apocalypse. The author also argues for freedom to expound scripture beyond the four gospels while rejecting any fifth gospel, and defends the continuation of prophecy among believers. For readers of intertexts the work is valuable chiefly for its dense fabric of biblical quotation in Old Latin forms, its use of apocryphal material such as Enoch, and its evidence for how a late antique polemicist assembled and repurposed scriptural parallels.
la.priscillian_bishop_of_avila.canones_in_p: A Latin dogmatic handbook of Late Antiquity by Priscillian, bishop of Avila, framed as a reply to a correspondent who had asked for a compact scriptural weapon against heretics who twist apostolic testimony to their own perverse reading. After the prefatory letter, the work sets out ninety canones, brief doctrinal propositions on such themes as the truthfulness of God, the two spirits, the two wisdoms, and Christ as mediator and foundation of the faith, each supplied with numerical citations locating its supporting passages in the fourteen Pauline epistles from Romans to Hebrews. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it an early witness to the systematic harvesting and numbering of Pauline proof-texts and to the vocabulary of Late Antique doctrinal controversy.
la.proba_active_4th_century.cento: A late antique Latin biblical epic of the fourth century, the Cento of Proba retells sacred history from the creation, fall, and flood through the life, miracles, Passion, and resurrection of Christ, with a dedication to the younger Arcadius and a preface presenting Virgil as a poet transformed to Christian ends. Nearly every line is assembled from Virgil's poems, so that the narrative of creation, Eden, and the Gospels proceeds through recombined Virgilian diction. For readers of intertexts, the work stands as a landmark of cento practice, in which phrases from the Aeneid, Georgics, and Eclogues are redeployed in new doctrinal contexts and almost every clause invites comparison with its source.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_novatianum: A pseudonymous Latin treatise transmitted under Cyprian's name and printed among his works in Hartel's 1871 Vienna edition, of uncertain authorship and later-imperial date, which polemicizes against Novatian and his followers for denying penance and reconciliation to Christians who lapsed under persecution. The author adopts the exhortative voice of a bishop addressing his 'fratres dilectissimi,' casts Novatian as the priest and Levite of the gospel parable who abandoned the wounded traveler, and answers his rigorism with an allegory of Noah's ark in which the raven that never returns figures irremediable apostates while the dove bearing the olive branch prefigures baptism and the church's exclusive saving power. Its dense tissue of scriptural quotation and allusion, Genesis, Isaiah, the gospel of John, the Apocalypse, offers rich material for readers tracking biblical intertexts and Cyprianic diction in later Latin anti-schismatic prose.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_vigilium_de_iudaica_in: Ad Vigilium de Iudaica incredulitate is a brief Latin theological treatise of uncertain date and authorship, transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage and printed among the works assembled in Hartel's Vienna edition of 1871.
