Framed as an exhortation to a certain Vigilius, it denounces the obstinate and inherited unbelief of the Jewish people, who despite prophecy and divine teaching prefer the darkness of the mind to the light of Christ. The argument strings together Gospel sayings, Christ as the light of the world, the lament over Jerusalem, the Magi from the East, Simeon in the temple, with testimonies from the Psalms, Isaiah, and other prophets to show that salvation was offered and wilfully refused. Readers of intertexts will find a dense lattice of scriptural quotation and a further specimen of the pseudo-Cyprianic polemic against the Jews.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_disciplina_et_bono_pud: A short Latin Christian homily or episcopal exhortation on discipline and the good of chastity, transmitted under Cyprian of Carthage's name and printed among his works in Hartel's Vienna edition of 1871, but bearing the spuriously attributed designation Pseudo-Cyprian and of uncertain date within the later imperial period. Cast as a direct address to the faithful, it urges preservation of pudicitia by ranking virginity, continence and marriage, grounding its argument in Pauline teaching on the two-in-one flesh, the headship of the husband and the church as bride of Christ, and celebrating chastity through a catalogic sequence of definitions ('honor corporum, ornamentum morum, sanctitas sexuum'). Readers hunting verbal parallels will find scriptural quotation embedded in cadenced, antithetical prose and a conceptual repertoire of virginity, concordia and spiritual temple that invites comparison with the Latin ascetic treatises of the third and fourth centuries.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_laude_martyrii: De Laude Martyrii is a brief Latin theological treatise of the later Roman Empire, transmitted under Cyprian's name and printed among his works in Hartel's 1871 Vienna edition of the Opera Omnia, though its authorship and date are uncertain. Composed in prose and running to only thirty lines, it opens with an apology for the inadequacy of speech before so great a subject and then sets out to declare what martyrdom is, how great it is, and of what profit it is. The speaker defines martyrdom as the end of sin and the terminus of peril, praises the confessor's immobility under torture, and grounds the whole in Christ's own passion, through which mortal humanity is made immortal. For readers hunting textual parallels its interest lies in its scriptural quotation, its Cyprianic diction, and its place in the wider late antique rhetoric of praise for the martyrs.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_rebaptismate: The De Rebaptismate is a brief Latin prose treatise of the later imperial period, of uncertain date and authorship, transmitted under Cyprian's name and printed among his works in Hartel's Vienna edition of 1871. It takes up the dispute over converts from heresy: whether baptism performed in the name of Christ outside the church is null, so that rebaptism is required, or whether episcopal imposition of hands for the reception of the Holy Spirit suffices. Defending the latter position, the author appeals to the most ancient custom and tradition of the churches, denounces novelty as a source of schism, and gathers scriptural chapters on John the Baptist's baptism in water and the apostles' baptism in the Spirit, especially from Acts. Readers hunting parallels will find a dense weave of biblical phrasing and diction close to genuine Cyprianic prose, a useful witness to the formulae and arguments in circulation on both sides of the rebaptism controversy.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_spectaculis_liber: The De Spectaculis liber is a later-imperial Latin prose treatise against attendance at the theatre, circus and arena, attributed to Cyprian but transmitted among the pseudo-Cyprianic works and printed in Hartel's 1871 Vienna edition of the Cyprianic corpus. Cast as an admonition to the faithful, it argues that idolatry is the mother of all ludi, that every spectacle traces back to sacrifice offered to idols or daemons, and that scripture's silence on the games functions as a prohibition, illustrating its case with instances such as the Christian who carried the eucharist through a brothel on the way to the shows. Its argument and diction overlap so extensively with Tertullian's treatise of the same title that readers hunting textual parallels will find it a prime witness to the afterlife of that work in later imperial Christian moralising.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_xii_abusionibus_saecul: A Latin prose treatise on the twelve 'abuses' that corrupt the world, transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage (hence Pseudo-Cyprian) and of uncertain date, though assigned to the later imperial period. It opens with a compact catalogue of social and ecclesiastical types perverted by the lack of their proper virtue, the wise man without works, the old man without religion, the youth without obedience, the rich man without almsgiving, the woman without chastity, the lord without virtue, the contentious Christian, the proud pauper, the unrighteous king, the negligent bishop, the undisciplined people, the lawless people, and then expands each type into moral exhortation, as in the treatment here of the preacher, the elder, and the youth. The fixed, numbered enumeration of estates and offices lent itself to borrowing and rearrangement in later Latin moral and homiletic writing, making its formulas a productive hunting ground for verbal parallels. The brief excerpt printed here, from Hartel's Vienna edition of the Cyprianic corpus, covers the opening list and the first three abuses.
la.pseudo_cyprian.epistulae: A group of four Latin epistolary pieces transmitted under the name of Cyprian but of uncertain authorship, edited in Hartel's Vienna edition of 1871. Composed in later imperial prose and belonging to the genre of theological correspondence, the letters address the discipline of reading scripture, the rebaptism controversy with its formula 'unus Deus, una fides, unum baptisma', the treatment of traditores who surrendered the sacred books, and a long consolatio to a bereaved father on the death of his daughter, urging hope in the resurrection. For readers of intertexts the collection offers dense citation and adaptation of scripture, including Job, the Gospels, the Psalms and the Pauline epistles, alongside deliberate echoes of Cyprianic diction, and so illustrates how biblical language circulates in pseudonymous early Christian letters.
la.pseudo_cyprian.liber_de_aleatoribus: The Liber de Aleatoribus, a Latin Christian treatise transmitted under Cyprian's name and printed with his works in Hartel's Vienna edition of 1871, belongs to the later imperial period, though its date of composition is uncertain. Written in prose in an episcopal voice, it opens with an exhortation on the duties of bishops as shepherds and stewards of evangelical teaching, stitched together from Pauline and gospel quotations, before turning to a sustained denunciation of the gaming table as a snare of the devil. Catalogues of the gambler's vices, from perjury and discord to squandered patrimonies and nocturnal revels, make the work a witness to Christian moralising on leisure, and its scriptural cento style rewards readers tracing biblical allusion and the circulation of vice catalogues in later Latin prose.
la.pseudo_eucherius.de_situ_hierusolimitana: A very brief late-antique Latin prose treatise in letter form, De situ Hierusolimitanae urbis atque ipsius Iudaeae is transmitted under the name of Eucherius (hence the conventional designation Pseudo-Eucherius) and is addressed to the priest Faustus of the islands. It surveys the topography of Jerusalem and Judaea from a scriptural and pilgrimage standpoint, moving through the Martyrium, Golgotha, and the Anastasis erected under Constantine, Mount Sion with its clerical and monastic dwellings, the ruined Temple, the pool of Bethsaida, and the spring of Siloam, before turning to Bethlehem, Jericho, the Jordan, and the dimensions of the land from Dan to Beersheba. The treatise closes with two lengthy excerpts from Jerome's letter to Dardanus on the land of promise, which the author expressly says he compiled for the work. Its condensed dossier of biblical place-names and holy sites makes it a natural point of comparison for pilgrimage itineraries, Jerome's correspondence, and later descriptions of the Holy Land.
la.pseudo_severus_sulpicius.epistolae_septe: A collection of seven Latin prose letters transmitted under the name of Sulpicius Severus and classed as pseudo-Sulpician, belonging to the Late Antique period and of uncertain date. The letters are moral and ascetic exhortations to steadfastness in the Christian life: the opening epistle, addressed to a woman styled as a sister, urges perseverance through the image of the ploughman who looks back, the armor of the believer against the devil, and the loss of rewards by those who lapse after conversion. A dramatic set-piece on the Last Judgment has the damned protest that no prophet, lawgiver or apostle ever warned them, while Noe, Abraham, Moses, David and Isaias refute them with scriptural exempla. For readers hunting parallels, the work offers a dense fabric of biblical echo and formulaic exhortation characteristic of late antique epistolography.
la.pseudo_tertullian.adversus_omnes_haerese: A brief Latin prose treatise of the later imperial period, transmitted among the works of Tertullian under the title Adversus omnes haereses, though the authorship implied by that attribution is uncertain. It catalogues heresies in rapid succession, moving from Jewish groups such as the Sadducees, Pharisees, and Herodians to Simon Magus, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, Nicolaus, and the Ophite, Cainite, and Sethian sects, compressing each system's cosmology and Christology into a few lines. For readers hunting parallels, its value lies in these dense, formulaic Latin summaries of Gnostic teaching, which preserve phrasing that can be set beside other heresiological catalogues and supply a compact point of comparison for tracing how such dossiers of heresy circulated in early Christian polemic.
la.pseudo_victor_vitensis.passio_septem_mon: The Passio Septem Monachorum is a short Late Antique Latin prose passion (twenty lines) transmitted under the name of Victor of Vita but of uncertain authorship, celebrating seven monks of a monastery in the territory of Capsa in Roman Africa, Bonifatius, Servus, Rusticus, Liberatus, Rogatus, Septimus and the boy Maximus. After a preface asking divine aid for narrating the triumphs of the martyrs, it surveys the persecution of Catholics by the Vandal king Huneric, his edicts of exile and church closure and his drive for Arian rebaptism, then recounts the seven's refusal of rebaptism before the authorities at Carthage and their martyrdom by fire at sea. The monks are styled a new band of Maccabees, and the narrative is dense with scriptural citation and liturgical formula ('unus dominus, una fides, unum baptisma', the Gloria in excelsis), so readers hunting parallels will find here a compact witness to biblical diction, Maccabean martyr typology and the rhetoric of the rebaptism controversy in Late Antique hagiography.
la.q_cicero.on_running_for_consul: A short Latin prose treatise of the Republican era, attributed to Quintus Cicero and cast as a letter of advice on running for the consulship. Across 58 lines it counsels a novus homo candidate on presenting himself at Rome, sets out the support to be secured from publicani, equites, municipia, and noble youth, and rehearses scathing attacks on the rival candidates Antonius and Catilina. Its allusions to Demosthenes, Pompeius, Sulla, and Marius, together with its dense vocabulary of petitioning and patronage, make it a compact repository of Republican campaign language and anecdote for readers hunting parallels.
la.quintilian.institutio_oratoria: The Institutio Oratoria is a Latin prose treatise on rhetorical education and oratory by Quintilian, a writer of the early imperial period, presented here in twelve books. The opening lines supplied, from the final book, enter the treatise's hardest task: defining the perfect orator, whom they frame with Cato's formula of the good man skilled in speaking (vir bonus dicendi peritus) and measure against Cicero, figured as the solitary master on the vast sea of eloquence. Across its full course the work follows the orator's formation from earliest schooling through invention, arrangement, style, and delivery, repeatedly quoting and debating Greek and Roman predecessors. For readers of intertexts it offers dense engagement with Ciceronian idiom, Cato's auctoritas, and the moral vocabulary that later Latin prose absorbed from Roman rhetorical schooling.
la.remigius_of_auxerre.expositione_in_pasch: An early medieval Latin prose commentary by Remigius of Auxerre on the Paschale Carmen of the Christian poet Sedulius, transmitted with the CSEL edition of Sedulius's works. The commentary opens with an account of Sedulius's life drawn from Jerome's catalogue of illustrious men as continued by Paterius, then glosses the text word by word, explaining vocabulary, Greek etymologies, metaphors, and the dedicatory epistle to the priest Macedonius. Its allegorical readings, such as the sea as the depth of the paschal mystery, the small boat as the poet's modest talent, and the anchor as firmness of faith, alongside its explication of biblical allusions like the parable of the talents, record how Sedulius was studied in the medieval schoolroom. Readers tracing the poem's intertexts will find here a repository of interpretive commonplaces and of classical lore, from Campus Martius training to nautical metaphor, mediated through Carolingian exegesis.
la.rufius_festus.breviarium: A compressed Latin summary of Roman history in prose by Rufius Festus, a Late Antique author of uncertain precise date, addressed to an emperor ('gloriosissime princeps') whose joint rule with a brother the prologue invokes. The work organises Roman history under its kings, consuls, and emperors, counting 1,117 years from the founding of the city to the rise of the brothers' shared imperium and running its list of rulers from Augustus down to Jovian. After a chronological skeleton of Roman chronology and territorial growth, it offers a province-by-province account of how Sicily, Africa, Spain, Gaul, Britain, and the eastern lands were acquired, conquered, and currently governed. For readers hunting parallels, its terse, formulaic narratives of conquest invite comparison with the Latin historical epitome tradition, especially Florus and Eutropius and the annalistic material inherited from Livy.
la.ruricius_i_bishop_of_limoges.epistulae: The Epistulae of Ruricius I, bishop of Limoges, form a compact body of late antique Latin correspondence, printed here from August Engelbrecht's 1891 CSEL edition alongside the works of Faustus of Riez. The letters are cast as humble petitions to revered priestly and episcopal correspondents, begging for prayer, correction, and spiritual medicine, and they elaborate their pleas in ornate prose through scriptural figure, notably an extended reading of the parable of the prodigal son, and through classical allusion, from the dove's wings of escape to the speaker transformed from Arion into Orpheus. Readers hunting textual parallels will find a dense weave of epistolary formula, biblical citation, and rhetorical commonplace characteristic of late antique Gallic letter writing, useful for tracing shared diction and themes across the letter collections of the period.
la.sallust.histories: The Histories of Sallust, a Latin prose historiographical work of the Roman Republic, are preserved only in fragments, of which the corpus retains a relatively small portion. The extant lines consist largely of set-piece oratory, opening with a long address to the Roman people denouncing the tyranny of L. Sulla and urging backing for the consul M. Aemilius Lepidus, followed by a speech before the senate. Readers hunting intertexts value the fragments for Sallust's compressed, archaising diction and for his formulations of libertas, dominatio, and civil discord, phrases and topoi that recur throughout later Latin literature.
la.salutati.de_laboribus_herculis: An epistolary Latin treatise of the Renaissance by Salutati, the De Laboribus Herculis opens with a compendious defence of poetry against its detractors, prefaced to an account of what the poets sang concerning the labours of Hercules. The argument rebukes self-styled Aristotelians who scorn the poets their master everywhere cites, contends that Plato banished only the base and comic poets rather than poetry itself, and adduces poets honoured as warriors and counsellors, from Tyrtaeus and Sophocles to Euripides at the Macedonian court. Tracing the origin of the art to the praise of divinity and virtue held in common by gentile and sacred tradition, Salutati maintains that the figurative veiling of divine mysteries in Moses and the prophets is itself poetic speech. Woven densely with quotation from Virgil alongside allusions to Hermes Trismegistus, Augustine and Gellius, the work offers a rich quarry for readers tracing classical and biblical intertexts in humanist apology.
la.salutati.de_tyranno: De Tyranno is a Latin prose epistle of the Renaissance by Coluccio Salutati, chancellor of Florence, addressed to Antonio da Aquila, a student of arts at Padua, and written in answer to his questions about tyranny. Salutati defines the tyrant and distinguishes its kinds, weighs whether it is ever lawful to kill a tyrant, and then argues that Julius Caesar ruled lawfully and was therefore no tyrant, so that his assassins killed him unjustly. The closing sections defend Dante's placement of Brutus and Cassius in the deepest hell and take up whether Antenor and Aeneas were traitors to their homelands. The work serves as a dense gathering point for authorities on tyranny, Caesar's rule, and Dante's infernal punishment of Caesar's killers.
la.salvianus.de_gubernatione_dei: The De Gubernatione Dei of Salvian, presbyter of Massilia (Marseilles), is a prose treatise of Late Antique theology, some 540 lines in extent, which answers the objection that God is careless of human affairs and lets the wicked prosper while the righteous suffer. Its opening marshals testimonia from pagan philosophy and poetry, including Pythagoras, Plato and the Stoics, Cicero, and Virgil's deum namque ire per omnes terrasque tractusque maris caelumque profundum, to show that even writers without revealed religion acknowledged divine providence, before turning to scriptural argument and criticism of those who profane the Christian name. Readers hunting intertexts will find here an explicit late antique repository of classical quotation, in which pagan poets and philosophers are cited, paraphrased, and redirected to a Christian apologetic end.
la.saxo_grammaticus.gesta_danorum: A medieval Latin history of the Danes by Saxo Grammaticus, of uncertain date, composed at the urging of Archbishop Absalon and addressed to King Valdemar. Opening with the geographical situation of Denmark, it recounts Danish deeds from legendary antiquity down to the author's own day in ornate prose punctuated by verse renderings of traditional Danish songs, and its preface names Danish oral tradition, Icelandic antiquarian learning, and Roman historiographical style among its sources. Because its deliberately classical diction fuses the manner of ancient Latin authors with Northern heroic material, it offers abundant ground for readers tracing textual parallels between classical literature and medieval Scandinavian narrative.
la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium_altera: A short Latin dedicatory epistle by the Late Antique Christian poet Sedulius, addressed to the priest Macedonius and transmitted as the prose preface to the Paschale Opus, the prose counterpart of his verse Paschale Carmen. Sedulius explains that, at Macedonius's prompting, he has recast the Paschal poem into rhetoricised prose, defends the doubled edition against prospective critics by citing the multiple recensions of Hermogenianus and Origen, and distinguishes genuine completion from illegitimate alteration. The letter offers a rare ancient rationale for verse-to-prose conversion and for authorial self-revision, making it valuable for readers tracing the relation between the Carmen and the Opus, the mechanics of biblical paraphrase, and Late Christian conventions of preface and dedication.
la.sedulius.hymnus_ii_a_solis_ortus_cardine: A Late Antique Latin Christian hymn by Sedulius, A solis ortus cardine is an alphabetic Nativity poem whose stanzas run from A to Z and rehearse the whole life of Christ, from the annunciation and virgin birth through the adoration of the magi, the massacre of the Innocents, the baptism, and a catalogue of miracles, to the betrayal, crucifixion, and resurrection. The alphabet itself organises the narrative, with each stanza's initial letter advancing the sequence, and the hymn closes by summoning all singers to proclaim Christ's triumph over hell. Its compact letter-by-letter retelling of the Gospel story and its memorable phrasing made it a durable template and quarry for later Latin hymnody and Nativity verse.
la.sedulius.opus_paschale: The Opus Paschale of Sedulius is a late-antique Latin work of Christian poetry in ornate prose, the prose counterpart to his verse Paschale Carmen. Its preface sets the trivial fables of gentile poets against the truth of Scripture, invokes the Davidic psalter, and closes with a prayer for divine guidance before beginning a march through the wonders of salvation history, from creation and Enoch toward the passion and Easter mystery of Christ. Its rhythmical, allusive style and its programmatic opposition of pagan myth to Christian truth offer rich hunting grounds for parallels with classical topoi and biblical phrasing in later Latin literature.
la.seneca.ad_lucilium_epistulae_morales: Seneca's Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales is a collection of prose letters on moral philosophy addressed to his correspondent Lucilius, written in the Early Imperial period and preserved in the corpus as thirteen book files totaling 2,263 lines. Each epistle opens with the salutation 'Seneca Lucilio suo salutem' and closes with 'vale', and the sequence works through Stoic themes such as the right use of time, discriminating reading, the trials of friendship, poverty, and death, often weighing Greek authorities like Epicurus and Theophrastus. For readers of intertexts, the letters serve both as a dense nexus of Seneca's engagement with Greek philosophy and Roman literary tradition and as a formative quarry for later European moral and epistolary writing.
la.seneca.carminum_fragmenta: A tiny corpus of thirty-three lines of lyric verse by Seneca, belonging to the early imperial period and surviving only as disconnected fragments in mixed meters. The pieces are gnomic and Stoic in temper: the opening poem, addressed to a supreme parent and ruler of the lofty heaven, yields the famous sententia 'Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt' on willing submission to fate, while other fragments declaim against the pursuit of wealth and measure it against virtue, honor for parents, and the goods of nature. A handful of stray verses on truth, on profit in dying, and on fine clothing complete the collection. For readers of intertexts, the fragments offer compact comparanda for Stoic commonplaces on fate and riches and for sententious formulations that circulated widely in Greek and Latin moral verse.
la.seneca.de_beneficiis: De Beneficiis is a philosophical treatise in seven books by Seneca, composed in Latin prose of the Early Imperial period and addressed to Liberalis. It sets out how benefits should be given and received, examining ingratitude, the motives and conduct of the giver, the obligations of the recipient, and the position that liberality must never degenerate into a form of lending. The opening book laments that benefits are squandered when given or reclaimed badly, and urges perseverance in generosity even amid widespread ingratitude, since the worth of giving lies in the act itself. Its aphoristic moralizing and accumulation of illustrative cases make it a rich hunting ground for verbal and thematic parallels in later ethical and didactic literature.
la.seneca.de_clementia: The De Clementia is a Latin prose treatise in which Seneca addresses the young emperor Nero, holding up clemency as the virtue that most becomes a ruler who w power of life and death over nations. The opening presents the work as a mirror in which the princeps may see himself, and the argument proceeds to define clemency, distinguish it from cruelty and from indiscriminate pardon, and show how the mind may acquire and confirm it. Written in the early Imperial period, it is a central witness to Stoic political thought and to the mirror-for-princes tradition, and its diction and imagery of rulership offer rich ground for parallels in later panegyric and advice literature as well as in Seneca's own philosophical and tragic corpus.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_marciam: Seneca's De Consolatione ad Marciam is a Latin prose treatise in the consolatory tradition, composed in the early Imperial period and addressed to Marcia, a woman who has spent three years in unrelenting grief for her son. The work praises Marcia's virtue and that of her father, the historian Cremutius Cordus, whose books were saved and restored to public use after his prosecution under Sejanus, and it sets out Stoic arguments for restraining excessive mourning. Its argument rests largely on contrasting exempla: Octavia, sister of Augustus, whose mourning for Marcellus never ended, and Livia, who recovered composure after similar losses. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a dense repertoire of consolatory topoi, exempla, and phrasing that later Latin and early modern consolation literature repeatedly reworked.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_polybium: The Consolatio ad Polybium is a short prose treatise of philosophical consolation from the Early Imperial period, attributed in its edition to L. Annaeus Seneca, in which the author seeks to comfort Polybius on the death of his brother. It opens with a meditation on the mortality of cities, monuments, and even the universe itself, and then deploys the standard consolatory arguments: the equality of fate as a shared human condition, the futility of uncontrolled grief and tears, and an expansive survey of the universal causes of human sorrow. The work is rhetorically elaborate, staging imagined laments and apostrophes to an arbitrary Fortune, with pointed references to Caesar's favour and its limits. For readers tracing intertexts, it offers a dense repository of consolation topoi, sententiae on mortality and impermanence, and phrases that echo across the consolatio tradition.
la.seneca.de_constantia: De Constantia is a Latin prose treatise by Seneca of the early imperial period, addressed to Serenus and arguing on Stoic grounds that the wise person can receive neither injury nor insult. The work opens by ranking the Stoics above other professors of wisdom and then answers Serenus's indignation, occasioned by the mob treatment of Cato, that the sage's apparent exposure to outrage and contempt refutes Stoic claims. Seneca replies with the exempla of Cato, Ulysses, and Hercules and with imagery of adamant and wave-beaten cliffs, showing that the sage's soul stands beyond the reach of any thrown weapon. Readers of intertexts will find here compact formulations of Stoic commonplaces on constancy and invulnerability that echo throughout later moral and literary tradition.
la.seneca.de_ira: De Ira is a prose philosophical treatise on anger by L. Annaeus Seneca of the Early Imperial era, framed as a reply to Novatus' request for advice on how anger may be calmed. Opening with a famous diagnosis of anger as a brief madness, it surveys the passion's bodily symptoms and its public devastations, weighs rival definitions including Aristotle's, and argues that anger, as the enemy of reason, belongs to no animal but man. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it a dense source of loci on the passions, animal imagery, and moral psychology that later ethical and rhetorical writing repeatedly echoes.
la.seneca.de_providentia: De Providentia, a brief Latin philosophical essay in prose by Seneca of the early Imperial period, answers Lucilius's opening question why many evils befall good men if the world is governed by divine providence. Its argument, that hardship is the discipline by which god trains and proves the virtuous, as a stern father toughens a son or a trainer matches his athlete against the strongest opponent, culminates in the exemplum of Cato standing upright amid the collapse of the republic. For readers of intertexts it is a compact source of Stoic commonplaces, from the spectacle of the good man contending with evil fortune to maxims such as 'virtue without an adversary languishes' and 'nothing evil can happen to a good man,' formulations that recur throughout Senecan prose and later moral literature.
la.seneca.de_tranquillitate_animi: De Tranquillitate Animi is a Latin prose philosophical dialogue of the early Roman Empire, in which Serenus confesses to Seneca a restless instability of mind that is neither sickness nor health, and Seneca answers with counsel on how to attain steadiness of soul. The speaker's grievances range from austerity tempted by luxury, to public service, literary ambition, and the pull between otium and civic life, while the reply draws on Stoic authorities named in the exchange such as Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus. A reader of intertexts may value its medical metaphors for disorders of the spirit, its analyses of ambition, wealth, and retirement, and its coinage tranquillitas animi, a phrase and therapeutic model that reverberated through later writing on contentment and melancholy.
la.seneca.de_vita_beata: De Vita Beata is a Latin philosophical treatise in prose by Seneca, written in the Early Imperial period and addressed to his brother Gallio. It argues that the happy life consists in living according to nature, attained through a sound and courageous mind that uses the gifts of fortune without serving them, and it repeatedly opposes such Stoic contentment to the life led by the crowd, where people follow reputation and example rather than reason. Along the way Seneca considers rival definitions of the highest good, defends the freedom of the philosopher to adapt Stoic doctrine, and closes with a portrait of the wise man contented with virtue and contemptuous of pleasure. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a compact statement of Senecan Stoic ethics, with its imagery of error, the herd, and the storm-tossed crowd, that echoes throughout later moral and literary tradition.
la.seneca.hercules_furens: Hercules Furens is a Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period by L. Annaeus Seneca, preserved in the Teubner edition of Rudolf Peiper and Gustav Richter (1921) and running to 1,394 lines of dramatic verse. Opening with Juno's monologue of hatred for Hercules, the play brings on Amphitryon, Megara, the usurper Lycus, Theseus, and a Theban chorus, and dramatizes the hero's return from the underworld and the madness in which he destroys his own wife and children. For readers of intertexts it offers the principal Roman tragic treatment of the Heracles myth, densely mythological in diction, and invites comparison with Greek drama, above all Euripides' Heracles, and with the epic and philosophical traditions on madness, heroism, and apotheosis.
la.seneca.hercules_oetaeus: Hercules Oetaeus, a Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period attributed to Seneca, dramatizes the hero's death on Mount Oeta: supplanted by the captive Iole, Deianira sends the robe steeped in Nessus' blood, and Hercules perishes in agony before his apotheosis. Opening with Hercules' enumeration of his labours and his demand for a place in heaven beside Jupiter, the play runs to 2,039 lines, by far the longest of the tragedies transmitted under Seneca's name, and assigns speaking parts to Iole, Deianira, Alcmene, Hyllus, Lichas, and Philoctetes alongside its lyric choruses. Its reworking of a story known from Sophocles' Trachiniae and Ovid's Metamorphoses makes it a central point of reference for tracing the Hercules legend through Roman tragedy and its later reception.
la.seneca.phaedra: The Phaedra of L. Annaeus Seneca is a Latin drama of the early imperial period, running to 1308 lines in dramatic meters. It retells the myth of Phaedra's destructive passion for her stepson Hippolytus, opening with a chorus of hunters dispatched through the hills, coasts, and plains of Attica in an extended hymn to Diana. Because the legend had already been treated by Euripides and Ovid, the play's diction, scenes, and structural choices offer rich material for readers tracing parallels among classical versions of the story.
la.seneca_the_elder.excerpta_controversiae: The Excerpta Controversiae preserves excerpts from the Controversiae of Seneca the Elder, an early imperial Latin prose compilation of declamatory oratory. The excerpts set out controversiae, fictional legal cases such as a son disinherited for supporting his impoverished uncle, a former captive and prostitute seeking a priesthood, and prosecution under an adultery statute, together with the sententiae, divisiones, and colores delivered by the opposing declaimers. For readers of intertexts, the collection is a rich storehouse of epigrammatic phrasing, rhetorical topoi, and schoolroom themes that circulated through later Latin literature.
la.seneca_the_elder.suasoriae: The Suasoriae form part of Seneca the Elder's collection of the sententiae, divisiones and colores of the orators and rhetoricians, a prose record of declamation compiled in the early Imperial period. The work preserves model deliberative speeches composed on historical themes, opening with the suasoria in which counsellors seek to dissuade Alexander from sailing the Ocean, and records the striking utterances of named declaimers together with the author's critical commentary and anecdotes about rhetorical practice under the principate. A reader hunting textual parallels will find in it a dense storehouse of early Imperial sententiae and topoi, such as the limits of empire and the terrors of Ocean, whose phrasings echo throughout the poetry and prose of the era.
la.servius_honoratus.in_virgilii_georgicon_: A Late Antique prose commentary on Virgil's Georgics, attributed to the grammarian Servius Honoratus and transmitted in four books corresponding to the four books of the poem. Working lemmatically through Virgil's lines, the commentary explains diction, grammar, mythology, astronomy, and agricultural lore, drawing on Hesiod's Works and Days, Varro, Sallust, Terence, Orpheus, and other Greek and Roman authorities, with an opening preface that sets the Georgics against the Aeneid, the Bucolics, and their poetic models. For readers hunting intertexts it serves as a dense repository of verbal parallels, aetiological myths, and learned quotations, as well as evidence for how Virgil was read and glossed in late antiquity.
la.silius_italicus.punica: The Punica of Silius Italicus is an Early Imperial Latin epic in dactylic hexameters, comprising seventeen books and some 12,200 lines, which treats the Second Punic War from Dido's foundation of Carthage and Juno's enduring hatred of the Trojan race down to Hannibal's campaigns in Italy and Rome's narrow deliverance. Its opening invocation and the long scene in which Juno inflames the young Hannibal with ancestral hatred of the Aeneadae, naming the Trebia, Lake Trasimene, Cannae, and the Aufidus, advertise the poem's pervasive recasting of Virgilian diction and of the Aeneid's themes of fate, empire, and Dido's curse. For readers of intertexts, the work offers a dense web of allusion to earlier Latin epic, above all to Virgil, and provides a monumental verse treatment of the war that Roman epic repeatedly returned to as an emblem of national destiny.
la.suetonius.de_vita_caesarum: Suetonius's De Vita Caesarum, a Latin prose work of imperial historiography from the Early Imperial period, is arranged in twelve books of imperial lives, the first and opening one devoted to Julius Caesar. Rather than strict annalistic narrative, each life assembles its subject's ancestry, omens, offices, habits, appearance, and scandals in topical sections, drawing on letters, archives, and anecdotal tradition; the opening account of Caesar's priestly office, defiance of Sulla, early campaigns, and sexual rumors exemplifies the method. The work preserves a vast stock of anecdotes, phrases, and characterizations that later Latin writers echo and reuse. Readers hunting textual parallels will find it a dense source of recurring imperial motifs, from prophetic sayings to patterns of vice and virtue.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_Bassulae_p: A brief late-antique Latin prose letter of Sulpicius Severus, addressed in the salutation to the venerable Bassula as his parent. It opens in a mock-forensic key, indicting Bassula for carrying off every scrap of his writing, no page, booklet, or epistle left at home, and broadcasting even jests dictated in play, before shifting register to recount the holy bishop Martin's final journey to reconcile quarrelling clergy, his exorcism of a flock of rapacious birds, and his austere deathbed self-offering, sealed by the angelic radiance of his body at death. The letter also refers back to an earlier missive on Martin's passing, sent to the deacon Aurelius, and pointedly disclaims the role of sole chronicler of the saint. For readers hunting intertexts it serves both as a companion to the same author's Martinine hagiography and as an early locus for deathbed formulas such as 'si adhuc populo tuo sum necessarius, non recuso laborem' that later ascetic writers echo, while its witty preface offers a rare metaliterary reflection on the leakage and circulation of private correspondence.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_aurelium: A short Late Antique Latin prose letter by Sulpicius Severus, addressed to Aurelius, mourning the death of Martin, bishop of Tours. The writer narrates a dream in which Martin appears to him in radiant form, blesses him, and is borne up to heaven, followed by the priest Clarus, whereupon a messenger arrives from Tours with word that Martin has died; the letter then offers consolation through an extended argument that Martin, though denied a bloody martyrdom, achieved a martyr's crown by ascetic endurance, with pointed allusions to the Hebrew children in the furnace, Isaiah, and the apostle Paul. The letter also refers to a life of Martin the writer had composed, and its blend of epistolary consolation, visionary narrative, and scriptural and classical echoes makes it a key witness to the Martinian hagiographic tradition and a rich hunting ground for readers tracing intertexts.
la.terence.eunuchus: The Eunuchus is a comedy in dramatic verse by Terence, a poet of the Roman Republic, running to some 1,120 lines. It adapts Menander's Greek play of the same name and opens with a prologue in which the poet defends himself against the charge that he stole the parasite and the braggart soldier from Menander's Colax and from an older Latin play linked in the prologue to Naevius and Plautus. The exchange between an aggrieved lover and his adviser, who argues that love admits neither counsel nor measure and that the captive lover must simply be ransomed at the lowest price he can get, supplies some of the most quotable sententiae in Roman comedy. Readers hunting parallels will value its explicit negotiation of Greek-to-Latin adaptation, from the transfer of stock personae to the claim that no saying exists that has not been said before.
la.terence.phormio: Phormio is a Latin comedy by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic, composed in dramatic verse for the stage. Its prologue replies to an older poet's attacks on Terence's manner of writing and announces the Greek original, the Epidicazomenon, whose Latin title derives from the parasite Phormio through whom the action chiefly proceeds. The opening scene introduces Geta, slave in the household of the brothers Chremes and Demipho, whose absent masters leave their sons' affairs of secret marriage and money to set the plot in motion; the play runs to 1,079 lines. Readers hunting textual parallels value the work as a Republican reworking of Greek New Comedy, whose stock figures, the parasite, the clever slave, the deceived senex, invite comparison with Plautine comedy and with Terence's other plays.
la.tertullian.ad_martyres: Ad Martyres is a short Latin prose exhortation by Tertullian, the early Christian writer of Late Antiquity, addressed to the 'blessed martyrs designate' imprisoned and awaiting trial. The work consoles and instructs the confessors in second-person direct address: it urges them to nourish the spirit alongside the body supplied by the church, to preserve concord against diabolical discord, and to reframe imprisonment as separation from a world that is itself the true prison. Its imagery draws on the athletic contest, with God as agonothetes, the Holy Spirit as xystarches, and Christ as epistates, together with military discipline and the Pauline contrast between corruptible and incorruptible crowns. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a dense nexus of scriptural allusion, martyr and athlete motifs, and the prison-as-desert trope that recurs throughout later ascetic and martyrological literature.
la.tertullian.adversus_valentinianos: A late antique Latin prose treatise of anti-heretical theology by Tertullian, edited by Emil Kroymann in the 1906 Vienna volume of his Opera. It opens with an extended satire on the studied secrecy of the Valentinians, likened to the initiatory reticence of the Eleusinian mysteries, and then traces the sect's origins to Valentinus's disappointed ambition for a bishopric and its diffusion through Ptolemaeus, Heracleon, Secundus, Marcus, Theotimus, and the Antiochene Axionicus. Readers hunting intertexts will find it a dense weave of classical and biblical allusion, Eleusis, the towers of Lamiae, Solomon as Sophia, the serpent-and-dove saying, and an early example of Latin polemic that treats esoteric concealment itself as the heretics' defining vice.
la.tertullian.de_carnis_resurrectione: De Carnis Resurrectione is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on theology by Tertullian, defending the resurrection of the flesh against philosophers such as Epicurus, Seneca, Plato and Pythagoras and against heretics including Marcion, Basilides, Valentinus and Apelles. The work presents itself as the third in a sequence following the author's De carne Christi and anti-Marcionite writings, and it argues from scripture, from the common notions of humankind (communes sensus), and from the works of the creator God. Its dense, combative Latin and its sustained negotiation between Christian doctrine and Greek philosophical positions on body, soul and death make it a rich source of intertexts for readers tracing classical and biblical parallels in early Christian argument.
la.tertullian.de_ieiunio_adversus_psychicos: De Ieiunio Adversus Psychicos is a Latin prose treatise on fasting by the Christian theologian Tertullian, transmitted in the Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum and belonging to the Late Antique era of polemical theology. Writing against the 'psychics' who resist the Paraclete and the New Prophecy of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, the author turns from his earlier defense of monogamy to argue that frequent fasts, extended stations, and xerophagies, abstinence from meat, wine, and moist foods, are no human novelty but a remedy for the gluttony by which Adam fell. Scripture is mobilized throughout, from the Day of Atonement in Leviticus and Isaiah's chosen fast to the Gospel sayings on what enters the mouth and the strictures of Galatians, as the treatise answers its opponents' proof-texts while building a case for ascetic rigor. Its dense biblical quotation and combative engagement with rival exegesis make it a rewarding quarry for readers tracing scriptural reception and ascetic discourse in Latin Christian prose.
la.tertullian.de_patientia: De Patientia is a Latin prose treatise on patience attributed to Tertullian, a Christian author of the late antique period, edited here by Emil Kroymann (Vienna, 1906). The work opens with the author's confession that he writes on patience despite being himself wanting in it, then argues that patience belongs to the very nature of God: it appears in the divine forbearance shown to the ungrateful world and, pre-eminently, in Christ's humble life, his submission to baptism and temptation, and his unresisting Passion. Against the philosophers, who honour patience as a human attainment, Tertullian grounds the virtue in heavenly discipline and closes by binding it to the obedience owed to God, on which turn eternal reward or punishment. Readers of intertexts will find dense scriptural allusion, the wounded Malchus, the unquenched flax, the Lamb dumb before the shearers, alongside an early Christian Latin reworking of the philosophical virtue tradition.
la.tertullian.de_spectaculis: De Spectaculis is a Latin theological treatise by Tertullian, a Christian author of the late antique period, which argues that the discipline incumbent on those turning to God requires the renunciation of the public entertainments of the circus, the theatre, the athletic contest, and the gladiatorial show. The work sets out and answers the objections of pagans and of more scrupulous Christians who demand explicit scriptural warrant, maintaining that things instituted good by the creator are perverted to idolatrous and violent use, and that scripture, above all the first Psalm of David, condemns such gatherings implicitly though not by name. Composed in vigorous rhetorical prose, it provides a hostile but detailed witness to Roman spectacle culture and a dense specimen of Christian argument reworking classical moralising commonplaces, making it a productive point of comparison for readers tracing parallels between Latin Christian literature and Greco-Roman tradition.
la.tertullian.de_testimonio_animae: The De Testimonio Animae is a brief Latin theological treatise by Tertullian, a Christian author of the late antique period. It summons the human soul, not the learned soul trained in schools and libraries, but the untutored soul of the street corner and the workshop, as a witness to Christian truth, drawing on ordinary pagan speech and on the admissions of poets and philosophers to confirm the one God, his goodness and judgment, the reality of demons, and the figure of Satan. For readers hunting intertexts, the work offers a dense web of allusion to Greek philosophical traditions, from Epicurean atomism to Chrysippus and the Academy and Porch, and to Greco-Roman cult and common idiom, exemplifying a Christian polemic that turns secular literature and everyday language into evidence for its own claims.
la.thedulf_of_orleans.carmina_appendix: A Latin poem of fifty-two lines attributed to the Carolingian author Theodulf of Orleans and transmitted as an appendix to his Carmina. The verse consists chiefly of first-person riddles in which unnamed speakers, bodiless beings with as many eyes as the heavens hold stars, figures marked by five breasts, six wings, or three faces, invite the reader to identify them, before the closing lines turn to a prayer that the soul be transplanted from earthly to heavenly soil. The combination of enigmatic self-description with devotional conclusion makes the piece relevant to readers tracing the Latin riddle tradition, personification formulas, and the shared motifs of such speaking objects across medieval poetry.
la.theodosius.de_situ_terrae_sanctae: The De Situ Terrae Sanctae is a short Late Antique Latin prose treatise attributed to Theodosius, measuring in Roman miles the distances from Jerusalem and other cities to the holy places of Palestine, from Jericho and the Jordan through Galilee and Samaria to Gaza, Hebron, and the coastal towns. Alongside the itineraries it records the associations of individual sites with patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs, and describes the principal sanctuaries of Jerusalem itself, including Calvary, Golgotha, the Sepulchre, and holy Sion. Compact as it is at some thirty-three lines, it belongs to the pilgrim-itinerary tradition of the Holy Land and preserves topographical formulae, etymologies, and local legends that recur in other descriptions of Palestine, offering a compact witness for readers tracing shared traditions of biblical geography.
la.valerius_maximus.facta_et_dicta_memorabi: Facta et Dicta Memorabilia, a nine-book Latin prose compilation by the early imperial writer Valerius Maximus, gathers memorable deeds and sayings of Romans and foreigners alike, arranged thematically rather than chronologically and prefaced by an invocation of the reigning Caesar as patron. Each chapter assembles exempla, anecdotes of piety, virtue, vice, and fortune, such as the opening book's accounts of priestly discipline and religious observance, distilled from earlier historians and orators into a handbook of moral illustration. For readers of intertexts the work is a central storehouse of Latin exempla: many anecdotes circulating across poetry and prose appear here in condensed, often influential form, so it serves both as a source of commonplaces behind an allusion and as evidence of a later author's own borrowings.
la.vergil_pseudo.catalepton: The Catalepton is a small collection of short Latin lyric poems of the Augustan period, transmitted under the name Pseudo-Vergil, the attribution to Vergil himself being uncertain, and edited by R. Ellis (Oxford, 1907). Its 222 lines gather occasional verse in the Catullan manner: an exchange with a Tucca, an attack on a rhetorician who mangles Greek and Gallic words, a renunciation of rhetoric upon leaving the school of Siro, letters to friends such as Varius, and a greeting to a young victor in his triumph. Its dense verbal play on Catullus and its diction standing close to Vergil's youthful manner make it a fertile source for readers tracing Augustan intertexts.

grc.septuaginta.genesis: The opening book of the Greek Pentateuch, translated from Hebrew in Alexandria in the third century BC and the oldest portion of the Septuagint. It runs from the creation of the world and the flood through the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to the story of Joseph and his brothers in Egypt. This Greek text is the version the New Testament writers quote when they invoke Adam, Abraham, or the promises made to the patriarchs.
grc.septuaginta.exodus: The second book of the Pentateuch, continuing the third-century BC Alexandrian translation of the Torah. It tells of the Israelites' bondage in Egypt, the plagues, the escape through the sea, and the giving of the law at Sinai, then turns to detailed instructions for building the tabernacle. Its Greek vocabulary for covenant, law, and sacrifice became the standard later drawn on by the New Testament and the early Christian writers.
grc.septuaginta.levitikon: The priestly law code at the center of the Pentateuch, covering sacrifice, ritual purity, the priesthood, and the annual festivals, including the Day of Atonement. It is organized as instructions delivered to Moses at Sinai rather than as narrative, and its vocabulary for sacrifice and purity later shaped Christian theological language. Traditionally ascribed to Moses, like the rest of the Pentateuch, and translated into Greek in the third century BC.
grc.septuaginta.arithmoi: The fourth book of the Pentateuch, named in Greek for the two censuses of the Israelite tribes that frame it. It narrates the forty years of wandering in the wilderness after Sinai, including the rebellion of Korah, the crisis at Kadesh, and the story of Balaam and his donkey, before ending with preparations to enter Canaan. Genealogical and legal material is interwoven with the narrative throughout.
grc.septuaginta.deuteronomion: The last book of the Pentateuch, presented as Moses's farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before his death. It restates the law given at Sinai, adds the Shema and other core declarations of Israelite faith, and closes with blessings, curses, and the account of Moses's death. Its Greek phrasing for exclusive devotion to God is quoted directly in the New Testament, including by Jesus in the temptation narrative.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_a: The first of the four Books of Kingdoms in the Septuagint, corresponding to 1 Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. It follows the judge and prophet Samuel, the rise and fall of King Saul, and the young David's anointing, his years as an outlaw, and his friendship with Saul's son Jonathan. The four Kingdoms books together form one continuous history running from Samuel through the fall of the two Israelite monarchies.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_b: The second Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 2 Samuel, narrating David's reign after Saul's death: his consolidation of power, the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, the dynastic promise delivered through the prophet Nathan, and the family disasters that follow his affair with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, including Absalom's revolt. It continues directly from 1 Kingdoms, divided from it for length rather than content.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_g: The third Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 1 Kings, opening with the succession struggle in David's final days and Solomon's accession. It covers Solomon's wisdom, wealth, and construction of the Jerusalem temple, the kingdom's split after his death into Israel and Judah, and the early kings of both, including the prophet Elijah's confrontations with King Ahab and Jezebel.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_d: The fourth and final Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 2 Kings, continuing the parallel histories of Israel and Judah through the ministry of Elisha and other prophets. It narrates the Assyrian conquest of Israel in 722 BC, the reforms and failures of Judah's later kings, and ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
grc.anthologia_graeca: The Palatine Anthology, some four thousand Greek epigrams by several hundred poets spanning the Hellenistic period to the Byzantine era, gathered by Constantinus Cephalas around 900 AD and preserved in a tenth-century manuscript rediscovered at Heidelberg in 1606. Its sixteen books cover epitaphs, dedications, erotic and convivial verse, and epideictic epigrams, and include celebrated short poems like Meleager's welcome to spring (9.363) that were widely read and imitated.
grc.achilles_tatius.leucippe_et_clitophon: The Leucippe and Clitophon of Achilles Tatius, an ancient Greek prose romance of uncertain date, is presented here from Hercher's Teubner edition of the Erotici Scriptores Graeci (1858). After an extended ekphrasis of a painting of Europa at Sidon, the story unfolds as the first-person narration of Clitophon of Tyre, whose love for the Byzantine maiden Leucippe is driven through oracle, elopement, shipwreck, piracy, banditry, and a sequence of apparent deaths and recognitions as far as Egypt. The romance is celebrated for its descriptive brilliance, erotic rhetoric, dreams, and digressions, and its knowing play with the conventions of the ideal Greek novel makes it a fertile hunting ground for verbal and thematic parallels.
grc.acta_joannis.acta_joannis: The Acta Joannis is a Greek apocryphal act of the apostle John, of anonymous authorship and uncertain date, preserved and printed in Bonnet's edition of the Acta Apostolorum Apocrypha (1898). Its opening narrative places John before the emperor Domitian, who has begun a persecution of Christians: the apostle travels from Ephesus to Rome, drinks deadly poison unharmed, raises a condemned criminal from death, and is exiled to Patmos, whence he returns to Ephesus after Nerva's recall of the exiles. The subsequent episodes recount John's miracles in Ephesus, notably the resurrections of Cleopatra and Lycomedes, Lycomedes' painted portrait of the apostle and John's discourse on the true colors that paint the soul, a sermon and healings in the theatre, and the collapse of the altar and temple of Artemis. Readers of intertexts will find here a dense web of motifs shared with the canonical Acts, the other apocryphal acts of the apostles, and Greco-Roman traditions of miracle, martyrdom, and sacred portraiture.
grc.aelian.de_natura_animalium: The De Natura Animalium of Claudius Aelian, presented here in Greek from Rudolf Hercher's Teubner edition of 1864, is a collection in seventeen books of short chapters on the traits, intelligence, and remarkable behaviour of animals. Its prologue argues that creatures lacking reason nonetheless share in virtue, prudence, and affection, and the work assembles anecdotal proof in the form of devoted fish, grieving dolphins, industrious bees, vengeful morays, and other exempla that blend natural history with moralising and marvels. Aelian describes the compilation as a treasury gathered in his accustomed literary style and acknowledges earlier writers on the same themes as predecessors. For readers of intertexts, its set pieces and stock animal lore offer a dense control for tracing motifs and their recombination in later Greek and Latin writing.
grc.aelian.varia_historia: Aelian's Varia Historia is a Greek miscellany of short anecdotes and notices on animal behaviour, human customs, historical episodes, and memorable sayings, compiled from earlier writers. The collection, given here in Rudolf Hercher's Teubner edition of 1866, runs to nearly two thousand lines and opens with accounts of the cunning of octopuses, the weaving of spiders, and the resourcefulness of Egyptian frogs, dogs, and foxes, before proceeding to further stories of animals and men. Aelian names and paraphrases earlier authorities such as Aristotle and preserves versions of many anecdotes otherwise lost, making the work a rich quarry for readers tracing parallels in ancient natural lore and moralising narrative.
grc.aelius_aristides.orationes: A collection of Greek orations attributed to Aelius Aristides, printed from William Dindorf's recension in the two-volume Weidmann edition (Leipzig, 1829). The speeches open with a cycle of prose hymns to the Olympian gods, Zeus, Athena, Poseidon, Dionysus, Heracles, and Asclepius, framed as votive thank-offerings and dream-visions and recounting each deity's birth, dominion, titles, and benefactions to gods and mortals. Recasting the archaic hymnic tradition in elevated rhetorical prose, the hymns are saturated with Homeric and Pindaric diction, Platonic theological language, and mythological exempla, and repay close attention from readers hunting textual parallels.
grc.aeschines.against_ctesiphon: A forensic speech in Attic Greek by the Athenian orator Aeschines, prosecuting Ctesiphon by a graphē paranomōn for proposing a decree that Demosthenes be crowned with a golden wreath for his services to the city. The argument centres on the liability of every public official to audit and examination, and it presses each point by quoting Athenian laws, decrees, oaths and public records verbatim against the defence. As the direct counterpart to Demosthenes' reply On the Crown, the speech forms half of the most celebrated exchange in classical oratory, making it a prime node for tracing parallels in legal diction, civic ideology and personal invective between rival rhetoricians.
grc.aeschines.on_the_embassy: A Greek forensic oration attributed to Aeschines, the Athenian orator and adversary of Demosthenes, delivered in his own defence at his trial on Demosthenes' charge of bribery and misconduct arising from the embassies to Philip II of Macedon and the peace negotiated with him. The speech answers the prosecution point by point, retelling the origins of the peace, the conduct of the second embassy at Philip's court, and earlier Athenian relations with the Macedonian dynasty, while mounting sustained invective against Demosthenes and citing decrees, letters and witness testimony. As the direct rejoinder to Demosthenes' On the False Embassy, covering the same diplomacy from the opposite side, it offers a prime site for intertextual comparison, from mirrored narratives and document citations to Homeric and tragic colouring in its invective.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon: The Agamemnon is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, running to 1,645 lines and opening with the watchman on the palace roof at Argos who sights the beacon fire announcing the fall of Troy. The play follows Agamemnon's homecoming and his murder at the hands of Clytemnestra, and it stands as the first part of a trilogy tracing the curse on the house of Atreus. Its choral odes, gnomic lyric passages, and celebrated episodes, the beacon speech, the carpet scene, Clytemnestra's exultation over the corpse, have made it one of the most heavily echoed works of ancient drama for readers hunting textual parallels.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon_hypothesis: The Agamemnon Hypothesis is a brief ancient argument, or prose summary, transmitted with Aeschylus' tragedy Agamemnon, the first play of the Oresteia, and printed in Herbert Weir Smyth's Loeb edition of 1926. In a handful of lines it recounts the plot, the beacon watched for at Clytemnestra's command, Agamemnon's return with Cassandra, her prophecy of her own death and of Orestes' future matricide, the killing of the king, and the rival claims of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, and then appends the didascalic notice and a list of the dramatis personae. The didascalia places the production in the archonship of Philocles, second year of the 80th Olympiad (458 BC), with Xenocles of Aphidnae as choregus and Aeschylus placed first with the Agamemnon, Choephoroi, Eumenides, and the satyr play Proteus. Readers tracing parallels value the hypothesis for its ancient critical observations, including its praise of Cassandra's silent death and its remark on Aeschylus' distinctive handling of Agamemnon's murder, and for the performance data against which echoes of the play are commonly measured.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides: The Eumenides, the concluding play of Aeschylus' Oresteia, dramatises Orestes' pursuit by the Erinyes after the murder of his mother, his trial before the Areopagus at Athens under Athena's presidency, and the transformation of the vengeful goddesses into the benevolent Eumenides. Opening with the Pythia's prayer and alarm at Delphi, the action moves from Apollo's sanctuary to Athens and closes with a choral performance instituting the cult of the Kindly Ones. Its treatment of justice, civic institutions, and ritual aetiology makes it a recurrent point of comparison for readers tracing legal, theological, and tragic intertexts.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides_hypothesis: A Greek hypothesis, or prose argument, transmitted with the Eumenides attributed to Aeschylus, of uncertain authorship and date. The hypothesis summarizes the drama's action: Orestes, pursued by the Erinyes and directed by Apollo, comes from Delphi to Athens and the sanctuary of Athena, is tried and acquitted through Athena's counsel, and returns to Argos, whereupon the appeased Erinyes are renamed Eumenides; it closes with the critical note that the story is found in neither of two unnamed poets. Such plot summaries are valuable to readers tracing the mythographic tradition of the Orestes legend, the motif of trial before an Athenian court, and the transformation of the Erinyes into benevolent goddesses across classical and later literature.
grc.aeschylus.persians: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, preserved here in Herbert Weir Smyth's 1926 edition, dramatizing the reaction of the Persian court to the defeat of Xerxes' invasion of Greece. The play opens with the chorus of Persian elders appointed by Xerxes to guard his wealthy palaces, who voice anxiety over the king's long absence and name the vast host of commanders he has led from Susa and Ecbatana; it then traces the report of the naval disaster at Salamis, the summoning of Darius' ghost, and the king's dishevelled return. As the only surviving Greek tragedy on a contemporary historical subject, it presents the Greek victory through the eyes of the vanquished, and its epic-style catalogue, funerary lament, and reworking of Homeric language make it a frequent reference point for intertextual comparison.
grc.aeschylus.persians_hypothesis: A brief Greek hypothesis, or prefatory notice, to Aeschylus' Persians, anonymous and of uncertain date, transmitted with the play. It reports the ancient claim preserved by Glaucus that the Persians was modeled on Phrynichus' Phoenissae, contrasts the openings and staging of the two dramas, and places the scene at the tomb of Darius with a chorus of elders in place of Phrynichus' eunuch messenger. It then summarizes the action of Xerxes' expedition against Greece, defeated by land at Plataea and by sea at Salamis, adds the didascalic note that Aeschylus won the tragic competition with Phineus, Persians, Glaucus Potnieus, and Prometheus, and closes by distinguishing Darius' ill-fated advance on Marathon from Xerxes' second invasion. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable chiefly for its ancient testimony to Aeschylus' debt to Phrynichus and for the didascalic information attached to the play.
grc.aeschylus.seven_against_thebes: Seven Against Thebes is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, preserved in Herbert Weir Smyth's Loeb edition of 1926 and running to 1,068 lines. It dramatizes the Argive assault on the city of Cadmus: King Eteocles rallies the Thebans, assigns champions to the seven gates in response to the scout's report of the enemy leaders, and the play ends with the mutual slaughter of Oedipus' sons and the chorus's anguished lament. The long catalogue of shields and their blazons, dense with simile and allusion to the wider Theban and Argive saga, makes the play a central witness to the myth and a key point of comparison for later treatments, from Euripides' Phoenissae to Statius' Thebaid.
grc.aeschylus.suppliant_women: The Suppliant Women (Hiketides) is a Greek tragedy of uncertain date by Aeschylus, preserved in some 1,072 lines in the edition of Herbert Weir Smyth. It opens as the Danaids, daughters of Danaus, land on the Argive coast after fleeing Egypt, invoking Zeus and recounting their descent from Io and their escape from a forced marriage with the sons of Aegyptus. The action centres on their ritual supplication of the king and people of Argos and on the city's deliberation over whether to grant them asylum. Its sustained supplication vocabulary, its handling of the Io myth, and its place in the Danaid legend make it a natural point of comparison for readers tracing asylum, marriage, and pursuit motifs in Greek poetry.
grc.andocides.on_the_mysteries: On the Mysteries is a forensic oration of uncertain date in which Andocides defends himself before an Athenian jury against charges of impiety arising from the profanation of the Mysteries and the mutilation of the Herms. The speech rehearses the series of denunciations brought by informers such as Andromachus, Teucrus, Agariste, and Diocleides, recites the names of the men accused in each, produces witnesses, and rebuts the claim that Andocides informed against his own father. Its dense fabric of personal names, legal formulas, and ritual vocabulary, together with its narrative of political crisis surrounding Alcibiades and the Sicilian expedition, makes it a rich source of parallels for readers of Attic oratory and Athenian civic history.
grc.anonymous.stadiasmus_magni_maris: The Stadiasmus Magni Maris is an anonymous Greek coastal sailing guide, of uncertain date, preserved in Karl Müller's Geographi graeci minores (Paris, 1855). Framed as a letter promising a learned correspondent the most accurate possible periplus of the great sea, its 358 lines record stade distances between successive ports, anchorages, headlands, islands, watering places, and cult sites, beginning at Alexandria and running through the Mediterranean coasts to the Pontus as far as Dioscurias, and onward to the Pillars of Heracles and Gades. Its dense toponymy, notices of harbours, temples, and oracles, and remarks on winds and sailing conditions make it a rich source of parallels for readers tracing place-name traditions, itineraries, and geographical formulae shared with other periploi, itineraries, and poetic accounts of the sea.
grc.apollodorus.library: The Library is a prose compendium of Greek mythology attributed to Apollodorus, printed in Frazer's Loeb edition of 1921, and of uncertain date and authorship. It opens with the rule of Uranus and proceeds genealogically through the castration of Uranus, the Titanomachy, the accession of Zeus, the Gigantomachy and Typhoeus, Prometheus and the flood of Deucalion, to the offspring of Zeus and the descendants of Hellen. Variant versions are flagged throughout with formulas such as 'as some say,' together with occasional appeals to Homer and other poets. Since it condenses the divine and heroic traditions presupposed by epic, lyric, and tragedy, it offers readers hunting intertexts a compact index of mythic material.
grc.apollonius_of_perga.conica: The Conica of Apollonius of Perga is a Greek geometrical treatise of uncertain date, edited by J. L. Heiberg in the second volume of his Teubner Apollonii Pergaei quae graece exstant (Leipzig, 1893). Composed in the proposition-and-proof manner of Euclidean mathematics, the portion preserved here establishes properties of tangents and secants drawn from external points to conic sections and circles, with particular attention to the hyperbola, its asymptotes, and its opposite branches, and repeatedly argues by reductio ad absurdum. For readers hunting intertexts, the excerpt offers dense examples of ancient technical mathematical diction, terms such as ἐφαπτομένη, ἀσύμπτωτος, and ἀντικείμεναι τομαί, and of ratio-based geometric argumentation later authors echo or reuse.
grc.apollonius_rhodius.argonautica: The Argonautica of Apollonius Rhodius is a Greek epic in four books, totalling 5,834 lines, opening with an invocation to Phoebus Apollo. It recounts Pelias' charge to Jason, the building of the Argo under Athena's guidance, and the muster of heroes beginning with Orpheus, then follows the voyage through the Cyanean Rocks toward Colchis in quest of the Golden Fleece, with Medea's passion for Jason at its centre. As the fullest surviving treatment of the Argonautic saga, it offers rich material for readers tracing epic diction, heroic catalogues, and the Jason–Medea story across later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.archimedes.arenarius: The Arenarius or Sand-Reckoner, a short prose treatise in Doric Greek by Archimedes, addressed to King Gelon and written against those who hold the number of grains of sand to be infinite. To carry the argument it devises a nomenclature of orders and periods of numbers reaching far beyond the traditional myriad, and then demonstrates by geometric proof that named numbers can exceed the grains of sand needed to fill a sphere the size of the cosmos, even as enlarged under the hypotheses of Aristarchus of Samos, whose account of an unmoving sun with the earth revolving about it is set out in some detail. Along the way it records assumptions about the earth's circumference, ratios among the diameters of sun, moon, and earth attributed to earlier astronomers including Eudoxus and Archimedes' own father Phidias, and an instrumental measurement of the sun's apparent diameter. For readers of intertexts its chief interest lies in the Aristarchus passage, among the clearest ancient testimonies to heliocentric speculation, and in its dense allusion to earlier mathematical and astronomical writing.
grc.archimedes.de_corporibus_fluitantibus: A Greek mathematical treatise in two books by Archimedes, De Corporibus Fluitantibus sets out the behaviour of solid bodies in fluids as a sequence of postulates, definitions, numbered propositions and proofs. The first book postulates a mechanical model of fluid pressure, shows that the surface of a fluid at rest is spherical with the same centre as the earth, and establishes the laws of buoyancy and flotation, including the result that a body immersed in fluid loses weight equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. The second book determines when segments of a right-angled conoid, floating at any given ratio of weight to fluid, return to the upright or remain inclined, drawing on centres of gravity and conic geometry and referring to Archimedes' mechanical works. Preserved partly in Doric Greek and partly in a Latin rendering, the treatise exemplifies the deductive prose of ancient applied mathematics and supplies the technical vocabulary and formulae of hydrostatics, mechanics and conics for readers tracing parallels in Greek scientific writing.
grc.archimedes.de_lineis_spiralibus: De Lineis Spiralibus (On Spirals) is a Greek geometrical treatise by Archimedes, cast in the form of a letter and opening with a preface that reviews problems once sent to Conon, some since proved and some shown false, before announcing its own subject. The work defines the spiral traced by a point moving uniformly along a straight line that rotates uniformly about a fixed end, then demonstrates the areas swept out in successive turns, the ratio of the spiral's area to the containing circle, and the properties of tangents to the curve, prefacing these with lemmas on ratios, circles, and the squares of lines in arithmetic progression. Composed in the Doric dialect characteristic of Archimedes' mathematical prose, it supplies parallels for the conventions of Greek mathematical prefaces, definitions, and lemma-based argument, and documents the earliest systematic treatment of the curve later known as the Archimedean spiral.
grc.archimedes.de_planorum_aequilibriis: A treatise on statics by Archimedes, the De Planorum Aequilibriis (On the Equilibrium of Planes) derives, from seven postulates on weights suspended from a balance, the law of the lever and the properties of the centre of gravity of plane figures, with propositions on commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes, composite bodies, and the parallelogram. It is written in the Doric dialect characteristic of ancient Greek mathematical prose, with forms such as τᾶς for τῆς, μακέων for the beam of the balance, and σαμεῖον for σημεῖον, which distinguish it sharply from Attic literary Greek. For readers tracing intertexts it offers the canonical formulation of mechanical vocabulary, κέντρον τοῦ βάρεος (centre of gravity), ἰσορροπέω (to balance), ῥέπω (to incline), on which later discussions of the lever and the balance in Greek technical and literary authors draw.
grc.archimedes.problema_bovinum: A short Greek epigram attributed to Archimedes, the Problema Bovinum challenges a 'stranger' to reckon the bulls and cows of Helios in four colours, white, dark, yellow and piebald, grazing in Sicily, and closes with added conditions on square and triangular totals that make the arithmetic famously demanding. The verse presents itself as a problem devised by Archimedes for the mathematicians working at Alexandria and sent in a letter to Eratosthenes of Cyrene, while a prose appendix recaps the solution in archaic numeral notation. Composed in Homericising hexameters, the poem reworks the cattle of the Sun familiar from the Odyssey as a computational exercise and stands as the outstanding instance of mathematics dressed in epic diction. Readers of intertexts will find here a nexus of learned epigram, verse epistle and number problem, bridging poetic form and Hellenistic geometrical enquiry.
grc.archimedes.quadratura_parabolae: A Greek geometrical treatise by Archimedes, edited in the second volume of Mugler's Budé Archimède (Paris, 1971) and running to some fifty-four lines, the Quadratura Parabolae takes the form of a letter to Dositheus that opens by mourning the death of the geometer Conon. It establishes that every segment bounded by a straight line and a section of a right-angled cone, the parabola of the title, is four-thirds of the triangle on the same base and of equal height, first by mechanical balancing arguments on a lever and then by purely geometrical demonstration, with preliminary lemmas drawn from conic elements. For readers of intertexts, the work preserves Archimedes' explicit engagement with the quadrature attempts of earlier geometers, appeals to results from his Mechanics, and the formulaic propositional and reductio style of Greek mathematical prose that later technical writers perpetuate.
grc.aretaeus.curatione_acutorum_morbum: The Curatione acutorum morborum (On the Cure of Acute Diseases) of Aretaeus the Cappadocian is a Greek medical treatise on the treatment of acute illness, composed in prose of markedly Ionic coloring. Aretaeus' own date is uncertain; the opening lines preserved here furnish a sustained clinical portrait of the epileptic fit, tracing its visual aura, flickerings likened to a rainbow in the sky, through the fall, the convulsions compared with those of slaughtered oxen, and the numb, dispirited aftermath. Such close observation and vivid simile earned Aretaeus a lasting place in the ancient medical tradition, and readers of intertexts will find in his wording and imagery a fertile quarry of parallels for later descriptions of disease, seizure, and the body in extremis.
grc.aristophanes.clouds: Clouds (Nephelae) is a Greek comedy by Aristophanes, preserved complete in 1,481 lines and edited by F. W. Hall and W. M. Geldart in the second volume of their Oxford Clarendon edition of 1907. The plot opens with the elderly Strepsiades lying awake over debts run up through his son Pheidippides' passion for horses, and follows his attempt to enrol in the thinking-house of Socrates to master specious argument and evade his creditors, an education that rebounds when the son turns his new skills against his own father. The comedy's caricature of Socrates, its satire of sophistic instruction, and its debate between Just and Unjust Argument made it a touchstone for ancient and later portrayals of philosophy, and its scenes, characters, and phrases supply plentiful parallels for readers tracing intertexts.
grc.aristophanes.ecclesiazusae: Aristophanes' Ecclesiazusae, a Greek comedy of uncertain date running to 1219 lines, is edited by F. W. Hall and W. M. Geldart in their Oxford Clarendon Press edition of 1907. The play opens before daybreak with a woman apostrophising a lamp while the women of Athens, disguised as men, prepare to infiltrate the assembly and vote themselves into power; the plot then follows their rule of the city and the communal regime of property, wives, and daily life that they establish. Readers hunting intertexts will find Aristophanic parody of assembly rhetoric and civic ritual alongside a comic enactment of community of property and wives that invites comparison with Platonic speculation on the same themes.
grc.aristophanes.frogs: Aristophanes' Frogs (Batrachoi) is an Attic comedy of uncertain date, running to 1545 lines in the Hall–Geldart Oxford edition of 1907.
