grc.aelius_theon.progymnasmata: A Greek rhetorical treatise on the preliminary exercises (progymnasmata), attributed to Aelius Theon, a rhetorician of uncertain date, and printed under the title Ars rhetorica in Spengel's Rhetores Graeci (Teubner, 1855). The brief surviving portion is the work's programmatic opening: it argues that the finest ancient orators drew their power from philosophical training, defines and surveys the preparatory exercises, fable, narration, ecphrasis, chreia, prosopopoeia, common topic, comparison, thesis, encomium, paraphrase, and insists on their utility for judicial, deliberative, and epideictic speaking. It is studded with quoted and reworked passages from Homer, Archilochus, Thucydides, Theopompus, Demosthenes, Aeschines, Lysias, and Isocrates, and offers an explicit defence of paraphrase, with celebrated demonstrations of how Homer was recast by Archilochus and Demosthenes reworked himself. Readers of intertexts will therefore find here both direct echoes of classical authors and a contemporary account of the very practice of imitation and rewriting by which such parallels were generated.
grc.aeschines.against_timarchus: A forensic speech in Attic Greek, the Against Timarchus (Kata Timarchou) presents Aeschines' prosecution in an Athenian court at Timarchus' dokimasia, arguing that a dissolute and shameful life debarred a citizen from speaking in the assembly and that the city's laws demand his exclusion. The orator first surveys, with extensive quotation, the statutes of Solon and earlier lawgivers on the supervision of boys, youths, teachers, gymnasia, and choregoi, before turning to Timarchus' own conduct as the direct violation of those enactments. Readers tracing intertexts will find the speech a dense repository of legal formulas, moralising commonplaces, and civic-constitutional argumentation with close affinities in Demosthenic and other Attic oratory.
grc.aeschylus.libation_bearers: Libation Bearers (Choephoroi) is a Greek tragedy in about 1,073 lines by Aeschylus, printed here in Herbert Weir Smyth's two-volume Loeb edition of 1926, and it forms the second play of the Oresteia trilogy. Its action centers on Orestes' secret return from exile: with Pylades he comes upon Electra and a chorus of captive slave women bearing offerings at Agamemnon's tomb, and the drama goes on to stage the vengeance owed for Agamemnon's murder, the deaths of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, and Orestes' final appearance harried by the avenging Furies. Readers hunting textual parallels will find the classic ancient treatments of tomb-side lament and libation ritual, recognition by tokens such as the lock of hair and footprints, prophetic dream omens, and the moral problem of blood-for-blood requital, motifs that resonate with the Electra plays of Sophocles and Euripides and with the later tradition of revenge drama.
grc.aeschylus.prometheus_bound: Prometheus Bound is a Greek tragedy transmitted under the name of Aeschylus and printed here in Herbert Weir Smyth's Loeb edition (1926). The drama opens as Power and Force drive the reluctant Hephaestus to rivet Prometheus to a high crag in Scythia as punishment for stealing fire for mortal kind, after which the chained Titan receives the chorus of Oceanids, Oceanus, Io, and Hermes, contrasting craft and foreknowledge with the harsh supremacy of Zeus. Across its 1095 lines it stages the suffering benefactor of humankind, the harshness of the new ruler, and Io's tormented wanderings, motifs that later poets and dramatists repeatedly reworked. Readers tracing intertexts will find here the canonical articulation of fire theft, prophetic defiance of Zeus, and the alliance of necessity with brute force.
grc.aesop.fabulae: A Greek prose collection of animal fables transmitted under the name of Aesop, the traditional Greek fabulist, and of uncertain date in the form preserved here; the text follows Halm's Teubner edition of the Fabulae Aesopicae Collectae (Leipzig, 1872). Its 736 lines consist of short fable narratives, such as Zeus and the goods, the eagle and the fox, and the eagle and the dung beetle, each typically closed by an epimythion stating the moral, and the same tale often appears in several parallel versions. For readers of intertexts it is a central reservoir of fable plots that saturate ancient oratory, poetry, and moralising literature and that passed into Latin, Byzantine, and later European collections, making it useful for tracing shared motifs such as betrayed friendship, the vengeance of the weak, and the slowness of good fortune.
grc.aesop.αισώπειων_μύθων_συναγωγή: A Greek prose collection of Aesopic fables attributed to Aesop and of uncertain date, transmitted under the title Αισώπειων Μύθων Συναγωγή. Its 965 lines consist of short fables, largely with animal protagonists, the eagle and the fox, the eagle and the dung beetle, the nightingale and the hawk, most of which close with a moralising epimythion introduced by formulae such as ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ or ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ. For readers hunting intertexts the collection is a primary witness to the traditional fable repertoire, whose plots, animal types, and moralising topoi recur across Greek and Latin literature from Hesiod onward.
grc.agatharchides.ex_agatharchidis_de_maris_: Excerpta from the De Mari Erythraeo of Agatharchides, a Greek prose account of the Erythraean Sea printed by Karl Müller in the first volume of the Geographi graeci minores (Didot, Paris 1855). The opening discusses Ptolemy son of Lagus as an organizer of elephant hunts and surveys competing explanations of the sea's name, ranging from the reddening glare of the sun to the genealogy of Erythras, before turning to a long critical survey that rejects the mythological marvels surrounding Perseus, the heroes, and the gods themselves. Alongside its geographical and ethnographic interests, the work preserves a dense inventory of mythical tales drawn from epic and tragic tradition, with explicit reference to Hesiod's ages of man, making it a productive source for mythographic and rationalizing parallels.
grc.alcidamas.ὀδυσσεύς: A short Greek forensic declamation attributed to Alcidamas, giving Odysseus' prosecution of Palamedes for treason before the assembled Greeks at Troy, with the charge supported by a letter supposedly carried on an arrow from Alexander (Paris) that offers Cassandra and reward for betrayal. The speech also digresses into the story of Nauplius, Auge, Heracles and Telephus, retelling material from the Trojan cycle in the manner of classical rhetorical display. Readers of intertexts will find it a prose reworking of the Palamedes myth and a natural parallel to the defence speeches composed within the same tradition.
grc.anacharsis.epistulae: A short collection of Greek letters attributed to Anacharsis, the Scythian sage of Greek tradition, preserved in Rudolf Hercher's Epistolographi Graeci (1873) and of uncertain date and authorship. Composed in Anacharsis' voice and addressed to figures such as the Athenians, Solon, and Croesus, the letters defend barbarian wisdom against Greek mockery of a Scythian's solecisms and attack drunkenness, envy, luxury, tyranny, and hoarded wealth from the standpoint of Scythian frugality. Readers of intertexts may find here formulaic treatments of the Hellene-barbarian contrast, the simple life, and the shipwreck exemplum of the Ister, material that recurs across the wider literary tradition surrounding Anacharsis and Cynic diatribe.
grc.andocides.against_alcibiades: A brief Greek oration attributed to Andocides and of uncertain date, printed in Karl Fuhr's Teubner edition, in which an Athenian speaker facing ostracism alongside Alcibiades and Nicias attacks a law permitting exile without trial and then turns to indict Alcibiades' life. After arguing from the oath of the demos and council against unjudged punishment and from his own repeated acquittals, the speaker catalogues Alcibiades' offences: his doubling of the tribute once assessed by Aristides, his adultery and private violence, and the hatred of the allies that will harm Athens in a future naval war with Sparta. Its treatment of ostracism, the Aristidean assessment, and the rivalry of Alcibiades and Nicias, together with its phrasing on the dangers of public life and the claims of the common good over private interest, makes it a fertile source of parallels for readers tracing themes of exile, demagoguery, and civic judgment across classical prose.
grc.andocides.on_the_peace: An Attic deliberative oration of uncertain date, attributed to Andocides, in which the speaker urges the Athenians to make peace with Sparta rather than continue the war. The speech contends that peace has never brought about the overthrow of the Athenian democracy, marshalling a review of earlier settlements with the Lacedaemonians, the fifty years' peace, the thirty years' peace, and the Peace of Nicias, while distinguishing a mutually agreed peace from the imposed truce that followed Athenian defeat. For readers tracing intertexts, its rehearsal of treaty history offers close parallels to Thucydides' narrative of the Peace of Nicias and to the broader fourth-century debate over empire, naval power, and democratic politics that recurs in Xenophon and the orators.
grc.anonymous.geographiae_expositio_compendi: An anonymous Greek prose compendium of geography, of uncertain date, printed by Karl Müller in the second volume of the Geographi graeci minores (Paris, 1861). The work gives in stades the circumference of the earth, the seventy-thousand-stade length of the inhabited world from the Ganges to the Sacred Promontory of Lusitania beyond the Pillars of Heracles, and the breadth of its habitable band, then divides the oikoumene into Asia, Libya, and Europe by isthmuses and straits. The bulk of the piece is a province-by-province survey of Europe, naming the three Spains, the Gauls, Germany, Italy, Sarmatia, Dacia, Moesia, Macedonia, and Thrace, together with their rivers, seas, and islands as far as Ireland, Britain, Thule, and Scandia. Its inherited measurements and compact ethnographic catalogues make it a useful point of comparison for geographical formulae and place-lists circulating in Greek and Latin literature.
grc.antiphon.speeches: Attic forensic speeches transmitted under the name of Antiphon, of uncertain date, preserved in six book files totaling some 295 lines and printed in Maidment's edition of the Minor Attic Orators. The opening oration is a prosecution for murder in which a young man charges his stepmother with poisoning his father, over the opposition of the half-brothers who now defend her, and argues at length from their refusal to submit their slaves to interrogation under torture (basanos). The collection is composed in the antithetical prose and argument-from-probability style prized in Athenian courts, and its recurring material, household murder, homicide procedure, oaths, and the torture of slaves, makes it a rich source of verbal and thematic parallels for readers of oratory and drama.
grc.antisthenes.αἴας: A short Greek speech attributed to Antisthenes and transmitted under the title Ajax, its date uncertain. Ajax is the speaker, protesting that the contest for the arms of Achilles is being judged by men who took no part in the deeds, denouncing his rival Odysseus as a coward who won repute by a night-time theft of the goddess's image, and demanding that the case be decided by works rather than words. The piece turns the mythical judgment of arms into an argument that virtue is proved by deeds alone, with the eloquent but devious Odysseus cast as its foil. Readers of intertexts will find here a rhetorical reworking of the Ajax-Odysseus rivalry familiar from epic and tragedy, closing on an echo of the Iliadic Ajax as the fighter always posted first, alone, and without the protection of walls.
grc.antisthenes.ὀδυσσεύς: A short Greek prose piece in four units and attributed to Antisthenes, of uncertain date, preserving a single sustained defence speech in which Odysseus answers Ajax's insults in the contest for the arms of Achilles. The speaker argues that intelligence, endurance and cunning rather than brute strength constitute true valour, cataloguing his services to the Greek army, the recovery of the Palladium, night raids, espionage behind Trojan walls, against the mindless ferocity of Ajax, who boasts unbreakable armour and can barely stay awake at his post. The closing prophecy that a wise poet will one day style Odysseus polytlas, polymetis and sacker of cities makes the speech a self-conscious engagement with Homeric diction and with the epic tradition of the arms debate, of obvious interest to readers tracing the reception of the Iliad and Odyssey and the Ajax–Odysseus rivalry.
grc.apollodorus.epitome: The Epitome is a short Greek prose summary transmitted with the mythological compendium known as the Bibliotheca or Library, attributed to Apollodorus and of uncertain date. In 177 lines it runs through heroic myth in rapid, compendious style, frequently recording alternative versions with phrases such as 'some say'; the opening portion narrates Theseus's labours on the road to Athens, his recognition by Aegeus, the Minotaur and Ariadne, Daedalus and Icarus, Minos's death in Sicily, and the tales of the Amazons, Phaedra and Hippolytus. For readers hunting parallels it offers a dense mythographic précis of stories elaborated at length in epic and tragedy, preserving variants and details that make it a standard reference point for tracing ancient allusion.
grc.apollonius_dyscolus.περὶ_ἀντωνυμίας: Περὶ Ἀντωνυμίας (On Pronouns) is a short Greek grammatical treatise by Apollonius Dyscolus, preserved in the Teubner edition of his extant works prepared by Schneider and Uhlig (Grammatici Graeci 2.1, 1878) and running to some 240 lines. The author opens by reviewing rival names and definitions of the pronoun, Aristarchus' 'words conjugated according to person', Dionysodorus' 'paronomasiae', Tyrannion's 'signs', and defends the definition of the pronoun as a part of speech used in place of a noun. He then argues at length against the Stoic and Peripatetic practice of classifying pronouns as articles or 'indefinites', adducing numerous Homeric verses, dialect forms and sound-changes as evidence. For readers of intertexts the treatise offers a dense repository of quoted poetry and of named earlier authorities, Aristarchus, Apollodorus of Athens and Dionysius Thrax among them, whose terminology it both transmits and disputes.
grc.appian.civil_wars: Appian's Civil Wars, a Greek prose history of uncertain date preserved in five books in Mendelssohn's Teubner edition of 1879, narrates Rome's internal conflicts from the earliest quarrels between plebs and senate through the death of Tiberius Gracchus, the dictatorship of Sulla, the struggle between Caesar and Pompey, and the rise of Octavian, who appears under the Greek name Sebastos. The opening survey treats civil discord as a single escalating sequence, from lawful contention to proscriptions, massacre, and dynastic war, naming Coriolanus, Brutus and Cassius, Antony, and Lepidus, and closing with Actium, the taking of Egypt, and Augustus' settlement of hereditary rule. For readers tracing intertexts, the work supplies compact Greek formulations of famous episodes, the plebs' withdrawal to the sacred mount, Gracchan legislation, the decisive battle in Thessaly, that later poets and historians repeatedly rework.
grc.archimedes.ad_eratosthenem_methodus: The Method is transmitted as a Greek letter from Archimedes to Eratosthenes, opening with the claim that mechanical procedures, which balance magnitudes about their centers of gravity, can furnish discoveries in geometry that later receive formal demonstration. It restates the propositions earlier sent to Eratosthenes, among them that a segment of a right-angled cone equals a third of the triangle on the same base and height, sets out the mechanical arguments together with lemmas on centers of gravity, and promises the geometric proofs appended at the end. Its preface assigns the first proof of the cone and pyramid theorems to Eudoxus while crediting Democritus with their unproved statement, and it cites Archimedes' treatise on Conoids, making the work a valuable node for readers tracing links between Archimedes' writings and earlier Greek geometry.
grc.archimedes.fragmenta: A short Greek fragment of twenty-four lines, attributed to Archimedes and printed in Charles Mugler's edition of Archimède, Volume 4 (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1972), preserves an enumeration of the thirteen semiregular solids said to have been discovered by Archimedes. Opening from the five regular figures expounded by Plato, it lists each polyhedron bounded by equilateral and equiangular but dissimilar polygons, octahedron, tetradecahedra, icosahedra, and the rest, specifying its faces, edges, and solid angles, and closes with an account of how individual figures are generated by truncating a pyramid, cube, or octahedron so that designated vertices are cut away. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the mathematical continuation of the Platonic regular solids and a locus for the technical vocabulary of Greek stereometry.
grc.aretaeus.signorum_acutorum_morbum: The Signs of Acute Diseases (De signis acutorum morborum) is a Greek medical treatise belonging to the surviving corpus of Aretaeus the Cappadocian, a physician of uncertain date who wrote in an Ionicising prose; the wording here follows the Greek printed in Francis Adams's edition of 1856. The work catalogues the diagnostic signs of acute conditions: the present section opens with the premonitory aura of epileptic convulsion, from rainbow-like shimmering before the eyes and ringing ears to the fall 'as if struck by a blow', proceeds through a vividly detailed account of the fit itself, and then sets out the signs of tetanic spasms in their three postures (straight, opisthotonos, emprostotonos), their causes in cold, wounds, season, sex and age, and their grim prognosis. For readers hunting intertexts, the treatise offers some of the most striking clinical portraiture in ancient medicine, with symptom vocabulary and phrasing that invite comparison with the Hippocratic corpus and later Greek and Latin medical writers.
grc.aristophanes.acharnians: A Greek comedy by Aristophanes, edited from the manuscripts of Hall and Geldart in their Oxford Comoediae and running to 1188 lines. The play centres on the Athenian farmer Dicaeopolis, who, weary of the long war celebrated and deplored in the opening assembly scene, negotiates a private peace with Sparta while the chorus of Acharnian charcoal-burners pursues him as a traitor. Its satire ranges over politicians, ambassadors and civic ritual, and its action is studded with parodic imitation of tragedy, above all of Euripides, whoseTelephus supplies the beggar disguise for Dicaeopolis' self-defence. For readers of intertexts it is among the richest ancient loci for tragic allusion, comic self-commentary and topical reference in fifth-century Athenian drama.
grc.aristophanes.birds: A comedy by Aristophanes, edited here in Hall and Geldart's Oxford text of 1907, the Birds runs to 1,725 lines and opens with two Athenians wandering in search of Tereus the hoopoe, hoping to find among the birds a refuge from the litigiousness of their native city. The plot builds on the myth of Tereus transformed from man into bird and moves toward the founding of a city in the sky, from which the birds intercept the sacrifices that bind gods and men. The play offers a comic cosmogony, a lengthy catalogue of bird names, sustained parody of tragic diction, and pointed satire of Athenian public life. For readers of intertexts it is a dense repository of mythological allusion, utopian invention, and paratragedy in classical Athenian comedy.
grc.aristophanes.thesmophoriazusae: Thesmophoriazusae is a Greek comedy by Aristophanes, running to some 1,228 lines, in which the women of Athens, assembled for the festival of the Thesmophoria, resolve to punish Euripides for his stage portrayals of them, while the poet counters by sending a kinsman disguised as a woman into their assembly. The opening scenes bring Euripides and his relative to the house of the tragic poet Agathon, whose performance of a hymn in refined lyric is staged in detail, and the play goes on to parody Euripidean tragedy in both diction and scenario, with rescue and recognition scenes in the manner of the Telephus and the Andromeda. The artificial antitheses of the opening dialogue on hearing and sight already signal its sustained comic engagement with tragic and sophistic language. Its dense, identifiable verbal echoes of Euripides and Agathon make it a rich hunting ground for tragic and rhetorical intertexts.
grc.aristotle.categoriae: The Categoriae, or Categories, is a short Greek treatise attributed to Aristotle, printed here from Immanuel Bekker's Aristotelis Opera (Oxford, 1837); its date of composition is uncertain. It opens by distinguishing homonyms, synonyms, and paronyms, then classifies things said without combination and sets out the ten categories, substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, having, acting, and being acted upon, with a sustained discussion of primary and secondary substance and of predication. As one of the foundational works of the ancient logical tradition, it supplied a vocabulary of ousia, accident, and categorial predication that recurs throughout later Greek and Latin philosophical and literary writing, making it a rich source of verbal and conceptual echoes for readers hunting parallels.
grc.aristotle.constitution: The Athenaion Politeia (Constitution of the Athenians), a Greek prose treatise attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date, edited by Kenyon (Oxford, 1920), recounts Athens' constitutional history from the early kings and the synoecism of Ion through the reforms of Draco, Solon, and Cleisthenes, and then sets out the offices and workings of the later democracy, including the nine archons, the Areopagus, the councils, and the courts. As a systematic account of the evolution and machinery of one Greek polis' government, it offers a dense field of political and institutional vocabulary for readers tracing parallels. Its practice of citing authorities, from Homer's ship catalogue in the opening lines to Aristotle himself, makes it a productive witness to how historical and political writing cross-referenced one another.
grc.aristotle.de_anima: Aristotle's De Anima, transmitted here in the Greek text of Bekker's Oxford edition of 1837, is the foundational treatise of ancient philosophical psychology, inquiring into the nature, definition, and faculties of the soul. After surveying the doctrines of predecessors such as Democritus, Anaxagoras, and Empedocles, it develops its characteristic account of the soul as the first actuality of a natural organic body and examines nutrition, sense-perception, imagination, and intellect, asking which psychic activities are inseparable from matter and whether mind alone might survive the body. Its technical vocabulary and arguments, entelechy, hylomorphic definition, phantasia, the distinction between active and receptive intellect, became a reservoir for later ancient, medieval, and Renaissance writers on mind, perception, and affect, making it an indispensable source for intertextual study.
grc.aristotle.de_insomniis: De Insomniis (On Dreams) is a short Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle on the nature of dreaming, printed in Immanuel Bekker's Oxford edition of the Aristotelian Opera (1837). Posing the question whether dreams present themselves to the thinking or to the perceiving faculty of the soul, it argues that a dream is a phantasma, an appearance generated by sense-perception that persists after its object has ceased to act, and illustrates the claim with after-images, the marks left on mirrors by the gaze of menstruating women, and the delusions of the fevered, the fearful, and the desiring. For readers tracing intertexts, the work offers a central ancient account of dreams, imagination, and the fallibility of the senses, on which later philosophical and literary treatments of sleep and appearance could draw.
grc.aristotle.de_iuventute_et_senectute_de_v: A Greek prose treatise by Aristotle, printed by Immanuel Bekker in the Oxford Aristotelian Opera of 1837, opening an inquiry into youth, old age, life, and death that its author declares inseparable from an account of breathing. The surviving opening argues that the nutritive and sensitive faculties of the soul reside in a single central organ, the heart, which serves as the common sensory seat and the first principle of life in blooded animals, in contrast to plants. Along with the neighboring short natural-philosophical works of the Parva Naturalia, it supplied later Greek and Latin authors with their standard physiological doctrines of the heart, vital heat, and the conditions of life and death, and so remains a key point of reference for readers tracing such commonplaces across ancient literature.
grc.aristotle.de_longitudine_et_brevitate_vi: A short Greek treatise transmitted among Aristotle's physical works, printed from the Greek in Immanuel Bekker's 1837 Oxford edition of the Aristotelian corpus. It asks why some animals and plants are long-lived and others short-lived, answering in terms of the quantity and quality of innate moisture, natural heat, bodily size, habitat, climate, and the balance of elemental contraries, and proceeds by aporia and solution in the Peripatetic manner. Its opening points back to a prior treatment of sleep and waking and forward to fuller accounts of life, death, disease, and health, placing the work within the sequence of Aristotle's shorter inquiries into living nature. Readers hunting parallels will find compact statements of doctrines on ageing, the moist and the dry, and the dependence of soul on body that recur throughout Aristotelian biology and natural philosophy.
grc.aristotle.de_partibus_animalium: A Greek prose treatise in four books attributed to Aristotle, transmitted here in Bernhard Langkavel's Teubner edition (Leipzig, 1868). It opens with a methodological prologue on how the study of nature should proceed, insisting on the priority of final causation over material necessity and criticising Empedoclean explanations of animal structure as products of chance, before turning to the causes and functions of the parts of animals. Its arguments, formulas of teleological explanation, and vocabulary of cause, form, and generation recur throughout Aristotle's biological and physical writings and were echoed by later ancient scientific and philosophical authors. For readers tracing intertexts, it supplies some of the classic Greek statements on the relation between necessity and purpose, on generation ('man begets man'), and on the contrast between art and nature.
grc.aristotle.de_sensu_et_sensibilibus: The De Sensu et Sensibilibus is a Greek treatise by Aristotle, presented here in Immanuel Bekker's edition of the Aristotelian Opera (Oxford, 1837). Continuing directly from the De Anima, it takes up the affections shared by soul and body, sensation, memory, waking and sleep, youth and age, respiration, life and death, and goes on to examine the several senses, their objects and organs, and the medium through which sight operates. Throughout, Aristotle tests earlier accounts of perception against his own, quoting and criticizing Empedocles, Democritus, and the Timaeus of Plato. For readers hunting intertexts, the work offers a dense witness to Presocratic and Platonic doctrines of sense and to the Peripatetic response to them.
grc.aristotle.de_somno_et_vigilia: De Somno et Vigilia (On Sleep and Waking) is a short Greek treatise by Aristotle, printed in Bekker's 1837 Oxford edition of his works. It asks what sleep and waking are, whether they belong to the soul or the body or both, why all animals with perception but no plants share them, and what dreams are and whether they can foretell the future. The argument defines sleep as a privation or binding of the primary organ of perception, locates its cause in processes of cooling around the heart, and defers fuller treatment of dreams to a later discussion. Readers tracing intertexts will find here a hub for ancient psychology and physiology, with explicit cross-references to the De Anima and standing behind later reflection on sleep, dreams, and divination.
grc.aristotle.eudemian_ethics: Aristotle's Eudemian Ethics, presented here in F. Susemihl's Teubner edition of 1884, is a Greek ethical treatise whose opening argues that a life must be ordered toward a chosen mark of the noble and surveys the rival claims of virtue, practical wisdom, and pleasure to constitute happiness. The discussion opens by quoting the maxim that a certain wise man wrote up at the gateway of the temple of Leto on Delos, dividing the good, the beautiful, and the pleasant, and then asks whether the happy life arises by nature, teaching, habituation, divine inspiration, or luck. The treatise distinguishes the vulgar and commercial trades from the lives of politics, philosophy, and enjoyment, insisting that one must first settle what living well consists in and what it cannot do without. Readers hunting intertexts will find value in the echoed Delian inscription, the dialectical inventory of earlier views on eudaimonia, and the verbal overlap with the Nicomachean Ethics.
grc.aristotle.fragmenta_deperditae_partis_pr: Fragments of the lost first part of the Constitution of the Athenians attributed to Aristotle, preserved in the Kenyon edition of the Aristotelis Res Publica Atheniensium (Berlin, 1903) and surviving only as quotations in lexicographers, scholiasts, and biographers. The twelve lines assembled here carry the Aristotelian account of earliest Athenian history: Ion's synoecism and the naming of the Ionians, Theseus' appeal to civic equality and his division of the citizen body into eupatridae, geomoroi, and demiourgoi, and the pre-Cleisthenic four-tribe system with its trittyes, phratries, and gene. Because the fragments are embedded in sources such as Harpocration, Plutarch's Theseus, and the scholia to Plato, they offer readers of intertexts verbatim Aristotelian phrasing against which to measure parallel traditions of Athenian antiquarian writing.
grc.aristotle.poetics: Aristotle's Greek treatise on poetry, edited by R. Kassel, opens by defining the poetic arts as forms of imitation distinguished by medium, object, and manner, and surveys epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyramb, and related musical forms. It traces the natural origins of poetry in the human instinct for imitation and rhythm, credits Homer with the first dramatic depiction of serious and comic action, and proceeds to analyze the elements and construction of tragedy, including plot, character, recognition, and reversal. For readers of intertexts, the work supplies the ancient critical vocabulary of mimesis and tragic form that later poets, commentators, and theorists invoke and debate throughout Western literary history.
grc.aristotle.topica: The Topica, a treatise by Aristotle transmitted in the Bekker edition of the Aristotelian Opera (Oxford, 1837), sets out a method for finding dialectical syllogisms, arguments that proceed from generally accepted opinions (endoxa) rather than from true and primary premises, and distinguishes them from demonstration and eristic reasoning. It defines the four predicables of definition, property, genus, and accident, and organizes lines of argument for reasoning about each, claiming utility for intellectual exercise, everyday encounters, and inquiry into the first principles of the philosophical sciences. For readers of intertexts, the work is a foundational inventory of dialectical argumentation, repeatedly quarried by later writers on rhetoric, logic, and disputation for its account of commonplaces and its model of reasoning from reputable opinion.
grc.aristotle.μηχανικά: The Μηχανικά (Mechanics) is a short Greek treatise attributed to Aristotle and transmitted within the Aristotelian corpus, of uncertain date. Its prologue defines mechanics as the branch of art (τέχνη) that aids human purposes where nature falls short, tracing all mechanical wonders back to the paradoxical properties of the circle, before proceeding through a series of mechanical problems on the balance, the lever, and the movements of wheels and other devices. Because it sets mathematical and physical explanation side by side, quotes the poet Antiphon on art mastering nature, and frames each puzzle as a problem demanding its cause, it offers fruitful ground for readers tracing shared phrases, topoi, and arguments across Greek philosophical and technical writing.
grc.aristoxenus.elementa_harmonica: Aristoxenus' Elementa harmonica, preserved in Greek and printed in Macran's Clarendon edition of 1902, is the foundational treatise of ancient harmonics, the branch of the science of melody that concerns itself with tones, intervals, and systems of notes. The work sets out the scope and proper order of the inquiry, the movement of the voice, the definition of interval and system, the continuous and the composite, and the division of melody into the enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic genera, while polemicising against earlier harmonikoi such as Eratocles and Lasos, who confined themselves to the enharmonic genus and argued without demonstration. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the technical vocabulary of tetrachords, genera, and melodic ordering on which Greek authors, and their later imitators, draw whenever they speak of the structure of music.
grc.arrian.anabasis: Arrian's Anabasis, here in A. G. Roos's Teubner edition (Leipzig, 1907) and divided into seven books running to some 1,400 lines, is a Greek prose narrative of the campaigns of Alexander son of Philip. Its preface sets out the author's method of weighing divergent earlier accounts, declaring Ptolemy son of Lagus and Aristobulus the most trustworthy witnesses, before proceeding from Philip's death and Alexander's operations in Thrace and Illyria toward the war against Persia. The title invites comparison with Xenophon's Anabasis, and the work's classicising prose makes it a fertile source of verbal and structural echoes for readers hunting intertexts.
grc.artemidorus.onirocriticon: The Onirocriticon, a Greek prose treatise on the interpretation of dreams attributed to Artemidorus and of uncertain date, opens with a defence of dream divination against its critics and a classification of dreams into the direct (theorematikoi) and the allegorical. Distinguishing the prophetic oneiros from the enypnion, the author draws on his professed experience of collecting dream cases and their outcomes in Greece, Asia, Italy and the islands, and cites Homer and earlier writers such as Artemon of Miletus and Phoebus of Antioch in support of his categories. As the fullest surviving ancient handbook of oneiromancy, it offers a rich source of parallels for dream scenes, symbolic interpretation, and divinatory vocabulary throughout classical and later literature.
grc.aspasius.in_ethica_nicomachea_paraphrasi: An ancient Greek commentary on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, attributed to Aspasius and preserved in the Commentaria in Aristotelem graeca (Heylbut, 1889); its date is uncertain. The work opens by weighing ethical and political philosophy against theoretical wisdom, invoking Socrates and the Pythagoreans on moral training, and then proceeds lemma by lemma through the opening of Book I, expounding Aristotle's treatment of technē, methodos, praxis, and proairesis and the argument that every art and pursuit aims at the good, whose attainment is eudaimonia. Readers hunting intertexts will find early exegetical paraphrase of Aristotle's ethical vocabulary and formulations that circulated in later Greek philosophical prose.
grc.athenaeus.deipnosophists: A lengthy Greek prose dialogue of uncertain date, the Deipnosophists (Learned Banqueters) of Athenaeus stages a banquet given by a wealthy Roman, Larensius, at whose table an erudite company, legal experts, grammarians, physicians such as Galen, philosophers, rhetors, and a musician, converses in self-consciously Platonic fashion. The speakers discourse on fish, vegetables, animals, music, jests, drinking vessels, royal wealth, and ships, and their talk is woven through with quotations from Greek poets, historians, and philosophers. Because many of the works cited survive only or chiefly in its pages, the Deipnosophists is a principal repository of fragments and a rich hunting ground for verbal parallels; the corpus presents it in Charles Burton Gulick's edition (1927), running to some 4,175 lines.
grc.babrius.fabulae_aesopeae: Fabulae Aesopeae is a Greek verse collection of Aesopic fables transmitted under the name of Babrius, of uncertain date, presented here in Schneidewin's 1865 Teubner edition. Its 285 lines open with a prologue addressed to a certain Branchus that retells the Hesiodic myth of the ages of mankind and promises Aesop's old tales recut into 'bitter iambs', followed by short beast fables, lion and huntsman, goatherd and she-goat, horse and ass, fisherman and piper among them, many closed by moral summaries introduced with 'that...'. For readers of intertexts the collection preserves the principal Greek verse form of the fable tradition, offering plots and gnomic morals that recur across Latin fabulists, proverb collections, and later Aesopic corpora.
grc.barnabas.barnabae_epistulae: The Epistle of Barnabas is a Greek Christian epistle of uncertain date, attributed to Barnabas and transmitted with the Apostolic Fathers; the Greek here follows Kirsopp Lake's 1912 edition and runs to some 194 lines. Addressed to its readers as sons and daughters in the name of the Lord, it gives thanks for their spiritual gifts, sets out the three doctrines of the Lord as hope of life, righteousness, and love, and argues from the prophets that God requires no sacrifices, burnt offerings, or outward fasts but a contrite heart and works of mercy. Its argument opposes the ceremonial observances of the law to the new law of Jesus Christ, warns of the completion of scandal in the evil days at hand, and strings together long scriptural quotations, including one introduced with the words 'as Enoch says.' A reader hunting intertexts will find in it a dense web of prophetic citation, often freely recast, and an early instance of Christian appropriation of Enochic apocalyptic material.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.de_legendis: An admonitory address in Greek prose by Basil of Caesarea, printed among his Letters in Deferrari's edition and known by the Latin title De legendis. The work counsels young men to read the poets and prose writers of pagan Greece with discernment, taking whatever serves virtue as a preparation of the soul for sacred learning, an argument introduced through a quotation of Hesiod and illustrated by Moses trained in the wisdom of the Egyptians and Daniel among the Chaldaeans. Its dense quotation and reinterpretation of classical authors make it a key witness to patristic engagement with Greek literature and a productive source of parallels for readers tracing intertexts.
grc.callimachus.aetia: The Aetia ('Causes'), an elegiac poem attributed to Callimachus and of uncertain date, survives only in fragments assembled from papyri and from quotations in ancient epigrams, lexicographers, scholiasts, and Stobaeus. Its design was to recount the origins of myths, cults, and customs, opening with the Dream in which the poet is carried from Libya to Helicon and questions the Muses, and including the papyrus-preserved tale of Acontius and Cydippe. The fragments are prefaced by ancient epigrams in praise and blame, from the hostile notice attributed to Apollonius Rhodius to Martial's allusion to the work. Readers hunting intertexts care both for its programme of learned, allusive poetry and because its quotation-contexts preserve mythological details echoed throughout later Greek and Latin verse.
grc.carmina_delphis_inventa.carmina_delphis_: Carmina Delphis Inventa preserves three Greek cult songs, a prosodion, a paean, and a hymn to Apollo, recovered from inscriptions in the Athenians' treasury at Delphi and edited with their ancient musical notation by Karl von Jan (Teubner, 1895). The accompanying civic decree honors Cleochares son of Bion, an Athenian poet of melē, whose songs for the theoxenia sacrifice the city ordered its annual chorus-master to teach the boys, while the poems themselves are of uncertain date. Across 117 lines the singers invoke Apollo as the slayer of the serpent on Parnassus, summon the Pierian maidens and the Castalian spring, and praise the Pythian lord with Theoxenia imagery of altars and sacrifice. Readers hunting parallels will find hymnic formulas and Apolline epithets echoing epic and lyric tradition, alongside rare epigraphic evidence for how Greek sacred song was performed and notated.
grc.chariton.de_chaerea: The Greek prose romance of Chaereas and Callirhoe, of uncertain date, opens with its narrator Chariton of Aphrodisias, under-secretary to the rhetor Athenagoras, announcing an erotic story set in Syracuse: the love of the young Chaereas for Callirhoe, divinely beautiful daughter of the general Hermocrates, the victor over the Athenians. Eros engineers their meeting at the festival of Aphrodite and the city itself arranges their marriage, while the rejected suitors conspire out of envy, setting in motion the separations and reversals that carry the couple far from Sicily before their eventual reunion. Readers hunting intertexts will find the novel saturated with Homeric and tragic resonance, from the comparisons of Chaereas with Achilles, Nireus, and Hippolytus to the wedding likened to that of Peleus and Thetis, all couched in diction that recalls historiography as much as fiction.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.eclogae_prophetica: A brief Greek collection of exegetical extracts and scholia attributed to Clement of Alexandria, transmitted in Otto Stählin's 1909 edition alongside the Stromata and the Excerpta ex Theodoto; its date of composition is not given in the source record. The work moves through Old Testament passages, the hymn of the three youths in the fiery furnace, Daniel, Hosea, and Genesis 1:1, and reads them allegorically on the ordering of the powers of creation, the abyss as matter, baptism with water and Spirit as regeneration, and the purification and filling of the soul. Besides its dense sequence of biblical quotations it cites Enoch alongside Daniel, making the collection a useful point of comparison for readers tracing scriptural, apocryphal, and early Christian exegetical parallels.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.paedagogus: The Paedagogus of Clement of Alexandria, written in Greek and edited by Otto Stählin in 1905, is a Christian didactic treatise that presents the divine Logos as the paedagogus or tutor who trains the soul of the believer, healing the passions and preparing it for higher instruction. The corpus preserves the opening of the work, headed by a chapter synopsis treating the Logos' philanthropy, his discipline of sin, his equal guidance of men and women, and his education of humanity through law and prophets. Explicitly framed as the sequel to the Protrepticus, which it names as the foundation of faith, the treatise addresses Christians as children and describes the sinless, impassible Logos as working toward the betterment of the soul rather than formal teaching. Dense with quotation and paraphrase of Moses and the prophets and cast in philosophical Greek, it offers rich material for tracing biblical and classical intertexts.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.quis_dives_salvetu: A Greek Christian work by Clement of Alexandria on whether the rich can be saved, opening with a denunciation of those who fawn upon the wealthy with encomiastic speeches and then taking up the Gospel saying that a camel passes through a needle's eye more easily than a rich man enters the kingdom of heaven. The work quotes at length the Gospel episode of the man who asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life, and argues that the Lord's words need not drive the prosperous to despair, since salvation remains attainable through obedience to the commandments and a rightly ordered life. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in it an extended citation of the Gospel narrative together with moralising exegesis of wealth and its perils, making it a fruitful witness to early Christian reinterpretation of biblical language; it is edited here from Otto Stählin's 1909 Leipzig edition.
grc.colluthus.rape_of_helen: The Rape of Helen (Harpagē Helenēs) is a Greek epic in hexameters, a single continuous book of 394 lines attributed to Colluthus, a poet of uncertain date. Opening with an invocation to the Trojan nymphs of the Xanthus, the poem recounts the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the snubbing and vengeance of Eris with the golden apple, the judgement of Paris among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, and the ensuing rape of Helen that set the Trojan War in motion. Its compressed reworking of episodes familiar from Homer, Hesiod, and the cyclic tradition of the Cypria makes it a dense site of verbal and thematic allusion, and a rewarding comparand for readers tracing the post-Homeric afterlife of the judgement of Paris and the abduction of Helen.
grc.cratetis_epistulae.epistulae: The Epistulae attributed to Crates, edited by Rudolf Hercher in the Epistolographi Graeci (1873), form a brief collection of Greek letters of uncertain date, composed in the voice of the Cynic philosopher and addressed to assorted friends and pupils. Their content is almost wholly paraenetic: exhortations to simplicity, self-sufficiency and endurance of toil, a summons to catch the dying Diogenes of Sinope while he still breathes, praise of the tribōn and pēra as 'the weapons of the gods', a temperance homily on wine backed by Homeric quotation, and reflections on training, law and philosophy. Exempla such as Penelope and Alcestis, along with the closing claim that to philosophise concisely is 'to kynizein', tie the letters firmly to the Cynic diatribe tradition associated with Diogenes and Antisthenes. For readers of intertexts, the collection offers dense clusters of Cynic topoi and Homeric citation that recur throughout later Greek moral and epistolographic writing, making it a compact index of that tradition.
grc.demosthenes.against_androtion: An Attic forensic oration of the Demosthenic corpus, preserved in the Butcher-Rennie Oxford edition of the orations, in which Demosthenes prosecutes Androtion for proposing that the Athenian Council be granted an honorary crown despite having failed to complete the triremes owed to the people. Speaking also on behalf of Euctemon, who claims to have suffered outrages at Androtion's hands, the orator defends the law barring the Council from requesting a crown until the ships are built and dismantles the defendant's contentions about probouleusis and the legality of the decree. For readers of intertexts, the speech offers characteristic Demosthenic argument over nomos and psephisma, civic honors, and procedural legality, with phrases and lines of reasoning that recur throughout the public prosecutions of the corpus.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_1: An Athenian forensic speech in Attic prose, preserved among the private orations of Demosthenes as the first of the speeches Against Aphobus. Speaking in his own person as a young plaintiff, the orator prosecutes his former guardian Aphobus for squandering an inheritance of some fourteen talents entrusted to him and his co-guardians, recounting his father's bequest, the terms of the guardianship, and the estate in meticulous detail, two workshops, maritime loans deposited with Pasion and other bankers, household goods, and the witnesses who assessed his property for the symmoria. Its self-conscious opening on youthful inexperience before the jury and its catalogue-style proof of wealth made the speech a set piece in later rhetorical education, and its guardianship narrative, legal formulas, and economic vocabulary supply frequent material for readers tracing textual parallels.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristocrates: A forensic oration of the Demosthenic corpus, Against Aristocrates (Kata Aristokratous) prosecutes a decree of Aristocrates granting personal immunity (asulia) to the general Charidemus, arguing that it contravenes the laws and endangers Athens' hold on the Chersonese. The speaker, who presents himself as a former trierarch in the Hellespont, rehearses the aftermath of Cotys' death, the rival Thracian kingships of Cersobleptes, Berisades and Amadocus, and the intrigues by which Charidemus and his partisans allegedly sought to steer Athenian policy. Attributed to Demosthenes in the transmitted corpus and printed in Butcher and Rennie's Oxford edition, the speech offers readers of intertexts a dense cluster of Attic legal vocabulary, diplomatic narrative, and the rhetoric of civic danger that recurs across fourth-century oratory.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_1: Against Aristogeiton I is a Greek forensic oration transmitted among the speeches of Demosthenes and of uncertain date, spoken before an Athenian court as the second prosecution speech in a public action (endeixis) against Aristogeiton, following an opening address by Lycurgus. The speaker heaps invective on the defendant as a habitual wrongdoer and sycophant who corrupts the assembly and the courts, and urges the jurors to regard their verdict as a public test of their hatred of wickedness and of their standing as guardians of the laws. Closing with an appeal to the personified Eunomia and Dike, the latter imagined, through an Orphic image, as seated beside the throne of Zeus, and to the jurors' oath, the speech offers a dense repertoire of moralising legal rhetoric valuable for readers tracing intertexts in Attic oratory.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_2: A brief forensic speech transmitted among the works of Demosthenes, the second prosecution speech against Aristogeiton, an Athenian who owed money to the public treasury and stood disfranchised (atimos) in consequence. The speaker contends that the laws expressly bar such men from addressing the people, invokes Solon's provision of swifter penalties for magistrates and demagogues than for private citizens, and illustrates with the figure of a helmsman whose error wrecks the whole crew how the misconduct of office-holders damages the entire polis. Historical exempla, Aristides, Miltiades and Pericles submitting to public penalties, and the decree of Hyperides after the disaster at Chaeronea restoring civil rights to the disfranchised, support the case against allowing Aristogeiton a public voice. For readers of intertexts, the speech offers dense parallels on atimia, democratic legality and the accountability of public men, in diction close to other Demosthenic forensic oratory.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_1: A short Attic forensic oration handed down among the speeches of Demosthenes, in which the speaker Mantitheus brings a private action against his half-brother Boeotus, who has had himself enrolled under the same name in the deme registers. Opening with the admission that the suit may seem officious, the speech argues that two citizens sharing one name would breed confusion in liturgies, court summonses, military levies and the allotment of offices, and it rehearses the oaths sworn by the mother, the enrolments in the phratries at the Apatouria, and the father's deathbed arrangements. For readers of intertexts it offers characteristic Attic oratorical material on names, kinship and civic administration, together with the recurrent figure of the sycophant and the rhetoric of household enmity.
grc.demosthenes.against_callippus: A short classical Athenian forensic oration preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes and attributed to him, belonging to the group of Demosthenic speeches concerned with disputes over the banking house of Pasion and Phormion. The speaker, presenting himself as a son of Pasion, defends the bank's payment of a sixteen-mina deposit left by Lycon of Heraclea against the claim of Callippus, who styles himself proxenos of the Heracleans; the case turns on the deposit entry in the banker's ledger, the testimony of witnesses, and the argument that an opponent of high reputation and influence must not be believed over the facts. For readers hunting parallels, it offers compact instances of banking vocabulary (trapeza, grammateion, apodounai), the formal witness citations, and the recurring forensic topos that eloquence and standing must not outweigh evidence in the judges' deliberations.
grc.demosthenes.against_dionysodorus: A Greek forensic speech from the Demosthenic corpus, one of the private orations and of uncertain date, delivered in an Athenian maritime commercial suit. The speaker, a co-financier in a loan contracted in the name of the banker Pamphilus, prosecutes Dionysodorus and his partner Parmeniscus for breach of contract: they had borrowed three thousand drachmas on a grain ship bound for Athens, but unloaded and sold the cargo at Rhodes when prices there proved better, violating the written agreement read out in court. The speech contrasts the security of the lender with the opportunities of the borrower, invokes the laws governing merchants and shipmasters, and attacks Cleomenes, the man in power in Egypt, for colluding in grain-price speculation. For readers of intertexts it preserves the formulae of the maritime contract (syngraphe), documents the Egypt–Rhodes–Athens grain route, and shares legal and commercial diction with the other Demosthenic commercial speeches.
grc.demosthenes.against_eubulides: A forensic speech transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus, of uncertain date, in which a speaker defends his claim to Athenian citizenship after being rejected by a vote of his demesmen. The speech attributes that vote to the machinations of Eubulides, who had earlier prosecuted the speaker's sister for impiety and now, the speaker argues, secured the deme's rejection through procedural trickery, including a ballot taken hastily at dusk with no chance for a proper defence. Readers of intertexts will find dense material on the dokimasia procedure, deme politics, and impiety prosecutions, together with courtroom formulae and narrative patterns that invite comparison with other Attic orators' speeches concerning citizen status.
grc.demosthenes.against_lacritus: A courtroom speech attributed to Demosthenes and of uncertain date, preserved in the corpus of his orations, in which the moneylender Androcles of Sphettus prosecutes Lacritus of Phaselis for failing to repay a maritime loan of three thousand drachmae contracted with Lacritus' late brother Artemon for a voyage to the Pontus. The speaker opens with an attack on the Phaselites as notorious abusers of commercial credit and then sets out the terms of the loan contract, quoted at length with its interest rates, sailing deadlines, and security provisions, followed by witness depositions. A compact specimen of Attic commercial litigation, the speech supplies the formulae of accusation, documentary diction, and maritime vocabulary that invite comparison with the other shipping cases transmitted under Demosthenes' name.
grc.demosthenes.against_leochares: A forensic speech of the Demosthenic corpus, attributed to Demosthenes and preserved among the private orations, delivered in an Athenian court in a dispute over the estate of the childless Archiades. The speaker contests the claim of Leochares, who asserts a right to the inheritance through an alleged posthumous adoption, and traces his own genealogy at length to establish nearer kinship to the deceased in the male line. Compact even by the standards of the inheritance speeches, it offers dense formulaic vocabulary for adoption, kinship (anchisteia), and testamentary litigation that recurs across the Attic orators, making it fertile ground for verbal and thematic parallels.
grc.demosthenes.against_macartatus: A short Athenian forensic speech of the fourth century BC, attributed to Demosthenes and transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus as Against Macartatus, addressed to a dikastery in a dispute over the estate of Hagnias of Oe. Speaking for a boy adopted into the house of Eubulides, the litigant recounts earlier litigation over the same inheritance, denounces a fraudulent will concocted by Macartatus' family, and describes their courtroom tricks, including the manipulation of the water-clock, before defending the boy's adoption on the strength of the phrateres' verdict at the altar of Zeus Phratrios. For readers hunting intertexts, the speech offers dense parallels to Isaeus and to Demosthenes' other private orations, rich in the vocabulary of Athenian inheritance law: next-of-kin claims, adoption, wills, and phratry adjudication.
grc.demosthenes.against_nausimachus_and_xeno: A short forensic speech preserved in the Demosthenic corpus under Demosthenes' name, composed for the courts of classical Athens. The speaker, who with a brother has entered upon an inheritance, pleads a paragraphē (preliminary objection) against a suit for thirty minae brought by Nausimachus and Xenopeithes, who had acted as guardians of his father; he maintains that an earlier legal discharge (aphesis) bars the same matters from being litigated afresh, and refutes their claim that the father recovered debts owed in the Bosporus. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the standard vocabulary of Athenian civil procedure, including paragraphē, aphesis, epitropē, and enkēma, together with argumentative and formulaic material that recurs throughout the Demosthenic private orations on guardianship and inheritance.
grc.demosthenes.against_olympiodorus: A brief forensic oration preserved among the speeches of Demosthenes and edited by W. Rennie (Oxford, 1931), Against Olympiodorus concerns a private suit over the estate of Comon, an elderly kinsman who died childless. The speaker, whose wife was the defendant's sister, recounts how a claim on the inheritance arose despite his prior care for the dying man, how the parties divided the property under oaths and a written agreement deposited with a trustee, and how Olympiodorus' subsequent demands drove him to court unwillingly. The speech displays the standard apparatus of Attic private oratory: witness depositions, citation of a law, and the stock pose of the kinsman forced into litigation against his own kin. Its treatment of inheritance, arbitration, and family obligation offers close parallels for readers tracing stock motifs and legal formulae across the Attic orators.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_31: An Attic forensic oration by Demosthenes, transmitted with his private speeches under the title Against Onetor, in which the speaker prosecutes a dispute over a dowry allegedly paid to Aphobus. Continuing a proof set out in a previous speech, the speaker argues that Onetor's shifting valuations of a house and a country estate show that no dowry was ever given, and he exposes the opposing case as perjury and collusion designed to shield Aphobus. The speech repays readers hunting intertexts with its compact display of Demosthenic reasoning from documents and witness testimony, its legal vocabulary of proofs, valuations and sureties, and its close links to the other orations arising from the same affair.
grc.demosthenes.against_phaenippus: A short forensic speech preserved among the private orations of Demosthenes, 'Against Phaenippus' belongs to the courtroom oratory of fourth-century BC Athens and arises from the antidosis procedure, by which a citizen called upon a wealthier man either to exchange estates with him or to undertake the advance of the city's property tax among the Three Hundred. The speaker charges Phaenippus with defying the sworn deadlines for declaring the value of his estate and with obstructing the lawful inspection of his property, from the boundary marks of his farmland to his stored barley and his timber carted off by donkeys. The speech offers a compact demonstration of Attic legal diction, courtroom formulas such as the opening invocation of Solon's antidosis law, and the procedural steps of the challenge, making it useful for readers tracing legal and rhetorical parallels across the Demosthenic corpus.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_1: A courtroom speech in Attic Greek, attributed to Demosthenes and transmitted among his private orations, in which an Athenian litigant prosecutes Stephanus of Acharnae for giving false witness. The speaker recounts his grievances against Phormion, who controls the estate left by his father Pasion and has married his mother, and argues that Stephanus committed perjury by attesting a challenge concerning the opening of Pasion's will. As the first of the speeches Against Stephanus, it belongs to the group of orations arising from the dispute over the banking house of Pasion, and its dense interweaving of testimony, documentary evidence, and procedural challenges (prokleseis) makes it fertile ground for readers tracing legal formulas and narrative motifs across Athenian forensic oratory.
grc.demosthenes.against_theocrines: Against Theocrines is a short forensic speech transmitted among the orations of Demosthenes. The speaker, a young Athenian whose father had been ruined and fined ten talents through Theocrines, prosecutes his enemy for withdrawing a phasis, a written denunciation against the shipwrecked vessel of Mikon of Cholleidai, after allegedly accepting money and thus failing to pursue the charge as the laws on informers required. The speech quotes the relevant statutes verbatim and incorporates testimony concerning the phasis, the ship, and the merchants and shipowners whom Theocrines is said to have extorted. Its compact argument over commercial litigation, sycophancy, and the procedural vocabulary of Athenian law makes it a productive source of parallels for readers tracing legal formulae and rhetorical commonplaces across the orators.
grc.demosthenes.erotic_essay: An epideictic speech attributed to Demosthenes and transmitted in his corpus, the Erotikos (Erotic Essay) is a short prose work in which a lover praises the youth Epicrates for his beauty, courage, and temperance and offers him advice on education and the conduct of life. Its preface self-consciously frames the piece as a written logos composed for reading rather than delivery, and it reflects on how erotic writing can bring honor rather than shame to its subject. Of uncertain date, it belongs to the Greek tradition of erotic encomium and advice literature, and it offers readers of intertexts a prose parallel for the paederastic and epideictic themes familiar from Plato and the orators.
grc.demosthenes.for_the_megalopitans: A short deliberative oration transmitted in the corpus of Demosthenes and edited from Butcher's Oxford text of 1903, For the Megalopolitans addresses the Athenian assembly in the aftermath of the battle of Mantinea, when envoys of both Arcadians and Lacedaemonians are canvassing for Athenian support. The speaker argues that Athens should aid the Megalopolitans so that neither Thebes nor Sparta grows strong enough to injure her, weighing the oaths sworn to the Messenians, the justice of the case, and the proposed recovery of Oropus. Readers hunting intertexts will find its balance-of-power reasoning, its pairing of τὸ δίκαιον and τὸ συμφέρον, and its diction closely parallel to the other fourth-century Athenian demegories on Peloponnesian policy.
grc.demosthenes.funeral_speech: An epitaphios logos, the ceremonial oration delivered at Athens for the public burial of the war dead, transmitted under the name of Demosthenes and printed from W. Rennie's 1931 Oxford edition. Opening with the conventional protest that the fallen, who chose a noble death over life, defy adequate praise, the speaker proceeds from the autochthony and ancient nobility of the Athenian stock through mythical exploits, victory over the Amazons and Eumolpus, shelter for the Heraclidae, the burial of the Seven against Thebes, to the repulse of the Persian invasion and the virtue of the dead. Its compressed sweep through the standard topoi of Athenian self-praise makes it a useful locus for tracing shared material with the other surviving funeral orations and with tragic treatments of the same legends.
grc.demosthenes.letters: A collection of Greek prose letters transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus and attributed to the Athenian orator Demosthenes, edited by W. Rennie in the Oxford Clarendon edition of the orations (1931) and running to 107 lines. The letters are addressed to the council and people of Athens and deliver political counsel, opening with a prayer to the gods and urging concord among the citizens, forbearance toward former opponents, and clear-sighted vigilance in the unsettled moment after Alexander's death, which one epistle expressly presupposes. For readers of intertexts the collection matters as the epistolary counterpart of Demosthenic deliberative oratory, offering the formulae of salutation and advisory preface alongside recurring political vocabulary of homonoia, stasis, and civic leadership.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_1: The First Olynthiac is a deliberative speech by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, urging the assembly to vote immediate and wholehearted assistance to Olynthus in its war with Philip of Macedon. It opens by declaring that no price is too high for sound counsel, then argues from Athens' repeated failures at earlier crises, Amphipolis, Pydna, Potidaea, Methone, that a spontaneous opportunity against Philip must not again be squandered. The speaker portrays Philip as an untrustworthy tyrant whose sole command of generals, rhetors, and treasury makes him formidable in war but suspect in alliances, and warns that if Olynthus falls nothing will bar his advance. Its compact antitheses, formulaic civic addresses, and historical exempla make it a frequent locus of verbal parallels within the Demosthenic corpus and the later rhetorical tradition.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_3: An assembly speech by Demosthenes, the third of the three Olynthiac orations, addressed to the Athenians while the campaigns of Philip of Macedon threatened the Greek cities. The speaker urges vigorous aid for Olynthus, arguing that the preservation of Athens' allies must take precedence over talk of revenge, and recalls earlier failures to act on resolutions hastily passed. Its boldest proposal is a call to suspend the laws governing the theoric funds, so that public money may be diverted from festivals to military needs. For readers of intertexts the speech is a central witness to Athenian debate over Macedonian expansion and a frequent reference point in later discussions of public finance and frank political counsel.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_halonnesus: A short deliberative oration of forty-six lines, transmitted among the works of Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian assembly in answer to Philip of Macedon's claims over the island of Halonnesus. The speaker dismantles Philip's offer to 'give' the island as a sham gift concealing seizure, attacks his proposals for treaties (symbola) and joint policing of pirates, and recalls Macedonian injuries such as the treatment of Athenian settlers at Potidaea. Its close verbal engagement with Philip's letter and the arguments of his envoys makes it a natural point of comparison for studies of Philippic rhetoric, interstate arbitration, and the diplomatic vocabulary of Athenian-Macedonian relations.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_liberty_of_the_rhodia: A deliberative oration of Demosthenes, On the Liberty of the Rhodians addresses the Athenian Assembly and urges the restoration of democratic government at Rhodes, which Mausolus of Caria had stripped of its freedom after the recent war involving the Chians and Byzantines. The speaker invokes the city's aid to Ariobarzanes through Timotheus and the liberation of Samos as precedents, weighs the risk of letting the Persian King secure the island while Artemisia controls its affairs, and argues that Athens should act in the interest of all Greeks rather than from enmity toward any one power. Readers hunting textual parallels will find here the standard furniture of Attic deliberative rhetoric, the opening claim to parrhesia, argument from precedent, and the balancing of advantage, justice, and reputation, along with phrasing and themes that recur across the Demosthenic corpus and earlier oratory on interstate liberty.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_navy: A Greek deliberative oration attributed to Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian people on the question of naval and financial preparedness against the Persian king. The speaker opens by dismissing praise of the ancestors as flattering but unprofitable, then argues that the king is a common enemy of all the Greeks, that Athens must not be the first to begin the war, and that openly visible preparation in ships, money and men will both avert attack and draw the other Greeks to Athenian leadership. For readers of intertexts, the proem's antithesis between encomiastic and useful counsel and the recurring formula of the king as the common enemy of the Hellenes are motifs that circulate widely in panhellenic political oratory.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_peace: An assembly speech from the Demosthenic corpus, On the Peace belongs to the deliberative oratory preserved in Butcher's Oxford edition of the orations. Addressed to the Athenians, it surveys recent civic misjudgements, the Euboean intervention on behalf of Plutarchus, the intrigues of the actor Neoptolemus, and the abandonment of the Phocians, and defends the speaker's earlier counsels concerning Philip of Macedon and the oaths sworn over the peace. The argument urges that the existing settlement be neither rashly broken nor complacently trusted, while warning against those who invoke the Amphictyons as a pretext for a common war. For readers of intertexts, its formulaic exordium, its self-justifying recapitulation of past advice, and its recurring phrases offer close parallels with the other Demosthenic deliberative speeches on Athenian policy toward Philip.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_trierarchic_crown: A public oration of the Demosthenic corpus, addressed to the Athenian council and people, in which the speaker defends his claim to a crown for being the first trierarch to fit out his ship and attacks rivals who obtained the same honour while hiring out their liturgies. The argument draws on precedent, including the Athenians' punishment of trierarchs after their naval defeat by Alexander, and insists on equal treatment of rich and poor in civic rewards and penalties. Its recurring vocabulary of naval equipment, liturgies, crowns, and legal procedure supplies parallels for readers of Attic oratory and students of civic honour and public finance. The work is filed as a single unit of 22 lines with no book divisions, in Rennie's Oxford edition of 1931.
grc.demosthenes.philip: A brief Greek prose letter written in the voice of Philip II of Macedon and addressed to the council and people of Athens, transmitted under Demosthenes' name in the Demosthenic corpus, though its attribution is disputed. The writer rehearses a catalogue of Athenian offences against their sworn oaths and agreements: the imprisonment of his herald, protection of pirates and Byzantine triremes, the raids of the strategos Diopeithes in Thrace, overtures to the Persian king, decrees concerning the Thracian rulers Teres and Cersobleptes, and the treatment of the Cardians and Peparethians. As a composition staging the Macedonian king's own case against Athens in the quarrel that produced Demosthenes' Philippics, it offers a counter-voice of interest to readers tracing the rhetoric of the Athenian-Macedonian conflict.
grc.didymus_alexandrinus.mensurae_marmorum_a: Attributed to Didymus Alexandrinus and of uncertain date, the Mensurae marmorum ac lignorum is a short Greek metrological handbook, edited by Hultsch in 1864, that explains how to compute the bulk of marble slabs and timber in three modes: linear, areal, and solid measurement. After a preamble distinguishing straight, plane, and cubic measure, its forty-three lines work through problems for square, round, triangular, and semicircular pieces, then tabulate the palms, digits, and feet of the Ptolemaic and Roman systems and give conversion ratios between them and the royal cubit. The coexistence of Ptolemaic and Roman measures points to an Egyptian setting, and the work offers useful parallels for Greek technical prose, Heronian-style stereometric problems, and the vocabulary of ancient measurement.
grc.dinarchus.against_aristogiton: An Attic forensic prosecution speech attributed to Dinarchus, transmitted in the Minor Attic Orators. Addressed to the Athenians as they weigh the verdict of the Council of the Areopagus, the accusers press for the death penalty against the notorious Aristogeiton, citing his record of convictions, his conduct toward his own father, and above all his acceptance of money from Harpalus as proof of incorrigible treachery toward the city. Vigorous and relentlessly abusive in manner, the speech offers fertile intertexts for the rhetoric of habitual wrongdoing and bribery, for the Harpalus affair, and for democratic debates over overturning the judgments of the Areopagus.
grc.dinarchus.against_demosthenes: The 'Against Demosthenes' of Dinarchus is a Greek forensic prosecution speech for the Athenian trial over the money Demosthenes and others received from Harpalus, transmitted among the Minor Attic Orators. Speaking after the charges laid by Stratocles and the inquiry of the Areopagus council, the speaker argues that Demosthenes, proved to hold twenty talents of Harpalus' gold, must suffer the death penalty he himself had agreed to accept if convicted, while rebutting his attacks on the council and invoking Chaeronea and the alleged betrayal of Thebes. The speech thus preserves a hostile contemporary account of Demosthenes' public career and shares its diction, procedural vocabulary, and recurring topoi with the wider corpus of Attic oratory, making it a rich source of verbal and thematic parallels for readers tracing intertexts.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.ad_ammaeum: A short Greek treatise in epistolary form by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, addressed to Ammaeus and of uncertain date, which refutes the Peripatetic claim that Demosthenes owed his mastery of rhetoric to Aristotle's rhetorical technai. Dionysius answers by setting out the chronology of Demosthenes' public career, from the Against Androtion to the Philippic orations, to demonstrate that the famous speeches were composed and delivered before Aristotle's treatises circulated. In the course of the argument the letter preserves an outline of Demosthenes' life drawn from biographical tradition and lists earlier writers of rhetorical handbooks, among them Isocrates, Alcidamas, and Theodectes. For readers of intertexts the work is valuable as a catalogue of Demosthenic speeches by title and occasion and as evidence for the lost Aristotelian technai against which Greek oratory was measured.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.antiquitates_: The Antiquitates Romanae of Dionysius of Halicarnassus is a Greek prose history, transmitted here in twelve book files totalling some 4,250 lines, devoted to Rome and its rise to universal dominion. The opening preface sets out a theory of historiography, criticises predecessors such as Anaximenes and Theopompus, and praises Roman rule as surpassing in extent and duration the Assyrian, Median, Persian, Macedonian, Athenian, and Spartan hegemonies. Readers hunting parallels will find in it a self-conscious engagement with earlier Greek historiography and a sustained comparison of Greek and Roman traditions.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_antiquis_o: De Antiquis Oratoribus is a short Greek critical treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, of uncertain date, though its preface speaks of an age in which Rome commands the allegiance of the Greek cities and shapes their taste. Addressed to one Ammaeus, it celebrates the restoration of philosophic, Attic rhetoric after the sway of an ignorant 'Asianic' style and announces a two-part survey of six canonical orators, Lysias, Isocrates and Isaeus among the older writers, Demosthenes, Hyperides and Aeschines among their successors. The record preserves only the four lines of the prefatory discourse. It repays readers hunting intertexts with the often-echoed simile of the wronged wife and the brazen courtesan representing the rival rhetorics, a borrowed Pindaric tag on time as the saviour of just men, and a programmatic statement of the standards later applied orator by orator.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_demosthene: A short Greek treatise of rhetorical criticism by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, On Demosthenes examines the style of the great Athenian orator and the prose traditions from which his art arose. The opening chapters characterise the austere, densely wrought manner whose rule and canon is Thucydides and the plain, unforced manner perfected by Lysias, setting out the two poles between which Demosthenes' blended style is to be placed. Dionysius contrasts the effects of the two manners on the hearer, the one able to overawe and concentrate the mind, the other to charm and relax it, and rates both supreme exponents as unmatched yet incomplete. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a dense ancient engagement with Thucydidean and Lysian phrasing, as well as a useful witness to how Demosthenic style was analysed and classified in later Greek criticism.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_dinarcho: A brief Greek critical essay by Dionysius of Halicarnassus on the orator Dinarchus, written to supply what earlier accounts, from Callimachus to Demetrius of Magnesia, had left inaccurate or unexamined. It reconstructs Dinarchus' life, from his Corinthian origins and his associations with Theophrastus and Demetrius of Phalerum to his fifteen years of speechwriting after Alexander's death, his exile at Chalcis, and his lawsuit against Proxenus, and characterises a style that falls short of Demosthenes only in bitterness and force while lacking nothing of Hyperides' charm. The essay also distinguishes the four men named Dinarchus, separates genuine speeches from spurious ones among the more than a hundred and sixty attributed to the orator, and quotes the opening deposition of the speech against Proxenus together with excerpts from Philochorus' Attic histories. Readers hunting intertexts will find here verbal fragments of lost prose writers alongside an ancient critic's comparisons of Dinarchus' diction with that of Demosthenes, Hyperides, Lysias, Isocrates and Isaeus.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_lysia: A short Greek treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus on the orator Lysias, opening with a biographical account of Lysias' Syracusan parentage, his birth at Athens and residence at Thurii, and his career writing speeches for courts, councils, and assemblies. The essay then assesses his style, praising him as a canonical model of pure Attic diction, plain and ordinary vocabulary, brevity, and clarity, while contrasting him with the poetic and figurative manner of Gorgias and Thucydides and setting Isocrates above later imitators.
