Readers hunting intertexts will find here a dense web of named parallels, Andocides, Critias, Timaeus, Demosthenes among others, offering an ancient evaluative framework for how Lias was read, ranked, and imitated in later rhetorical tradition.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_thucydide: A Greek critical treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, addressed to Quintus Aelius Tubero and devoted to the historical writing of Thucydides. Following the author's earlier notes on imitation and taking the place of a promised study of Demosthenes, it defends the audacity of finding fault in a writer ordinarily revered as the greatest of historians, adducing Plato's and Aristotle's critiques of their own predecessors as precedent. Dionysius disclaims any intention of attacking Thucydides, proposing instead a survey of the character of his writing that weighs both its virtues and the faults bordering on them, and asks where Thucydides resembles other authors and where he is distinctive, treating both his choice of subject and his powers of expression. The work offers readers of intertexts a dense record of the ancient critical reception of Thucydides and of Dionysius' evaluative terminology for historiography and rhetoric.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.epistula_ad_p: The Epistula ad Pompeium is a brief rhetorical treatise in epistolary form by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, addressed to a Pompeius who had taken exception to the strictures on Plato in Dionysius' comparative study of Demosthenes, Isocrates, and Plato. The letter defends synkrisis, the testing of authors against one another, as the surest route to critical truth, and finds a precedent for such censure in Plato's own practice, from his treatment of Lysias in the Phaedrus to his rivalry with Homer and his portraits of Gorgias, Protagoras, and other predecessors. Dense with quotation and close appraisal of Demosthenes, Isocrates, and Plato, it offers valuable evidence for ancient critical method and for the reception of classical prose, and its embedded citations and paraphrases make it productive ground for tracing textual parallels.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.libri_secundi: Brief Greek fragments surviving from the second book of Dionysius of Halicarnassus' treatise On the Ancient Orators, introduced by formulas such as ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς φησίν ('the Halicarnassian says') and transmitted as short scholia and excerpts. The remaining lines preserve Dionysius' judgements on Demosthenes and Aeschines, including criticism of the proem to the speech On the Embassy as too tragic and epilogic in manner, censure of Aeschines' use of παρακαταθέσθαι, and a note on a colon said to echo Euripides. Though only a few lines in length, the collection offers readers of intertexts a point of contact between ancient rhetorical criticism and the Attic orators and tragedians whom it quotes and evaluates.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnassus.de_compositio: An abridged Greek summary of Dionysius of Halicarnassus' treatise on literary composition, prefaced as a birthday gift to the young Rufus Melitius in deliberate imitation of Helen's gift to Telemachus in the Odyssey. The work expounds Dionysius' doctrine of word arrangement (synthesis), ranking it second in order among the divisions of lexis yet greater in power than the mere selection of words, and supports the claim through close analysis of Homer's Eumaeus episode, Herodotus' account of Candaules, and the reordering of the sentence on Croesus' origins. A compact witness to ancient stylistic criticism, the epitome is of interest to intertextual readers for its verbatim Homeric and Herodotean quotations and for its evidence of how classical prose writers deployed epic and historiographic diction.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnasus.de_imitatione_: Fragments in Greek of the treatise On Imitation by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, preserved in the Teubner edition of Usener and Radermacher (1904); the work's original form and date of composition are not indicated here. The opening definitions distinguish rhetoric, imitation (mimesis), and emulation (zelos), and the fragments exhort the student to steep himself in earlier writers, illustrated by the story of Zeuxis and the Crotonian maidens. A survey follows of the characteristic excellences of Homer, Hesiod, Antimachus, Panyasis, Pindar, Simonides, Stesichorus, Alcaeus, the tragedians, comedy, and the historians Herodotus, Thucydides, Philistus, and Xenophon. For readers of intertexts the fragments offer an ancient account of how the virtues of one author were to be selected, combined, and reworked by later writers, making the piece a guide to ancient practices of literary modeling.
grc.epictetus.gnomologium_epicteteum_e_stoba: A compact Greek gnomologium of sixty-seven lines, assembling maxims attributed to Epictetus as excerpted from the anthology of Stobaeus and printed in Heinrich Schenkl's 1916 Teubner edition of the Dissertationes. The sayings, cast in aphoristic gnomic style and often built on images of torrents, springs, ships, and animals, exhort simplicity, self-control, and independence from fortune, with particular attention to wealth, luxury, dining, and the pursuit of truth. Readers tracing intertexts will find here gnomic material circulating under Epictetus' name in the florilegium tradition, its phrasing inviting comparison with parallel sayings collections and Stoic moral prose.
grc.epicurus.ratae_sententiae: The Ratae Sententiae (Sovereign Maxims) of Epicurus, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, set out the core doctrines of Epicurean ethics in forty brief numbered statements. They treat the blessed and passionless gods, the nothingness of death, the measurement of pleasure and pain, the classification of desires, the need for physics to dispel fear, justice, friendship, and the senses as the criterion of truth. Because these compressed formulations were repeatedly quoted, paraphrased, and contested by later ancient authors, the collection functions as a compact reference point for identifying Epicurean echoes and allusions in Greek and Latin literature.
grc.euripides.heracles: Heracles is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, of uncertain date, running to 1428 lines and printed here from Gilbert Murray's Oxford edition of 1913. The prologue, spoken by Amphitryon, sets the scene at Thebes, where Megara and the children of Heracles await death at the hands of the usurper Lycus while Heracles is below the earth fetching the three-bodied hound of Hades. The play then follows his return and slaughter of Lycus, the madness inflicted on him by Hera, his killing of his own wife and sons, and the arrival of Theseus, who offers him refuge at Athens. Its dense treatment of the labours, the descent to the underworld, and the hero's madness makes it a central point of reference for readers tracing the Heracles legend across Greek and later literature.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_aulis: Greek tragedy transmitted under the name of Euripides, of uncertain date, printed here in 1,626 lines from Gilbert Murray's Oxford Clarendon Press edition of the Euripidis Fabulae (1913). Set at the Greek camp at Aulis, it dramatises Agamemnon's dilemma when the seer Calchas demands the sacrifice of his daughter Iphigenia to win fair winds for the fleet, moving through his secret letter to Clytemnestra, the deception of Achilles, and the confrontation between father and daughter. Its opening survey of Tyndareus' oath, Helen's wooing, and the muster of the Achaeans condenses much of the prehistory of the Trojan War, making the play a natural comparand for treatments of the house of Atreus, the sacrifice motif, and the mythic prelude to the expedition across Greek and later literature.
grc.eusebius_caesarea.historia_ecclesiastica: Eusebius of Caesarea's Historia Ecclesiastica is a Greek prose history of the Christian church from its origins down to the author's own day, transmitted here in ten books. The opening preface sets out a programme of recording the successions of apostles and bishops, the teachers of the most celebrated churches, the rise of heresy, the catastrophes that overtook the Jewish nation, and the persecutions and martyrdoms endured by the faithful. Because earlier writers had left only scattered notices, the author gathers and arranges excerpts from ancient authorities as from a flowery meadow, quoting extensively from documents and authors otherwise lost or fragmentary. Its dense citation of scripture and of earlier Christian and profane writers makes it a central hunting ground for intertextual parallels in patristic prose.
grc.flavius_josephus.contra_apionem: An apologetic treatise in Greek in two books by Flavius Josephus, addressed to Epaphroditus and printed here from B. Niese's Berlin edition of 1892. Written as a companion to the author's Greek Antiquities, it answers detractors who slander the Jewish nation and deny its antiquity, and explains why Greek historiography says so little about it. Josephus contrasts the recent and mutually contradictory writings of the Greeks, from Hellanicus and Acusilaus to Herodotus and Thucydides, with the far older public records of the Egyptians, Chaldaeans and Phoenicians, and promises to refute false accounts of his people by producing reliable witnesses. For readers of intertexts the work offers a Jewish historian's appraisal of Greek scholarship on early history, together with abundant references to earlier historians and their disagreements.
grc.flavius_josephus.de_bello_judaico_libri_: The seven books of the De Bello Judaico, printed in B. Niese's Berlin edition of 1895, recount the war between the Jews and the Romans, from the outbreak of factional strife in Judaea through the siege, capture, and burning of Jerusalem. The preface identifies the author as Iosepos, son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem who first took up arms against the Romans and afterwards fell into their hands, and who had earlier composed an account in his ancestral tongue before translating the work into Greek. He frames the history as a corrective to predecessors moved by flattery or hatred, insists on eyewitness accuracy, and argues with the authority of Titus, the captor of the city, that native tyrants rather than Roman arms alone drew fire to the temple. Readers hunting parallels will find a Greek historical voice indebted to the Thucydidean preface, an apologetic stance poised between Jewish and Roman worlds, and a narrative of the fall of Jerusalem that resonates throughout later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.galen.ad_glauconem_de_methodo_medendi: A brief run of twenty-nine lines of Greek medical prose by Galen, addressed to Glaucon, from the treatise on the method of healing preserved in the Kühn Leipzig edition. The speaker argues that the physician must know not only the common nature of humankind but the individual patient, defends a diagnostic method of repeated division after Plato and the physician Mnesitheus of Athens, and applies it to the simplest fevers, the 'ephemeral' ones of Hippocratic usage, listing their causes (fatigue, anger, grief, sleeplessness, chilling, burns) and their distinguishing signs in pulse, urine, complexion, and eyes, with counsel on bathing, diet, and wine. Readers of intertexts will find the passage useful for its explicit invocations of Hippocrates on prognosis and individualised treatment, its Platonic vocabulary of genus, species, and division, and its otherwise rare notice of Mnesitheus.
grc.galen.an_in_arteriis_sanguis_contineatur: A brief Greek medical treatise by Galen, printed in Kühn's Claudii Galeni Opera Omnia (Leipzig, Knobloch, 1822) under the Latin title An in Arteriis Sanguis Contineatur, 'Whether blood is contained in the arteries.' The opening demonstration argues syllogistically that blood must be present in the arteries from the start, since a wounded artery discharges blood at once, whereas pneuma, had it alone filled the vessels, would have escaped visibly beforehand. The discussion then rebuts the Erasistratean objections that pneuma drains away unobserved because of its fine texture or is expelled by the heart's compression, with an appeal also to the doctrine of Praxagoras. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact witness to Galen's polemic against Erasistratean physiology and to his dialectical treatment of rival medical theories.
grc.galen.de_anatomicis_administrationibus: A Greek manual of anatomical dissection by the physician Galen, preserved in the corpus as printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Claudii Galeni Opera omnia (Leipzig, 1821). In the preface Galen explains that he undertook a new and fuller account of anatomical operations to replace an earlier one written for Flavius Boethus, a Roman consul devoted to anatomical study, at a time when the emperor Antoninus ruled. The instruction that follows directs the student to begin with the bones, urging direct inspection of human skeletons and, where those cannot be seen, dissection of apes, whose structure most closely resembles the human, before proceeding to muscles, vessels, nerves, and viscera. Readers hunting intertexts will find the treatise peppered with named allusions to Hippocratic and Erasistratan anatomy and to Galen's own teachers, making it a natural hub for tracing medical traditions and their borrowings.
grc.galen.de_antidotis: A Greek prose treatise on antidotes (De antidotis) by Galen, printed in Kühn's Claudii Galeni Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1827). The opening chapters define the antidote, trace the ancestry of the theriac from the Mithridateion of Mithridates through Andromachus, Nero's archiatros, to the daily dose taken by the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, whose remedy Galen himself prepared, and go on to explain how the finest theriac is compounded, how simples are tested for strength and provenance, and how adulteration is detected. Readers hunting parallels will find dense pharmacological terminology, named authorities such as Dioscorides, Heraclides of Tarentum, Crateuas, Niger, Iollas and Rufus of Ephesus, and anecdotes about Mithridates, Attalus and the imperial court that recur throughout ancient medical and historical writing.
grc.galen.de_causis_morborum: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Causis Morborum, printed in Kühn's Leipzig edition of the Opera Omnia (1824). The work classifies diseases as simple and compound and takes up their causes, treating affections of the homogeneous parts of the body as dyscrasias or breaches of continuity, and then examines in detail how immoderate heat generates fever from exercise and fatigue, putrefaction, contact with hotter bodies, confinement of vapours beneath the skin, and heating foods and drinks, while rebutting the objection that such causes do not invariably kindle fever. Galen repeatedly directs the reader to companion books on the genera of diseases and on predisposing (prokatarktic) causes, marking the treatise's place in a larger medical sequence. For readers hunting intertexts it supplies core Galenic vocabulary, dyskrasia, homoiomere parts, organic disease, prokatarktika aitia, and a characteristic specimen of his adversarial, didactic medical exposition.
grc.galen.de_constitutione_artis_medicae_ad_: Galen's De constitutione artis medicae ad Patrophilum, preserved in Greek and printed in Kühn's Opera omnia (Leipzig, 1821), is a methodological treatise addressed to a Patrophilus whose hunger for a demonstrated, methodical account of medicine the opening praises at length. The work argues that every art takes its constitution from the conception of its end, as the ancient philosophers taught, surveys the genera of arts as theoretical, practical, productive and acquisitive, and assigns medicine to the productive arts that restore what has failed, on the analogy of the mender of clothes and the builder of houses. From that starting point it derives the physician's obligation to know, through anatomy, the body's simple and organic parts, their composition and their functions, since only the end of the art determines what knowledge is necessary. Readers hunting parallels will find here a dense node of craft analogies, teleological doctrine and the claim that one and the same method establishes every art, themes that resonate across Greek philosophical and medical writing on method.
grc.galen.de_consuetudinibus: A short Greek medical treatise attributed to Galen, edited by Iwan von Müller in 1879 as a single libellus, De Consuetudinibus defends habituation (ethos) as one of the principal therapeutic indications in medicine. The opening argument answers critics who scoff at appeals to custom, adducing the authority of Hippocrates' Aphorisms and Regimen in Acute Diseases and of Erasistratus' second book On Paralysis, each quoted at length, together with a clinical anecdote about Aristotle of Mytilene, whose refusal of cold drinking water proved fatal. Readers hunting textual parallels will find here extensive verbatim citation of Hippocratic and Erasistratean passages on the perils of sudden changes in diet and the power of habit over both body and mind, making the work a useful witness to the reception of earlier medical writing.
grc.galen.de_crisibus: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Crisibus (On Crises), printed in Kühn's Opera omnia (Leipzig, 1825), teaches how the crisis of a disease may be foreknown and judged. It surveys the possible senses of krisis, whether the sudden change in an illness, its turn toward the better, or its complete resolution, and defines the four periods of disease (beginning, growth, acme, decline), then shows how worsening or remission is diagnosed by comparing paroxysms in their timing, length, severity, and attendant symptoms. The argument repeatedly invokes Hippocrates' doctrine of periods and prognosis, presenting such foreknowledge as the mark of a genuinely skilled physician. Readers of intertexts will find the treatise a central witness to Hippocratic reception and to the technical vocabulary of krisis, kairos, akmē, and paroxysmos in ancient medical prose.
grc.galen.de_curandi_ratione_per_venae_secti: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, preserved in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1826), the De Curandi Ratione per Venae Sectionem ('On the Method of Cure by Venesection') organises the practice of bloodletting as a sequence of questions: which bodily conditions require evacuation, which patients can tolerate it, which veins should be opened, and how much blood should be withdrawn. Galen defends the remedy against the school of Erasistratus, Chrysippus of Cnidus, Medius, and Aristogenes in particular, while appealing to Hippocrates and the most reputable physicians for the view that the choice of vein matters greatly. The treatise also points repeatedly to Galen's own earlier writings, such as the Therapeutic Method and his two books against Erasistratus and the Erasistraleans of Rome, so that a reader hunting intertexts finds a dense web of allusions to Hippocratic doctrine and to the rest of Galen's corpus.
grc.galen.de_diebus_decretoriis: De diebus decretoriis ('On Critical Days') is a Greek medical treatise by Galen, printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's edition of the Opera omnia (Leipzig, 1825). Its opening argues that sudden resolutions of disease are trustworthy only when marked by ample evacuations or unmistakable crises, and it sorts crises as complete, reliable, safe, clear, or ominous according to their symptoms and outcomes. Galen holds that crises fall on determinate days, above all the seventh, which he finds complete and dependable, in contrast with the uncertain and dangerous crises of the sixth and twelfth, and supports the claim from the Hippocratic Aphorisms, Prognostics, and Epidemics and from the observations of Archigenes, Heracleides of Tarentum, Philotimus, and Diocles. For readers of intertexts, the treatise offers a dense web of Hippocratic quotation and allusion and names a chain of earlier physicians through whom critical-day doctrine was carried.
grc.galen.de_difficultate_respirationis: A short Greek medical treatise on difficulty of breathing (δυσπνοία), transmitted under the name of Galen and printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Leipzig edition of his Opera Omnia of 1824. It opens by defining dyspnoea as an impairment of respiration analogous to impaired sensation or impaired motion, then classifies its simple and compound forms according to the parts of respiration, inspiration, expiration, and the pauses between them, arguing that natural, measured breathing supplies the canon against which abnormal breathing must be judged. Throughout, the work defends the terminology familiar from Hippocrates and the ancient physicians against recent doctors who reassign terms such as 'rapid', 'slow', 'dense' and 'sparse' between the movements and pauses of breath. Readers hunting intertexts may value its explicit appeals to Hippocratic usage and its systematic treatment of Greek medical vocabulary for respiration.
grc.galen.de_elementis_ex_hippocrate: The De elementis ex Hippocrate is a Greek treatise by Galen on the elemental constitution of human nature as taught by Hippocrates, printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Claudii Galeni Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1821). Opening with the argument that sense-perception cannot be the criterion of what is truly an element, since much that is too small to be perceived is nonetheless real, the work proceeds to show that the element of bodies cannot be a single entity. Against Democritus, Epicurus, Leucippus, and the champions of one first principle under whatever name, atom, unstructured mass, or indivisible minimum, Galen sets Hippocrates' reasoning that a being of simple, uniform substance could never suffer pain, quoting Hippocratic passages in support. For readers of intertexts the treatise offers extended Hippocratic quotation alongside a systematic Galenic refutation of atomist doctrines of impassible, senseless first bodies.
grc.galen.de_foetuum_formatione: De Foetuum Formatione ('On the Formation of the Foetus') is a brief embryological treatise in Greek by the physician Galen, preserved in the Kühn edition of his Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1822). It opens by censuring philosophers who wrote on the shaping of the embryo without anatomical experience, crediting Hippocrates as the first to ground such inquiry in observation, and reproduces at length the famous case of the six-day embryo from the Hippocratic work on the nature of the child, which Galen attributes to Hippocrates himself or to his pupil Polybus. The surviving account then describes the chorion, amnion, allantois, umbilical vessels and urachus, and the blood-derived liver as the first organ formed, nourished through the vessels uniting foetus and mother. Readers of intertexts will find the treatise valuable chiefly as a learned reworking and explicit quotation of Hippocratic embryology, glossing that material in the technical vocabulary of ancient anatomy.
grc.galen.de_hirudinibus_revulsione_cucurbit: A short Greek therapeutic treatise of uncertain date attributed to Galen, printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1826), comprising compact chapters on the medicinal use of leeches, on revulsion (antispasis) as a means of diverting superfluous humours from one part of the body to another, on cupping-glasses, and on incision and scarification in place of venesection. The opening section gives practical instructions for catching and keeping bdellae, preparing the skin, detaching the animals, and treating the resulting wounds, while the later chapters set out rules for applying revulsion and cupping according to the direction of humoral flow. For readers hunting parallels, the work furnishes tidy formulae for doctrines and practices, leech therapy, revulsion, cupping, scarification, that recur throughout the Hippocratic and Galenic corpora and in later medical excerptors.
grc.galen.de_inaequali_intemperie: De Inaequali Intemperie, a short Greek prose treatise by Galen printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1824), is concerned with anōmalos dyskrasia, an uneven imbalance of the bodily qualities that affects some parts of an organism differently from others. It distinguishes such conditions of the whole body, as in certain fevers and skin diseases, from those confined to a single part, and explains how an influx of hot humour produces pain and inflammation in vessels, nerves, and membranes, with therapy by resolution of the humour or by pus formation and suppuration into neighbouring cavities. The argument quotes Hippocrates on pain accompanying change of nature and refers back to Galen's own works on mixtures and anatomical procedures, giving readers of intertexts a compact specimen of humoral pathology diction and Galenic self-reference.
grc.galen.de_instrumento_odoratus: A brief Greek physiological treatise on the organ of smell, preserved under Galen's name and printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia (1821). Opening from the observation that Greeks use osphrēsis both for the discrimination of odours and for the faculty that performs it, the argument surveys the anatomy of the nasal passages, the ethmoid bones, the membranes continuous with mouth, pharynx and trachea, and the cerebral nerves, and adduces experiments with incenses and aromatic drugs to show that odours are apprehended only in inhalation. It proceeds by elimination to place the seat of smell deeper in the head than the nasal membrane, palate, pharynx and windpipe, comparing the fitness of each sense organ to its proper object and appealing to Aristotelian terminology for bodily residues. For readers of intertexts it offers dense anatomical description and sensory doctrine of a kind readily echoed in later medical and philosophical Greek prose.
grc.galen.de_locis_affectis: De Locis Affectis (Greek Peri tōn peponthotōn topōn, 'On the Affected Parts') is a prose medical treatise by Galen, printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1824). The work teaches diagnosis by locating the affected part or region of the body, arguing that treatment alters with the seat of disease and that the physician must combine anatomy, knowledge of each organ's functions and uses, and a 'technical conjecture' standing between exact knowledge and complete ignorance. Vivid case histories, a youth at Mytilene wounded near the bladder, a child passing a stone after therapeutic shaking, bronchial tissue expelled by coughing, support the argument, alongside approving citation of Hippocrates and criticism of Archigenes, Asclepiades, and Erasistratus. For readers hunting parallels, the treatise offers a dense quarry of Galenic diagnostic terminology and explicit signposts to Galen's other writings, such as the works on the doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato and on the natural faculties.
grc.galen.de_marcore: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen, preserved in Kühn's complete Leipzig edition of his works, De Marcore defines marasmus as the destruction of a living body through dryness and distinguishes its simple form, seen in starvation, from compound forms accompanying old age and certain fevers. Galen locates the condition in the drying of the heart as the source of the whole body, sorts proper from metaphorical uses of the term, and rejects the doctrine, favored by nearly all recent doctors and philosophers, that innate heat consumes the body as a flame consumes its fuel rather than drying it by a natural sequence. The argument quotes the Hippocratic Prognostic on the visible signs of old age and the maxim that what kindled the body also destroys it, and it includes an anecdote about a philosopher of Galen's own day who promised to rear infants to be ageless and immortal. The treatise offers intertext readers a compact node of Hippocratic quotation and of the shared medical-philosophical discourse on innate heat, aging, and dryness.
grc.galen.de_morborum_differentiis: De Morborum Differentiis is a Greek medical treatise by Galen, printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's edition of the Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823). Its opening argument defines health as the due symmetry of the body's constituents and disease as their asymmetry, then establishes the simple primary diseases, excessive width or constriction of the pores of the homogeneous parts, as the elements from which all other diseases are compounded, with further distinctions reserved for the organic parts and the body as a whole. In defending this framework Galen argues against atomistic physiology, invoking the Epicurean indivisible and the anarmoi of Asclepiades. The treatise offers readers of intertexts a central locus for Galenic nosological vocabulary, νόσημα, συμμετρία, εὐκρασία and δυσκρασία, and for arguments on the definition of disease that later medical writers repeatedly rehearse.
grc.galen.de_motu_musculorum: De Motu Musculorum ('On the Motion of Muscles') is a Greek medical treatise by Galen, represented in the corpus by a short excerpt drawn from the Kühn edition of his Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1822). The passage defines the muscles as the organs of voluntary motion, explains the tendons as a mixed body partaking of both ligament and nerve, and traces the power of movement and sensation from the brain and spinal marrow through the nerves to the muscles, distinguishing psychic, deliberate movement from the involuntary motions of arteries and veins. Readers of intertexts will find here Galen's influential physiological vocabulary, 'neuron', 'tonos', 'syndesmos', and the phrase 'kath' hormēn' for voluntary action, which later medical, philosophical, and literary writers repeatedly drew upon and transformed.
grc.galen.de_nervorum_dissectione: De Nervorum Dissectione, or On the Dissection of Nerves, is a brief Greek anatomical treatise by Galen, printed among his works in Kühn's Leipzig edition. It opens from the axiom that no part of the living body possesses voluntary, 'prohairetic' motion or sensation without a nerve, whose origins lie in the brain and spinal cord, and then proceeds pair by pair through the cranial nerves: the optic nerves, the nerves moving the eyes, the third pair spread to face, jaws, teeth, and tongue and dubbed 'gustatory' as the instruments of taste, and the fourth and fifth pairs, the latter including the acoustic nerve. Several of these pairs are credited to the anatomist Marinus, whose findings Galen recounts and refines. The treatise offers a compact witness to Galenic neuroanatomy and to a vocabulary, above all the notion of prohairetic motion, that links ancient medical writing with philosophical debate about the soul's governance of the body.
grc.galen.de_parvae_pilae_exercitio: A short Greek treatise by Galen, cast as an address to Epigenes, on the merits of exercise with a small ball. The author grants that the best philosophers and physicians of old have sufficiently treated gymnastic in general, but argues that ball play surpasses hunting, running, and wrestling: it needs no costly equipment, moves every part of the body with adjustable intensity, sharpens sight and judgement, and by blending pleasure with exertion benefits soul as well as body, even drilling the seizing and guarding that lawgivers require of generals. Its playful subject, its contrasts between athletics and military virtue, and its insistence on measured exercise make the work a compact source of parallels for discussions of gymnastic, health, and the care of body and soul together. The seven lines follow Marquardt's edition of 1879.
grc.galen.de_placitis_hippocratis_et_platoni: De Placitis Hippocratis et Platonis ('On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato') is a Greek medical and philosophical treatise by Galen, preserved in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Opera Omnia printed at Leipzig in 1823 and recorded here as a single continuous passage of 150 lines. The passage argues from animal dissection and vivisection, and from the case of a boy whose heart lay exposed after part of the sternum was cut away, that the heart's left ventricle is always full of blood and that psychic pneuma resides instead in the ventricles of the brain. Chrysippus, Erasistratus, Herophilus, Aristotle, and Praxagoras are quoted and refuted by name, with Hippocratic phrasing threaded through the argument. For readers of intertexts, the work offers a dense cluster of borrowed diction and doctrine drawn from Hippocratic medicine and from earlier physicians and philosophers.
grc.galen.de_plenitudine: De Plenitudine ('On Fullness') is a brief Greek medical treatise by Galen, printed in Kühn's Leipzig edition of his Opera Omnia (1824). Its opening surveys the confusion among contemporary physicians about what plēthos, excess or plethora in the body, actually is, distinguishing those who deny innate faculties altogether, in the manner of Asclepiades and the Empiric and Methodical sects, from those who measure abundance only against the capacity of the containing vessels rather than the body's power (dynamis). Everyday evidence, the distended stomach, the laden bladder, vessels ruptured by an abundance of blood, supports the argument that fullness is relative both to the container and to the faculty that bears it. Readers of intertexts will find compact formulations of Galenic doctrines on dunameis and plethora, framed as polemic against rival medical schools, that recur throughout his larger works and later learned medical writing.
grc.galen.de_praenotione_ad_epigenem: Galen's De praenotione ad Epigenem, a Greek prose treatise on medical prognosis preserved in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1827), is framed as a discourse to Epigenes on whether and how a physician can foresee the course of a patient's disease. The work denounces practitioners who win reputation through flattery, luxury, and display rather than skill, and it invokes Hippocrates as the supreme guide for the art of prediction in medicine. Its opening narrative recounts Galen's practice in Rome, above all his anticipation of the quartan fevers of the Peripatetic philosopher Eudemus and the anatomical demonstrations subsequently requested by prominent Romans. Readers of intertexts will find in it a key witness to the rhetoric of prognostic authority inherited from Hippocratic medicine and to the ethical polemic surrounding the learned physician in Roman society.
grc.galen.de_praesagitione_ex_pulsibus: De Praesagitione ex Pulsibus (On Prognosis from the Pulse) is a Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen, printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Leipzig edition of his collected works (1825). Invoking Hippocratic authority, it argues that prognostic knowledge drawn from the pulse extends to present and past conditions as well as future ones, and it teaches how to diagnose from the pulse alterations of size, speed, and frequency, tracing them to causes such as bodily heat, leanness, exercise, bathing, wine, food, anger, and febrile crises, with an anecdote in which Galen exposes a wealthy patient secretly taking warming drugs by reading his pulse and tongue. The work repeatedly sends readers back to Galen's own earlier treatises on the diagnosis and the causes of the pulse, which it presents as prerequisites. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense junction of Hippocratic prognostic tradition and Galen's self-citing pulse corpus, together with a rich technical vocabulary of pulse terms.
grc.galen.de_propriorum_animi_cuiuslibet_aff: A short Greek ethical treatise by Galen, preserved in the Kühn edition of his Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823), composed as memoranda of the author's answers to a questioner who asked about the book he had written for Antonius the Epicurean on the ambushing and detection of one's own passions. It distinguishes errors arising from false opinion from passions arising from an irrational power in the soul that disobeys reason, enumerates the passions, anger, wrath, fear, grief, envy, excessive love or hatred, and prescribes self-examination, the honest criticism of friends, and readiness to accept correction as the means of diagnosing and curing one's own failings. Readers of intertexts will find the argument thickly woven with allusions to Plato, Aristotle, Chrysippus, Zeno, Diogenes and the Delphic 'know thyself', including Aesop's fable of the two sacks, all deployed to show why each person is blind to his own faults.
grc.galen.de_ptisana: A short Greek dietetic treatise by Galen, De ptisana sets out the preparation and therapeutic use of ptisan, the barley gruel given to the sick. Opening from the complaint that physicians administer it without defining when, how, and in what quantity it can help patients, the work discusses the selection of the best water and barley, the proper manner of boiling, and the grain's cooling, moistening, and cleansing powers, with particular attention to its value in acute fevers. Galen writes throughout as an expositor of Hippocrates, whose sayings on ptisan are quoted and glossed, so the piece serves as a compact witness to Hippocratic reception and to the vocabulary of ancient dietetics and pharmacology. The Greek is that printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823).
grc.galen.de_pulsibus_ad_tirones: A brief Greek treatise on the pulse by Galen, preserved in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1824) and addressed in its opening lines to a pupil named Teuthras, who is told that the fuller art of sphygmology is treated elsewhere. It functions as an elementary handbook: after explaining which arteries can be palpated at the body's surface, with a strong recommendation of the radial arteries at the wrist, it classifies pulse differences by the extent of diastole (large, long, high, and their opposites), by speed and slowness, by the force or faintness of the impact, by the softness or hardness of the arterial wall, by the intervals between beats, and by regularity and irregularity, including ordered irregularities and anomalies within a single beat such as the 'gazelle-like' (dorkadizon) and dicrotic pulses. The work offers readers of intertexts a compact locus for Galen's technical pulse vocabulary and for the diagnostic categories that recur throughout ancient medical writing and its later reception.
grc.galen.de_purgantium_medicamentorum_facul: 'De purgantium medicamentorum facultate' ('On the Power of Purging Medicines'), a Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen printed in Kühn's Opera omnia (Leipzig, 1826), argues that cleansing drugs possess a specific attractive faculty by which each draws out its own proper humor, against the view, associated with Asclepiades and Erasistratus, that purgatives alter whatever humors they touch. Galen invokes the silence of Hippocrates on the rival doctrine, rehearses the opponents' arguments, and challenges the sophists to clinical demonstrations, cases of jaundice and dropsy purged before witnesses in the most populous of cities, rather than to verbal disputation. For readers of intertexts, the work offers dense and recurring exposition of humor theory and drug faculties (attraction, catharsis, cholagogue and hydragogue action) that echoes across Galenic therapeutics and his polemics against the earlier medical sects.
grc.galen.de_sanitate_tuenda: De Sanitate Tuenda, a Greek treatise on the preservation of health (Ὑγιεινά) by the physician Galen, is preserved here in the Kühn edition of his Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823). The work divides the medical art into a hygienic and a therapeutic branch, defines health as a due balance of the hot, cold, wet and dry constituents of the body, traces the inevitable harms inherent in generation, growth and aging, and prescribes the regimen of food, drink, respiration and evacuation by which that balance is kept. Its opening passages refer expressly to Galen's other writings, including the treatise on the elements according to Hippocrates, and its dense humoral and physiological vocabulary offers rich material for tracing Hippocratic doctrine as refracted through Galen's language.
grc.galen.de_sectis_ad_eos_qui_introducuntur: A short Greek introductory treatise on the schools of medicine, addressed to beginners and transmitted under Galen's name in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1821). The work defines medicine by its goal, health, and sets out the two principal sects of the art: the Empiric school, which grounds the discovery of remedies in accumulated experience, observation (autopsia), recorded history, and experiment guided by similarity, and the Rationalist or Dogmatic school, which requires knowledge of the body's nature, causes, and surrounding conditions before treatment. Worked examples, such as the management of a painful, swollen part and the decision whether or not to cut a vein, show how indications are drawn from cause, strength, age, season, place, and habits. Readers hunting parallels will find here Galen's standard formulation of the experience-versus-reason debate and a dense store of technical vocabulary, peira, theōrēma, autopsia, historia, the transition by similarity, that recurs throughout ancient medical and philosophical writing.
grc.galen.de_sophismatis_seu_captionibus_pen: A short Greek treatise attributed to Galen, printed in Kühn's Opera Omnia (1827), on sophisms that arise from diction (παρὰ τὴν λέξιν). Its opening chapter follows Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations in enumerating six modes of verbal fallacy, homonymy, amphiboly, accent, combination, division, and figure of speech, and then argues, with a passing appeal to Plato, that every such fallacy reduces to ambiguity (τὸ διττόν). Readers hunting parallels will find a compact witness to the reception of Aristotelian logic within the Galenic corpus, replete with the stock equivocal examples (κύνα τεθήρακα, Ὄρος ἕστηκε) that recur throughout ancient philosophical prose.
grc.galen.de_substantia_facultatum_naturaliu: A Greek fragment by Galen on the substance of the natural faculties, printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Leipzig edition of the Claudii Galeni Opera Omnia (1822) and surviving as a single continuous passage. It opens by defending Plato against an apparent inconsistency over whether plants are ensouled, drawing on the Timaeus and observing how Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus reserved strict demonstrations for private audiences while writing for the many. It then sets out the natural faculties of attraction, retention, alteration and excretion, endorses mixture of the four elemental qualities against Empedocles' breaking of the elements into minute parts, and argues that knowledge of the soul's substance is unnecessary for medicine or for moral philosophy. Readers hunting intertexts will find dense verbal engagement with Platonic psychology and a shared vocabulary of faculties, mixtures and perception running between Galen and the philosophers he cites.
grc.galen.de_symptomatum_differentiis: De Symptomatum Differentiis (On the Differences of Symptoms) is a Greek medical treatise by Galen, printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's edition of the Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1824). Following earlier works on diseases and their causes, it takes up symptoms in order to complete an account of all conditions contrary to nature, defining health as a natural disposition productive of activity and disease as an unnatural constitution that impairs it. Galen distinguishes symptom, disease, affection (pathos and pathēma), and disposition (diathesis), and analyses primary versus incidental causation through the analogy of a row of falling mosaic tiles. The treatise appeals to Plato's use of pathēma and defends ordinary Greek medical vocabulary against disputes over names, making it useful to readers tracing the shared conceptual vocabulary of medical and philosophical prose.
grc.galen.de_temperamentis: De Temperamentis (On Mixtures), a Greek medical and philosophical prose treatise by Galen, explains how the four elementary qualities, hot, cold, dry, and wet, combine in the bodies of animals and plants, and sets out to classify all the resulting temperaments by kind and species. Composed as a sequel to the author's examination of the elements in Hippocratic doctrine, the work surveys and adjudicates the competing opinions of earlier physicians and philosophers on how many mixtures exist and which qualities can coexist in a single body. The corpus preserves the opening portion of the treatise, in which Galen distinguishes the senses of the quality terms and rehearses arguments for two- and four-mixture positions. Readers hunting intertexts will find it useful both as the classic systematic statement of the four-quality doctrine underlying Galenic physiology and for its explicit engagement with Hippocratic tradition and an allusion to Homer.
grc.galen.de_theriaca_ad_pisonem: A Greek treatise on theriac, the famous compound antidote against venomous bites and poisons, preserved in Kühn's edition of the works of Galen (Leipzig, 1827) and transmitted under his name. It is cast as a discourse addressed to a cultivated Roman named Piso, opening with praise of Andromachus, a Cretan physician and expert in drugs honoured by the emperors of an earlier reign, and with an anecdote of Piso's solicitous care for his son after a riding injury. The work goes on to celebrate the glory and efficacy of theriac, describing its testing on roosters and on condemned criminals, the alarm-driven daily use of the drug by 'the divine Marcus', and its generous distribution under the reigning emperors. Explicit appeals to Platonic doctrines of recollection and to Hippocratic maxims, along with the imperial anecdotes and pharmacological lore, make it a rewarding hunting ground for parallels in the traditions of ancient medicine, court rhetoric, and philosophical quotation.
grc.galen.de_totius_morbi_temporibus: A brief Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Totius Morbi Temporibus ('On the Times of the Whole Disease'), edited in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1824), which divides the course of a disease considered as a whole into four kairoi, genesis, increase (anabasis), acme, and decline (paracme), by analogy with the ages of living creatures. After canvassing disputes over how the acme and the beginning of a disease are to be defined, the argument applies the scheme to inflammation, fevers with and without inflammation, ulcers, ophthalmia, and catarrhal discharges, reading each stage from signs of digestion and indigestion in stools, urine, and sputum. Hippocratic maxims on intervention at the onset and crisis of illness are quoted and interpreted at length, with reference back to Galen's own discussions of crises, dyscrasia, and abnormal swellings. The passage offers a compact statement of Galenic disease-periodization and is a natural stopping point for readers tracing Hippocratic echoes and the theory of critical times in imperial medicine.
grc.galen.de_tremore_palpitatione_convulsion: A short Greek treatise on disordered bodily motion, printed among the works of Galen in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1824), devoted to tremor, palpitation, convulsion, and rigor, which it distinguishes from one another and locates in the muscles and nerves rather than, as Praxagoras held, in the arteries. The opening chapter takes issue with Praxagoras son of Nicarchus, recalls that Herophilus, once his pupil, had already refuted him, and proposes to supply what that physician left out rather than simply to censure him. Tremor is explained as the visible effect of a weakened motive power conveyed through the nerves, illustrated from old age, illness, fear, and the straining bearer of heavy burdens. Readers hunting parallels will find Galen quoting and interpreting Hippocrates, notably the dictum that standing is least helpful for sufferers of wounds and the discussion of errhipsis ('casting down') from the work on humours, making the treatise a compact node for Galen's reception of Hippocratic and Hellenistic medicine.
grc.galen.de_tumoribus_praeter_naturam: A brief Greek medical treatise by Galen, printed in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Claudii Galeni Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1824) and of uncertain date. It distinguishes swellings (onkoi) contrary to nature from ordinary natural variation in bodily bulk, and then treats inflammation at length, arguing from incision, wounds, and everyday observation that the enlargement of inflamed parts arises from an accumulation of blood rather than from pneuma or heat alone. Its dense, recurrent vocabulary of humours, pneuma, temperaments, and pathological categories makes it useful ground for readers tracing parallels across the Galenic and wider ancient medical corpus.
grc.galen.de_uteri_dissectione: A brief Greek anatomical treatise by the physician Galen, printed in Kühn's 1821 Leipzig edition of his Opera Omnia, De Uteri Dissectione treats the position, size, shape, attachments, and blood supply of the uterus, together with the membranes and vessels that envelop the embryo in pregnancy. In discussing the lateral outgrowths called 'horns' or 'plexuses', it records and criticises the rival descriptions of earlier anatomists, Herophilus, Diocles, Eudemus, Praxagoras, and Philotimus, and appeals to Hippocrates on the curvature of the spine. For readers hunting intertexts, the work matters both as evidence of Galen's anatomical terminology and as a source of reported fragments from authorities whose own writings are lost.
grc.galen.de_utilitate_respirationis: De Utilitate Respirationis, a Greek medical treatise by Galen of uncertain date, edited in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1822), asks what benefit breathing confers and proceeds through a doxographic survey of rival answers: generation of the soul with Asclepiades, strengthening of the innate heat with Praxagoras and Nicarchus, its cooling with Philistion and Diocles, nourishment with Hippocrates, and the filling of the arteries with Erasistratus. Galen then mounts a sustained refutation of Erasistratus, debating whether the heart can draw air from the lung when respiration is held, the motion of the arteries, the void, and whether animals need the substance or only the quality of inhaled air. Readers tracing intertexts will find dense quotation and paraphrase of Hippocratic and Hellenistic medical authorities, several otherwise poorly preserved, alongside characteristic vocabulary of pneuma, innate heat, and psychic respiration.
grc.galen.de_venarum_arteriarumque_dissectio: A brief Greek synopsis of the anatomy of the veins and arteries, addressed by Galen to his dear friend Antisthenes as a record of what the latter had watched being demonstrated in the body of a monkey. Opening with the tree analogy of roots, trunk, and branches ascribed to Hippocrates and the most reputable anatomists after him, the work follows the portal vein from the 'gates' of the liver to the stomach, spleen, intestines, mesentery, and omentum, then turns to the hollow vein and to the arteries springing from the heart. For readers hunting parallels it offers a compact register of ancient anatomical nomenclature, crediting the name 'aorta' to Aristotle and that of the duodenum to Herophilus, and stating the doctrine that nutriment is carried by the veins through the liver to the whole body in phrasing that recurs across Galen's anatomical writings.
grc.galen.de_victu_attenuante: A brief Greek treatise on the 'thinning' regimen, attributed to the physician Galen and edited by Kalbfleisch in the Teubner series in 1898. It opens by claiming that a diet of attenuating foods can on its own arrest chronic complaints such as kidney and joint disease, persistent breathlessness, enlarged spleen, and early epilepsy, then classifies vegetables, herbs, and seasonings, garlic, onion, cress, mustard, rocket, wild greens, salads, and relishes, by the acrid, biting, bitter, or saline impressions they make on taste and smell. Further passages treat the effect of dressing foods with vinegar, oxymel, salt, and oil, and warn that the physician must control both the occasion and the measure of use. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact witness to Galenic dietetics and to the humoral vocabulary of thinning and thickening powers that recurs throughout ancient medical writing.
grc.galen.institutio_logica: The Institutio Logica is a short Greek primer on logic attributed to the physician Galen, of uncertain date but evidently composed for readers who needed a working command of the discipline before approaching demonstrative science. It distinguishes sense-perception, thought, and demonstration, then sets out propositions, terms, axioms, and syllogisms, illustrating each with simple exempla such as the equality of Theon and Philon to Dion. Notably, the treatise preserves two sets of technical labels side by side, contrasting the usage of the 'older philosophers' with that of the 'newer', and explains terms like synemmenon and diezeugmenon for conditional and disjunctive statements. Readers of intertexts may find it valuable as a compact witness to the logical vocabulary and stock examples circulating in imperial Greek prose, and to how a non-philosophical author mediated Peripatetic and Stoic doctrine.
grc.galen.quod_optimus_medicus_sit_quoque_ph: Quod Optimus Medicus Sit Quoque Philosophus ('That the Best Physician Is Also a Philosopher') is a Greek treatise by Galen, printed in Kühn's Leipzig Opera Omnia of 1821. It opens by likening most physicians to athletes who dream of Olympic crowns without undertaking any training, and then argues that Hippocratic medicine requires all three parts of philosophy: logic for dividing diseases by species and genus, natural philosophy for knowledge of the body, and ethics in the form of contempt for wealth and mastery of the appetites. Hippocrates serves throughout as the exemplar whom doctors praise yet fail to imitate, as the argument moves over prognosis, regimen, and the corrupting pull of money. Its allusions to figures such as Phidias, Apelles, Artaxerxes, and Perdiccas, together with its programmatic union of medicine and philosophy, make it a recurring point of reference for later writing on the physician's intellectual and moral formation.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ἑλένης_ἐγκώμιον: The Encomium of Helen (Ἑλένης Ἐγκώμιον) is a short Greek epideictic speech of uncertain date by Gorgias of Leontini, composed to acquit Helen of Troy of the blame attached to her by the poets and their audiences. After surveying her divine parentage, beauty, and the gathering of suitors, it successively treats four possible causes of her voyage, the designs of Fortune, the gods, and Necessity, forcible abduction, persuasion by speech, and love, as grounds for exculpation. Its most celebrated passage presents logos as a great dynast, comparing the effect of persuasion upon the soul to that of drugs upon the body and illustrating it through poetry, incantations, and contests of philosophical argument. For readers hunting parallels it offers the locus classicus of the power-of-speech topos and a self-conscious rereading of the Helen of poetic tradition whose arguments and phrasing resurface throughout later rhetorical and literary discussion.
grc.hermogenes.progymnasmata_dub: A short Greek treatise on the preliminary rhetorical exercises (progymnasmata), of uncertain date and transmitted under the name of Hermogenes, printed among the dubia in Rabe's Teubner edition of his Opera (1913). Across some fifty-seven lines it defines and classifies the fable, the narrative, and the chreia, treating their subdivisions (Aesopic, Cyprian, Libyan, and Sybaritic fables; mythical, dramatic, historical, and political narratives) and demonstrating the elaboration (ergasia) of a chreia with stock examples from Plato, Isocrates, and Demosthenes. Readers of intertexts will find here the schoolroom vocabulary and exemplary phrasings, from Hesiod's nightingale and Archilochus' fox to Medea's betrayal of the golden fleece, through which fable and narrative were processed in ancient rhetorical education and passed into later literary use.
grc.hermogenes.περὶ_τῶν_στάσεων: A Greek treatise on rhetorical staseis, or issues, attributed to Hermogenes, concerned with how civic and forensic questions are to be divided and argued. It defines the political question, ranks the kinds of persons and acts that may be brought under examination, and catalogues both the classes of wholly untenable issues and those nearly untenable types still practised in declamation. Its hypothetical cases invoke figures from classical history and oratory, among them Pericles, Demosthenes, Alexander, Socrates, Critias and Cleon, and its framework for classifying arguments is of value to readers tracing the technical rhetoric and commonplaces that lie behind ancient speeches.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.belopoeica: A compact Greek treatise, some eighty lines in the edition of E. W. Marsden (Greek and Roman Artillery: Technical Treatises, Oxford, 1971), transmitted under the name of Hero of Alexandria and concerned with the building of artillery engines. Its preface strikingly presents mechanics as an aid to ataraxia and finds fault with earlier writers on belopoeika for recording dimensions without explaining construction or use, before distinguishing straight-spring euthytona, or scorpions, which shoot only bolts, from palintonoi engines that hurl stones as well. The surviving portion defines the art of belopoeike, traces the machines' development from hand bows, and sets out the parts, assembly, measurements, and operation of the engines in precise technical vocabulary. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense vein of military-mechanical terminology and a programmatic account of the genre's history well suited to comparison with other ancient artillery and engineering writings.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_automatis: A short Greek treatise of uncertain date by Hero of Alexandria on the construction of automata. It defines the art of automatopoietike and distinguishes two kinds of device: movable temples and altars (hypagenda) that travel of themselves to appointed places, and stationary tableaux (stata) whose doors open and shut automatically to reveal successive arrangements of figures enacting a chosen myth. The surviving discussion sets out the required level ground, light dry timber, axles, wheels, and cords, together with a falling weight trickling through millet, mustard seed, or dry sand that measures out each motion. Readers hunting intertexts may care for its picture of mechanical theatre in which a story unfolds through moving images, and for its report that the ancients called such makers thaumaturgoi, wonder-workers.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_mensuris: De Mensuris is a brief Greek manual of practical mensuration transmitted among the works attributed to Hero of Alexandria and printed alongside the Stereometrica in the fifth volume of the Teubner Heronis Alexandrini Opera. Opening with a division of measurement into linear, planar, and solid kinds, the treatise works through numerical exercises in alphabetic numerals that measure pits, wells, squared and rounded stones and timbers, columns, walls, drums, vaulted chambers, and towers, and that compute the grain capacity of ships and the filling rates of cisterns, using feet, dactyls, cubits, modii, artabas, and other ancient units. Its problem types, especially the cistern filled by inflows working at different rates, belong to a didactic metrological tradition with far-reaching parallels in later practical arithmetic and geometry, making the work a useful witness for readers tracing the afterlife of Heronian measurement problems.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.mechanicorum_fragment: Attributed to Hero of Alexandria, the Mechanicorum Fragmenta comprise a short set of Greek prose fragments on mechanics, printed from the Teubner edition of Schmidt and Nix (1900). The surviving passages address the problem of moving a given weight with a given force by mounting toothed drums on parallel axles, with worked numerical examples in talents that reduce, for instance, the drawing of a thousand talents to the strength of a single child. In doing so they recall the doctrine of the five powers, wedge, lever, screw, pulley, and wheel-and-axle, and invoke the saying ascribed to Archimedes that, given a place to stand, he would move the earth. For readers hunting parallels, the fragments offer a Greek technical witness to the currency of that Archimedean boast and to mechanical problem-formulations circulating under Hero's name.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.metrica: Metrica, a Greek treatise on mensuration by Hero of Alexandria and of uncertain date, opens with a preface tracing geometry from the survey and division of land to the measurement of solid bodies, crediting Eudoxus and Archimedes with the decisive advances and recalling the latter's theorems on the sphere and cylinder. The opening chapters fix conventions for reckoning areas and volumes in cubits, feet, and fractions thereof, and then demonstrate rules for the areas of rectangles and of right-angled, isosceles, and scalene triangles through worked numerical examples. Readers hunting parallels will find in it a dense store of Greek mathematical terminology and formulaic exposition, including paraphrases of celebrated results on the relation of the sphere to its enclosing cylinder that could echo elsewhere in Greek geometrical prose.
grc.heronis_alexandrini.liber_geeponicus_sp: The Liber Geeponicus is a short Greek handbook of geometry and mensuration transmitted under the name of Hero of Alexandria and printed among his geometric and stereometric remains in Hultsch's Berlin edition of 1864; its date is uncertain. It proceeds largely in question-and-answer form, first defining plane and solid figures such as the circle, triangles, quadrilaterals, gnomon and trapezia in terms that track the definitions of Euclid's Elements, then working practical problems that compute the areas, diagonals and heights of squares, rectangles and right triangles in body-based measures such as the finger, palm, span, foot, cubit and orguia. The printed text cross-refers throughout to Hero's Definitions and Geometrica, so readers hunting parallels will find it a convenient node for tracing the reuse of Euclidean definitions and Heroic mensurational routines within the Greek geometrical tradition.
grc.hesiod.works_and_days: A didactic poem in dactylic hexameters, running to 829 lines, of uncertain date and attributed to Hesiod. Opening with an invocation of the Muses and the famous distinction between two kinds of Strife, it addresses Perses over their disputed inheritance and recounts the myths of Prometheus and the fashioning of Pandora before passing into precepts on labour, farming, seafaring, and piety, together with a calendar of lucky and unlucky days, the myth of the ages of mankind, and the fable of the hawk and nightingale. For readers of intertexts it stands among the most generative of archaic Greek poems, supplying Pandora, the ages of man, gnomic maxims, and a template of divine justice that later epic, lyric, and prose writers continually echo and rework.
grc.hippocrates.coa_praesagia: The Coa Praesagia (Coan Prognostics) is a Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and edited by Émile Littré in his 1846 Paris edition of the complete works. Arranged in two books of short numbered judgements, it catalogues the signs by which the physician may foretell crisis, relapse, or death in acute disease, listing rigors, sweats, fevers, pains, urinary changes, and disturbances of mind and colour. Its aphoristic formulas and symptom-lists stand close to the Prorrheticon, the Prognostic, and the Aphorisms, making it a key witness for readers tracing shared prognostic diction across the Corpus and the medical writing that followed it.
grc.hippocrates.de_alimento: De Alimento (On Aliment), a Greek prose treatise of uncertain date attributed to Hippocrates, belongs to the Hippocratic Corpus. In barely fifty-five lines of dense, antithetical aphorisms it surveys the nature and power of nutriment, its assimilation by flesh, bone, vein, artery and marrow, the place of breath and heat in nourishment, the sympatheia of the body's parts, and the recognition and treatment of disease through diet, drugs and external applications. Its gnomic paradoxes, in which nutriment is at once food and drug, physis is one and many, and the beginning of all things is their end, rank among the most compressed formulations in the Corpus. For readers hunting parallels, the work offers rich points of contact with other Hippocratic treatises in aphoristic style and with Greek philosophical writing on nature, unity and causation.
grc.hippocrates.de_arte: De Arte (On the Art) is a short Greek prose treatise attributed to Hippocrates, printed among his works in Émile Littré's Oeuvres complètes d'Hippocrate (Paris, Baillière, 1849). Of uncertain date, it mounts a sustained defense of medicine as a genuine technē against detractors who disparage the healing arts, arguing that recoveries achieved through regimen, drugs, or diet, even without a physician, testify to the art's existence, and that the fixed distinction between what helps and what harms implies a rational method rather than mere chance. Composed in an adversarial, epideictic style that rehearses and refutes opposing arguments, it offers readers of intertexts a hub for verbal and thematic parallels concerning technē, tuchē, and the status of the arts within the Hippocratic Corpus and classical rhetorical prose at large.
grc.hippocrates.de_genitura: De Genitura (On Generation) is a short prose treatise attributed to Hippocrates in the file and of uncertain date, preserved in the Hippocratic Corpus as printed in Littré's Oeuvres complètes. Opening with the claim that 'law rules all things' (Νόμος μὲν πάντα κρατύνει), it argues for pangenesis, that seed is secreted as the strongest and richest portion of the body's fluid from every part of the body, and then traces the seed's route through the spinal marrow and kidneys, explains nocturnal emission, the sterility of eunuchs, the delayed menstruation of virgins, female pleasure and secretion in intercourse, conception, and the determination of a child's sex by the stronger of two seeds supplied by both parents. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a compact early Greek account of heredity, sexual difference, and generation, against which later medical and philosophical theories of likeness, seed, and descent define themselves.
grc.hippocrates.de_humoribus: Περὶ χυμῶν (De Humoribus, On Humours) is a very brief Greek medical treatise of uncertain date, transmitted under Hippocrates' name in the Hippocratic Corpus and printed in Émile Littré's Oeuvres complètes (Paris, 1846). It sets out diagnostic and therapeutic doctrine concerning the humours: their colours, the upward or downward direction of their flows, crises and critical days, the timing of purges, and the signs by which disease is judged, including dreams, odours and bodily discharges, before closing with remarks on periodic fevers and metastases, such as the coughs and quinsies of the patients at Perinthus. Its material recurs in other treatises of the Corpus, notably the Regimen and the Prorrhetics, which makes it a useful node for readers tracing verbal parallels and borrowed passages across Hippocratic writings.
grc.hippocrates.de_liquidorum_usu: A short Greek medical treatise on the therapeutic use of liquids, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, preserved in Émile Littré's Oeuvres complètes d'Hippocrate (Paris, Baillière, 1849) under the Latin title De Liquidorum Usu, 'On the Use of Liquids'. In seven compact sections it treats fresh water, seawater, and vinegar, explaining how drinking, pouring, and bathing with hot or cold liquids act on different parts of the body, which conditions they relieve or aggravate, and how the safe degree of each application must be judged case by case. Its terse, aphoristic style and its systematic opposition of heating and cooling, moistening and drying qualities make it a productive source of verbal and doctrinal parallels for readers tracing intertexts in Hippocratic and later ancient medical writing.
grc.hippocrates.de_natura_hominis: A Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, preserved in the Hippocratic Corpus and printed in Émile Littré's Oeuvres complètes d'Hippocrate. It opens with a polemic against thinkers who reduce human nature to a single element, air, fire, water, or earth, naming Melissus as a target, and argues instead that the body contains blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile, whose proper mixture yields health and whose displacement or imbalance causes disease. As the founding statement of humoural physiology and an early witness to the quarrel between medicine and Presocratic philosophy, it is a central locus for intertexts in later medical, philosophical, and literary writing.
grc.hippocrates.de_salubri_diaeta: A short Greek medical treatise on regimen attributed to Hippocrates and printed by Émile Littré in his Oeuvres complètes d'Hippocrate (Paris, 1849), of uncertain date. It opens with seasonal prescriptions for laypeople, recommending abundant food and unmixed wine in winter, softer fare and diluted drink toward summer, with gradual transitions between regimes. Further sections distinguish fleshy from lean body types and youth from age, prescribe exercise, bathing, and clothing by season, give regimens for losing and gaining weight, direct the use of emetics and clysters, and close with dietetic rules for infants and women. For readers tracing intertexts it offers a compact instance of Greek regimen literature's seasonal and humoral logic, with phrasing and classifications that recur in later dietetic prose.
grc.hippocrates.praeceptiones: A brief Greek medical treatise transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus under the name of Hippocrates, of uncertain date and authorship. The Praeceptiones ('Precepts') opens with the celebrated aphorism on the relation of time (chronos) and the opportune moment (kairos) and argues that medicine is mastered through practice and observation rather than through plausible reasoning alone. Subsequent sections take up the physician's fees, urging generosity toward poor and foreign patients, and counsel cooperation among practitioners instead of rivalry and displays of cleverness. Readers hunting parallels will find here an early and influential pairing of kairos with chronos, a programmatic defence of experience (empeiria) over mere argument, and ethical commonplaces about the medical art that echo through later Greek and Latin writing.
grc.hippocrates.prognosticon: The Prognosticon is a Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic corpus, transmitted under Hippocrates' name, of uncertain date, and printed in Émile Littré's edition of the Hippocratic writings (Paris, 1840). Opening with the claim that the best physician practises prognosis, declaring to patients the present, past and future course of disease, it sets out the signs by which outcomes in acute illnesses are to be foretold: the characteristic changes of the face, the eyes and their secretions, the posture of the sick, the plucking of the hands at bedclothes, the quality of breathing, and the kinds of sweat, together with the critical days on which fevers resolve. Its catalogue of fatal signs and its assumption that disease follows a predictable course made it a model for later prognostic writing, and its vocabulary offers parallels for ancient discussions of prognosis, the limits of the medical art, and the presence of the divine in disease.
grc.hippocrates.vectiarius: A short Greek surgical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus under the Latin title Vectiarius, printed in Émile Littré's nineteenth-century edition, of uncertain date and authorship. Opening with an osteological survey of the nature of bones and joints, it proceeds to practical instructions for treating broken ribs, injured ears, dislocated jaws, and dislocated shoulders, with detailed methods of reduction, manipulation, and bandaging. Its dense technical anatomical vocabulary and its explicit allusion to a Homeric phrase concerning the ox's shoulder joint make it a source of interest for readers tracing verbal echoes between ancient medical prose and epic poetry.
grc.isidore_of_charax.mansiones_parthicae: The Mansiones Parthicae (Stathmoi Parthikoi) is a brief Greek itinerary attributed to Isidore of Charax and of uncertain date, preserved in Müller's Geographi Graeci Minores. It records the overland route from the crossing of the Euphrates at Zeugma through Mesopotamia and Babylonia to Seleucia on the Tigris, and thence through Media, Hyrcania and the eastern satrapies as far as Arachosia, listing stations, villages, fortified posts, cities, temples and royal treasuries with distances measured in schoeni. Along the way it preserves notices of Macedonian and Alexandrian foundations, of Parthian royal history, and of sanctuaries such as those of Artemis and Anaitis, and the edition appends a fragment on pearl fishing in the Persian Gulf quoted from Isidore by Athenaeus. For readers of intertexts, the work offers dense toponymy and geographical lore of a kind echoed throughout the classical and late-antique geographical tradition.
grc.isocrates.letters: A collection of nine Greek letters transmitted under the name of the Athenian orator Isocrates, printed in Hercher's Epistolographi Graeci (Paris, 1873). The correspondence addresses powerful figures of the Greek world in the manner of political advice literature: the opening letter counsels a ruler on the salvation of the Hellenes, on the dangers of reckless heroism in war, and on the worth of honest admonition over flattery, and the remaining epistles continue in the same vein of moral and political exhortation. The authenticity of the individual letters varies, but the collection closely reworks the themes, diction, and self-presentation of Isocrates' speeches, and readers tracing parallels will find in the epistles a condensed echo of his stylistic habits and recurring ideas.
grc.libanius.declamations: Libanius' Declamations, preserved in the Teubner edition of Richard Foerster (Leipzig, 1913), comprise nearly 2,900 lines of Greek prose in the form of imaginary forensic speeches composed for rhetorical display. The opening declamation casts its speaker as a friend of Socrates pleading before the Athenian jury at his trial, countering Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon, arguing that the jurors' oath binds them to judge from the facts rather than from hostility, and defending a philosopher who himself declines the arts of courtroom persuasion. The speeches reinvent situations drawn from classical Greek history and legend, so that readers hunting intertexts will find dense allusion throughout to Plato, the Attic orators, and the institutions of the Athenian courts.
grc.libanius.orations: The Orations of Libanius are Greek rhetorical speeches transmitted in Richard Foerster's Teubner edition (Lipsiae, 1913). The corpus opens with an autobiographical oration in which the speaker weighs rival judgements on his fortune, narrating his childhood in a leading family of Antioch, the early deaths of his parents, and the consuming passion for eloquence that carried him from rural schooling to the lecture rooms of the sophists. Composed in ornate classicising prose that constantly recalls earlier literature, the speeches invoke Homer's defenders at Pylos and Aristophanes' Acharnians among their models, and so offer readers of intertexts a dense record of how a Greek orator reworked the poetic and prose inheritance of earlier centuries.
grc.libanius.orations_1-11: Orations 1-11 gathers the opening speeches of Libanius, a Greek rhetorician of Antioch, printed here from Richard Foerster's Teubner edition. The first oration is his autobiography, in which he corrects those who call him either the most fortunate or the most wretched of men by narrating his family history at Antioch, his orphaned childhood, and his ardour for the study of rhetoric. Because Libanius frames his life through allusion to earlier Greek literature, citing Aristophanes' Acharnians outright and recalling his memorization of the ancient orators, the autobiography offers rich pickings for readers tracing intertextual parallels.
grc.lucian.abdicatus: Abdicatus (The Disinherited) is a brief Greek forensic declamation by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, spoken in the persona of a son cast off by a father subject to fits of madness. Trained as a physician abroad, the speaker returned and cured the father, only to be disinherited a second time for refusing to practise medicine at the father's command rather than by the rules of the art, and the speech pleads his case before the judges. A reader hunting parallels will find here the stock topoi of the disinheritance trial, paternal anger, filial obedience, madness and its cure, set out in Lucian's characteristic blend of courtroom rhetoric and medical imagery.
grc.lucian.adversus_indoctum_et_libros_multo: A brief Greek satirical invective of uncertain date by Lucian of Samosata, directed against an uneducated man who amasses many fine books in the hope of appearing learned. The speaker mocks the collector's inability to tell valuable old volumes from worthless ones, whether of Callimachus, Demosthenes, or Thucydides, and argues that ownership without paideia is futile, illustrating the point with exempla such as Ismenias's seven-talent purchase of auloi at Corinth, the bow of Heracles useless without a Philoctetes, and Sulla's shipment of books from Athens to Italy. The ridicule culminates in proverbial hits, including the ape with golden coins and the question 'what has a dog to do with a bath-house?'. Readers tracing intertexts will find a compact quarry of mythological exempla, proverbs, and allusions bearing on ancient book collecting and attitudes to education.
grc.lucian.anacharsis: Anacharsis, or On Gymnastics, is a short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, printed here from Karl Jacobitz's Teubner edition of 1896. It stages a conversation between the legendary Scythian sage Anacharsis and the Athenian lawgiver Solon: watching youths wrestle in the mud, box, and leap in the dust of the gymnasium of the Lyceum, Anacharsis demands to know what good such violent exercise can do, and Solon answers with a defence of Greek athletics, its contests, and its prizes, from Panhellenic crowns of pine, celery, and laurel to the Panathenaic olive oil. The exchange turns the outsider's ethnographic gaze, familiar from Herodotean accounts of Anacharsis in Scythia, onto Greek athletic custom, while its Solonic interlocutor and question-and-answer form recall Platonic dialogue. Readers tracing intertexts will find it a compact locus for descriptions of the gymnasium, palaestra, and pankration, and for arguments over the worth of toil, wounds, and glory in competitive sport.
grc.lucian.bacchus: A brief Greek prose piece attributed to Lucian of Samosata, here from Jacobitz's 1896 Teubner edition and of uncertain date. The speaker mounts a mock-defence of Dionysus, retelling the god's campaign against the Indians, whose scorn for his army of Maenads, Satyrs, Silenus and Pan ends in their own capture, and then likens readers who dismiss new and satirical writing to those Indians, closing with an Indian grove of vines watered by springs named for Silenus, Pan and Satyrs. Students of intertexts will find in it a compact witness to the Dionysiac Indian-campaign tradition and to Lucianic self-conscious play with symposiastic, comic and satyr-choric imagery.
grc.lucian.calumniae_non_temere_credundum: A short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, arguing that slander (diabolē) must not be lightly believed.
