The speaker laments the blindness that ignorance works in human affairs, points to disasters of tragic legend such as the houses of Labdacus and Pelops as material furnished by misjudgment, and recounts how the painter Apelles of Ephesus, falsely accused before Ptolemy of joining a conspiracy at Tyre, escaped the charge and later depicted Calumny in an allegory attended by Ignorance, Suspicion, Envy, Deceit, Repentance and Truth. The closing lines turn to an analysis of slander under three roles, like the persons of a comedy: the slanderer, the slandered, and the one to whom the slander is told. Readers tracing intertexts will find here the celebrated ekphrasis of Apelles' painting of Calumny and Lucian's habitual play with tragic and comic material.
grc.lucian.cataplus: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, whose title denotes the voyage down to Hades; it runs to only twenty-eight lines and is presented here from Karl Jacobitz's Teubner edition of 1896. The scene is set at the edge of the underworld, where Clotho and Charon chafe at delays while Hermes drives down a flock of the newly dead, including a tyrant who has tried to slip away from his allotted fate. With its cast of Clotho, Charon, Hermes, and Aeacus, the piece turns the traditional furniture of the descent to Hades, the ferryman's obol, the counting of souls, the thread of the Fates, into farce at the expense of the reluctant dead. Its compact parody of underworld convention makes it a useful touchstone for readers tracing Charon scenes and katabasis motifs across ancient and later literature.
grc.lucian.de_domo: De Domo ('The Hall') is a short rhetorical piece in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, edited from Jacobitz's Teubner text. It argues that a magnificent private hall deserves more than mute admiration: its proportion, light, and restrained ornament naturally invite eloquence, so that praise spoken within the building becomes part of its beauty, unlike the ostentatious but speechless luxury of Persian palaces. The argument unfolds through vivid exempla, Alexander bathing in the Cydnus, Telemachus astounded by the house of Menelaus, Socrates conversing with Phaedrus beneath the plane tree by the Ilissus, making the work a compact test case for how a trained rhetorician redeploys Homeric and Platonic scenes and for ancient thinking on the relation between spectacle, judgement, and speech.
grc.lucian.de_luctu: A brief satirical piece in Greek prose by Lucian of Samosata, De Luctu (On Mourning) ridicules the notions of death and the underworld that the many derive from Homer, Hesiod and the other mythmakers, together with the funerary customs founded upon them. The speaker surveys the imagined geography of Hades, Pluto and Persephone, the Acherusian lake and its ferryman, Cerberus, the judges Minos and Rhadamanthys, the Elysian plain and the torments of Tantalus, before turning to the obol placed in the mouth of the dead, the washing, anointing and garlanding of the corpse, and the theatrical lamentation of the survivors. Its dense reworking of epic underworld material, invoked through returnees such as Alcestis, Protesilaus, Theseus and Odysseus, makes the work a rewarding site for tracing Homeric and Hesiodic motifs and their ironic reuse in Greek prose.
grc.lucian.de_mercede: A short Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, preserved under the title De Mercede ('On Salaries') and printed in Jacobitz's Teubner edition of 1896. The speaker warns his friend Timocles against taking salaried positions in wealthy households, cataloguing the servility, humiliations, and loss of freedom suffered by philosophers, grammarians, rhetors, and musicians who live as paid companions of the rich, an argument elaborated through sustained metaphors of shipwrecked survivors telling their tales and fish greedily swallowing a baited hook. Educated men, the dialogue insists, degrade themselves more than common flatterers by accepting such terms, and should rather reclaim their independence. For readers of intertexts, the piece offers a compact treatment of patronage, parasitism, and flattery that resonates with Greek comic and philosophical traditions and with Lucian's wider satiric corpus.
grc.lucian.de_sacrificiis: A brief satirical essay by Lucian of Samosata, presented in Jacobitz's Teubner edition of 1896, De Sacrificiis ridicules the logic of Greek sacrifice, imagining gods who sell health, wealth, kingship, and safe return for the price of cattle, hecatombs, or a royal maiden. The speaker catalogs scandalous divine biographies drawn from epic and mythographic tradition: Chryses extorting Apollo's plague from Agamemnon, Artemis' murderous pique at Oeneus' omitted offering, Apollo's servitude to Admetus and Laomedon, Cronus' castration of Uranus and swallowing of his children, Zeus' goat-nursed infancy and shape-shifting amours, Hera's parthenogenetic Hephaestus, and Prometheus crucified on the Caucasus with the eagle feeding on his liver. At barely fifteen lines in this edition the piece is slight, but it packs a dense repertory of Homeric and theogonic allusions into a mocking, rationalist argument, and readers hunting intertexts will find archaic myth openly reworked to subversive effect.
grc.lucian.de_saltatione: The De Saltatione of Lucian of Samosata is a Greek prose dialogue in which the speaker Lycinus answers his friend Crato's attack on pantomime dancing, rebutting the charge that attendance at such spectacles is unmanly and disgraceful. Lycinus defends the art as no recent invention but a practice coeval with the primordial Eros, visible in the ordered dance of the stars, and argues that it delights and educates its viewers, shaping the souls of those who watch. The opening exchange is dense with allusive material: Homer's lotus-eaters and Sirens from the Odyssey, a quoted Homeric line on the joy of seeing, and mentions of Plato, Aristotle, and Chrysippus alongside mythological dancers such as Phaedra and Rhodopis. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a compact example of Lucian's dialogic irony and a rich repository of references bearing on music, theater, and the Greek pantomime tradition.
grc.lucian.de_syria_dea: The De Syria Dea, a Greek prose treatise of uncertain date attributed to Lucian of Samosata, purports to be an account written by an Assyrian narrator of the great sanctuary of Hera at Hierapolis near the Euphrates and of the sanctuaries, rites, and myths of Syria and Phoenicia. Composed in an artificial Ionic dialect that deliberately imitates Herodotus, it describes temples at Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos, the Adonis rites and the annual reddening of the river Adonis, and the sweating, speaking cult statues and treasures of the Hierapolitan temple. Readers hunting intertexts will find a sustained Herodotean pastiche whose autopsy claims, ethnographic formulae, and aetiological stories rework material parallel to Herodotus' Egyptian logos while preserving traditions about Astarte, Europa, Osiris, and Cinyras.
grc.lucian.deorum_consilium: A brief Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, staged as an assembly of the gods convoked by Zeus to weigh complaints against unworthy newcomers. Momus, the licensed fault-finder, denounces the promotion of mortals to Olympus, dwelling on Dionysus and his rustic retinue of Pan, Silenus and the Satyrs, while Zeus shields Asclepius and Heracles from censure and is himself implicated through his amours and shape-changings. Rich in Homeric diction and parodic of the epic council scene, the piece offers a compact satirical reworking of mythological deification that repays readers tracing echoes of Homer and the comic tradition of divine censure.
grc.lucian.dialogi_marini: Dialogi Marini ('Dialogues of the Sea Gods') is a series of short satirical prose dialogues in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, staged among the deities and monsters of the sea. Its scenes include the teasing of the musical but monstrous Cyclops Polyphemus by the Nereids Galatea and Doris, the Cyclops' complaint to Poseidon about his blinding by Odysseus, and Alpheus' account of his love for the Sicilian spring Arethusa. Lucian recasts Homeric epic, above all Odyssey 9, and the bucolic Cyclops of Theocritus into witty Attic prose dialogue, so the work offers valuable evidence for the ancient comic reception and parody of epic and pastoral themes.
grc.lucian.dialogi_mortuorum: Lucian of Samosata's Dialogi Mortuorum, presented here in Jacobitz's Teubner text, is a series of short dramatic dialogues set in the Greek underworld, where Diogenes, Menippus, Pluto and other figures converse with the newly dead. The scenes turn on death as the great leveller: Croesus, Midas and Sardanapallus lament their vanished wealth and luxury, philosophers quarrel to no purpose, the beautiful and strong are reduced to bare skulls, and even oracular heroes such as Trophonius and Amphilochus are exposed to Cynic mockery. The opening exchange between Diogenes and Polydeuces already shows the work's pointed reuse of the Delphic 'know thyself' and its relish for taunting the powerful. For readers of intertexts, the dialogues rework Homeric and tragic katabasis material within a Cynic diatribe framework, making them a natural comparand for underworld scenes and for the later tradition of dialogues of the dead.
grc.lucian.dipsades: A brief Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, the Dipsades is a mock-didactic account of the burning sands of southern Libya, the hunting expeditions of the Garamantes, and the region's monstrous serpents, culminating in the dipsas whose bite breeds an unquenchable thirst that no drink can relieve. The narrator supplements his description with an epitaph likening the snake's victim to Tantalus and the Danaids, then closes by professing a rivalrous thirst of his own, framing the performance as an emulation of the poet Nicander and capping it with a quotation from Plato that there is no satiety of the beautiful. Its playful reworking of Nicandrean theriology together with Tantalean and Danaid imagery makes it a compact stop for readers tracing how Lucian's satire metabolizes didactic poetry and mythological topos. Running to only nine lines in Jacobitz's Teubner edition, it stands among the shortest of the pieces transmitted under Lucian's name.
grc.lucian.electrum: A very short Greek satirical piece by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a first-person anecdote in which the narrator converses with local boatmen. He recounts how the poets' tale that poplars on the Eridanus weep drops of amber for their brother Phaethon drew him up that river, where he was laughed at for his credulity, and how the same boatmen disabused him of the companion myth of melodious swans, Apollo's transformed retainers, singing on the banks; the closing address contrasts the plain, myth-free prose of the author with poetic discourse that drips gold and sings more sweetly than swans. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a compact comic reception of the Phaethon legend and the swan-song topos, as well as a programmatic statement of Lucian's stance toward poetic mythmaking.
grc.lucian.eunuchus: A brief comic dialogue in thirteen lines, the Eunuchus is by the satirist Lucian of Samosata and stages a conversation between Lycinus and Pamphile. Lycinus recounts a courtroom farce in which two Peripatetic philosophers, the aged eristic Diocles and Bagoas, a eunuch, disputed succession to a handsome royal stipend until Diocles argued that a eunuch must be barred from philosophy, its festivals and its prizes. Bagoas replies by summoning Aspasia, Diotima and Thargelia as advocates, while the judges weigh whether a deep beard rather than a blameless life is the true credential of a sage. Readers hunting parallels will find Lucian's mockery of the philosophical schools, a Homeric tag on prizes, and comic play with the paradox of the eunuch as a creature counting neither with doves nor ravens.
grc.lucian.gallus: Gallus, or The Cock, is a brief comic Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, printed in the third volume of Jacobitz's Teubner edition. Its scene is a dawn quarrel in which the poor cobbler Micyllus curses his rooster for rousing him from a dream of wealth, only for the bird to speak and reveal itself as the reincarnated soul of Pythagoras, arguing that the sleeping rich man is less blessed than the penniless dreamer. In the course of the exchange the rooster adduces Homer's prophetic horse Xanthus, the tale of Ares' youthful favourite transformed into a cock for failing to guard the assignations of Ares and Aphrodite, and Pythagorean doctrines of transmigration, silence, and abstention from beans. The dialogue's dense cluster of Homeric, mythographic, and Pythagorean allusions makes it a rewarding point of comparison for ancient speaking-animal tales and for satirical treatments of wealth and poverty.
grc.lucian.harmonides: Attributed to Lucian of Samosata and of uncertain date, Harmonides is a very brief prose dialogue in which the aulos-player Harmonides asks his celebrated teacher Timotheus how a performer may win renown, and is told that the approval of a few expert judges brings the applause of the many far more surely than direct appeal to crowded theatres. The anecdote closes with Harmonides dying, uncrowned, while competing at the Dionysia, after which a speaker applies Timotheus' maxim to orators who seek public fame and to the judgement of audiences. For readers of intertexts the piece is valuable for its dense musical lore, from the technique of auletes and the characters of the Phrygian, Lydian, Dorian and Ionian harmoniai to figures such as Marsyas, Olympus and the Boeotian musician-poet Timotheus, and it stands among Lucian's shorter dialogues on fame, expert judgement and the favour of the powerful.
grc.lucian.hercules: A brief Greek prose piece by the satirist Lucian of Samosata, transmitted among his minor essays and printed here from Jacobitz's Teubner edition. It is an ecphrasis of a painting of Heracles as the Celts' Ogmios: a silver-haired old man whose pierced tongue draws after him a delighted crowd bound to it by fine chains of gold and amber, an image a Greek-speaking Celt explains as an allegory of Logos, whose persuasive speech rather than brute force performs the god's labours. The ending turns the emblem on the author himself, justifying his return to public declamation in old age with allusions to Homeric and lyric poetry. Readers hunting parallels will find in it a compact source for the allegorised Hercules Ogmios, for the iconography of eloquence that binds hearers to the speaker's tongue, and for playful redeployments of Homeric formulas about winged and honeyed speech.
grc.lucian.hermotimus: A short Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, in which Lycinus gently quizzes his friend Hermotimus about the twenty years of study and toil he has devoted to following his philosophical teacher up the long, steep road towards virtue and happiness. Beneath the banter lies an ironic assault on the philosophical schools, whose professors promise an ascent to blessedness that no pupil can ever be sure of completing within a lifetime. Readers hunting parallels will find the exchange thick with allusion, reworking Hesiod's rough uphill path to Virtue, Homer's golden chain let down by Zeus, and the Coan physician's maxim that life is short while art is long.
grc.lucian.hippias: A short Greek encomium by Lucian of Samosata, the rhetorician and satirist of the Roman imperial period, in praise of a contemporary engineer named Hippias. After arguing that true wisdom lies in matching words with deeds, the speaker surveys celebrated sages and technicians, Epeius with the wooden horse, Thales diverting the Halys for Croesus, Archimedes and Sosistratus of Cnidus, before giving an extended ekphrasis of Hippias' bath complex, from its levelled site and foundations to its plunge baths, decoration, lighting and orientation to the winds. Readers of intertexts will find Homeric and Herodotean exempla, a quoted Pindaric maxim on the far-shining face of a work's beginning, and a compact example of the rhetoric of praise applied to technical achievement.
grc.lucian.iudicium_vocalium: A brief comic pleading by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a courtroom speech in which the letter Sigma prosecutes Tau before the seven vowels sitting as judges, accusing it of violently usurping Sigma's place in words and driving it out of names, verbs, conjunctions, and prepositions. Personified letters from Lambda and Rho to Gamma, Kappa, Delta, Theta, and Zeta figure as fellow litigants and victims, and the grievance turns on the doublet of Attic -tt- spellings against -ss-, with jokes about the alphabet's invention by Cadmus, Palamedes, or Simonides. The miniature parodies Athenian forensic oratory in only a dozen lines of prose. Readers hunting intertexts will find it a locus for the personification of grammatical entities and for Lucianic mock-legal comedy echoed in later alphabetical satire.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_confuatus: A brief Greek prose dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, the Iuppiter Confutatus ('Zeus Cross-Examined') stages an interrogation in which the Cynic Cyniscus quizzes Zeus himself on whether all things come to pass by fate. Drawing on Homeric and Hesiodic material - the Moirai, Heimarmene, Tyche, and Zeus's threat in the assembly of the gods to suspend everything from a golden chain - the speakers reduce the gods to dependents of Fate and expose prayer and sacrifice as futile if nothing can be altered. Its tight compression of Homeric allusion, Cynic questioning, and debate over determinism and providence makes the dialogue a rich quarry for intertextual echoes.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_tragoedus: A short Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, printed in Jacobitz's Teubner edition of 1896, in which Zeus, alarmed by a public debate on providence between the Stoic Timocles and the Epicurean Damis, fears the gods' honours are at stake and resolves to summon a divine assembly. The opening scene travesties tragic and epic diction, splicing parodied iambics and Homeric lines into comic dialogue, while Hermes' proclamation to the gods is built from borrowed epic verses and the arriving deities are seated according to the material worth of their statues. Dense quotation and parody of Homer and of tragedy, with Euripides explicitly invoked, make the work a rich hunting ground for epic and tragic echoes and for Lucian's comic exploitation of philosophical argument.
grc.lucian.marcrobii: The Macrobii ('Long-Lived'), a short Greek paradoxographical piece attributed to Lucian of Samosata and of uncertain date, is framed as a birthday offering to a dedicatee named Quintillus and promises a survey of men and whole peoples who reached extreme old age through diet, exercise and piety. Its brief catalogue runs from mythical figures such as Nestor and Tiresias through eastern sages and nations like the Brahmans, Magi, Seres and Chaldaeans to Roman kings including Numa Pompilius and Servius Tullius and rulers such as Arganthonius, Agathocles and Hiero. For readers of intertexts it serves as a compact repertory of longevity notices, citing Homer, tragedy, Herodotus, Anacreon, Theopompus and Timaeus among its authorities and gathering ethnic lore useful for tracing parallels in later rhetorical and paradoxographical prose.
grc.lucian.muscae_encomium: The Muscae Encomium is a brief Greek prose satire attributed to Lucian of Samosata and of uncertain date, in which the lowly fly receives a deadpan laudatio in the paradoxical-encomium tradition. Its twelve lines catalogue the insect's winged anatomy, melodious flight, feeding habits, and sexual licence, its guerrilla warfare with the spider, and its resurrection from ashes, culminating in the claim that the fly proves the soul immortal. Readers hunting intertexts will find the piece dense with Homeric material, since Homer's praise of heroic boldness and his similes are reworked around the fly, and with a knowing echo of Plato's argument for the immortality of the soul via the myth of Hermotimus of Clazomenae.
grc.lucian.navigium: A short Greek dialogue of Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, in which Timolaos, Lycinus, and Samippos recall their excursion to the Peiraieus to view a colossal Alexandrian grain ship. The conversation dwells on a beautiful youth glimpsed aboard, the vessel's extraordinary dimensions and Isis-headed ornament, and the master's tale of a storm driven past Sidon and the Chelidonian islands. The speakers themselves invoke Thucydides on early Greek luxury, and the detailed ship ekphrasis and technical nautical vocabulary make the piece a rewarding point of comparison for readers tracing maritime description and Lucianic dialogue form across Greek prose.
grc.lucian.necyomantia: A brief Greek dialogue attributed to the satirist Lucian of Samosata, the Necyomantia forms a companion piece to Lucian's Menippus: Menippus, freshly returned from the world of the dead, tells a friend why he descended to Hades to consult the seer Tiresias, what he saw there, and what verdicts the dead have passed against the wealthy. The prose conversation is punctuated by rhapsodic verse, since Menippus, having met Homer and Euripides in the underworld, cannot help paraphrasing epic and tragic lines, while his interlocutor repeatedly urges him to abandon tragic declamation and speak plainly. The opening also carries a long autobiographical account of his disillusionment with the poets and the philosophers whose contradictory counsels drove him to seek truth below. Readers tracing intertexts will find a dense web of allusion to the Homeric Nekyia, Hesiod's moralising verses, and Euripidean katabasis scenes, all bent to satire of philosophers and plutocrats.
grc.lucian.philopseudes: A short Greek prose satire in dialogue form by Lucian, of uncertain date, in which Tychiades and Philocles debate why people lie for the sheer pleasure of lying rather than out of necessity. Tychiades indicts poets, historians, and whole cities alike, Homer, Herodotus, Ctesias, and civic foundation legends, and then recounts a visit to the sick Eucrates, whose circle of philosophers, a physician, and dabblers in the occult trade tales of ghosts, demons, exorcism, and sorcery, including a story of a magician's animated implements that stands at the head of the later 'sorcerer's apprentice' tradition. Its parody of Platonic dialogue, mockery of historiographic marvel-telling, and dense repertory of supernatural folk motifs make it a rich node for readers tracing the transmission of mythic and folkloric material across Greek literature.
grc.lucian.pro_imaginibus: A brief Greek prose dialogue by Lucian, the Pro Imaginibus presents Lycinus' account, framed as an address to Aucinus, of a woman's criticism of the eulogistic portrait of her that he had written. Her complaint ranges over the absurdities of hyperbolic praise, from flatterers who credit their subjects with a beauty they do not possess to patrons who commission painters to improve their features, and she takes particular offense at being likened to Hera and Aphrodite and to the heroines Penelope, Arete, and Theano; the piece closes with the anecdote of Alexander declining the architect's promise to transform Mount Athos into his image. Running to only twenty-nine lines in Jacobitz's Teubner edition, the work is dense with allusion, drawing on Cassiopeia and the Nereids, Nireus, Phaon, Pelias, and the poets hired to praise the bald Stratonice. It offers rich material for parallels on flattery, encomium, portraiture, and the ethics of comparing mortals with gods.
grc.lucian.prometheus: A brief Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, staging the punishment of Prometheus at the moment Hephaestus and Hermes arrive to nail him to the Caucasus. In place of the tragic grandeur of the Aeschylean Prometheus Bound, the scene offers burlesque: Prometheus, left hanging before the eagle comes, presses for a formal hearing and trades courtroom repartee with Hermes over the rigged division of sacrificial meat, the creation of humankind, and the theft of fire. The dialogue quotes Hesiod by name and gestures repeatedly to 'the poet', making it a pointed witness to the comic reception of the Prometheus myth and to Lucian's parodic reuse of tragic and epic diction.
grc.lucian.prometheus_es_in_verbis: A brief comic dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, printed among the minor pieces in Jacobitz's Teubner edition of 1896. The speaker deflects the compliment of being called a new Prometheus for his verbal creations, disclaiming both claylike imitation and rash novelty, and illustrates the reception of startling innovations with the anecdote of Ptolemy son of Lagus, whose exhibited Bactrian camel and parti-coloured man won only derision from the Egyptians. He closes by defending his hybrid of dialogue and comedy, whose ill-assorted union he figures through images drawn from Aristophanic comedy, from philosophers consorting with clouds and measured flea-leaps to comedy's anapaestic gait. For readers tracing intertexts, the piece offers a compact manifesto of Lucian's mixed form and a dense cluster of allusions to Old Comedy and the Prometheus tradition.
grc.lucian.saturnalia: A short comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a conversation between Cronus and a priest during the festival of the Saturnalia, when Cronus briefly resumes his kingship. Cronus hears the petitioner's plea for wealth and instead lists the modest privileges of his seven-day reign, drinking, dicing, the crowning of mock kings, and the license granted to slaves, defending the egalitarian topsy-turvy of his festival. Challenged over the stories of his devouring his children, the stone substituted by Rhea, and his deposition and imprisonment in Tartarus, he blames Hesiod and Homer as the sources of such tales and recasts his abdication to Zeus as a voluntary retirement in gouty old age. The dialogue's explicit engagement with Hesiodic myth and its parodic echoes of epic diction and the Golden Age make it a rewarding locus for tracing ancient receptions of theogonic and festival material.
grc.lucian.soleocista: A very brief comic dialogue in Greek, attributed to Lucian of Samosata and of uncertain date, preserved in the Lucianic corpus under the title Soleocista. In its dozen lines two speakers contest the ability to recognise and avoid solecism, the first repeatedly committing errors, culminating in a quadruple solecism, that the second fails to detect, while the close reports anecdotes of Socrates the Cynic of Mopsus, encountered in Egypt, who corrected solecisms and counterfeit Atticisms without giving offence. The resulting catalogue of solecisms and false Atticisms, together with the vignettes of the Cynic sage, makes the piece a compact storehouse of grammatical humour for readers tracing parallels in Atticist and grammatical writing.
grc.lucian.symposium: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian, the Symposium presents a conversation between Lycinus and Philo about a wedding banquet hosted by Aristaenetus, at which philosophers of the rival schools, Stoic, Epicurean, Peripatetic, and Platonist, drank, quarrelled, and finally came to blows, so that the evening ended in wounds and blood. The dialogue operates as a burlesque counterpart to Plato's Symposium, replacing elevated banquet conversation with drunken disorder and turning the sympotic gathering into a scene of farce. Readers tracing intertexts will find in it Lucian's playful reworking of Platonic and broader symposium literature, together with a satirical gallery of philosophical sects and their pretensions.
grc.lucian.zeuxis: A brief Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, here spanning only a dozen lines in Jacobitz's Teubner text, in which the speaker answers admirers who praise nothing in his writing but its novelty. To make his case he recalls the painter Zeuxis, who scorned conventional subjects such as gods, heroes, and battles and instead dared to depict a female centaur nursing twin infants, and offers a lively description of a copy of that picture then in Athens, the original having been lost at sea while being shipped to Italy by Sulla. The paired defence of artistic and literary originality, together with allusions such as Homer's 'new song', makes the piece a compact witness both to Lucian's self-fashioning as a stylist and to the ancient anecdotal tradition surrounding Zeuxis' lost art.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.excerpta: The Excerpta is a brief Greek compilation of harmonic material, of uncertain date, attributed to Nicomachus of Gerasa and printed by Karl von Jan in the Teubner Musici Scriptores Graeci of 1895. It opens with a legendary history of the lyre, from its invention by Hermes and transmission through Orpheus, Linus, Amphion, and Terpander, and then sets out Pythagorean numerical demonstrations of the diatessaron (in 4:3 ratio) and the diapente (in 3:2) as composites of tones and the leimma. A closing section, citing Nicomachus in the third person, connects the names of the strings (hypate, mese, nete) with the planets from the Moon to Saturn. Readers of intertexts will find here compact parallels for the mythic genealogy of music, the arithmetic of the epogdoic tone, and the string-to-sphere correspondences that recur throughout Greek musical writing.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.ἐγχειρίδιον_ἁρμονικ: The Encheiridion Harmonikes of Nicomachus of Gerasa is a short Greek manual on harmonics, of uncertain date, composed as a rapid epitome during a journey and addressed to a lady whom the author hails as the finest and most reverend of women. After a table of chapter headings it treats the intervallic and continuous kinds of the voice, the cosmic music of the planets, the numerical ratios of the notes, Pythagoras' addition of the eighth string to the seven-stringed lyre, the diatonic division of the octave, and the harmonic passages of Plato's Timaeus, closing with testimony from Philolaus. Written from a Pythagorean standpoint, it promises a fuller and more detailed introduction to follow in the author's leisure. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in it a compact witness to the harmony of the spheres and to the Pythagorean reading of the Timaeus that echoes through later Greek and Latin writing on music.
grc.nonnus_of_panopolis.dionysiaca: The Dionysiaca of Nonnus of Panopolis is a monumental Greek epic in dactylic hexameter, running to more than 21,000 lines, of uncertain date, edited by W. H. D. Rouse in three volumes (1940–1942). Its programmatic opening invokes the shapeshifting Proteus as an emblem of the poem's own variety before turning to Zeus' abduction of Europa, the birth of Dionysus from Semele, and the god's career, including his war against the Indians. The verse is dense with Homeric and Hellenistic diction and continually recasts earlier epic, hymnic, and tragic material, making the work a major hub for readers tracing intertexts across Greek poetry.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_galatas: The Epistle to the Galatians (Ad Galatas) is a Greek letter of the New Testament whose opening verse presents it as the work of Paul the Apostle, sent with all the brothers to the churches of Galatia. It is printed in the Society of Biblical Literature's Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010), in 149 lines of prose of the Imperial era. The letter argues for justification by faith apart from works of the law, recounts Paul's call and his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, and contrasts promise, faith, and the Spirit with the Mosaic law through sustained engagement with Abraham and the scriptures. Its dense quotation and reworking of the Greek Jewish scriptures, drawing on Genesis, Deuteronomy, Habakkuk, and Leviticus among other books, make it a central node for tracing biblical parallels and a pervasive source of diction for later Christian writing.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philippenses: A canonical epistle of the New Testament, here given in the Greek text of the SBL edition (2010), addressed to the Christian congregation at Philippi and sent in the names of Paul and Timothy, with the date of composition left open. The letter, written in Imperial-era Koine prose, combines thanksgiving and news of the writer's imprisonment with exhortations to unity and humility, a celebrated passage on Christ's self-emptying and exaltation, an autobiographical claim to Jewish pedigree, and warnings against rival teachers. Because its compact formulations circulated constantly in later Greek Christian writing, it stands among the most heavily reused sources for verbal parallels and intertextual echoes.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_thessalonicenses_ii: The Second Letter to the Thessalonians is a brief Christian epistle in Koine prose from the Imperial era, preserved in the New Testament and given here in the SBL Greek New Testament (Holmes, 2010); it opens in the names of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, writing to the church at Thessalonica amid persecution. Across 47 lines it moves from thanksgiving for the community's growing faith to an apocalyptic account of the 'man of lawlessness' who must appear before the day of the Lord, and closes with exhortations to hold fast to tradition, work quietly, and discipline the idle. Its scenes of the parousia, final judgment, and eternal destruction became touchstones for later Christian apocalyptic writing, and its dense scriptural diction makes it a frequent node for readers tracing verbal parallels across biblical and post-biblical literature.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_titum: The Epistle to Titus is a brief prose composition of the Greek New Testament belonging to the Imperial era, attributed to Paul, who is named as sender in the opening salutation; the Greek follows the SBL edition of 2010. Addressed to Titus, whom Paul says he left in Crete to set right what was lacking and to appoint elders in each city, the letter prescribes qualifications for bishops, duties for older men, older women, younger women, and slaves, warnings against foolish controversies, genealogies, and legal quarrels, and a saying about Cretans attributed to 'a prophet of their own,' before closing with travel plans and greetings. Readers of intertexts value its dense overlaps with the other Pastoral Epistles, its Hellenistic virtue and vice catalogues, and memorable formulae such as the 'washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit,' which recur throughout later Christian discourse.
grc.novum_testamentum.lucas: The Gospel of Luke, one of the four canonical gospels of the New Testament, is written in Koine Greek prose of the Imperial era and transmitted under the name of Luke. It opens with a dedicatory preface to one Theophilus and an infancy narrative steeped in Septuagintal idiom, featuring the canticles known as the Magnificat and the Benedictus, before moving through the ministry, parables, passion, and resurrection of Jesus. Its preface advertises reliance on earlier accounts and eyewitness tradition, and its distinctive diction and syntax make it a rich source of verbal parallels for readers comparing the Septuagint, the other gospels, and later Christian Greek prose.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_ii: Second Peter (Petri II) is a Greek prose epistle of the Imperial era, attributed in its opening verse to Simeon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, printed in the SBL Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010). Writing in anticipation of imminent death, the author urges readers through a chain of virtues, faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, love, warns against false teachers who promise freedom while serving corruption, and illustrates divine judgment with the fallen angels, the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Balaam. The letter recalls the Transfiguration as eyewitness confirmation of the prophetic word, insists that no prophecy of scripture is of private interpretation, and answers scoffers who mock the promise of the Lord's coming by arguing that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years and that the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire. Readers of intertexts will find dense reuse of biblical exempla, apocalyptic imagery including the verb Tartaroo and a cosmic conflagration to come, and distinctive Hellenistic diction such as the promise that believers become partakers of the divine nature.
grc.orphica.fragmenta: A short collection of Greek fragments attributed to Orpheus and the Orphic poets, preserved through quotation in Plato, Aristotle, Aelian, Tatian, and other ancient authors and printed as part of Hermann Diels' 1922 gathering of Presocratic remains. The excerpts record cosmogonic and theological doctrines of the Orphic tradition, Oceanus and Tethys as the first parents of the gods, the soul entering living beings from the whole on the winds, the body as a prison and tomb of the soul, Zeus as head and middle of all things, alongside ritual formulas such as the command to shut the doors against the uninitiated. Plato and Aristotle cite these lines when treating early Greek theology, the prehistory of Presocratic speculation, and the nature of the soul, so the fragments supply a stock of formulas and ideas repeatedly echoed by later poets, philosophers, and Christian apologists.
grc.paradoxographus_florentinus.mirabilia_de: A short Greek paradoxographical collection of uncertain date, transmitted anonymously and conventionally labelled the Florentine paradoxographer, cataloguing some forty marvels of springs, lakes, and rivers in Greece, Asia, Africa, and Italy. Each notice ascribes a strange property to a water, maddening horses, petrifying drinkers, souring wine, expelling bathers, sustaining floating islands, usually with an attribution to a named authority such as Isigonos, Ctesias, Aristotle, Theopompus, or Hellanicus, and two entries append epigrams said to be inscribed at the springs concerned. For readers hunting intertexts, the work offers a compact node of the ancient mirabilia tradition, preserving source attributions and shared phrasings that recur across the paradoxographical corpus and the lost historians it draws on.
grc.phalaridis_epistulae.epistulae: A collection of Greek prose letters attributed to Phalaris, son of Leodamas of Astypalaea and tyrant of the Agrigentines, edited by Rudolf Hercher in his Epistolographi Graeci (1873); the true date of composition and authorship are uncertain. The letters, each brief, are cast in the tyrant's own voice and address citizens, envoys, kinsmen and defeated enemies with a blend of menace, reproach, moralizing and calculated clemency. Several are self-characterizing, the writer names himself as Phalaris, 'experienced in wars', and one credits the poet Stesichorus with ransoming captives of Tauromenium. For readers of intertexts the collection matters as a principal vehicle of the Phalaris legend, offering a distinctive tyrant-epistolary voice and episodes, such as the Stesichorus connection, that recur across later Greek and Latin writing.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_abrahamo: A Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus on the patriarch Abraham as an exemplar of the Mosaic law, opening with a programmatic account of the biblical heroes as living laws whose lives preceded all written legislation. Drawing on Genesis, it treats hope in Enos and repentance in Enoch before turning to Abraham himself, whose virtue, faith, and departure from Chaldaea are read as moral paradigms. The work forms part of Philo's larger exposition of the Pentateuch and fuses Greek philosophical vocabulary with scriptural interpretation, making it a rich source of parallels for ancient Jewish exegesis of Genesis and for the reception of biblical narrative in philosophical prose.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_aeternitate_mundi: De Aeternitate Mundi, a Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus preserved in the Cohn and Reiter edition of the Opera quae supersunt (Berlin, 1915), addresses the question whether the cosmos is ungenerated or liable to destruction. Across some 150 lines it distinguishes the senses of 'world' and 'perishing' and surveys the doctrines of Democritus, Epicurus, the Stoics, Aristotle, the Pythagoreans, and Plato's Timaeus, before defending the view that the cosmos, though generated, is imperishable. Readers hunting intertexts will find the argument studded with verbatim quotation from earlier poets and philosophers, including Parmenides and the Timaeus, making the treatise a compact repository of doxographic and fragmentary material.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_agricultura: De Agricultura (On Husbandry) is a Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus, preserved in the second volume of the Opera quae supersunt edited by Paul Wendland (Berlin, 1897). Taking its cue from the verses in which Noah appears as a georgos who plants a vineyard and drinks of the wine (Genesis 9:20–21), it distinguishes the true farmer from the mere hireling tiller of the soil and reads agriculture allegorically as the tending of the soul, in which reason cuts away the trees of the passions and plants the virtues in their place. Along the way it treats the encyclical arts as the milk of childhood, contrasts disinterested knowledge with mercenary rhetoric and medicine, and expounds the ancient comparison of the three parts of philosophy to a field with its trees, its fruits, and its enclosing wall. Its dense interweaving of Greek biblical wording with philosophical allegory makes it a rich source for readers tracing echoes of Genesis exegesis and Hellenistic philosophical metaphor.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_cherubim: De Cherubim is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus that takes its starting point from Genesis 3:24, the expulsion of Adam and the stationing of the cherubim and the flaming sword before the tree of life. Distinguishing the man 'sent out', who may return to virtue through repentance, from the man 'cast out' into permanent exile, the work reads Hagar as the encyclical education driven away by wisdom and Sarah as virtue in its generic and incorruptible form, and proceeds to discussions of sophistry versus wisdom, Cain's settlement in the land of Naid opposite Eden, and the ritual of the suspected wife in Numbers 5. Its sustained allegorization of the Eden narrative, the cherubim, and the Hagar-Sarah story makes it a central witness to ancient Jewish allegorical exegesis of Genesis and a rich hunting ground for parallels in later interpretive tradition.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_confusione_linguarum: De Confusione Linguarum ('On the Confusion of Languages') is a Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus, edited here from the Opera quae supersunt (vol. 2, Wendland, Berlin 1897) in a continuous text of 198 lines. Taking Genesis 11:1–9 as its lemmatic starting point, it expounds the building of the tower of Babel and the division of tongues allegorically, weighing the biblical narrative against pagan analogues such as Homer's account of the Aloeidae piling Pelion upon Ossa and the myth of a primordial common language shared by animals. The treatise opens in mid-argument, continuing a running exposition, and stages the sneers of those who mock the ancestral laws before answering them point by point. Readers of intertexts will find a close juxtaposition of Greek Genesis citation, verbatim Homeric quotation, and Greek mythographic material, in which scriptural events are read through and against classical literary parallels.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_congressu_eruditionis_g: De Congressu Eruditionis Gratia is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, the Hellenistic Jewish exegete, preserved here in Wendland's 1898 Berlin edition. Taking Genesis 16:1-2 as its starting point, the work reads Abraham's union with Hagar at Sarah's command as the soul's congress with the encyclical studies, grammar, geometry, music, rhetoric, and dialectic, which figure as the handmaiden and 'middle education' preparatory to virtue and wisdom, figured as Sarah. Across roughly 180 lines Philo etymologizes the scriptural names, expounds the individual arts in turn, and defends preliminary learning as the necessary approach to philosophy proper. Readers of intertexts will find a locus classicus for the ancient case for the liberal arts as propaedeutic, together with dense quotation and reinterpretation of the Septuagint, a fruitful source of parallels for later patristic and medieval discussions of pagan learning and Scripture.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_decalogo: De Decalogo, 'On the Decalogue', is a Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus on the Ten Commandments and their place within the Mosaic law. It argues that God gave the law through Moses in the wilderness rather than in the cities, which it depicts as seats of vanity, idolatry, and corruption, and then presents the ten commandments as the divinely spoken 'heads' or summaries of the particular laws, opening its exposition with an excursus on the mathematical completeness of the number ten. Readers hunting intertexts will find a dense weave of biblical diction, Greek philosophical argument, and number symbolism, making the work a natural meeting point for parallels between Hellenistic ethics, biblical law, and later Jewish and Christian decalogue exegesis.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_fuga_et_inventione: De Fuga et Inventione ('On Flight and Finding') is a Greek treatise by the Jewish exegete Philo Judaeus, printed here from Paul Wendland's 1898 Berlin edition of the Opera quae supersunt. Taking its departure from Hagar's flight into the wilderness (Genesis 16), it distinguishes three causes of flight, hatred, fear, and shame, and unfolds allegorical readings of Jacob, Laban, Esau, and the Egyptian bondage, opposing the formless matter (ὕλη) of the ignorant soul to the mind shaped by the divine logos. Its close interleaving of Septuagint quotation with Greek philosophical vocabulary, including the image of the cosmos as the imprint (ἐκμαγεῖον) of the perfect logos, makes the work a productive hunting ground for parallels between scriptural exegesis and Hellenistic philosophy. The treatise is not divided into books and runs to some 213 lines.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_gigantibus: De Gigantibus is a short Greek treatise of uncertain date by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, an allegorical exposition of Genesis 6:1–4 on the giants and the unions of the 'sons of God' with the 'daughters of men'. Interpreting the angels of the biblical narrative as souls moving in the air, Philo distinguishes those that remain in the service of the creator from those that sink into bodies and senses, and reads the daughters and their offspring as figures for pleasure and the flesh prevailing over virtue. The work closes with an explanation, drawn from Genesis 6:3, of why the divine spirit does not abide for ever among human beings who are flesh. It offers readers of intertexts an early, philosophically inflected treatment of Genesis 6, angelology, and the descent of souls, themes that recur throughout Jewish, Christian, and Platonic literature.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_josepho: De Josepho (On Joseph) is a Greek treatise by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, cast as the fourth in a series of ideal lives: after the lives of learning, nature, and ascetic practice named after Moses, Philo here presents the political life (βίος πολιτικός) through the patriarch Joseph. The work retells the Genesis narrative of Joseph's prophetic dreams, his brothers' jealousy, his sale into slavery, and his eventual rise, expanding the biblical account into an ethical portrait of the wise ruler and statesman. Readers hunting intertexts will find in it a Hellenistic Jewish rewriting of Genesis, coloured by classical ideals of kingship, from the Homeric 'shepherds of the peoples' to Greek discourse on the education of the ruler.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_migratione_abrahami: De Migratione Abrahami is a Greek allegorical exposition by Philo Judaeus that reads the divine command to Abraham to leave his land, kindred, and father's house (Genesis 12:1–3) as a summons for the soul to depart from the body, from sense-perception, and from the word expressed in speech. Drawing closely on the Greek wording of Genesis and Exodus, the treatise elaborates the body as a prison, Lot as the soul's inclination toward the sensible, and the Exodus as the mind's deliverance from the Egypt of bodily pleasure. Its dense interweaving of scriptural quotation with Greek philosophical vocabulary, above all its treatment of the logos as the father's house and the dwelling of mind, makes it a rich locus for readers tracing parallels between biblical exegesis and Hellenistic philosophy.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_opificio_mundi: De Opificio Mundi is a Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus on the creation of the world as related at the opening of Genesis. It argues that Moses placed the cosmogony at the head of the law as its most beautiful beginning, refutes those who declared the cosmos unbegotten and God inactive, explains the fittingness of the six days and the number six, and presents the incorporeal ideas and the intelligible cosmos as the paradigm after which the sensible world was fashioned. In reading the biblical narrative through the vocabulary of Greek cosmology, the active and passive causes, providence, and the world of forms, the work offers a rich point of contact for parallels between Platonic and Stoic philosophy and the scriptural account of creation.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_plantatione: De Plantatione is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, continuing a running commentary on Genesis whose preceding book treated agriculture in general and turning here to viticulture in particular, occasioned by Noah's planting of the vineyard (Gen. 9:20). Philo presents God as the great planter and the cosmos as a plant rooted in the eternal divine Logos, then ranges across the ordering of the elements, the creation of plants, animals, and angelic souls, and the fashioning of man upright and in God's image. Readers of intertexts will find the work a dense meeting point of Greek philosophical cosmology and Mosaic exegesis, offering Greek phrasings of Genesis passages widely echoed in later literature. The treatise runs to 177 lines in the Wendland edition of the Opera quae supersunt (Berlin: Reimer, 1897).
grc.philo_judaeus.de_praemiis_et_poenis_et_d: A Greek treatise on rewards and punishments and on curses, preserved under the name of Philo Judaeus, opening with a division of the Mosaic scriptures into cosmogony, history, and legislation before taking up the prizes set before the virtuous and the penalties appointed for the wicked. The argument proceeds through a sequence of figurative athletic contests, hope, repentance, and the other seeds sown by God in the rational soul, with blessings and punishments traced across individuals, households, cities, and nations. Greek philosophical learning and biblical exegesis are tightly interwoven: alongside figures such as Enoch appear the myth of Triptolemus and the vocabulary of the gymnic agon, making the work a productive source of parallels between Platonic and Stoic idiom and Jewish scriptural interpretation.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_sacrificiis_abelis_et_c: A Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus on the sacrifices of Cain and Abel in Genesis 4, reading the two brothers as opposed movements of a single soul: Cain the self-loving mind that imagines it possesses all things, and Abel the God-facing understanding that refers everything to its cause. Moving verse by verse through the Greek biblical text, the exposition draws on Rebekah's warring twins, the deaths of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the figure of Moses to describe the soul's bearing of good and evil doctrines and its progress toward virtue and the knowledge of God. The constant interlacing of Genesis quotation with Greek philosophical psychology makes the work a dense source of parallels for readers tracing biblical allegory, Septuagint phrasing, and the afterlife of Philonic exegesis in Jewish and Christian tradition.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_somniis_lib_iii: The third book of the De Somniis of Philo, the Jewish exegete who wrote in Greek, continues his discussion of god-sent dreams by taking up their second kind, in which the dreaming mind, moved by the divine and held as though god-possessed, is thought to grasp and foreknow something of the future. Preserved here in Wendland's 1898 Berlin edition, the book opens with Jacob's dream of the ladder reaching from earth to heaven (Genesis 28:12-15) and proceeds from the questions raised by the well named 'of the oath' and the journey to Haran into extended allegory, in which the well figures the deep and boundless nature of knowledge. Across its 558 lines the work weaves Greek philosophical vocabulary, the four elements, the endlessness of learning, the maxim that life is short but art long, into scriptural interpretation, making it a dense source of biblical quotation and allegorical method for readers tracing parallels in dream theory and exegesis.
grc.philo_judaeus.quis_rerum_divinarum_heres: Quis Rerum Divinarum Heres Sit ('Who Is the Heir of Divine Things?') is a Greek philosophical-exegetical treatise by Philo Judaeus, preserved in Paul Wendland's 1898 Berlin edition of Philo's surviving works and running to 316 lines. Announcing itself as a sequel to a discussion of rewards, the treatise takes its departure from Genesis 15:1–3, where the childless Abraham asks what God will give him and names Eliezer of Damascus as heir, and inquires who the true heir of divine things must be. Drawing densely on Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, the opening argument expounds Moses' hesitancy of speech, the freedom of speech (parrhesia) with which the soul addresses God, and the disciplines of silence and attentive hearing, even quoting a comic tag along the way. Readers hunting parallels will find a characteristic weaving of Greek biblical quotation into philosophical prose and allegorical method typical of Philo's scriptural commentaries.
grc.philo_judaeus.quod_deterius_potiori_insi: Quod Deterius Potiori Insidiari Soleat ('That the Worse Is Wont to Lie in Wait for the Better') is a short Greek allegorical treatise of some 178 lines by the Jewish exegete Philo Judaeus, edited here from the Cohn edition of 1896. Opening from the Greek biblical text of Genesis 4:8, in which Cain lures Abel into the plain, it reads the plain as the arena of psychic contest and unfolds a chain of further Genesis passages, Jacob's summons of Leah and Rachel to the plain, Joseph's mission to his brothers at Shechem, and his 'variegated' coat, as allegories of the soul's irrational powers, of progress under gentler teachers, and of the division of goods into those of soul, body, and externals. Readers hunting intertexts will find a dense lattice of verbatim biblical quotation interwoven with the vocabulary of Greek gymnastic contest, askesis, and philosophical ethics, showing how scriptural narrative is moralised through Hellenic conceptual frames.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.de_gymnastica: A short Greek treatise on athletic training attributed to Philostratus the Athenian and of uncertain date, opening from a distinction between wisdom (sophia) and banausic crafts in order to claim gymnastics as an art worthy of written memorials. It sets out the causes and origins of the Greek contests, stadion, dolichos, diaulos, armed race, jumping, javelin, discus, wrestling, boxing, and the pankration, with the pentathlon as their combination, drawing on Elean traditions and heroic exempla from Peleus, Theseus, and Heracles down to Milo and Glaukos, and it defends nature against charges of decline by blaming defective training. Among its aetiological stories are the fire race at the altar that founded the stadion and the Arcadian running heralds behind the dolichos. Readers of intertexts will find in it a dense store of athletic terminology, etymologies, and foundation myths of the sort echoed throughout later Greek prose and verse.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.epistulae_et_d: A compact Greek collection of erotic letters and short prose pieces (dialexeis) attributed to Philostratus the Athenian and of uncertain date, running to only some 75 lines in Kayser's Teubner edition of 1871. The letters, nearly all addressed to beautiful youths, turn on the gift of roses and elaborate the flower through mythological exempla such as Adonis, Hyacinthus, Meleager, and Achilles and Patroclus, with witty arguments on beauty, wealth, poverty, and love for strangers. The dialexeis sustain the same polished, epideictic manner. The dense pattern of Homeric and mythological allusion makes the collection a rich hunting ground for verbal and thematic parallels in Greek erotic epistolography.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.vita_apollonii: The Vita Apollonii of Philostratus the Athenian is a Greek prose life of Apollonius of Tyana, the Pythagorean sage and wonder-worker, presented in eight books after Carl Ludwig Kayser's Teubner edition of 1870 and of uncertain date. The narrator frames the work as a reworking of the travel-notes kept by Damis of Nineveh, which he says he revised for the empress Julia, and he sets his hero beside Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Plato, and Socrates as a figure of divine wisdom whose contact with the magi of Babylon, the Brahmans of India, and the gymnosophists of Egypt drew mistaken charges of sorcery. The narrative follows Apollonius through his journeys, sayings, acts of foreknowledge, and letters to kings, cities, temples, and philosophers, gathered from urban traditions, sanctuaries, earlier accounts, and his own correspondence. Readers of intertexts will find in it a dense web of echoes of Homer, Plato, Herodotus, and the Pythagorean biographical tradition, and one of the fullest ancient portraits of a philosopher credited with superhuman knowledge.
grc.philostratus_the_lemnian.imagines: A Greek prose work attributed to Philostratus the Lemnian and of uncertain date, comprising ekphraseis, or rhetorical descriptions of paintings, preceded by a prologue that defends painting as a sibling of poetry and philosophy. The framing scene places an older speaker in a seaside gallery near Naples, expounding panels by various painters to an eager young boy, with subjects drawn first from Homer, such as the fire of Hephaestus overwhelming the river Scamander, and then from mythological figures like Komos. As an exemplary performance of the ancient ekphrasis tradition, it shows readers of intertexts how epic scenes and mythological types were translated into visual terms and interpreted through allusion.
grc.phlegon.de_mirabilibus: A brief Greek paradoxographical work, the De Mirabilibus attributed to Phlegon and of uncertain date, runs to sixty-six lines and collects accounts of prodigies and marvels. It opens with the story of Philinnion, a young woman six months dead who visits her lover Machates at an inn, until an official inquiry, the opening of her tomb, and purificatory rites prescribed by the seer Hyllos bring her returns to an end. The closing lines frame the material as a report sent to the king. Readers hunting parallels will find here a dense concentration of revenant and funerary motifs, the dead bride's nocturnal epiphany, the ring and cup left as tokens, the propitiation of Hermes Chthonios and the Eumenides, that recur across classical and later ghost and marvel literature.
grc.plato.alcibiades_2: Attributed to Plato and printed among his works in Burnet's Oxford edition of 1903, the Second Alcibiades is a short Socratic dialogue in Attic prose in which Socrates meets Alcibiades on his way to pray and questions whether it is safe to ask the gods for anything, since they sometimes grant requests that prove disastrous, as Oedipus' prayer for the division of his paternal inheritance showed. The ensuing discussion treats foolishness and madness as fundamentally the same, grades its milder forms under flattering names, and suggests that most citizens are thus 'mad', so that prayer requires knowledge of what is truly beneficial. Readers of intertexts may value the dialogue's close kinship with the first Alcibiades and its handling of madness, prayer, and Socratic ignorance, themes that echo elsewhere in the Platonic corpus.
grc.plato.apologia: Plato's Apologia, a compact work of Attic Greek prose in a single file, records the defence speech of Socrates before the Athenian jury at his trial, opening with his disavowal of rhetorical artifice and his distinction between the present accusers and the long-standing slanderers who have shaped public opinion against him. Socrates confronts the popular image of himself as an investigator of things in the heavens and beneath the earth who makes the weaker argument the stronger, an image he links explicitly to Aristophanes' comedy, before turning to answer the indictment brought by Meletus. For readers of intertexts, the work offers direct engagement with Aristophanic comedy, the conventions of forensic oratory, and the earliest full literary dramatisation of the trial that defined the Socratic tradition in later Greek and Roman writing.
grc.plato.charmides: Plato's Charmides is a Socratic dialogue of uncertain date, staged as Socrates' return to Athens from the campaign at Potidaea and his visit to the palaestra of Taureas, where Critias presents his young cousin Charmides, famed for beauty and philosophy. A pretext, Socrates' supposed remedy for the youth's morning headache, launches an inquiry into sophrosyne, pursued through successive definitions offered by Charmides and then Critias. Readers of intertexts find here an early locus for the Delphic precept of self-knowledge, for portraits of the historical Charmides and Critias, and for the Greek vocabulary of restraint and sound-mindedness that resonates through later literature. The Greek follows Burnet's Platonis Opera (Oxford, 1903).
grc.plato.euthyphro: Plato's Euthyphro, presented in John Burnet's Oxford edition of 1903, is a short Greek dialogue set outside the stoa of the king archon, where Socrates, awaiting trial on Meletus' indictment for impiety, meets Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his own father for the death of a farm labourer. The conversation repeatedly asks what piety (to hosion) is, examining in turn the definitions that piety is what the gods love, what they approve, and a kind of service or commerce between gods and men, each of which Socrates dismantles, and the dialogue ends in unresolved aporia. It is the classic ancient source for the problem of whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious or pious because it is loved, and as such a standing intertext for later treatments of piety, divine command, and the relation of religion to morality. Its picture of Socrates under an impious indictment also links it closely with the Apology and the other trial dialogues.
grc.plato.hipparchus: Hipparchus, a short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato and printed in Burnet's Oxford text, opens with Socrates and an unnamed friend attempting to define the lover of gain (philokerdes) and to settle whether gain itself is good. A string of elenctic exchanges, built on analogies with the farmer, horseman, helmsman, and other experts who know the worth of their equipment, dismantles the friend's successive accounts, until the two concede that everyone loves gain and that the reproached philokerdes is the one who profits from things from which the good do not dare to profit. A later digression praises Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, as a benefactor who brought the poems of Homer to Athens, giving the dialogue its title. Its aporetic handling of value, profit, and the appetite for more affords close parallels with the definitional dialogues of the Platonic corpus and with later Greek discussions of pleonexia and acquisition.
grc.plato.hippias_maior: Plato's Hippias Maior (Greater Hippias) is a Socratic dialogue in which Socrates questions Hippias of Elis, a travelling sophist and envoy, about the nature of the beautiful (to kalon), successively testing definitions drawn from the fitting, the useful and beneficial, and the pleasant. The opening exchange sets Hippias' boastful accounts of his earnings and diplomatic successes against Socrates' reflection on the impractical wisdom of the ancients, from Thales, Bias and Pittacus to Anaxagoras, and the dialogue goes on to display the sophists Gorgias and Prodicus in passing. Edited in Burnet's Oxford Platonis Opera (1903), the work stands as an early and influential treatment of beauty as an object of definition, making its formulations of the kalon a natural point of comparison for readers tracing ancient aesthetic vocabulary and argument across Greek literature and philosophy.
grc.plato.ion: A short Platonic dialogue, in Attic prose and of uncertain date within Plato's career, staging a conversation between Socrates and Ion of Ephesus, a prize-winning rhapsode met on his way from victory at the Asclepieia in Epidaurus. Socrates questions whether Ion's celebrated skill in interpreting Homer constitutes a technē like medicine or arithmetic, pressing him on why he excels on Homer alone while dozing over Hesiod and Archilochus, and concludes that rhapsody and poetry alike arise not from knowledge but from a divine gift akin to inspiration or prophecy. Readers of intertexts will find here sustained quotation and discussion of Homer and other poets, an early theorisation of the poet as hermēneus or interpreter, and one of the most influential ancient formulations of poetic inspiration.
grc.plato.lovers: The Lovers (Erastai) is a brief Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato and of uncertain date, preserved in the Platonic corpus as printed in Burnet's Oxford edition of 1903. Socrates comes upon two young men, one devoted to gymnastics and the other to music, quarrelling about philosophy, and questions whether philosophy is fine and good, seeking to distinguish it from mere polymathia or much learning. The conversation cites Solon's maxim that one grows old ever learning many things and mentions Anaxagoras and Oinopides, giving readers of intertexts a locus for Platonic quotation of early Greek poetry and for the dialogue's play with rival ideals of education. Its brevity makes it a natural point of comparison for verbal and thematic parallels among the shorter dialogues of the corpus.
grc.plato.philebus: Plato's Philebus is a Greek philosophical dialogue in which Socrates, with Protarchus acting as spokesman for the largely silent Philebus, contests the claim that pleasure, enjoyment, and delight constitute the good for all living creatures, defending instead thought, understanding, memory, correct opinion, and true reckoning. The conversation moves from the diversity and heterogeneity of pleasures, those of the intemperate, the temperate, the foolish, and the wise, to the broader question of what state of soul can render human life happy. Its date is uncertain within Plato's corpus, and the dialogue is printed here in John Burnet's Oxford edition of the Opera (1903). Its systematic weighing of hedonic against intellectual goods made it a standard reference in ancient debates over pleasure and the good life, and a natural source of parallel and allusion for later ethical writers.
grc.plato.symposium: The Symposium is a dialogue in Attic Greek by Plato, transmitted here in Burnet's Oxford Classical Text. Framed as Apollodorus' retelling of Aristodemus' report to a circle of friends, it stages a drinking party held the day after Agathon's first tragic victory, at which the guests successively praise Eros, culminating in Socrates' account of Diotima's teaching and Alcibiades' drunken encomium of Socrates himself. Aristophanes' myth of severed lovers and Diotima's ladder of ascent toward beauty belong among the most frequently cited passages in the Western tradition on desire. For readers of intertexts, the dialogue offers a dense reservoir of Homeric quotation and of formulas about love and beauty that later poetry and philosophy repeatedly echo.
grc.plato.theaetetus: Plato's Theaetetus, presented here in Burnet's Oxford text, is a philosophical dialogue in which Euclides and Terpsion at Megara have a slave read out a written record of a conversation between Socrates, the geometer Theodorus, and the young Theaetetus on the question 'what is knowledge?'. The discussion tests and discards three successive definitions, knowledge as perception, as true judgement, and as true judgement with an account, pausing over Protagoras' claim that man is the measure, Heraclitean flux, the wax-tablet and aviary images of memory and judgement, and the contrast between the philosopher and the man of the courts, and it ends without a settled answer. A central ancient locus for epistemological vocabulary, sophistic doctrine, and the Socratic method of definition, it offers abundant hooks for readers tracing textual parallels.
grc.plutarch.ad_principem_ineruditum: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, transmitted in the Moralia under the Latin title Ad Principem Ineruditum ('To an Uneducated Ruler'), argues that a ruler lacking education must take philosophy as the companion and guardian of power, so that law, 'king of all, mortals and immortals' in the words of Pindar, reigns enthroned within the ruler's own soul. The argument is studded with borrowed material: Plato's refusal to legislate for the prosperous Cyrenaeans, the Spartan king Theopompus and the ephors, the Persian attendant who woke the king to his duties, Anaxarchus's defense of Alexander after the murder of Cleitus, Epameinondas keeping watch while Thebes feasted, Cato's death at Utica, and the fearful sleeping arrangements of the tyrants Clearchus and Aristodemus. For readers tracing intertexts, the essay offers a compact cluster of quotable maxims and historical exempla on kingship, law, and the ruler as image of god that circulated in later moral and political writing.
grc.plutarch.adversus_colotem: A Greek prose polemic by Plutarch, transmitted with his Moralia in the Bernardakis Teubner edition of 1895. Framed as a dialogue with Aristodemus of Aegium and addressed to a Saturninus, it answers Colotes, the Epicurean whom Epicurus used to call by the pet names Colotarân and Colotarion, whose pamphlet had argued that according to the doctrines of the other philosophers it is not even possible to live. Plutarch replies point by point on behalf of Democritus, Empedocles, Parmenides, Melissus, Plato, Stilpon, Socrates and the rest, defending the possibility of a good and social life under the older philosophies and exposing Colotes' habit of wrenching stray phrases from their context. For readers of intertexts the work is valuable for its extensive direct quotation of Homer, Plato and Democritus and as a principal source for the teachings of Epicurus and the arguments of Colotes' book.
grc.plutarch.agesilaus: A Greek prose biography of the Spartan king Agesilaus, son of Archidamus, by Plutarch, printed here in Perrin's edition of Plutarch's Lives. The narrative opens with Agesilaus' upbringing in the Spartan agoge and his contested succession over Leotychides, secured through Lysander's patronage, and proceeds to his reign, campaigns, and character, including his lameness, cheerfulness, and deference to the ephors and ancestral laws. Plutarch names and quotes a range of authorities, among them Xenophon, Theophrastus, and Duris, and cites oracles and a Simonidean epithet for Sparta, while cross-referring to his own life of Lycurgus. Readers hunting parallels will find dense verbal and thematic echoes of Xenophon's writing on Agesilaus and of the Laconian exempla that recur throughout the Lives.
grc.plutarch.agis: Plutarch's Life of Agis is a Greek biographical account of Agis, the Eurypontid king of Sparta who tried to restore the ancestral constitution against entrenched wealth, composed as one half of a pair with the Life of Cleomenes and formally compared by Plutarch with the Gracchi. The opening chapters reflect on love of glory and the servitude of demagogues to popular opinion, citing a line of Sophocles on herdsmen who are slaves to their flocks and a remark of Theophrastus on the role of praise, before turning to the causes of Sparta's decline and the genealogies of the two royal houses down to Agis and his contemporary Leonidas son of Cleonymus. The dense allusive texture, Ixion's cloud, the serpent whose tail rebels against its head, Phocion's rebuke of Antipater, and the standing comparison with Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, makes the Life a productive site for tracing how Plutarch embeds poetic and philosophical quotation in moralizing historical prose.
grc.plutarch.alcibiades: Plutarch's Greek Life of Alcibiades, printed here in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives, follows the Athenian aristocrat and general from his double descent from Eurysaces son of Ajax and the Alcmaeonids, through his guardianship under Pericles, into the vicissitudes of his turbulent public career. The narrative dwells on his beauty, eloquence, and restless ambition, and on the formative attachment of Socrates, enlivened by childhood anecdotes such as his exposure of the aulos and his defiance of the cart-driver. Aristophanes, Euripides, Antiphon, and Plato are among the authors quoted or reported in the course of the biography. Readers hunting parallels will find the Life a dense nexus of allusion, preserving anecdotes and verses that interact with the Platonic portrayals of the Socrates–Alcibiades relationship and with the comic and tragic treatments of its subject.
grc.plutarch.alexander: Plutarch's Life of Alexander, a Greek prose biography written as one of the Parallel Lives and paired by design with the Life of Caesar, is presented here in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition. Its prologue announces the author's program of writing lives rather than histories, seeking the revelation of character in small sayings and anecdotes rather than in vast battles and sieges. The narrative proceeds from Alexander's Heraclid and Aeacid ancestry and the portents surrounding his birth to Philip and Olympias, the serpent, Philip's dream, the burning of the Ephesian Artemision, into his appearance and campaigns. Readers hunting parallels will find the work dense with named sources such as Eratosthenes, Theophrastus, and Aristoxenus, and with omen-and-anecdote material that circulated widely in later Greek and Latin tradition.
grc.plutarch.amatoriae_narrationes: Attributed to Plutarch and printed among the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1892, the Amatoriae Narrationes preserve a compact group of Greek prose love-tales. The narratives gathered here, the fatal wooing and abduction of Aristocleia at Haliartus, the Corinthian tragedy of Actaeon and Archias that ends in suicide, pestilence and the founding of Syracuse, and the outrage against the daughters of Scedasus later avenged at Leuctra, turn on erotic pursuit, rape and divine vengeance. Readers of intertexts will find in them a store of localised mythic exempla, rich in named springs, cults and omens, of the kind that recurs throughout Greek love-literature and historical exempla collections.
grc.plutarch.an_recte_dictum_sit_latenter_es: A polemical ethical essay in Greek by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia, disputing the Epicurean precept to 'live in obscurity' (lathe biosas) and asking whether that saying is well put. The speaker contends that virtue requires recognition and public exercise, citing Epaminondas, Themistocles, Camillus, and Plato's liberation of Sicily through Dion as benefactors whose worth depended on being known, and depicts Epicurean withdrawal as darkness, idleness, and the slow decay of the soul. Quoting Epicurus, Democritus, and Sophocles, and ridiculing Epicurean letters, communal meals, and instructions about burial, the work offers dense material for readers tracing the topos of the hidden life and the reception of Epicurean doctrine in Greek philosophical prose.
grc.plutarch.an_virtus_doceri_possit: A short Greek prose essay by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia under its Latin title An Virtus Doceri Possit, which takes up the Platonic question of whether virtue can be taught. The speaker argues that those who declare virtue unteachable make it non-existent, since people are taught singing, letters, riding and every minor craft, yet supposedly acquire the supreme art of living well by unreasoned habit alone. The case is built on analogies with the learned arts and on anecdote and quotation, including Diogenes punishing the boy's tutor, Aristippus on tutors' wages, Iphicrates' answer to Callias, and cited lines from Plato, Heraclitus, Herodotus and Aristophanes. Its dense texture of borrowed sayings and versified fragments makes it productive ground for readers tracing verbal parallels.
grc.plutarch.an_vitiositas_ad_infelicitatem_: A short dialectical ethical treatise among Plutarch's Moralia, transmitted under the Latin title An Vitiositas ad Infelicitatem Sufficia ('Whether Vice Suffices for Unhappiness'), argues that wickedness alone, without any assistance from Fortune, suffices to make a life wretched. In its central set piece Fortune and Vice appear as rival contractors bidding to construct a miserable man, and Vice's inventory of wars, tyrannies, fevers, griefs and remorse proves the richer, while sages such as Diogenes, Socrates and the Roman general Decius are cited as having defeated Fortune's threats outright. Opening with a quotation from Euripides and woven through with poetic tags, Cynic anecdote and ethnographic exempla, the piece offers dense hunting ground for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels.
grc.plutarch.aratus: Plutarch's Life of Aratus, a Greek prose biography of uncertain composition date, forms part of the corpus of Plutarch's Lives and runs to roughly 232 lines. Addressed to Polycrates, a Sicyonian who claimed descent from its subject, it opens with a debate over a proverb and a quotation of Pindar before narrating Aratus of Sicyon's childhood exile after his father Cleinias' murder by the tyrant Abantidas, the liberation of Sicyon, and his career in Achaean League politics against Macedonian power. Readers hunting intertexts will find in the Life a dense lattice of allusion, with quoted proverbs and verse, anecdotes patterned on earlier historians, and explicit appeal to Aratus' own memoirs, all shaped by Plutarch's moralizing method.
grc.plutarch.brutus: Plutarch's Life of Brutus, a Greek prose biography from his Parallel Lives, presents Marcus Junius Brutus through his ancestry, philosophical formation, and political career down to the conspiracy against Julius Caesar and the civil wars that followed. The opening chapters weigh disputed points of genealogy, citing Posidonius on the line of Junius Brutus, and sketch Brutus's devotion to the Old Academy and his famously terse letter style, quoting his messages to the Pergamenians, Samians, Xanthians, and Patareans. The narrative then follows his conduct in the struggle between Pompey and Caesar and his attachment to his uncle Cato, blending Roman history with moral characterization. For readers hunting intertexts, the Life is dense with embedded letters, apothegms, and digressions that invite comparison with Plutarch's own related lives, the Roman historical tradition, and the Ciceronian correspondence.
