grc.plutarch.caius_marcius_coriolanus: Plutarch's Greek Life of Caius Marcius Coriolanus, printed in Bernadotte Perrin's edition of Plutarch's Lives (1916), is a moralizing biography of the early Roman patrician commander celebrated for his martial prowess and his intractable pride. Opening with the pedigree of the Marcius house and the hero's upbringing by a widowed mother, it follows his restless pursuit of distinction in battle, the civic crown he wins for shielding a fallen citizen, and the aristocratic rigidity that makes his excellence in war hard to reconcile with political life. As part of Plutarch's series of paired Greek and Roman lives, marked by such cross-comparisons as the reflection on Epameinondas, it stands as a principal ancient portrait of Coriolanus and a key antecedent for later literary treatments, most famously Shakespeare's tragedy. Readers hunting intertexts will find in its brief span dense material on Roman ancestral virtue, maternal ambition, and the ethics of glory.
grc.plutarch.caius_marius: A Greek biographical Life of the Roman general and statesman Caius Marius, composed by Plutarch as part of his Parallel Lives and printed here in Bernadotte Perrin's 1920 Harvard edition. The Life opens with a digression on Roman naming customs before following Marius from his poor upbringing near Arpinum through early service under Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia, his tribunate, his rise through the cursus honorum and successive consulships amid military crisis, and on to the savagery of his last years and his rivalry with Sulla. The opening's explicit engagement with Posidonius on the tria nomina, together with the dense web of anecdotes and phrasing shared with Roman historiography, makes the work a productive hunting ground for textual parallels, both to lost Hellenistic and Roman sources and to Plutarch's other biographies.
grc.plutarch.cato_minor: Plutarch's Cato Minor, written in Greek, is a biography of Cato the Younger, the Roman republican famed for Stoic incorruptibility. It opens with his lineage as great-grandson of Cato the Censor and his orphaned upbringing in the house of Livius Drusus, then builds a portrait of unbending character from childhood anecdotes, his defiance of Pompeius Silo, his demand for a sword against Sulla's proscriptions, before following his public career through the civil strife of the late Republic to his death at Utica. For readers of intertexts, the life offers a Greek window on late Republican Rome and a store of moral exempla, constancy under tyranny, austere virtue, patriotic suicide, that echo throughout later Greek, Latin, and European literature.
grc.plutarch.cimon: Plutarch's Cimon is the Greek Life of the Athenian statesman and general Cimon, composed as one of the Parallel Lives to be read against Plutarch's Lucullus, and printed here from Bernadotte Perrin's 1914 Harvard edition. The opening moves from Chaeronean local history, the seer Peripoltas and the outlaw Damon whose trial Lucullus's testimony ended, into Plutarch's programmatic defence of truthful and restrained biography before introducing the comparison of the two commanders. For readers of intertexts it offers a dense web of allusion to earlier Greek historiography and a paradigmatic instance of the paired Greek-Roman comparison that structures the Lives as a whole.
grc.plutarch.comparison_aegisalius_pompey: A short Greek synkrisis or formal comparison by Plutarch, serving as the concluding assessment of his paired Lives of Agesilaus and Pompey and preserved in Bernadotte Perrin's 1917 edition. It weighs the two commanders point by point, access to power, treatment of Sulla and Lysander, breaches of political justice, conduct under fortune, clemency toward enemies, and generalship, frequently to the advantage of the Spartan king over the Roman. Readers of intertexts will find it useful because it explicitly cross-references and re-evaluates episodes narrated in the two biographies, invokes Xenophon's portrait of Agesilaus, and lays bare the criteria by which Plutarch measured his Greek and Roman subjects against one another.
grc.plutarch.comparison_agis_cleomenes_gracc: The Comparison of Agis, Cleomenes, and the Gracchi is Plutarch's synkrisis concluding the paired Lives of the Spartan kings and the Roman reforming brothers, preserved in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition (Cambridge, MA, 1921); at nineteen lines it is a brief epilogic essay rather than a full biography. In it the Spartans and the Gracchi are weighed point by point, their natures and education, disinterestedness, the scale and legality of their political innovations, their military exploits, and the manner of their ends, with Agis and Cleomenes generally granted the greater resolve. A reader hunting intertexts will find the passage dense with allusive material: Plato's image of lopping off a hydra, the patriotic Rhetra of Lycurgus and the sanction of the Pythian oracle, and glancing references to Carthage, Numantia, Sardinia, and the contest for hegemony over Greece against Illyrian and Gallic arms, so that the comparison functions as a miniature cross-map of Hellenic and Roman moral exempla.
grc.plutarch.comparison_alcibiades_coriolanu: Plutarch's Comparison of Alcibiades and Coriolanus is the short formal synkrisis that closes the paired Lives of the Athenian Alcibiades and the Roman Marcius Coriolanus, printed in Bernadotte Perrin's edition of Plutarch's Lives (Cambridge, MA, 1916). In twenty-two lines of Greek it weighs the two men's military daring and generalship, their opposed political characters, Alcibiades' brilliant but unscrupulous charm against Marcius' harsh, oligarchic stiffness, and their conduct toward money, crowds, exile, and their native cities. Along the way it appeals to Thucydides and Dionysius as historical authorities and echoes a letter of Antipater on Aristotle and a saying of Plato. The chapter offers a compact specimen of Plutarch's comparative method and a dense node of cross-references for readers tracing how biographical judgement reuses historiographical material.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_demosthenes_with_: A short Greek synkrisis by Plutarch, serving as the formal comparison that concludes the paired Lives of Demosthenes and Cicero in the Perrin Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives. Across nineteen lines it weighs the two orators' rhetorical powers and stylistic distinctions, their temperaments as revealed in wit and self-praise, their conduct in commands and provincial office, their dealings with money and royal gifts, and the contrasting circumstances of their exiles. The comparison draws on Caesar's memoirs to Agrippa and Maecenas, alludes to Caelius' defense, Cato's mockery of Stoic paradoxes, Isocrates and Anaximenes, and the Platonic maxim on the conjunction of great power and wisdom, making it a useful node for readers tracing oratorical and ethical topoi across Greek and Roman literature.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_dion_and_brutus: A short Greek comparison by Plutarch, the concluding assessment attached to his paired Lives of Dion and Brutus, printed in Bernadotte Perrin's edition of Plutarch's Lives (Harvard University Press, 1918). It judges the two men point by point, resources for their enterprises, motives, generalship, and relations with the rulers they opposed, crediting Brutus with an untainted hatred of tyranny while arguing that Dion took up arms only after personal injury, a claim reinforced by an appeal to Plato's letters. Readers of intertexts find in it a concentrated repository of Plutarch's verdicts on Caesar, Cassius, Dionysius, and Pompey, formulations on tyrannicide and civic liberty that later writers repeatedly cite and rework.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lucullus_and_cimo: Plutarch's Comparison of Lucullus and Cimon is the short formal synkrisis that follows and weighs his paired Lives of the Roman Lucullus and the Athenian Cimon, edited by Bernadotte Perrin in the 1914 Loeb Plutarch's Lives. In a compact eighteen lines it judges the two generals point by point: their deaths, their leisure and luxury, their use of wealth, their land and sea command, Cimon's single-day double victory against Persia set against Lucullus's march beyond the Taurus and Tigris, and their fortunes with soldiers and allies, both falling short of overthrowing a hegemony. The comparison is densely intertextual, citing Plato's mockery of Orpheus, the ten-year silencing of Cimon's voice by ostracism, and the philosophies of Xenocrates and Epicurus, so that readers tracing echoes will find Plutarch's moralized historiography stitching biography to a wider web of Greek literary and philosophical commonplaces.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lycurgus_and_numa: A short Greek synkrisis by Plutarch, preserved in Perrin's Loeb edition of 1914, appended to the paired Lives of Lycurgus and Numa and weighing the two lawgivers against each other point by point. The comparison surveys their shared virtues, temperance, piety, and lawgiving sanctioned by the gods, before setting off their differences, from Lycurgus's harsh Spartan austerity and the harshness of the helot system to Numa's gentler civilizing of Rome, and then treats land redistribution, attitudes to wealth, and communal customs of marriage and childbearing. For readers of intertexts, the piece is a compact specimen of Plutarch's comparative method, rich in ethical commonplaces and cross-references to Spartan and Roman institutions that recur throughout the Parallel Lives.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_philopoemen_and_t: Plutarch's Comparison of Philopoemen and Titus is the short formal synkrisis that closes the paired Lives of the Achaean general Philopoemen and the Roman commander Titus Quinctius Flamininus, edited by Bernadotte Perrin in the Loeb Plutarch's Lives (1921). In nine lines of Greek prose it weighs the two men against each other: Titus' benefactions to the Greeks and victory over Philip are set against Philopoemen's far greater experience of war, while their faults are traced to ambition in one case and contentiousness in the other. The verdict awards the crown of military skill to the Greek, who raised armies and invented tactics in a Hellas already declining, and that of justice and magnanimity to the Roman, who commanded resources already at their height. The piece thus condenses Plutarch's comparative method into a compact specimen, and readers hunting parallels will find in it the verbal echoes, paired judgments, and Greek-versus-Roman topoi that bind the comparison to the two Lives it concludes.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_theseus_and_romul: The Comparison (synkrisis) of Theseus and Romulus is the formal concluding assessment that Plutarch appends to the paired Lives of Theseus and Romulus, preserved in Perrin's 1914 Harvard edition. In brief Greek prose it weighs the two founders' motives, deeds, political characters, and misfortunes, Theseus's self-chosen perils, his clearing of Sciron, Sinis, Procrustes, and other bandits, and the Cretan expedition with Ariadne against Romulus's rise from servitude, his killing of the tyrant of Alba, and his founding of Rome, before awarding a verdict that favors each man in different respects. For readers of intertexts the passage serves as a compact hub where Greek and Roman foundation traditions are set side by side, with explicit cross-references to the centauromachy, the Amazons, and a saying of Plato, and it supplied later writers with a paradigmatic framework for comparing lawgivers, founders, and the eros and anger of rulers.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_apollonium: A prose consolation attributed to Plutarch and preserved among the Moralia, of uncertain date, addressed to Apollonius upon the untimely death of his son, a young man of marked self-control and piety. The speaker argues for moderated grief rather than utter insensibility, using medical metaphors in which words act as physicians of the sick soul and defending metriopatheia against the harsh apatheia he rejects, while urging reasoned endurance of fortune's reversals. The argument is densely woven with quotation, Euripides, Menander, and the Academic Crantor are invoked in its opening movement, making the work a rich repository of fragments and verbal parallels for readers tracing intertexts.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_uxorem: A letter of consolation addressed by Plutarch to his wife on the death of their young daughter, the Consolatio ad Uxorem is transmitted among the Moralia and is printed here from Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891. Writing as both husband and philosopher, Plutarch urges measured grief, praises his wife's composure and records the child's winning and affectionate nature, and warns that grief, once admitted into the house, becomes an inmate hard to dislodge. The argument alludes to Homer, quotes from tragedy, and retells the Aesopic fable in which Zeus distributed grief among the gods. For readers of intertexts the letter offers a compact instance of the consolatio tradition, with embedded quotations and topoi of mourning ripe for comparison across Greek and Latin literature.
grc.plutarch.crassus: Plutarch's Life of Crassus, a Greek biographical account of the Roman triumvir Marcus Licinius Crassus as printed in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition (1916), opens with its subject's family and notorious love of wealth, property gathered cheap from Sulla's proscriptions, speculation in burning tenements, and a vast retinue of skilled slaves, before tracing his eloquence, hospitality, and political career through the civil violence of the late Republic to his fatal Parthian expedition. Composed in the moralizing manner of the Parallel Lives, it weighs character through anecdote, quoted sayings, and pointed comparisons, including reflections on the measure of wealth drawn from Marius and Archidamus. Its dense weave of maxims, verbal reminiscences of the historians of the late Republic, and episodes retold elsewhere in Plutarch's biographies makes it a productive meeting point for readers hunting textual parallels.
grc.plutarch.de_alexandri_magni_fortuna_aut_: Plutarch's De Alexandri Magni Fortuna aut Virtute, printed among the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1889, is a Greek rhetorical essay asking whether Alexander the Great won his empire through Fortune or through virtue, and it argues emphatically for virtue. The work stages Fortune's claim to credit for Alexander's conquests and the king's imagined reply, a catalogue of wounds and toils delivered in conspicuously Homeric diction, before crediting his achievement to philosophy, Aristotle's training above Philip's legacy. Readers hunting parallels will find direct engagement with Homer (the Iliad and Odyssey as the king's baggage for his campaign), citations of Alexander historians such as Aristobulus, Ptolemy, Onesicritus, Anaximenes, and Duris, and pointed comparisons of Alexander's hellenizing conquest with Socrates, Plato, Zeno, and Carneades.
grc.plutarch.de_amore_prolis: The De Amore Prolis is a Greek dialogue by Plutarch preserved among the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891, arguing that affection for one's children is implanted by nature rather than grounded in advantage. Its opening sets animals before a notional court: since beasts mate, bear, and rear their young without laws, contracts, or penalties for childlessness, their unforced philostorgia reproaches human beings, who calculate and argue from custom, and it rebuts the Epicurean position, quoted in the course of the discussion, that no one loves another person without profit. Examples run from the halcyon's woven nest and the bear's shaping of its formless cubs to Homeric similes of the lion and the bird provisioning her nestlings, alongside partridges, hens, and dogs defending their young. For readers of intertexts the dialogue offers a dense field of zoological exempla and direct Homeric quotation deployed in ethical argument.
grc.plutarch.de_capienda_ex_inimicis_utilita: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia and printed here from Bernardakis's Teubner edition, addressed to Cornelius Pulcher and arguing that a man of sense can profit even from his enemies. The author develops Xenophon's dictum that the intelligent benefit from their antagonists, illustrating the point with the saying of Chilon, the fable of Prometheus and the satyr, anecdotes of Zeno, Diogenes, and Crates, and Nasica's remark on Rome's security after the fall of Carthage. Woven through the argument are Homeric quotation, animal and elemental similes, and gnomic exempla of the kind collected elsewhere in the Plutarchan corpus. Its dense constellation of allusions to historians, philosophers, and poets makes it a productive site for readers tracking intertextual parallels in Greek ethical prose.
grc.plutarch.de_communibus_notitiis_adversus: Plutarch's De communibus notitiis adversus Stoicos, a Greek philosophical dialogue of uncertain date transmitted in the Moralia and printed from the Teubner edition of Gregorius N. Bernardakis (1895), stages a conversation between Lamprias and Diadoumenus against the Stoic appeal to common conceptions and preconceptions. The speakers contend that Stoic paradoxes, such as the claims that only the sage is king, rich, beautiful, or a judge, subvert the koinai ennoiai on which the school itself professes to found knowledge, and they direct particular invective at Chrysippus's dialectic. The dialogue also recalls the quarrel between the Stoa and the Academy through Arcesilaus and Carneades, and drops anecdotes about Cato and Caesar alongside mythological allusions. Readers of intertexts will find in it a compact repository of anti-Stoic polemic and its accompanying commonplaces.
grc.plutarch.de_cupiditate_divitiarum: A short Greek moral essay from Plutarch's Moralia, printed in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891, on the love of wealth (philoploutia). Opening from the saying of the trainer Hippomachus and arguing by analogy with bodily appetite and disease, the piece holds that greed is an insatiable sickness of the soul which money cannot cure, since wealth quenches no desire beyond itself. Along the way it cites the saying of Aristippus and embeds gnomic and comic verses from Solon, Menander, Hipponax, and a comedy, making it a productive place to trace borrowed sententiae on wealth and self-sufficiency within Greek moral prose.
grc.plutarch.de_curiositate: De Curiositate (Greek Peri polypragmosynēs), a Greek moral essay by Plutarch transmitted with the Moralia and printed from Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891, condemns polypragmosyne, the restless itch to pry into other people's affairs while overlooking one's own faults. The opening likens diseased passions to a dark or unhealthy house that can be made habitable by shifting the light, altering the staircase and opening or shutting particular doors, and the essay urges redirecting such curiosity inward toward self-examination, sustaining the architectural imagery throughout. Anecdotes of Odysseus questioning the shades of Homer's Nekyia, of Aristippus at Olympia and of Socrates pursuing Pythagorean argument sit beside the fable of the Lamia and Ariston's remark on winds that lift our cloaks, all mustered against meddlesomeness. Readers hunting parallels will find Homeric quotation, material drawn from Xenophon's Oeconomicus and moral commonplaces on curiosity packed into a short compass.
grc.plutarch.de_defectu_oraculorum: De Defectu Oraculorum (On the Obsolescence of Oracles) is a Greek dialogue by Plutarch, transmitted in the Moralia and edited here from Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891. Set at Delphi shortly before a Pythian festival, it stages a conversation among Ammonius the philosopher, Cleombrotus the Spartan traveller, and Demetrius the grammarian newly returned from Britain, on the question of why oracles have fallen silent; the discussion opens from the myth that eagles or swans once met at the earth's central omphalos and Epimenides' sceptical oracle on that story, and draws on reports such as the ever-burning lamp at the oracle of Ammon in Egypt, whose diminishing oil consumption is read as a sign of cosmic change. Its dense texture of quotation and allusion, Homer, Alcaeus, Epimenides, and Delphic lore, makes the work a rich point of reference for readers hunting classical intertexts.
grc.plutarch.de_e_delphos: A Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia in the Bernardakis Teubner edition, which takes as its puzzle the letter epsilon dedicated at Delphi. The conversation, framed as addressed to Sarapion and featuring Ammonius, Lamprias, and other speakers, moves from Dicaearchus' anecdote about Euripides and Archelaus to Apollo's role as philosopher rather than mere prophet, the Delphic maxims 'know thyself' and 'nothing in excess,' and the Five Sages' dedication of the wooden tablet, weighing symbolic, mathematical, and theological explanations of the letter. Readers hunting parallels will find dense engagement with Euripidean verse, with traditions about the Seven Sages and their sayings, and with number and planetary symbolism of the kind that circulated freely in later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.plutarch.de_esu_carnium: A short Greek ethical diatribe from Plutarch's Moralia, given in the Teubner text of Bernardakis, which opens with a question about the reasons for Pythagoras's abstinence from flesh-eating and turns that question against the first man who slew and consumed an animal. The speaker concedes that primordial scarcity and a disordered early world once drove humanity to eat flesh, but denies any such excuse now that Demeter and Dionysus yield the earth's unmixed abundance. Later passages attack the cruelty and waste of wealthy tables, where the meat left behind exceeds what is eaten, and rebuke the luxurious excuse that beasts' cries are mere wordless sound. Readers tracking intertexts will find here the classic Pythagorean arguments on blood-guilt, diet, and the rhetorical defence of vegetarianism that recur across Greek moral prose and verse.
grc.plutarch.de_esu_carnium_2: The second book of Plutarch's De esu carnium, printed among the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition, is a short ethical argument against the slaughter and eating of animals. It contends that flesh-eating springs not from hunger or necessity but from gluttony, luxury, and unbridled appetite, and it dwells on the elaborate cruelties practised by gourmets upon swine, cranes, and swans. Drawing on Pythagorean and Empedoclean doctrines of the transmigration of souls, the speaker warns that human and animal bodies may be exchanged across rebirths, and traces meat-eating from a first act of violence against a wild creature to wars, murder, and human suffering. Laced with allusions to Homer, Cato, Lycurgus' rhetrai, Herodotus' distant peoples, and Plato's Phaedo, the work offers rich ground for readers hunting classical echoes of Pythagorean vegetarianism and Plutarch's debts to earlier poetry and philosophy.
grc.plutarch.de_exilio: A short Greek prose consolation on exile, preserved among the Moralia of Plutarch and edited from Bernardakis's 1891 Teubner text. The speaker argues that exile, like loss of office or wealth, weighs upon a man only as his own judgment makes it weigh, and culminates in a cosmopolitan claim that the true fatherland is the whole ordered cosmos under one divine ruler who guides all things by nature and Dike. The argument is densely interwoven with embedded quotation, including Alcaeus on Sardis, Homer's two jars of good and evil, Plato's description of man as a celestial plant, and a hymnic passage on Zeus and Dike, which makes the essay a rewarding locus for readers tracing lyric, epic, and Platonic fragments through later Greek literature.
grc.plutarch.de_fato: A short Greek treatise on fate (Περὶ εἱμαρμένης, De Fato), printed among Plutarch's Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891 and framed as a written reply to a friend named Piso who had asked for a clear and concise account of destiny. The opening distinguishes fate as activity from fate as substance, supporting each with Platonic witnesses: the law of Adrasteia in the Phaedrus, the divine laws spoken by the god in the Timaeus, and Lachesis, daughter of Necessity, in the Republic. Fate is then argued to be finite rather than infinite, a bounded circle governing recurrent cosmic periods, and to hold of universals as a law of nature does, with particulars following by consequence. For readers of intertexts the work is a compact node of Platonic citation and determinist vocabulary, necessity, cosmic cycles, Adrasteia, Lachesis, that later Greek and Latin discussions of fate repeatedly reuse.
grc.plutarch.de_fortuna_romanorum: A Greek rhetorical essay by Plutarch preserved in the Moralia, 'De Fortuna Romanorum' ('On the Fortune of the Romans') stages a contest between personified Virtue and Fortune over which of the two brought Roman hegemony into being. The speaker resolves the quarrel by presenting the two powers as reconciled collaborators in Rome's rise, each attended by a retinue of Roman exempla, Fabricius, Camillus, Mucius Scaevola, Marcellus, the Scipios, Marius, Aemilius Paullus, and Sulla, who styles himself Fortune's child. The piece is densely allusive, citing or echoing Ion, Plato, Democritus, Pindar, Alcman, Sophocles, and Menander, and offers a compact specimen of Greek personification rhetoric applied to Roman history. Readers of intertexts will find it a focal point for the Fortune-versus-Virtue debate tradition and for the redeployment of classical poets in imperial prose.
grc.plutarch.de_fraterno_amore: On Brotherly Love (De fraterno amore) is a Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891. Addressed jointly to Nigrinus and Cynthus, it argues from nature and example, the Spartan dokana of the Dioscuri, the paired organs of a single body, and mythological and historical exempla, that fraternal concord is the pattern for all human cooperation and that discord among brothers is a self-mutilation. Readers hunting parallels will find the essay densely intertextual, with explicit quotation from Menander, allusion to Herodotus and the Molionidae, references to Anaxagoras, and a string of gnomic sayings on friendship, kinship, and the household.
grc.plutarch.de_garrulitate: De Garrulitate (Peri Adoleschias) is a short Greek prose treatise by Plutarch, preserved with the Moralia and printed here from Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891. The essay attacks talkativeness as a disease of the soul, likening the chatterer to an empty vessel resonating with noise, and argues that silence, listening, and brevity are the proper conditions of philosophical conversation. In support it deploys anecdotes about Aristotle, Bias, and Zeno and quotes Euripides, Homer, Archilochus, and Sophocles, so the piece offers abundant material for readers hunting poetic fragments and commonplaces on speech, silence, and drunkenness.
grc.plutarch.de_genio_socratis: A Greek prose dialogue by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia and printed here from Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891. Set at Thebes, it opens with Caphisias and Archidamus arranging a full account of the conspiracy that liberated the city from its Spartan-backed oligarchy, gathering figures such as Epameinondas, Pelopidas, Simmias and the seer Theocritus, and moving towards the celebrated question of the daimonion of Socrates that gives the work its title. An explicit quotation of Pindar in the opening exchange, Socratic characters inherited from the Platonic corpus, and the layered narration of an episode central to Greek historical memory offer readers of intertexts abundant points of verbal and thematic contact.
grc.plutarch.de_gloria_atheniensium: A Greek essay from Plutarch's Moralia (Gregorius N. Bernardakis, Moralia, Leipzig: Teubner, 1889), De Gloria Atheniensium asks whether the Athenians won greater renown from war or from wisdom, arguing that poets, painters, and historians share in the deeds they commemorate. It contrasts generals and statesmen with makers of words and images, invoking Simonides' dictum that painting is silent poetry and poetry speaking painting, surveying Athenian achievement from the Persian wars to Epameinondas' campaigns, and praising Thucydides for making his readers spectators of battle. Readers tracing intertexts will find extended engagement with Thucydidean phrasing, the anecdote of the messenger announcing Marathon, and testimony for lost historians such as Herakleides of Pontus, which makes the essay a central witness to ancient ideas of enargeia and the rivalry of word and image.
grc.plutarch.de_invidia_et_odio: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition, which compares the passions of envy (phthonos) and hate (misos) and opens abruptly, as if continuing an earlier discussion. It argues that the two are akin yet distinct: hate, born of the belief that its object is base, can attach even to animals, whereas envy arises only between humans and fastens on good fortune and growing virtue, illustrated through anecdotes about Themistocles, Charillus, Thersites, the persecutors of Socrates, Alexander and Cyrus. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a compact repository of ancient psychological commonplaces about envy, with allusions to Homer, Spartan history and Alexander's career that recur throughout later moral and literary tradition.
grc.plutarch.de_iside_et_osiride: A Greek philosophical essay by Plutarch on the Egyptian deities Isis, Osiris, and Typhon, printed among the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1889. Addressed to Clea, a devotee of Isis, it insists that true religion rests on knowledge and truth rather than superstition, and reads Egyptian myths and priestly observances such as purity rules, linen garments, abstention from salt, and the care of the Apis bull as vehicles of philosophical teaching. With explicit quotations from Homer, Hesiod, and Plato and a sustained habit of allegorical explanation, the essay offers rich material for readers tracing textual parallels between Greek literature and Greek interpretations of Egyptian religion.
grc.plutarch.de_primo_frigido: Plutarch's De Primo Frigido (“On the Principle of Cold”), a short Greek dialogue preserved in the Moralia, asks whether cold is a positive power and substance, as heat is rooted in fire, or merely the privation of heat, as darkness is of light and silence of sound. Opening with a question posed to Favorinus, the discussion marshals perceptual and physical arguments, cold is felt and admits degrees of more and less, acts in freezing and condensation, and mingles with heat within a cosmic order that God arranges like a musician, while the Stoic claim that the pneuma of embryos is solidified into soul by refrigeration is reported and dismissed as disputed. A closing appeal to Homer's “iaínesthai” for the pleasant relaxation that follows shivering typifies the work's blend of natural philosophy with literary citation. For readers of intertexts, the dialogue offers a compact node of Aristotelian privation theory, Stoic physics, and Homeric echo within the Plutarchan tradition of scientific dialogue.
grc.plutarch.de_pythiae_oraculis: A Greek dialogue by Plutarch, transmitted in the Moralia (Bernardakis, Teubner, 1891), set at Delphi and conducted among the interlocutors Basilocles, Philinus, Theon, and Diogenianus. Framed by a visitor's tour of the sanctuary's dedications, the conversation takes up the Pythia's oracles and the question why they are no longer delivered in verse, while the opening exchanges linger on the blue-green color of ancient bronze and offer physical explanations of it in terms of air and moisture. The speakers appeal to Aristotle's causal theories and cite Homer verbatim, making the work a dense meeting point of Homeric quotation, Peripatetic natural philosophy, and Delphic lore within a Platonic-style dialogue.
grc.plutarch.de_recta_ratione_audiendi: A Greek prose essay by Plutarch, transmitted in the Moralia and printed here from Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1888, De Recta Ratione Audiendi ('On the Right Way to Listen') offers advice to a young dedicatee, Nicander, on how to profit from lectures as he passes from boyhood to manhood. Plutarch argues that the ear is the principal channel through which reason can shape character, warning against the undisciplined 'lawlessness' of youth and illustrating his case with anecdotes about Xenocrates' ear-guards for his pupils, Bias's tongue sent to Amasis, and Spintharus's praise of Epaminondas as a sparing speaker. The essay is densely allusive, quoting or echoing Homer, Herodotus and Theophrastus in its argument, and will interest readers of intertexts both for its borrowed material and for its own later reception in the tradition of educational literature.
grc.plutarch.de_se_ipsum_citra_invidiam_laud: A short Greek moral essay from the Moralia corpus, attributed to Plutarch and addressed to a certain Herculanus, on how a statesman may praise himself without incurring envy. It opens with Euripides, Pindar, and Timotheus on the general odium of self-praise (periautologia), then distinguishes blameless cases, self-defence against slander, plain report of genuine deeds, illustrated by Pericles, Epaminondas and the Thebans, Homer's Sthenelus, Cicero, and Scipio. At twenty-two lines in Bernardakis's Teubner Moralia of 1891, the treatise is brief but densely supplied with verse quotations and historical exempla, making it fertile ground for readers hunting parallels.
grc.plutarch.de_sollertia_animalium: A Greek prose dialogue by Plutarch, transmitted in the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1895. Framed as a conversation between Autobulus and Soclarus on the morning after a display of speeches, the work prepares a contest in which Aristotimus pleads for land animals and Phaidimos for sea creatures on the question of animal intelligence, following a day given to the argument that all animals share in reason. The opening exchanges set an encomium of hunting recited the previous evening against the fear that praise of the chase drives the young toward bloodshed. Readers tracing intertexts will find the dialogue dense with poetic quotation, Euripides and Sophocles are cited at the outset, and rich in anecdotes and philosophical argument, including Stoic doctrine on the rational and irrational soul, that echo widely through later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.plutarch.de_tranquilitate_animi: De Tranquillitate Animi, a Greek moral essay by Plutarch preserved in the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition, is cast as a letter to Paccius in which the author explains his delayed reply by his friend Eros's sudden voyage to Rome at the summons of Fundanus, and compiles from his note-books a discourse on peace of mind. The essay rejects the view that freedom from disturbance is best secured by inactivity, arguing with examples from Homer, Hesiod, Menander, and Epicurus that the calm or troubled life is measured by the quality of one's undertakings rather than their number. Its extensive quotation of poets and its engagement with Hellenistic philosophy make it a rewarding source for readers tracing verbal parallels across Greek literary tradition.
grc.plutarch.lycurgus: Plutarch's Lycurgus is a Greek biographical essay, one of the Lives printed in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives (Cambridge, MA, and London, 1914). It treats the semi-legendary Spartan lawgiver, opening with a frank survey of the irreconcilable traditions about his genealogy, his death, and his chronology relative to the first Olympiad and Homer, before narrating his regency for the infant Charilaus and the laws and constitution he gave the Spartans. Throughout, Plutarch names and weighs earlier authorities, including Aristotle, Eratosthenes, Apollodorus, Timaeus, Xenophon, and Simonides, setting variant accounts side by side. For readers of intertexts the Life is a dense node of quotations and transmitted fragments bearing on early Sparta and on poets and historians otherwise imperfectly preserved.
grc.plutarch.marcellus: Plutarch's Life of Marcellus is a Greek biographical account of Marcus Claudius Marcellus, the Roman statesman who held the consulship five times, preserved in the Loeb edition prepared by Bernadotte Perrin (1917). The narrative opens with Marcellus' lineage, martial temperament, and early exploits, including his victories in single combat, the rescue of his brother Otacilius in Sicily, and the Gallic and Carthaginian wars that dominated Roman life from his youth to his old age. As one of the Parallel Lives, it interweaves Homeric quotation and Greek moral commentary with Roman history, offering rich material for readers tracing literary allusion, proverbial phrasing, and biographical conventions across Greek and Latin traditions.
grc.plutarch.marcus_cato: In Greek and printed in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives (1914), the Life of Marcus Cato traces the Roman statesman known as Cato the Elder from his Tusculan lineage and Sabine farmhouse upbringing through his service in the wars against Hannibal and his emergence as orator, advocate, and public figure. The narrative dwells on his habitual austerity, bodily hardiness, and imitation of exemplars such as Manius Curius, while crediting his late study of Greek letters and his debt to Thucydides and Demosthenes for his style. Plutarch seasons the account with verse, apothegms, and translated sayings, and the density of quoted and reworked material makes the life a rewarding hunting ground for readers tracing verbal and moral echoes across biographical literature.
grc.plutarch.numa: Plutarch's Life of Numa is a Greek biographical account of Numa Pompilius, the Sabine chosen to succeed Romulus as king of Rome, preserved in the Perrin Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives. The opening chapters weigh disputes over Numa's chronology and over the tradition linking him with Pythagoras, then narrate Romulus's sudden disappearance in a storm, the divine honors accorded him, the patrician interregnum, and the election of Numa to the throne. The file follows the story from these debates through Numa's acceptance of the kingship. For readers of intertexts, the narrative offers a dense weave of chronographical argument and Roman foundation legend, touching Sabine origins, Spartan ancestry claims, and early Roman religious institutions, and so serves as a natural cross-reference for other treatments of Rome's regal period.
grc.plutarch.pelopidas: Plutarch's Pelopidas is a Greek biographical essay, one of the Parallel Lives and expressly paired by its author with the Life of Marcellus. The prologue argues, through anecdotes about Cato the Elder, a soldier of Antigonus, Callicratidas, Timotheus and Chares, that a commander must weigh his own safety because the fate of an army hangs upon him, before turning to Pelopidas of Thebes, his distinguished birth, his generous use of inherited wealth, and his close friendship with the austere Epaminondas. Readers hunting parallels will find the passage densely intertextual, citing Homer, Euripides' Capaneus, Aristotle and a Spartan funeral elegy, and framing Pelopidas as a Greek counterpart to Marcellus, both soldiers celebrated for a daring that cost them their lives.
grc.plutarch.phocion: Plutarch's Life of Phocion is a Greek biographical narrative from the Parallel Lives, pairing the austere Athenian statesman and general Phocion with Cato the Younger, a comparison its prologue on Demades, frank speech, and the steering of the ship of state makes programmatic. The narrative follows Phocion through the era of Macedonian supremacy: his repeated generalships, his reluctant dealings with Philip, Alexander, and Antipater, and his condemnation and death at the hands of a fickle Athens. Dense with quoted verse, epigrammatic sayings, and moralising comparison, the life stands among the most excerpted of Plutarch's biographies and supplies a canonical exemplar of civic integrity whose echoes recur throughout later literature.
grc.plutarch.pompey: Plutarch's Life of Pompey (Pompeius), printed in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives (1917), is a Greek biographical narrative of the Roman general Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus. In under four hundred lines it follows Pompey from his youth under his father Strabo and the turmoil of Cinna's ascendancy through the growth of his reputation, dwelling on his self-command, his charisma before crowds and armies, and anecdotes of his love affairs and frugal habits, while the opening frames his fortunes through Aeschylus' Prometheus and his carefully cultivated resemblance to Alexander the Great. The Life's dense weave of quoted sayings, borrowed similes, and moralized anecdote makes it a productive source for readers tracing echoes of classical poetry, historiographical topoi, and parallels with Plutarch's other biographies.
grc.plutarch.pyrrhus: Plutarch's Life of Pyrrhus, one of the biographies that make up his Lives (here in the Greek as printed in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition of 1920), follows the Epirote king from his perilous infancy after the expulsion of his father Aeacides, his rescue across a flooded river and his reception by Glaucias of Illyria, through his exile, restoration to the Molossian throne, and entanglements with Demetrius and the successors of Alexander. Written in Greek, the narrative combines political and military history with anecdote, omen, and physiognomic detail in Plutarch's characteristic moralizing manner. Readers hunting intertexts will find it a dense repository of Hellenistic historical tradition, including Pyrrhus's campaigns in Italy against Rome, and a work whose episodes and phrasing were widely taken up by later Greek and Latin writers.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_graecae: Attributed to Plutarch and preserved in the Moralia (Babbitt's Loeb edition of 1936), the Quaestiones Graecae is a short antiquarian work of uncertain date that poses questions about obscure Greek local customs and answers them with etymologies and historical explanations. Its entries cover civic bodies, magistracies, rituals, and festivals, from the 'konipodes' of Epidaurus and the adulteress's 'onobatis' ride at Kyme to Delphic officials, the Bysios month, and the Charila rite, frequently appealing to Aristotle, Theophrastus, Callisthenes, and Aeschylus. For readers tracing parallels, it offers a dense repository of glossed rare words, cult aetiologies, and local traditions that surface elsewhere in lexicography, historians, and the moral essays.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_naturales: Quaestiones Naturales, a short treatise by Plutarch preserved among the Moralia (here in the Teubner edition of Bernardakis, Leipzig 1893), poses and answers a sequence of questions about natural phenomena: why seawater does not nourish trees or land animals, why rainwater feeds seeds better than irrigation, why herdsmen give salt to their beasts, and why rain accompanied by thunder benefits crops. The discussion proceeds by weighing rival explanations and invokes Plato, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Aristotle, Empedocles, Heraclitus and Aratus, quoting the Heraclitean river fragment and a line of Aratus on frogs as signs of rain. For readers of intertexts, the treatise supplies a compact repertory of Greek physical explanations and verbatim quotations from earlier philosophy that recur elsewhere in ancient poetry and prose.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_romanae: Plutarch's Quaestiones Romanae, a Greek treatise preserved in the Moralia and printed here in Frank Cole Babbitt's Loeb edition of 1936, takes the form of a succession of brief questions about Roman custom, wedding rites, the five wedding torches, temple restrictions, the treatment of those reported dead, kissing among kin, each followed by one or more conjectural explanations. The answers draw freely on antiquarian learning, citing authorities such as Varro, Juba, and Aristotle, and repeatedly set Roman practice beside Greek parallels and aetiological myths. For readers of intertexts the work offers a compact repository of Roman ritual lore, symbolic and etymological reasoning, and explicit cross-cultural comparison.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_adolescens_poetas_audir: A Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia in Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1888 and addressed in its opening to Marcus Sedatus on the poetry his young sons should study. The work argues that verse is a nourishing but dangerous food for the young, to be tempered rather than banned: readers must learn that poets deliberately fabricate, weigh the pleasurable against the profitable, and apply philosophical judgement to tales of gods, heroes, and the underworld. Richly studded with quotation and discussion of Homer, Hesiod, Empedocles, Xenophanes, Pindar, Simonides, and the tragedians, it offers a dense node for intertextual study, showing how a Second Sophistic moralist redeploys canonical epic, lyric, and philosophical verse as pedagogical evidence.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_quis_suos_in_virtute_se: A short Greek philosophical dialogue from Plutarch's Moralia, addressed to Sossius Senecio, on how a person may come to perceive their own progress toward virtue. The speaker asks whether moral advance is gradual or an instantaneous transformation, objects to the doctrine that all short of the perfect sage are equally wicked, and begins to set out signs by which improvement in philosophy may be detected, likening steady progress to a ship running before a constant wind. Its dense weave of Homeric quotation, historical exempla such as Aristides, Phalaris, Brasidas, and Dolon, and the Delphic oracle's command to the Cirrhaeans makes the dialogue a rich hunting ground for readers tracing literary and philosophical intertexts in Plutarch's prose.
grc.plutarch.romulus: Plutarch's Life of Romulus is a Greek biographical treatment of Rome's legendary founder, transmitted in the Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives prepared by Bernadotte Perrin (1914). Its opening chapters survey the rival traditions about the origin of Rome's name and its eponymous founders, then turn to the narrative of Amulius, Numitor, Rhea Silvia, and the exposed twins fed by the river and a she-wolf. A reader hunting parallels will find a dense assembly of variant foundation legends and etymologies, together with named earlier authorities such as Diocles of Peparethus and Fabius Pictor, making the work a natural crossroads for motifs of exposed infants, divine parentage, and city naming.
grc.plutarch.septem_sapientium_convivium: The Septem Sapientium Convivium ('Dinner of the Seven Sages'), a Greek dialogue by Plutarch preserved in the Moralia, recounts the banquet that Periander hosts at Lechaeum beside the sanctuary of Aphrodite, attended by the renowned wise men of Greece. The opening narrative follows the guests on their way to the feast, taking in Neiloxenus of Naucratis with his riddling commission from Bias, the celebrated story of the sacrificial animal whose best and worst portion is the tongue, and Thales's measurement of the Egyptian pyramid by its shadow. At table the company ranges over tyranny, flattery, and the art of agreeable dinner conversation, and the dialogue's accumulation of sententiae, exemplary anecdotes, and sympotic staging makes it a productive hunting ground for readers tracing gnomic wisdom and the literary tradition of the philosophical banquet.
grc.plutarch.sertorius: Plutarch's Life of Sertorius, transmitted in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives, is a Greek biographical prose work from the Parallel Lives of the Roman imperial period, paired with the Life of Eumenes of Cardia. It opens with a digression on the coincidences of chance, cataloguing deaths by the same kinds of creatures, cities captured more than once, and one-eyed commanders such as Philip, Antigonus, Hannibal, and Sertorius, before narrating the Roman general's career from Sabine Nursia through service under Caepio and Marius against the Cimbri and Teutones, command in Iberia, and resistance to Metellus and Pompey at the head of exiles and Spanish allies, ending in assassination. For readers hunting intertexts, the programmatic preface and the explicit comparison of Sertorius with Eumenes make the work a central locus for tracing Greek and Roman correspondences and for Plutarch's treatment of tyche in paired biography.
grc.plutarch.sulla: Plutarch's Life of Sulla (Greek Σύλλας), preserved in Greek in the Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives prepared by Bernadotte Perrin (1916), is a biographical account of Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the patrician Roman general who rose from straitened circumstances to supreme power at Rome. Opening with Sulla's ancestry, unpretentious means, forbidding appearance, and temperamental love of jest and pleasure, the narrative proceeds through his quaestorship under Marius, his part in the capture of Jugurtha through the Numidian king Bocchus, and the rivalry with Marius that his growing repute provoked, before going on to his dominance and the bloodshed that attended it. For readers of intertexts the Life matters as a dense repository of anecdote, quoted verse, and morally shaded portraiture whose phrasing and material recur throughout Plutarch's corpus and the Roman historical tradition.
grc.plutarch.timoleon: Plutarch's Life of Timoleon, presented here in Bernadotte Perrin's Loeb edition of Plutarch's Lives (1918), pairs the Corinthian general Timoleon with Aemilius Paulus as men favoured alike in judgement and fortune. The work opens with a programmatic reflection on biography as a mirror for shaping one's own character, quoting Democritus on ethical improvement, before turning to Sicily's descent into tyranny after the murder of Dion, the restoration of the tyrant Dionysius, and the Corinthian expedition that placed Timoleon at the head of Syracusan liberation and resistance to Carthage. For readers of intertexts, the prologue's meditation on the moral uses of historiography, together with its embedded citations and allusions, makes the Life a productive site for tracing Plutarch's borrowings and his dialogue with earlier historical writing.
grc.plutarch.παροιμίαι_αἷς_ἀλεξανδρεῖς_ἐχρῶν: A short Greek paroemiographic collection transmitted under Plutarch's name and titled as the proverbs which the Alexandrians used, arranged as a single sequence of entries in which each saying is followed by a concise explanation of its meaning and origin. The roughly 130 entries gloss idioms such as 'Milesian things at home', 'the Cestreus fasts', and 'the Heraclidean itch' with anecdotes and aetiological stories drawn from Greek myth, history, and daily life, ranging from Aristagoras of Miletus before the Spartan ephors to the Athenian marriage custom of carrying bread in a winnowing basket. For readers tracing intertexts, the collection preserves proverbial diction and the narrative explanations attached to it, often serving as an early or unique witness to individual sayings and the lore behind them, and thus helps illuminate allusive turns of phrase encountered elsewhere in Greek literature.
grc.plutarch_pseudo.de_musica: Attributed to Plutarch (Pseudo-Plutarch) and of uncertain date, the De Musica is a Greek dialogue set at a symposium hosted by Onesicrates, whose guests, notably the musician Lysias, discuss the origins of music and the earliest practitioners of song. Its speakers trace the invention of hymns, dirges, citharodic and aulos nomes to figures such as Amphion, Linus, Thamyris, Terpander, Clonas and Polymnestus, drawing on earlier compilers like Heraclides and citing the Sicyonian records, and they contrast the discipline of ancient music with its later corruption. The work preserves quotations from Homer and from many otherwise lost poets and theorists on music, making it a valuable witness for readers tracing musical and poetic intertexts in Greek literature.
grc.polybius.histories: The Histories of Polybius is a Greek prose universal history, presented here in the Teubner edition of Theodorus Büttner-Wobst after L. Dindorf (Leipzig, 1893–) and running to some 12,000 lines. The opening book argues that the study of history is the surest training for political life and the best teacher of how to bear the reversals of fortune, and announces as its theme how the Romans brought almost the whole inhabited world under one rule in fewer than fifty-three whole years, setting their achievement against those of the Persians, Lacedaemonians, and Macedonians. The narrative begins with the 140th Olympiad, embracing the Social War fought by Philip with the Achaeans against the Aetolians, the war of Antiochus and Ptolemy Philopator over Coele-Syria, and the Hannibalic war between Rome and Carthage, the era from which events, formerly scattered, become 'body-like' and converge on a single end. Its programmatic preface and sweeping political themes made the work a standing model and quarry for later historians, and a natural point of comparison for readers tracing ancient reflections on the purpose and method of history.
grc.pseudo_dicaearchus_messeniushe.dicaearch: A short Greek periegesis transmitted under the name of Dicaearchus of Messana, though the title itself notes that the work belongs more probably to an Athenaeus, and of uncertain date. Taking the form of a traveller's itinerary, it opens with a witty sketch of Athens, dry and ill-planned, yet rich in sights such as the Odeion, the Parthenon, the unfinished Olympieion, and its tree-shaded gymnasia, before following the road through Oropus, Tanagra, and Plataeae to Thebes, characterising each city's land and inhabitants with satirical bite. The account quotes verses of Lysippus and Xenon and names the comic poet Posidippus, preserving poetic fragments within a prose frame. Readers tracing intertexts will find a dense cluster of topoi on Athenian luxury and hospitality, Boeotian manners, and monumental sightseeing.
grc.pseudoarrianus.anonymi_arriani_ut_fertur: A Greek periplus of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Arrian and hence printed as Pseudo-Arrian in Karl Müller's Geographi graeci minores (1855), the work is a short coastal sailing guide to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Its chapters run from Berenice along the African shore of the so-called Barbaric country, past Ptolemais of the Hunts and the emporium of Adulis to the markets of Malao, Mundu, and Mosylon, cataloguing distances in stades, anchorages, imports and exports, local peoples, and rulers such as Zoskales, and naming the metropolis of the Auxomitae as the terminus of the ivory trade. The dense attention to merchandise, sailing conditions, and coastal ethnography makes the periplus a valuable quarry for readers seeking parallels in place names, trade vocabulary, and the phrasing of ancient geographical literature.
grc.pseudogalen.de_fasciis: De fasciis (On Bandages) is a short Greek surgical treatise transmitted under Galen's name but spuriously attributed to him, of uncertain date and authorship, printed in Kühn's 1829 edition of the Galenic corpus. After a defence of figured and patterned bandages against critics who cite Hippocrates against them, it sets out a taxonomy of bandages by material, shape, length, width, and construction, naming varieties used for fractures, wounds, and particular parts of the body. Its heavy quotation and interpretation of Hippocratic surgical writings make it productive for readers tracing the reception of Hippocratic medicine in later Greek technical prose.
grc.pseudogalen.de_remediis_parabilibus: De Remediis Parabilibus ('On Remedies Easily Procured') is a short Greek therapeutic handbook transmitted under Galen's name and printed among his works in Kühn's Leipzig edition of 1827; as the designation Pseudogalen records, its authorship and date are uncertain. The preface sets out a deliberately practical programme: to aid travellers and dwellers in villages, fields, and deserted places, who have access neither to expensive drugs nor to skilled physicians, with treatments made from ordinary and widely available materials. The treatise begins with the head, called the citadel of the body, and passes through a classified sequence of headaches arising from heat, chill, fumes, indigestion, wine, blows, and bruises, prescribing oils, vinegars, plant juices, garlands, and amulets, some credited to the earlier physician Archigenes. Formulaic entries marked 'another' and the reuse of named authorities make the work a convenient witness for readers tracing parallel remedies and shared therapeutic lore across the ancient medical tradition.
grc.pseudogalen.introductio_seu_medicus: A brief Greek treatise on the origins and divisions of medicine, transmitted under Galen's name and of uncertain date, preserved in Kühn's edition of Galen's Opera omnia (Leipzig, 1827). Under the title 'Introduction, or the Physician' it first recounts the mythical discovery of the art, Asclepius taught by Apollo, Chiron's herbal lore, and Egyptian pharmacy, with quotations from Homer and Herodotus, then distinguishes three kinds of beginning for medicine and characterises the three sects, the Logical, the Empiric, and the Methodist, each by four defining marks. Its compact doxography of the Hellenistic medical schools and its embedded poetic and historiographical quotations make it a ready source of intertextual parallels for readers of Greek medical prose.
grc.pseudolucian.δημοσθένους_ἐγκώμιον: The Demosthenes Encomium (Δημοσθένους Ἐγκώμιον) is a brief Greek dialogue, some fifty lines long, transmitted under Lucian's name and of uncertain date. It stages a chance encounter between the narrator and the poet Thersagoras, who has risen at night to sacrifice first-fruits of his verse to Homer, and the conversation becomes a paired celebration in which Homer and Demosthenes are set against each other as rivals in praise. In defending rhetoric against the claims of poetry, the speakers adduce close verbal and thematic correspondences between Homeric lines and Demosthenic oratory, and dwell on the orator's force, bitterness, inspired intensity, Attic wit, hostility to barbarians, and debt to Athens, his famous fatherland. Readers hunting intertexts will find an explicit ancient catalogue of Homer-Demosthenes parallels together with a literary argument about the kinship of poetic and rhetorical discourse.
grc.pseudolucian.κυνικός: A short Greek dialogue, the Κυνικός (Cynicus), transmitted under Lucian's name and counted among the pseudo-Lucianic pieces, of uncertain date and authorship. It stages an exchange between Lycinus and a Cynic philosopher, who defends his ragged, propertyless life against the charge of wretchedness by arguing that sufficiency, not abundance, constitutes virtue, and who attacks the acquisitiveness, luxury, and costly commerce of the wealthy. The work is dense with the characteristic topoi of Cynic diatribe, living according to nature, self-sufficiency, the plenty provided by the gods to those who take only what they need, and a closing allusion to Eriphyle's betrayal of her husband for gold illustrates its use of mythological exempla. Readers hunting intertexts will find here phrasing and arguments that echo Lucianic satire and the wider Cynic and Stoic tradition on poverty, pleasure, and the simple life.
grc.pseudolucian.λούκιος_ἢ_ὄνος: Λούκιος ἢ Ὄνος (Lucius, or the Ass) is a short first-person Greek novel transmitted under Lucian's name but pseudonymous, and of uncertain date. It tells how the young Lucius travels to Hypata in Thessaly, where his eagerness to witness magic, pursued through an intrigue with the maid Palaestra, leads to his transformation into a donkey and a chain of comic, often risqué adventures before he recovers human form. As the Greek counterpart of Apuleius' Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), it offers point-by-point parallels in episode, phrasing, and tone that make it a central witness for intertextual study of the ass-transformation tale.
grc.pseudolucian.φιλόπατρις_ἢ_διδασκόμενος: Φιλόπατρις Ἢ Διδασκόμενος (Philopatris, or The Learner) is a short prose dialogue in Greek transmitted among the works of Lucian under the name Pseudo-Lucian and of uncertain date. It stages a conversation between Triephon and Critias in which Critias, thrown into bewilderment by the teaching of certain 'accursed sophists,' is simultaneously reassured and entertained while the Olympian gods, Zeus, Apollo, Poseidon, Athena, are subjected to irreverent and scurrilous demystification in a broadly Lucianic manner. The dialogue is saturated with Homeric diction, mythological exempla such as Salmoneus, Tyro, Icarus, Cleombrotus of Ambracia and Niobe, and verbal echoes of the Lucianic corpus, so that readers tracing the afterlife of Lucianic satire and the reuse of mythological material will find it a dense point of intersection.
grc.pseudolucian.ἀλκυών: A short Greek dialogue transmitted under Lucian's name (Pseudo-Lucian) and of uncertain date, the Alcyon stages a conversation between Socrates and Chaerephon on the shore near Phaleron. Hearing the mournful cry of the halcyon, Socrates recounts the myth of Alcyone, daughter of Aeolus, transformed into a bird as she searched the seas for her dead husband Ceyx, and links her to the midwinter calm of the 'halcyon days'. The scene then widens into a reflection on human weakness and the incomparable power of divine nature, written in deliberately Platonic idiom. Readers of intertexts will find here a prose handling of the Ceyx and Alcyone legend and the halcyon-days motif that invites comparison with Ovid and with the Socratic dialogue tradition it imitates.
grc.rufus_of_ephesus.de_renum_et_vesicae_aff: A short Greek medical treatise by the physician Rufus of Ephesus (date uncertain) on diseases of the kidneys and bladder, setting out, ailment by ailment, how each is to be recognised and treated. In some 185 lines it distinguishes renal from vesical inflammation through symptoms such as flank pain radiating to hip, bladder, and groin, chills, and painful or suppressed urination, and prescribes diet, warm poultices, diuretic drugs, enemas, cupping, and phlebotomy, including a plaster credited to Chrysippus. Its formulaic symptom catalogues, dietary rules, and named recipes make it a useful source of parallels in urological vocabulary and prescription practice across the Greek medical tradition.
grc.rufus_soph.ars_rhetorica: A brief Greek rhetorical handbook attributed to the sophist Rufus, of uncertain date, printed by Spengel in his Teubner edition of the Rhetores Graeci (1853). The work defines rhetoric as the science of disposing a proposed speech well and persuasively, divides it into four species, judicial, deliberative, encomiastic, and historical, and then sets out the parts of the judicial speech, the sources of prooimia, the virtues and modes of narration, and the kinds of proof, each head illustrated by short exemplary sentences. Many of the illustrations quote or echo Demosthenic oratory (Meidias, Androtion, the Chersonese, against Neaera, Philip's deeds at Olynthus and Olympia), with a nod to Thucydides, so readers tracing verbal parallels will find in the work a compact witness to how Greek rhetorical handbooks mined the classical orators for their stock examples.
grc.scylax_of_caranda.periplus_scylacis: A Greek periplus transmitted under the name of Scylax of Caranda and preserved in Müller's Geographi Graeci Minores (1855), its date of composition being uncertain. The work offers a coastal survey of the Mediterranean, opening at the Pillars of Heracles and proceeding people by people along the shores of Iberia, Liguria, Italy, Sicily, and the Adriatic and beyond, recording cities Greek and barbarian, harbours, islands, rivers, and sailing distances measured in days and nights. Its terse geographic and ethnographic notices, punctuated by brief mythological aetiologies such as Odysseus's sojourn with Calypso, the grave of Elpenor, and the cult of Diomedes among the Ombrici, supply a dense repertory of place names, peoples, and foundation legends against which echoes and parallels elsewhere in Greek prose and verse can be traced.
grc.septuaginta.abdias: The book of Obadiah (Abdias) in its Greek form is the shortest of the Twelve Prophets, a prose oracle of judgement against Edom, the descendants of Esau, denouncing its pride and its betrayal of Judah and closing with the promise of deliverance from Mount Zion and the kingdom of the Lord. The translation belongs to the Septuagint, the Hellenistic-era Greek rendering of the Hebrew scriptures made by anonymous translators, and is printed here from Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905. Its twenty-one lines offer distinctive Greek phrasing of prophetic material that diverges in places from the Hebrew, and it is therefore useful to readers tracing biblical diction and its echoes in later Greek-Jewish and Christian writing.
grc.septuaginta.baruch: Baruch is a deuterocanonical book of the Greek Old Testament, preserved in the Septuagint and presented here in Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905; it is traditionally attributed to Baruch son of Neriah, whose genealogy the opening verse supplies, but the work is of uncertain date and Hellenistic era. The book opens with the words Baruch is said to have written in Babylon after the Chaldaeans took and burned Jerusalem, depicting the exiles as they read the book aloud, send money and instructions to Jerusalem, and recite an extended communal confession of sin together with prayers for deliverance. Its Septuagintal prose, only some 141 lines long, weaves dense phraseology from the law of Moses and the prophetic writings into the confession, which makes the book a fertile hub of verbal echoes for readers tracing intertexts within the biblical corpus and in later Jewish and Christian literature.
grc.septuaginta.bel_et_draco_translatio_grae: Bel and the Dragon is an anonymous Hellenistic Jewish prose narrative of uncertain date, preserved in Greek among the deuterocanonical additions to Daniel and printed here in the Septuagint version of Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905. In two linked episodes Daniel exposes the idol Bel by revealing that its priests secretly consume the offerings, destroys a live dragon worshipped by the Babylonians, and, cast into the lions' den, is fed by the prophet Habakkuk, whom an angel carries by the hair from Judaea. Its satirical treatment of idolatry, its Danielic legend material, and the angelic translation of Habakkuk supplied motifs that recur in later Jewish and Christian writing, making the work a frequent point of comparison for readers tracing biblical and apocryphal intertexts.
grc.septuaginta.esdras_b: Esdras B, given here in Henry Barclay Swete's Cambridge edition of the Septuagint (1901–1905), is the Greek version of the biblical books of Ezra and Nehemiah, rendered from Hebrew and Aramaic originals by an unknown translator at an uncertain date in the Hellenistic period. Opening with the decree of Cyrus that releases the Judean exiles and restores the Temple vessels from Babylon, the work proceeds through genealogies of the returnees, the rebuilding of the altar and Temple, and the reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah in Jerusalem. As prose scripture in Septuagintal Greek, it offers readers of intertexts a stock of biblical formulae, royal edicts, census lists, cultic and legal diction, that echo widely through later Greek and Christian writing, alongside a translation witness that often diverges from the Masoretic Hebrew.
grc.septuaginta.esther: The Greek Esther of the Septuaginta, given here from Swete's Cambridge edition of 1896, is the Hellenistic-era Greek version of the biblical book of Esther, the work of an anonymous translator or translators. The Greek retelling opens with Mordecai's apocalyptic dream of two dragons and a rising sun, then narrates the elevation of his ward Esther from exile in Susa to queenship under Artaxerxes and the threat posed to her people by Haman, expanding the Hebrew narrative with additional episodes, prayers, and documents. As Septuagintal prose it preserves Greek diction and idiom that later Jewish and Christian writers absorbed pervasively, so readers of intertexts will find in it a recurrent source of biblical echoes in post-classical Greek literature.
grc.septuaginta.habacuc: The Greek Habakkuk of the Septuagint, a Hellenistic rendering of one of the Twelve Prophets, preserved in Swete's Cambridge edition of the Old Testament in Greek (1905). The book contains the prophet's laments over violence and unpunished injustice, the oracle announcing the rise of the Chaldeans, a series of woes against the plundering nations, the command to write the vision clearly on a tablet together with the declaration that 'the righteous shall live by my faith', and a closing prayer with song narrating the Lord's theophany in prose punctuated by diapsalms. Its Septuagintal Greek diverges from the Hebrew at many points, and its phrasing, especially in the faith-vision and the theophanic hymn, circulated widely in early Christian and patristic quotation, making the book a productive source for readers tracing scriptural intertexts in later Greek literature.
grc.septuaginta.job: The Greek Book of Job preserved in the Septuagint, the anonymous Hellenistic-era translation of the Hebrew scriptures into Greek, edited here from Swete's Cambridge edition of 1896. In biblical prose it recounts how the devil challenges the righteousness of Job, a blameless man of the land of Ausitis, and how Job, stripped of his children, wealth, and health, converses with his friends Eliphaz, Baldad, and Sophar and curses the day of his birth. The Greek version differs in wording and scope from the Hebrew book, and because Greek-speaking Jewish and Christian writers generally encountered Job through the Septuagint, its phrasing lies behind most echoes of Job in later Greek literature and offers the natural basis for tracing such parallels.
grc.septuaginta.michaeas: Michaeas is the book of the prophet Micah in its Greek prose form within the Septuagint, presented here in Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905. Opening with the word of the Lord that came to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, the work passes through oracles of judgment against Samaria and Jerusalem, denunciations of grasping landowners, venal priests, and false prophets, and promises of a gathered remnant, culminating in the eschatological vision of nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord from which law goes forth out of Zion. Of Hellenistic date and anonymous Greek translation, it is a key witness for readers tracing intertexts, since its distinctive renderings of familiar prophetic passages, much echoed in later Jewish and Christian writing, at points diverge from the Hebrew, and its Greek phrasing is often the form in which the material circulated and was quoted.
grc.septuaginta.osee: Osee, as the Septuagint titles the book of Hosea, is the Hellenistic Greek rendering of the Hebrew prophetic book, the work of an unnamed translator, printed in Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905, where it stands first in the sequence running from Hosea to 4 Maccabees. The superscription places the word of the Lord to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash and the kings of Judah, and the opening chapters tell of the command to take Gomer, a wife of fornication, whose children bear the names Jezreel, 'Not Pitied', and 'Not My People'; subsequent oracles figure Israel's worship of the Baalim as harlotry, pronounce judgment on Ephraim, and promise healing and return. For readers of intertexts, the Septuagintal phrasing matters because later Jewish and Christian writers cite Hosea in this Greek form, most famously transforming 'Not My People' into 'sons of the living God'.
grc.septuaginta.sapientia_salomonis: The Wisdom of Solomon (Sapientia Salomonis) is a prose work in Greek of the Hellenistic period, transmitted as part of the Septuagint and bearing Solomon's name in its title, though of uncertain authorship. Opening with an exhortation to the judges of the earth to love righteousness and seek the Lord in singleness of heart, it contrasts the righteous and the wicked, asserts the immortality of the just, and includes the well-known scene in which the ungodly conspire against the righteous man and condemn him to a shameful death. Its fusion of Jewish wisdom teaching with Greek philosophical diction, and the extensive echoes of its language in early Christian literature, make it a productive source of intertexts.
grc.septuaginta.sophonias: Sophonias is the Greek Septuagint version of the prophetic book known in English as Zephaniah, printed here in Swete's Cambridge edition of the Old Testament in Greek. The opening superscription places the prophet in the days of Josiah, king of Judah, and the prose oracles that follow announce the coming 'day of the Lord' upon Judah and Jerusalem, denounce idolatry and injustice among leaders and people, and pronounce judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria before ending with promises of a humble remnant and the worship of the Lord among the nations. The Hellenistic Greek translation, rendered anonymously within the Septuagint tradition, frequently departs from the underlying Hebrew and became part of the shared scriptural diction of later Greek-writing authors, so its phrasing of wrath, remnant, and judgment often surfaces as a source or echo in intertextual study.
grc.sextus_empiricus.adversus_mathematicos: A Greek prose work of uncertain date by Sextus Empiricus, running to some 2,800 lines and comprising a sustained Pyrrhonian attack on the learned disciplines. After surveying Epicurean and Pyrrhonian hostility to formal education, including Epicurus' disparagement of his teacher Nausiphanes, it argues at length that nothing can be taught and then brings particular refutations against individual arts and sciences such as grammar, geometry and music. Rich in quotation, anecdote and doxographical material about earlier philosophers and schools, it serves as a central point of reference for tracing sceptical formulae and shared commonplaces across ancient literature.
grc.sophocles.electra: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, of uncertain date, surviving in some 1,428 lines and read here in the Loeb edition of 1913 with an English translation by F. Storr. The play stages the covert return of Orestes to Mycenae, where, aided by Electra and an old retainer, he spreads a false report of his own death in the chariot races at Delphi before killing Clytemnestra and Aegisthus in revenge for Agamemnon. Its treatment of Electra's unrelenting grief and of the deception that precedes the matricide offers a central point of comparison with Aeschylus' Choephoroe and Euripides' Electra for readers tracing the Orestes myth through Greek tragedy.
grc.soranus.vita_hippocratis_secundum_soranu: A Greek biography of Hippocrates transmitted as the life according to Soranus and printed among Soranus' works in Ilberg's Teubner edition. It traces Hippocrates' Coan lineage back to Asclepius and Heracles, records his birth in the first year of the 80th Olympiad and his teachers Herodicus, Gorgias, and Democritus, and narrates his celebrated cures, his refusal of Artaxerxes' gifts, the honors granted him by the Thessalians, Argives, and Athenians, his death at Larissa at an age variously reported, and a closing survey of the disputes over which writings are genuinely his. The narrative repeatedly invokes earlier authorities, including Eratosthenes, Pherecydes, Apollodorus, Areios of Tarsus, Ischomachus, Andreas, and Soranus of Cos, who is said to have searched the archives at Cos, making the life a rich gathering point for the ancient biographical tradition about Hippocrates and a useful quarry for readers tracing the sources and afterlives of the Hippocratic legend.
grc.strabo.geography: Strabo's Geography is a Greek prose treatise in seventeen books offering a systematic description of the inhabited world, its lands, seas, peoples, plants, and products, framed as an enterprise worthy of the philosopher and useful for political and military life. The opening books defend the study and argue that Homer stands as the founder of geographical knowledge, expounding his references to Ocean, the Ethiopians, the Elysian plain, and the Islands of the Blessed while engaging closely with predecessors such as Eratosthenes, Hipparchus, Polybius, and Posidonius. The work rewards readers of intertexts because it preserves extensive quotation from and debate with earlier geographers and historians, many now fragmentary or lost, and forms a major ancient witness to Homeric geography and to myth as geographical evidence.
grc.strabo.strabonis_geographiae_chrestomath: A Greek chrestomathy, or epitome in excerpt form, of Strabo's Geography, attributed to Strabo and printed among the Geographi graeci minores edited by Karl Müller (Paris, 1861). Its 834 lines consist of brief lemmata, each introduced by hoti ('that...'), condensing the work's argument: the opening asserts that Homer was the first to attempt geography, and the excerpts go on to treat the Ocean and its tides, the coasts and peoples Homer names, Anaximander's map, the dependence of geography on geometry and astronomy, Eratosthenes, and the relation of poetry and myth to truthful description. As a condensed repertory of Homeric quotations and judgments on earlier geographers and philosophers, the epitome offers readers of intertexts a compact witness to the poetic and scholarly material absorbed into the Strabonic geographic tradition.
grc.theophrastus.concerning_odours: Concerning Odours (Περὶ ὀσμῶν), a short Greek prose treatise of uncertain date attributed to Theophrastus and printed in Hort's Loeb edition of 1927, investigates the nature of smell, holding that odours, like juices, arise from mixture, and classifying them as pleasant or foetid. The discussion moves from the natural odours of plants, animals, and inanimate things, noting how feeble the human sense of smell is, to odours produced by craft, analysing the perfumer's combinations of dry and moist ingredients and the effects of grinding, cutting, and burning on substances such as myrrh and frankincense. Along the way it explains why perfume improves wine but spoils food, and why flowers scent the air from afar while roots and woods give out their odour only when cut or heated. Its recurring links between odour, juice, and flavour, and its catalogue of aromatic plants and unguents such as iris and nard, make it a productive source of parallels for ancient writing on sensation, botany, and perfumery.
grc.theophrastus.de_lapidibus: De Lapidibus, 'On Stones', is a Greek treatise on minerals transmitted with the surviving works of Theophrastus of Eresus in the third volume of Wimmer's Teubner edition. The opening chapter divides substances formed in the earth into those born of water, such as mined metals, and those born of earth, the stones, and surveys their distinguishing properties of colour, smoothness, density and transparency together with their more remarkable powers, such as melting or resisting fire, attracting other matter, and assaying gold and silver as the Heraclean and Lydian touchstones do.
